PAPER Holistic evaluation of a machine learning-based timing calibration for PET detectors under varying data sparsity Stephan Naunheim1,∗, Florian Mueller1, Vanessa Nadig1, Yannick Kuhl1, Johannes Breuer2, Nan Zhang3, Sanghee Cho3, Maciej Kapusta3, Robert Mintzer3, Martin Judenhofer3 and Volkmar Schulz1,4,5,6,∗ 1 Department of Physics of Molecular Imaging Systems (PMI), Institute for Experimental Molecular Imaging, RWTH Aachen University, Aachen, Germany 2 Siemens Healthineers AG, Forchheim, Germany 3 Siemens Medical Solutions USA, Inc., Knoxville, TN, United States of America 4 Hyperion Hybrid Imaging Systems GmbH, Aachen, Germany 5 Fraunhofer Institute for Digital Medicine MEVIS, Aachen, Germany 6 Physics Institute III B, RWTH Aachen University, Aachen, Germany ∗Authors to whom any correspondence should be addressed.
E-mail: stephan.naunheim@pmi.rwth-aachen.de and volkmar.schulz@pmi.rwth-aachen.de Keywords: PET, CTR, TOF, machine learning, residual physics, gradient-boosted decision trees Abstract Objective. Modern PET scanners offer precise TOF information, improving the SNR of the reconstructed images. Timing calibrations are performed to reduce the worsening effects of the system components and provide valuable TOF information. Traditional calibration procedures often provide static or linear corrections, with the drawback that higher-order skews or event-to-event corrections are not addressed. Novel research demonstrated significant improvements in the reachable timing resolutions when combining conventional calibration approaches with machine learning, with the disadvantage of extensive calibration times infeasible for a clinical application. In this work, we made the first steps towards an in-system application and analyzed the effects of varying data sparsity on a machine learning timing calibration, aiming to accelerate the calibration time. Furthermore, we demonstrated the versatility of our calibration concept by applying the procedure for the first time to analog readout technology. Approach. We modified experimentally acquired calibration data used for training regarding their statistical and spatial sparsity, mimicking reduced measurement time and variability of the training data. Trained models were tested on unseen test data, characterized by fine spatial sampling and rich statistics. In total, 80 decision tree models with the same hyperparameter settings, were trained and holistically evaluated regarding data scientific, physics-based, and PET-based quality criteria. Main results. The calibration procedure can be heavily reduced from several days to some minutes without sacrificing quality and still significantly improving the timing resolution from (304 ± 5)ps to (216 ± 1)ps compared to conventionally used analytical calibration methods.Significance. This work serves as the first step in making the developed machine learning-based calibration suitable for an in-system application to profit from the method’s capabilities on the system level.
Furthermore, this work demonstrates the functionality of the methodology on detectors using analog readout technology. The proposed holistic evaluation criteria here serve as a guideline for future evaluations of machine learning-based calibration approaches.
1. Introduction The functional imaging technique positron emission tomography (PET) (Cherry and Dahlbom 2006, Muehllehner and Karp 2006, Nadig et al 2022) facilitates the visualization of metabolic processes within a specimen of interest. A radiopharmaceutical is injected, which emits positrons resulting in © 2024 The Author(s). Published on behalf of Institute of Physics and Engineering in Medicine by IOP Publishing Ltd Phys. Med. Biol. 69 (2024) 155026 S Naunheim et al electron-positron-annihilation. This leads to the emission of two back-to-back γ-photons with an energy of 511keV each, registered by multiple PET detectors. Between a pair of detectors a line-of-response (LOR) can be established, which is subsequently used for image reconstruction. Incorporating time-of-flight (TOF) information into the reconstruction algorithms (Conti 2006, 2011, Nuyts et al 2023) can significantly enhance the resulting images’ signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). The TOF information is characterized by the temporal resolution of the detectors, known as coincidence time resolution (CTR). In addition to exploring novel scintillators (Gonzalez-Montoro et al 2022, Konstantinou et al 2022, Pagano et al 2022, Herweg et al 2023) and hardware innovations (Gundacker et al 2019, Pourashraf et al 2021, 2023, Merzi et al 2023, Nadig et al 2023, Gonzalez-Montoro and Levin 2024) advancements in detector calibration procedures are crucial to improve the image’s SNR further.
Traditional PET detectors consist of one or many scintillation crystals, which are coupled to photosensors (e.g. silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs)) read out by dedicated electronics. Measured timestamps are given as a superposition of true value and jitter effects contributed by the different parts of the detection system.
Concerning complex scintillator topologies, the coupling to the photosensor and the readout electronics, reaching low CTRs can become arbitrarily complicated. Calibration problems are an active area of research, especially in PET, where often calibration procedures are needed to provide information about the precise timing, γ-interaction location, or energy deposition. Concerning timing calibration, various traditional calibration approaches exist, e.g. using dedicated reference detectors (Thompson et al 2005, Bergeron et al 2009, Hancock and Thompson 2010), intrinsic characteristics of the scintillation material (Rothfuss et al 2013), or even clinical data (Werner and Karp 2013). Many approaches are founded on minimizing a matrix equation (Mann et al 2009) for a given norm (e.g. l2 (Reynolds et al 2011) or l1 (Freese et al 2017)) with the benefit that these procedures can be applied to coincidental detectors in benchtop experiments and complete PET systems (Luo et al 2003). The solution to the equation representing the estimated time skews can be found analytically or by using dedicated solver algorithms (e.g. ADMM (Freese et al 2017)).
Many of the traditional algorithms provide constant or linear corrections to a calibration object, which might be a readout channel, scintillation element, or crystal volume (Naunheim et al 2022). In the context of complex scintillator topologies, a complete analytical formulation of all involved skew effects can become arbitrarily complicated to realize in practice.
One way to approach this circumstance is the usage of machine learning, which is given as classical learning systems (Naunheim et al 2023a) or neural networks (Chen and Liu 2021), with its capabilities to transcend traditional static or linear timestamp adjustments by providing event-by-event corrections. Recent research demonstrated the capabilities of using waveform information to improve CTR (Berg and Cherry 2018, Ai et al 2021, Onishi et al 2022, Feng et al 2024). In most cases, the researchers decided to use convolutional neural networks (CNNs) due to their ability to capture local patterns and invariance against shifts given by the architecture that exploits convolutional filters. While precise waveform sampling might provide the richest information, its costs and complexity are nearly prohibitive for a complete PET scanner concerning practicability and data management. In a recent Monte-Carlo simulation study (LaBella et al 2021), the combination of sparsely sampled waveforms (given as multiple timestamps) in combination with CNNs was analyzed, successfully demonstrating improvement in the timing performance.
In our preceding studies (Naunheim et al 2023a, 2023b), we introduced a novel calibration methodology to improve the achievable CTR of PET detectors. Contrary to the aforementioned machine learning approaches, we do not use waveform sampling but work on single timestamps from different readout channels instead, minding practicability for a PET system. Furthermore, we decided to use the classical machine learning algorithm gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDT) (Chen and Guestrin 2016) because of its simplicity and potential benefits (Krueger et al 2023) for an in-system application. The proposed method uses the concept of residual physics (Zeng et al 2020), combining a traditional analytical calibration with machine learning. The residual physics calibration (Naunheim et al 2023a) relies on correcting major time skews prior to the machine learning application to provide a first guidance, e.g. by using conventional analytical calibration methods (Naunheim et al 2022). After this, each deviation from an expected value can be seen as a residual effect of higher order and might be corrected using computational intelligence. The approach necessitates the collection of coincidence data of a large number of source positions leading to extensive calibration times being prohibitive for translating the approach to PET systems (van Sluis et al 2019, Siemens Healthineers 2023) in clinical routine, which might require a recalibration in regular manner.
Therefore, multiple approaches for reducing the calibration time are described and evaluated in this article.
Furthermore, we applied the methodology for the first time to data from an analog readout and analyzed the effects of leaving out source positions (spatial sparsity) and reduced measurement time per position (statistical sparsity) of clinical relevant PET detectors.
Recent publications demonstrate the broad variety of approaches aiming to improve the achievable timing resolution in PET detectors. In our proof-of-concept study (Naunheim et al 2023a), we demonstrated 2 Phys. Med. Biol. 69 (2024) 155026 S Naunheim et al the proposed calibration concept to PET detectors utilizing digital SiPMs coupled to an array of eight lutetium–yttrium oxyorthosilicate (LYSO) slabs (3.9mm × 31.9mm × 19.0mm). We were able to significantly improved the CTR from 235ps to 185ps showing the capabilities of this calibration procedure.
Measured with the TOFPET2 ASIC (Di Francesco et al 2016, Bugalho et al 2018), Cucarella et al (2021) achieved with slabs (25.4mm × 12mm × 0.95mm) coupled to Hamamatsu SiPMs (S13361-3050AE-08) a CTR of 276ps by using an energy-weighted averaging of the reported timestamps. In a study performed by Zhang et al (2021), thick semi-monoliths (1.37mm × 51.2mm × 20mm) coupled to SiPM arrays from Hamamatsu (S13361) were measured at 28 ◦C and digitized with the TOFPET2 ASIC resulting in a CTR of 718ps. Terragni et al (2023), evaluated an array of 16 LYSO crystals (3.1mm × 3.1mm × 15mm) coupled to Hamamatsu S13361-3050AE-04 SiPMs, which was able to provide DOI information and readout with the TOFPET2 ASIC reaching a CTR of 224ps. Recently, Nadig et al (2023) tested 16-channel HF readout board connected to the TOFPET2 ASIC as back-end electronics and achieved with a 4 × 4 matrix of 3.88mm × 3.88mm × 19mm LYSO:Ce,Ca crystals one-to-one coupled to an array of Broadcom NUV-MT SiPMs an average CTR of 223ps.
2. Materials 2.1. PET detectors We used two PET detectors to acquire coincidence data. The photosensor arrays of both detectors consist of 4 × 4 S13-series MPPC SiPMs (Hamamatsu Photonics), which are optically coupled with a thin optical patch (<200µm thickness, refractive index of 1.47) to a 4 × 4 matrix of Lutetium oxyorthosilicate (LSO) scintillators. Each crystal element comprises a volume of 4mm × 4mm × 20mm and is coupled to a TOFPET2 ASIC (version 2c) channel via a custom-designed adapter board (Nadig et al 2023). The TOFPET2 evaluation kit was used with the adapter board being connected to the ASIC front-end board (FEB/A). A reduced input stage impedance (Rin = 10Ω) was implemented to operate the ASIC in default trigger mode.
After successfully triggering a SiPM channel (4mm × 4mm, 50µm microcell pitch, 53V breakdown voltage), a timestamp in picoseconds and energy value in arbitrary units is provided. Both detectors show the same crystal-to-readout topology, but differ in their light-sharing properties. While one detector allows light-sharing, the other detector does not.
2.2. Experimental setup The measurement setup was operated in a dark box and maintained at a controlled temperature of 16 ◦C.
The detectors are mounted at a total distance of 435mm, facing each other at positions z = −217.5mm and z = +217.5mm. In between the detectors, a 22Na radiation source was mounted on a translation stage system, allowing movement along all three spatial axes with sub-millimeter precision. The movement of the translation stage along the axis between the detectors is technically limited to zmin/max = ±130mm. The ASIC board temperatures were kept constant while operation and measured to be 24.5 ◦C, and 23.8 ◦C for the one-to-one coupled detector with and without light-sharing, respectively. The source activity was 7.3MBq during the acquisition.
3. Method 3.1. Calibration concept Since this work studies the possibility of accelerating the calibration procedure by analyzing modification on the training data, the calibration concept itself is seen as fixed. The important hyperparameters controlling the acceleration, namely step width (sw) and undersampling factor (usf), will be introduced and explained in detail in section 3.5.
A radiation source is moved to different off-centered positions zs in between two facing PET detectors (see figure 1). This results in different path lengths for the γ-photons, leading to different detection times (t1 and t2) of the annihilation quanta. Based on the known source location zs, one can conclude the expected time difference E[{∆t}] for the measured time differences {t1 −t2} using E[{∆t}] = E[{t1 −t2}] = −2 cair · zs.
(1) The expected time difference information is used as a label for a supervised learning approach, such that the model predicts one scalar value based on the given input sample. A detailed explanation of the features used can be found in section 3.3.
3 Phys. Med. Biol. 69 (2024) 155026 S Naunheim et al Figure 1. Scheme of the machine learning-based residual physics time skew calibration. Adapted from Naunheim et al (2023a) CC BY 4.0.
3.2. Data acquisition & pre-processing Data is acquired by collecting coincidences while moving the radiation source to different positions between the detectors. The measurement settings are listed in table 2. It is necessary to group hits, belonging to one γ-interaction, to a cluster based on the analysis of the initial timestamps of the hits. This allows for aggregating all related information associated with one single γ-interaction, e.g. concerning light propagation in a light-sharing matrix. Subsequently clusters are grouped to coincidences utilizing a coincidence window taking into account the timestamp difference among two clusters.
A step width of sw = 10mm is applied, resulting in 27 zs-positions covering a total range of 260mm. The distance between the grid positions (xs,ys) ∈G is 5mm resulting in a 3 × 3 grid G. Hits showing energy values (in arbitrary units) of less than 0 or more than 70 were excluded from clustering. A cluster window of 30ns was employed based on a prior statistical analysis. The coincidence window was set to 20ns to suppress a high fraction of randoms and prevent a possible cut-out of coincidences experiencing high time skews.
The γ-interaction is estimated using dedicated calibration measurements (Mueller et al 2023). The center of gravity (COG) of the detected optical photons is used to identify crystals. Furthermore, the light-sharing detector is able to provide DOI information, which is estimated by a trained GBDT model (Mueller et al 2018, 2019, 2022, 2023, Kuhl et al 2023). Spatially dependent energy calibrations (Bovelett et al 2023) are conducted by dividing the crystal into voxels, providing an estimated energy value in keV for each cluster.
Prior to the calibration, the data was corrected for saturation effects using the 511keV and 1275keV peak of the Na22 source.
3.3. Input features Each input sample consists of multiple features given as detection information of coincident clusters from both detectors. The two detectors contribute the same kind of input features (see figure 2), which are connected to information about the detected timestamps, the energy deposition in the respective readout channel, and the location of the γ-interaction within the sensitive volume. Due to their different light-sharing properties, we considered a fixed number of eight channels for the light-sharing detector and four channels for the non-light-sharing detector. Channels are selected based on their temporal occurrence.
The choice of the number of channels is mainly driven by computational limitations, such that the concept would also work if all available channels were included as features. In the following text, the features are described in detail.
Considering the feature group associated with timestamp information, n sorted timestamps and their channel IDs are provided (n = 8 for the light-sharing detector, n = 4 for the non-light-sharing detector). The timestamps are given in a relative way, such that the value represents the difference to the detector’s first detected timestamp of the corresponding cluster. In addition, the time spread is given, which is the difference between the last and first detected timestamp within a detector cluster. The saturation-corrected energy values of the channels mentioned above and the associated energy value of the cluster represent the information of feature group ‘energy’. Furthermore, information about the γ-interaction location and light distribution is given, represented as the COG, second moment, main channel ID, and potentially DOI information. Lastly, the measured time difference between the first timestamps of the light-sharing and the non-light-sharing detector is also used as a feature. For the case that the number of triggered channels is smaller than the above-defined number of channels to be used for the feature matrix, the missing values are filled with NaN. For example, consider the hypothetical case where the light-sharing detector’s coincident cluster consists of only five hits. The feature ‘sixth relative timestamp’ is assigned to NaN. This procedure is performed for all missing features.
4 Phys. Med. Biol. 69 (2024) 155026 S Naunheim et al Figure 2. Schematic overview of features which are fed into the machine learning models. The input features consist of information of both detectors. They can be grouped into (relative) timing information, information about the detected energy, and information about the γ-interaction position. Furthermore, the measured time difference, given as the difference between the first timestamps, is used as a feature that connects the data from both detectors. The word timestamp is abbreviated as TS.
Concerning the feature group ‘timestamp’, the first timestamp is not included into the feature matrix. This can be reasoned by the fact that the timestamp information is given relative to the first timestamp. Therefore, the value of the (relative) first timestamp is equal to zero for both detectors and each sample.
A detailed description with mathematical notation can be found in our proof-of-concept work (Naunheim et al 2023a).
3.4. Machine learning algorithm GBDT employ a supervised learning approach utilizing an ensemble of binary decision trees. Each tree in the ensemble is sequentially trained on the residuals from the preceding trees. We utilized XGBoost’s (Chen and Guestrin 2016) GBDT implementation, constructing the model as a combination of weak learner trees (Breiman et al 2017). Unlike the complex architectures of deep neural networks (Tang et al 2016, Li et al 2022), GBDT’s simpler structure has nonetheless demonstrated strong predictive capabilities across numerous applications (Torlay et al 2017, Xia et al 2017, Aaboud et al 2018, Zhang and Jung 2021, Naunheim et al 2023a). When speaking of ‘models’ within this work, we are referring to different instances of the same architecture that only differ in terms of the training data presented. There are many possibilities for fine-tuning an XGBoost GBDT through several hyperparameters like the maximum tree depth d, describing the maximal number of decisions within one tree, and the learning rate lr, measuring the training’s influence of the prior tree on the current one. Since this work focuses on exploring effects induced due to differences in the data presented during training, the learning rate for models was set to lr = 0.1, and the maximum tree depth to d = 18 based on prior experience (Naunheim et al 2023a, 2023b). The number of trees N within an ensemble is subject to XGBoost’s early stopping mechanism, allowing to prevent overfitting but also to fully train models out. The number of early stopping rounds for all presented models is set to ten rounds.
GBDT is a classical machine learning algorithm with several advantages for the proposed calibration procedure. Due to the simplicity of the decision-making process, GBDT have several options allowing for explainable AI (XAI) techniques that might be required in terms of monitoring, licensing, and risk management in safety-critical applications (EU Law 2024, Gilbert 2024) (e.g. nuclear medicine and medical imaging). In addition, the inference simplicity brings the further advantage that GBDT are particularly suited for high-throughput contexts, like PET systems or direct detector-level applications (Wassermann et al 2021, Krueger et al 2023). Contrary to deep neural networks, GBDT are able to internally handle missing values such that imputation techniques are not required. Furthermore, there is no urgent need to normalize or transform the input data because decisions are made on a simple thresholding if-else question.
3.5. Data generation & diminution In this work, two parameters are of interest studying the effects of spatial and statistical data sparsity, respectively. Both approaches come at the cost of a reduced amount of training data which is a multifaceted topic (Balki et al 2019, Nikolados et al 2022, Hammoudeh and Lowd 2023). The step width (sw) represents the distance between the source positions zs along the z-axis. For a given detector distance, an increased step width indicates a smaller amount of used source position and translates to a shorter calibration duration but also to sparsity concerning the topology of the training data domain. This alteration means that the data domain used for training will differ from the application domain, which might lead to non-physical predictions.
The undersampling factor (usf) controls the degree of statistical sparsity. A undersampling factor of usf = n indicates that only every nth data sample is considered for training and validation and translates into a smaller measurement time per position (∼1/n). For this study, the initially acquired dataset Dsw=10, usf=1 is 5 Phys. Med. Biol. 69 (2024) 155026 S Naunheim et al Figure 3. Schematic overview of the data generation depicted for the example of an originally acquired dataset with step width sw = 10mm.
split into a training, validation and test set. While the training and validation sets were further modified regarding their sw and sf parameters, the test dataset stays unchanged (see figure 3). By doing so, we simulate an actual in-system application of the trained models and evaluate their holistic performance regarding this.
1.22 × 108, and 2.43 × 107 samples are used for training and validation (80/20 split). To perform statistically well-founded evaluations, 2.43 × 108 test samples are used. Based on these numbers, the acquisition time for training and validation data comprising all source positions was 43 h, while for each source position a measurement time of 637 s was used.
3.5.1. Spatial sparsity Based on the training and validation dataset with the original step width, additional datasets are formed by artificially removing source positions in regular patterns from the data. It is ensured that the number of collected events per source position remains the same, and the removal of source positions is symmetrically distributed around the iso-center of the setup (zs = 0mm).
By following this procedure, five different step widths are used, namely sw [mm] ∈{10,20,··· ,50}.
(2) 3.5.2. 3.6. Evaluation metrics Prior works (Naunheim et al 2023a, 2023b) established a three-folded evaluation of trained models using data scientific, physics-based, and PET-based metrics. Before a model’s performance can be evaluated regarding its applicability in PET, the prior data scientific and physics-based assessment must have been passed. By posing this requirement, we want to exclude models that are not in accordance with physical laws and might produce predictions providing good CTRs but still cannot be trusted and therefore also not used for a later in-system application. All evaluations are based on unseen test data having the smallest step width and highest statistics. To exclude machine learning typical bias effects at the data edges, the evaluations are based on all measured source positions within the test range Z = {zmin + 6cm,...,zmax −6cm} (see figure 4). Each evaluation metric is explained in detail in the following subsections, however, for the sake of overview, the metrics are also listed below with a very short description which effect and key point the metric is addressing.
The data scientific metrics consist of the average mean absolute error (av. MAE) and the cumulative mean absolute error difference (cum. MAE diff.). The av. Gray boxes mark the beginning of the model’s performance deterioration due to reaching the boarders of the training data domain. For unbiased evaluations, source positions from these zones are excluded from the analysis. A clear trend is visible, indicating that very big step widths results in an oscillating behavior of the MAE and high undersampling factors lead to an overall worsening of the MAE performance.

The physics-based metrics are the linearity factor (L) and the σ-environments (S) of the ε-value. The L factor measures if the model’s predictions agree with the assumption of a linear relation between the spatial source location and the expected mean time difference. The S metric measures if the aforementioned linear dependence agrees with the speed of light. The PET-based metric is the CTR, which is commonly used to characterize the time-resolving capabilities of a system of detectors in PET.

If the sum-of-square metric of the fitting routine does not converge during the fitting procedure, the prediction distribution cannot be approximated by a Gaussian distribution and it can be assumed that the model’s predictions are strongly scattered and do not accumulate at a stable value (an example can be found in the appendix, see figure 8). The analysis of the averaged MAE and cumulative MAE difference suggests that both parameters, step width, and undersampling factor, affect the training quality of the models in different ways.
By increasing the spatial sparsity of the training above a certain step width, the predictions of trained models start to oscillate regarding their MAE. The exactness of predictions for input data, which was present during training, is high. On the other hand, the quality of predictions for data stemming from input data being in between the data presented during training strongly deteriorates, which is pronounced as the shape of the prediction distribution starting to deviate from a Gaussian shape. This might be reasoned by the simplification of the regression problem due to the fact that only a subset of target values is shown to the model and the regression model collapses to a classifier. Stronger oscillations indicate a degradation of the model’s interpolation capabilities and unstable behavior along the LOR, being impracticable concerning an in-system application. This rise in av. MAE is moderate, until a critical threshold undersampling factor is reached and the deterioration starts to become stronger due to not enough training samples.
Due to the degradation of the interpolation capabilities of models trained on data with high step width values, an oscillating-like behavior is also visible for the linearity analysis of these models. While small sw-usf combinations result in models that match the physical expectation, a very high spatial and statistical sparsity dataset is unsuitable for building reliable models, which can also be seen in the existence and magnitude of the corresponding PNGD parameter. The holistic evaluation testing for data scientific and physics-related measures was able to identify non-physical models and should be taken as a standard quality measure for machine learning-based timing calibrations.
Models that meet the quality criteria of sections 3.6.1 and 3.6.2 show a consistent picture regarding the improvement in CTR that can be achieved. Although no strict monotonic trend is visible, it can be stated that for a given step width setting, increasing the undersampling factor results in slight degradation of the timing performance for most of the evaluations. When looking at the effect of an increase in the step width for a fixed undersampling factor, all determined CTRs are within a 3σ interval, underlining consistency between the models.

Summary In this work, we analyzed how spatial and statistical data sparsity affects the quality of a machine learning-based PET detector timing calibration method in order to accelerate the calibration procedure for a possible in-system application. We proved the functionality of our novel timing calibration method for the first time on analog readout technology demonstrating the independence of technology. Furthermore, we established a holistic evaluation scheme for machine learning models used in the context of PET detector time skew calibration.
To analyze the concepts of accelerating the calibration procedure, 80 machine learning models were trained and evaluated using data scientific, physics-based and PET-specific metrics. The results indicate that high acceleration factors up to 2 × 500 = 1000 are possible while ensuring agreement with physical principles and still outperforming analytical calibration approaches. Based on these factors, the acquisition time for training and validation data can be reduced from 43 h to approximately 3 min. Furthermore, the work shows the capabilities of the residual physics-based calibration concept to improve the timing resolution significantly demonstrated by the achieved CTR of around 220ps for clinically-relevant PET detectors.

args.summary:
This scientific paper by Naunheim et al. (2024) in Physics in Medicine & Biology presents a holistic evaluation of a machine learning-based timing calibration method for PET detectors, specifically analyzing how varying data sparsity affects calibration quality. The study aims to accelerate the calibration procedure for practical in-system clinical applications.

**Key Objective:** To improve coincidence time resolution (CTR) in PET detectors using machine learning (gradient-boosted decision trees/GBDT) combined with residual physics, while reducing calibration time from days to minutes.

**Methodology:**
- Used two PET detectors with LSO scintillators and TOFPET2 ASIC readout.
- Collected coincidence data with a moving ²²Na radiation source at various positions.
- Introduced two parameters: step width (sw, spatial sparsity) and undersampling factor (usf, statistical sparsity) to simulate reduced measurement time.
- 80 GBDT models were trained with varying sw (10-50mm) and usf (1-100,000) combinations.
- Evaluation used three-tiered metrics: data scientific (av. MAE, cum. MAE diff.), physics-based (linearity factor L, σ-environment S), and PET-based (CTR).

**Key Results:**
- Calibration time can be reduced from 43 hours to approximately 3 minutes (acceleration factor of 1000) without sacrificing quality.
- CTR improved from 304±5 ps (conventional analytical calibration) to 216±1 ps (ML-based calibration) for the 450-550 keV energy window.
- Models trained with sw ≤ 20mm and usf ≤ 500 passed all quality criteria.
- The method was demonstrated for the first time on analog readout technology, proving technology independence.

**Conclusions:** The residual physics-based calibration approach significantly improves timing resolution and is feasible for in-system clinical application. The holistic evaluation criteria established serve as a guideline for future ML-based calibration approaches.

## Abstract

PET is a functional imaging method that can visualize metabolic processes and relies on the coincidence detection of emitted annihilation quanta. From the signals recorded by coincident detectors, TOF information can be derived, usually represented as the difference in detection timestamps. Incorporating the TOF information into the reconstruction can enhance the image’s SNR. Typically, PET detectors are assessed based on the coincidence time resolution (CTR) they can achieve. However, the detection process is affected by factors that degrade the timing performance of PET detectors. Research on timing calibrations develops and evaluates concepts aimed at mitigating these degradations to restore the unaffected timing information. While many calibration methods rely on analytical approaches, machine learning techniques have recently gained interest due to their flexibility. We developed a residual physics-based calibration approach, which combines prior domain knowledge with the flexibility and power of machine learning models. This concept revolves around an initial analytical calibration step addressing first-order skews. In the subsequent step, any deviation from a defined expectation is regarded as a residual effect, which we leverage to train machine learning models to eliminate higher-order skews. The main advantage of this idea is that the experimenter can guide the learning process through the definition of the timing residuals. In earlier studies, we developed models that directly predicted the expected time difference, which offered corrections only implicitly (implicit correction models). In this study, we introduce a new definition for timing residuals, enabling us to train models that directly predict correction values (explicit correction models). We demonstrate that the explicit correction approach allows for a massive simplification of the data acquisition procedure, offers exceptionally high linearity, and provides corrections able to improve the timing performance from (371  6) ps to (281  5) ps for coincidences from 430 keV to 590 keV. Furthermore, the novel definition makes it possible to exponentially reduce the models in size, making it suitable for applications with high data throughput, such as PET scanners. All experiments are performed with two detector stacks comprised of 44 LYSO:Ce,Ca crystals (each 3.8 mm × 3.8 mm x 20 mm), which are coupled to 4 × 4 Broadcom NUV-MT SiPMs and digitized with the TOFPET2 ASIC.

## 1 Introduction

The introduction of precise time-of-flight (TOF) information in positron emission tomography (PET) leads to a significant improvement in the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the reconstructed images, which could aid physicians in diagnosis [[1](#B1), [2](#B2)]. For this reason, in recent years, there has been increased research into various approaches that have the potential to further improve TOF-PET, with the ultimate goal of eventually achieving a timing resolution in the order of 10 ps [[3](#B3)].

The PET data acquisition begins with the detection of the emitted -photons using dedicated detectors consisting of a scintillation volume and attached readout technology. Recent research demonstrated the potential of co-doping approaches [[4](#B4), [5](#B5)], Cherenkov emitters [[6](#B6), [7](#B7)] like Bismuth germanate (BGO) [[8](#B8)–[12](#B12)] or composite materials like metascintillators [[13](#B13), [14](#B14)]. Furthermore, the research community investigates double-sided readout techniques [[15](#B15)–[18](#B18)] and waveform sampling approaches [[19](#B19)–[22](#B22)], both providing rich signal information but posing hardware-related challenges regarding the usage in full scanner configurations.

Besides previously mentioned research lines, a considerable number of studies are conducted on the development and improvement of calibration techniques aiming to minimize any deteriorating effects impacting the TOF measurement by estimating unaffected timestamps or providing corrections to them. Mathematically (see [Equation 1](#e1)), one can describe a timestamp  reported by the detection system as a superposition of unaffected, true timestamp  and a time offset  often called skew,

with the offset value being a composition of different deteriorating sub-offset  (see [Equation 2](#e2)), which can be parameterized by a set of parameters ,Here,  represents a set of parameters that governs the behavior of the sub-skew  without loss of generality. In reality, the sub-offset  might change from -interaction to -interaction (e.g., due to different energy depositions affecting the signal steepness, baseline shifts, depth of interaction (DOI)-related effects, etc. [[23](#B23), [24](#B24)]) leading to different magnitudes and constitutions of .

While in former times, primarily analytical calibration approaches were studied, artificial intelligence (AI) methods gained interest in recent years, so that machine learning approaches are also an active area of research. Classical PET timing calibration methods in the literature rely on solving matrix equations [[25](#B25)–[27](#B27)] or use timing alignment probes [[28](#B28), [29](#B29)]. Also, data-driven approaches without requiring specialized data acquisition setups have been investigated, e.g., using consistency conditions [[30](#B30)–[33](#B33)] or detector-intrinsic characteristics [[34](#B34), [35](#B35)]. Other approaches use statistical modeling under the premise of a maximum-likelihood approach [[36](#B36), [37](#B37)].

Many machine learning-based timing calibrations utilize supervised learning and, therefore, generate labeled data by measuring radiation sources at multiple positions [[38](#B38)–[42](#B42)] or at a single position [[43](#B43)]. Nearly all of the existing approaches work with the signal waveforms. Although this data represents a rich source of information, it often requires dedicated measurement hardware capable of high sampling rates, e.g., oscilloscopes, that might be challenging to implement in a full scanner setting.

In recent studies, we developed and demonstrated the functionality of a machine learning-based timing calibration for clinically relevant detectors (coupled to digital silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) [[44](#B44), [45](#B45)] and analog SiPMs [[46](#B46)]) without the need of waveform information. Instead, we utilized detector blocks coupled to matrices of SiPMs, as is done in pre-clinical and clinical settings. Furthermore, we proposed to follow a residual physics-based calibration concept, which separates the calibration effort into two parts.

In the first part, an analytical calibration procedure is conducted, which addresses so-called skews of first order that do not change during measurement and are similar for each event. After correction for those skews, each deviation from an expectation can be interpreted as a residual effect caused by higher-order skews that might change on an event basis. To address these higher-order skews in the second part, we endeavor to use machine learning techniques since they offer high flexibility and are suitable for finding characteristic patterns in the calibration data. The strength of the residual physics concept is the underlying idea that the experimenter can incorporate prior domain knowledge in the way the residual effects are defined.

When applying machine learning techniques in physical problems, one should ensure that the trained models produce results that are in alignment with physical laws. Therefore, we proposed in prior works, to use a three-fold evaluation scheme. In the first instance, models are assessed regarding their mean absolute error (MAE) performance. How well the models are with physics is tested in the second instance. Finally, models that passed the first two evaluation levels are tested in the third instance regarding the improvement in coincidence time resolution (CTR).

In our proof-of-concept study [[44](#B44)], we used a similar label generation like Berg and Cherry [[38](#B38)], which demands the collection of multiple source positions between two detectors in order to label the data for supervised training of the model. Successfully trained regression models are able to predict the expected time difference for a given input sample, e.g., consisting of information about the measured time difference, the detected timestamps, the detected energy signals, and the estimated -interaction position. In this sense, the trained models provide implicit corrections by directly predicting the corrected time difference.

Although this procedure demonstrated that significant improvements in CTR are possible, the acquisition of the labeled data was time-consuming considering future applications in a fully equipped PET scanner. In a follow-up work [[46](#B46)], we demonstrated that the acquisition time can be significantly reduced without losing the calibration quality making the approach more practical. However, the study also revealed a strong dependence of the trained regression models on the used training step width given as the distance between subsequent source positions. As soon as this stepping distance becomes too large, the regression model showed on finer sampled test data a form of collapse towards a classification model for positions present in the training data set. This resulted in a worse prediction quality for radiation sources located at positions being not present in the training data. Even though the overall prediction quality of the collapsing models was in an acceptable range regarding the MAE, it also led to a substantial loss of linearity. The linearity property of a calibration model, namely, that a source shift in the spatial domain translates linearly to shift of the time difference distribution in the time domain, is especially for TOF-PET one of the most important attributes, since it ensures a correct interpretation of the TOF information. The precise value of the maximum training step width at which the model remains functional might depend on the spatial sampling of the training dataset and on the timing resolution that can be achieved with the detectors being calibrated. While the precise derivation of the dependence on the measurement parameters is out of the scope of this work, one can safely assume that a training step width being large compared to either the testing step width or/and the timing resolution will likely result in a model collapse. The implication of this observation leads to the conclusion that the smaller the CTR value and/or testing step width is, the smaller the training step width used has to be, resulting potentially in an elaborate data acquisition.

In this work, we provide a new definition of the timing residuals (oriented on the work of Onishi et al. [[43](#B43)]), which allows us to train TOF-correction models explicitly providing correction values instead of expected time differences.

In the first part, we compare the novel residual formulation (explicit corrections) with the already established one (implicit corrections) regarding a three-fold evaluation scheme. The analyses use real measurement data and demonstrate that by using the explicit correction approach, the strong dependence on the step width is removed, the biased prediction distributions are suppressed, and the linearity property is preserved. Considering a typical PET scanner geometry, we will refer to this study as the *transaxial performance* study.

In the second part, we analyze how the in-plane distribution of sources for a given location between the detectors affects the calibration quality, minding a later in-system application with, e.g., dedicated phantoms or a point source located at a single position between the detectors. In the following, this study is called the *in-plane distribution* study.

## 2 Materials

### 2.1 PET detectors

Two clinically relevant PET detectors of identical design are used for the experiments. The scintillator topology is given by 4 × 4 LYSO:Ce,Ca crystals manufactured by Taiwan Applied Crystals (TAC), which have shown promising performance in previous studies [[5](#B5)]. ESR-OCA-ESR sheets with a thickness of 155 μm cover the lateral sides of the outer crystals. Each of the 4 × 4 crystal elements encloses a volume of 3.8 mm × 3.8 mm x 20 mm, features polished top and bottom faces with depolished lateral faces [[47](#B47), [48](#B48)], and allows for light-sharing. The crystals are coupled to a 4 × 4 array of Broadcom NUV-MT SiPMs (AFBR-S4N44P164M) having a pitch of 3.8 mm and 40 μm SPAD size. Each SiPM is coupled to one channel of the TOFPET2 ASIC (version 2c) [[49](#B49), [50](#B50)]. A timestamp in picoseconds and an energy value in arbitrary units is reported if an SiPM is triggered and defines a so-called hit. The trigger and validation settings can be found in [Table A4](#TA4). The overvoltage is set to 7 V to balance good timing performance [[5](#B5)] with a reasonable noise floor [[5](#B5), [21](#B21)].

### 2.2 Experimental setup and settings

The measurement setup is located in a light-protected climate chamber, which is controlled at a temperature of 16°C. The sensor tiles are mounted at a distance of 565 mm. In between the detectors, a 22Na point source with an active diameter of 0.5 mm is used. The source holder is connected to a custom-manufactured translation stage system, allowing movement along all three spatial axes with a precision of <1 μm. The activity of the source was given to 1.4 MBq. The ASIC board temperatures are kept constant while operation and are measured to be (33.9  0.1) °C and (36.3  0.1) °C, respectively. For all data acquisitions, the same measurement settings (listed in [Table A4](#TA4)) are used.

### 3.1 Defining timing residuals: implicit and explicit corrections

Labeling the acquired measurement data is essential to make it applicable for supervised learning algorithms. The labels represent a type of ground truth since they guide the training procedure of machine learning models. However, for PET timing calibrations, the underlying ground truth is not accessible since the time skews can vary on an event basis, and the only information available to the experimenter is the measured time difference given as the difference between the timestamps reported by two coincident detectors. Nevertheless, it is possible to obtain a certain level of ground truth by connecting the spatial location of a radiation source with the expected time difference, assuming that no systematic skews are present. In this regard, these models provide only implicit corrections to the timestamps, which is why we refer to them as implicit correction models. Following this approach, it becomes apparent that a certain number of source positions is needed to generate a sufficient label variability (or class cardinality for classifier problems), otherwise it will lead to poor generalization, as shown in [[46](#B46)].

Furthermore, this explicit correction formulation (see [Equations 6](#e6), [7](#e7)) introduces a translational symmetry into the labeling process. Therefore, it does not pose any restriction on the number of sources along the -axis such that the experimenter can decide if it is wanted to include a spatial sampling along  during the acquisition process or if a few or even one source position is sufficient regarding practicability. Mathematical considerations about the explicit correction formulation can be found in the [Appendix](#app1).

When comparing both label definitions (see [Figure 1](#F1)), one can see that the label distribution is discrete for the implicit approach. Precisely, the number of unique labels (unique expected time differences) is equal to the number of used source positions, which might result in a sparse coverage of the label domain. Contrary to this, the explicit correction approach generates a continuous spectrum of labels, which is independent from the number of measured source positions due to translational symmetry of the formulation resulting in a high coverage of the label domain. The various label approaches also lead to differences in terms of label balance or imbalance. In the implicit approach, it is very easy to generate a high balance of labels by using the same measurement time per source position. This promotes that all labels can be trained equally well. In comparison, the explicit approach leads to a label imbalance independent of the selected measurement time. This is because the labels are based, among other things, on the measured time difference spectrum, which is Gaussian-like distributed. As a result, corrections with a large magnitude are less often represented in the training data set than corrections with a smaller magnitude.

### 3.2 Evaluation metrics

In recent works, we proposed to use a three-folded evaluation scheme [[45](#B45), [46](#B46), [51](#B51)] for any kind of machine learning-based TOF correction or calibration. The scheme consists of a data scientific, physics-based and PET-based evaluation approach. Only models that pass the first two evaluation criteria are evaluated in a subsequent step regarding their application in PET.

#### 3.2.1 Data scientific evaluation

The data scientific evaluation approach assesses the models based on typical metrics known from machine learning. If the data scientific and physics-based evaluations are positive, finally, the performance of the model is tested assessing the achievable CTR. ### 3.3 Model architecture

We use gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs) as model architecture for the second part of the residual physics-based timing calibration. GBDTs are a classical machine learning approach with the advantage that they can handle missing values and allow the implementation in a field programmable gate array (FPGA) [[53](#B53)]. This makes it especially suitable for the application in PET scanners minding edge-AI approaches [[54](#B54), [55](#B55)]. The model is based on an ensemble of binary decision trees, which uses boosting as a learning procedure. Each tree that is added to the ensemble during the training process attempts to minimize the errors of the predecessor model. In this study, we worked with the implementation of XGBoost [[56](#B56)], which has proven it’s predictive power [[57](#B57)] in our prior studies [[44](#B44), [46](#B46)].

Like in many other machine learning algorithms, several hyperparameters can be set before training a model. The maximum tree depth  describes the maximum number of decisions inside a single tree. The learning rate  works as a smoothing parameter and controls the contribution of each new tree to the overall model. Another hyperparameter is the maximum number of trees within the ensemble, which is often used in combination with an early stopping criterion that stops the training procedure as soon as the validation loss has not improved for a certain amount of boosting rounds. ### 3.5 Data pre-processing

Hits corresponding to a single -interaction must be grouped into clusters by analyzing their initial timestamps. This clustering approach enables the aggregation of all relevant information linked to a specific -interaction. Following this step, clusters are further grouped into coincidences by applying a coincidence window, which considers the time differences between two clusters using their main SiPM. Hits with energy values (in arbitrary units) below 2.5 or above 100 were excluded from the clustering process. A cluster window of 8 ns was empirically chosen by analysis of the temporal distribution. Furthermore, a coincidence window of 50 ns was applied to significantly reduce the proportion of random events and minimize the risk of excluding true coincidences.

To each cluster, a -interaction position and timestamp value was assigned based on the coordinates and timestamp of the SiPM with the highest energy value. The energy signals were saturation corrected using the 511 keV and 1275 keV energy peak of the 22Na source. An energy value derived from the deposited energy on the main SiPM was assigned to each cluster.

Following our proposed residual physics-based calibration scheme, a conventional time skew calibration [[59](#B59)] is conducted in order to remove the major skews of the first order.

### 3.6 Input features

The input features for both models are derived from the detection information of coincident clusters and can be separated into a set with information from detector , and a set with information about detector . Since both sets are similar content-wise, we describe in a general way the information a sample is made up of.

The  first relative timestamp values, which have been corrected using the first-order analytical calibration, along with their SiPM ID, represent the temporal information. Furthermore, we use the magnitude of the detected energy signal on these SiPMs, and the ID, energy signal, and coordinates of the main SiPM (SiPM detecting the highest number of photons) as additional information. In addition to this, the row and column energy sums are used. Furthermore, the number of triggered SiPMs, and the difference between the first and last timestamp of a cluster are fed to the model. Finally, the first (center of gravity (COG)) and second moment of the light distribution are also included. Missing values are handled as NaN.

While these quantities represent the input for the explicit correction models, the implicit correction models use one additional feature: the measured time difference. Based on a prior statistical analysis on how many triggered SiPMs are contained in a cluster,  is set to twelve and nine. No filter is applied to the energy or light distribution of the input data to ensure that the trained models function effectively with any potential input sample.

## 4 Results

### 4.1 Transaxial performance study

#### 4.1.1 Data scientific evaluation

Prior to assessing the models with the three-fold evaluation scheme, we checked that the models were trained successfully by analyzing the training and validation curves. All models showed a smooth training progression and were fully trained out.

The MAE progression of the explicit and implicit correction models for different training step width is displayed in [Figures 5](#F5)–[7](#F7). For the models trained on data with a step width of 10 mm, both correction models show a smooth MAE progression without any outliers. While most of the MAE values of the implicit correction models are located in a region between 100 ps and 200 ps, the MAE rises towards the edges of the testing data. The labels of the training dataset for implicit correction models are, in good approximation, uniformly distributed. The MAE progression of the explicit correction models resembles a U-form, with the lowest MAE of sub-100ps being achieved at labels of small magnitude. args.summary:
This research article, published in Frontiers in Physics on April 17, 2025, presents a novel approach to time-of-flight (TOF) corrections in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) detectors. The authors (Naunheim et al.) introduce an "explicit correction" machine learning method that directly predicts correction values for timing residuals, as opposed to their previous "implicit correction" approach that predicted expected time differences.

The study uses two detector stacks of 44 LYSO:Ce,Ca crystals (3.8mm × 3.8mm × 20mm each) coupled to 4×4 Broadcom NUV-MT SiPMs and digitized with TOFPET2 ASIC. A 22Na point source was used for measurements.

Key findings and methodology:
- The explicit correction approach removes the strong dependence on training step width (distance between source positions), which was a major limitation of the implicit approach.
- The new method preserves linearity—a crucial property ensuring correct interpretation of TOF information—even when training data is sparsely sampled.
- The explicit correction approach improves timing performance from (371 ± 6) ps to (281 ± 5) ps for coincidences in the 430-590 keV energy window.
- The approach allows for massive simplification of data acquisition, potentially requiring only a single source position.
- Models can be exponentially reduced in size, making them suitable for high-throughput PET scanner applications.
- The method uses gradient-boosted decision trees (XGBoost) as the model architecture, which can be implemented in FPGAs for edge-AI applications.

The evaluation used a three-fold scheme: data scientific (MAE performance), physics-based (linearity and speed-of-light compatibility), and PET-based (CTR improvement). The explicit correction approach outperformed the implicit approach on all metrics, particularly when training data was spatially undersampled, and remained functional across the full measurement range without edge effects.

## Abstract

In PET systems, the SNR relies on the coincidence time resolution (CTR) of 511 keV photon pairs. This research investigates the impact of reflectors, surface treatments, materials, and scintillation crystal length on the CTR of a brainPET detector using dual-layer offset scintillators (DLOs). This study is based on a brainPET, under development at the University of Manitoba, to propose a new design to achieve an improved CTR. Four different pairs of LYSO crystals with distinct optical compositions, surface treatments, and reflective materials were simulated (using GATEv9.3). Each model comprises two LYSO crystal with dimensions of 3 × 3  × 10 mm3. Considering the initial experimental data from the brainPET lab, simulation results showed that the crystal with a roughened surface and ESR reflector demonstrated 13.6% energy resolution and an average 17.8% improvement in CTR compared to other models. In addition, a more comprehensive model, including a dual-layer offset detector was designed. The bottom and top layers have 25 × 19 and 24 × 18 crystals with thickness of 12 and 8 mm, respectively in the DLO model. The simulation investigation showed that the DLO configuration could enhance the time resolution by 17.5% and the energy resolution by 5.4% which are considerably comparable to the state-of-the-art brainPET systems.

## Introduction

Positron emission tomography (PET) is a widely used imaging modality in various medical fields, including oncology, cardiology, and neurology. Traditional PET scanners detect gamma rays resulting from the annihilation of positron-emitting radionuclides. The concept of using timing information to improve PET image quality was proposed in the development of PET scanners. By measuring the time difference between the detection of the two annihilation photons, Time of flight-PET scanners can determine the position of the emission event more accurately[1](#ref-CR1 "Arabi, H., Manesh, A. S. & Zaidi, H. Innovations in dedicated PET instrumentation: From the operating room to specimen imaging. Phys. Med. Biol. 69(11), 11TR03 (2024)."),[2](#ref-CR2 "Arabi, H. & Zaidi, H. Recent advances in positron emission tomography/magnetic resonance imaging technology. Magn. Reson. Imaging Clin. 31(4), 503–515 (2023)."),[3](#ref-CR3 "Sanaat, A. et al. Active-PET: A multifunctional PET scanner with dynamic gantry size featuring high-resolution and high-sensitivity imaging: A Monte Carlo simulation study. Phys. Med. Biol. 67(15), 155021 (2022)."),[4](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR4 "Allen, M. S., Scipioni, M. & Catana, C. New horizons in brain PET instrumentation. PET. Clin. 19(1), 25–36 (2024)."). This timing information allows for better localization and reconstruction of the emitted photons, resulting in improved image quality and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)[5](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR5 "Sanaat, A. et al. The quest for multifunctional and dedicated PET instrumentation with irregular geometries. Ann. Nucl. Med. 38(1), 31–70 (2024).").

The integration of time-of-flight (TOF) technology in PET scanners offers several advantages over traditional PET imaging. The SNR of PET images is directly related to the CTR of the scanner. By accurately measuring the time difference between the detection of the annihilation photons, TOF-PET scanners can reduce the impact of random coincidences and improve the overall SNR of the reconstructed images[6](#ref-CR6 "Du, J. & Jones, T. Technical opportunities and challenges in developing total-body PET scanners for mice and rats. EJNMMI Phys. 10(1), 2 (2023)."),[7](#ref-CR7 "Arabi, H. et al. Quantitative assessment of inter-crystal scatter and penetration in the PET subsystem of the FLEX triumph preclinical multi-modality scanner. Iran. J. Nuclear Med. 18(Supplement 1), 40 (2010)."),[8](#ref-CR8 "Sanaat, A. et al. Deep-TOF‐PET: Deep learning‐guided generation of time‐of‐flight from non‐TOF brain PET images in the image and projection domains. Hum. Brain. Mapp. 43(16), 5032–5043 (2022)."),[9](#ref-CR9 "Sanaat, A. et al. DeepTOFSino: A deep learning model for synthesizing full-dose time-of-flight Bin sinograms from their corresponding low-dose sinograms. NeuroImage 245, 118697 (2021)."),[10](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR10 "Arabi, H. & Zaidi, H. Assessment of deep learning-based PET attenuation correction frameworks in the sinogram domain. Phys. Med. Biol. 66(14), 145001 (2021)."). Another advantage of TOF-PET is the reduction in image artifacts. Artifacts can occur in PET images due to various factors, such as scatter, attenuation, and random coincidences. By incorporating timing information, TOF-PET scanners can mitigate the impact of these artifacts, resulting in cleaner and more accurate images[11](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR11 "Zeng, X. et al. A conformal TOF–DOI prism-PET prototype scanner for high‐resolution quantitative neuroimaging. Med. Phys. 50(6), 3401–3417 (2023)."). TOF-PET also enables shorter scan times and lower radiation doses[12](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR12 "Mehranian, A. et al. Deep learning-based time-of-flight (ToF) image enhancement of non-ToF PET scans. Eur. J. Nucl. Med. Mol. Imaging 49(11), 3740–3749 (2022)."),[13](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR13 "Sanaei, B. et al. Does prior knowledge in the form of multiple low-dose PET images (at different dose levels) improve standard-dose PET prediction? in 2021 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC) (IEEE, 2021)."). This not only improves patient comfort but also reduces the radiation dose delivered during the scan.

The performance of TOF-PET scanners heavily relies on the detectors used to measure the timing information accurately. Recent studies have focused on developing detectors with improved time resolution and photon detection efficiency[14](#ref-CR14 "Leem, H. et al. Optimized TOF-PET detector using scintillation crystal array for brain imaging. Nuclear Eng. Technol. 54(7), 2592–2598 (2022)."),[15](#ref-CR15 "Li, Y. et al. Simulation study of a brain PET scanner using TOF-DOI detectors equipped with first interaction position detection. Phys. Med. Biol. 68(1), 015011 (2022)."),[16](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR16 "Lecoq, P. et al. Roadmap toward the 10 Ps time-of-flight PET challenge. Phys. Med. Biol. 65(21), 21RM01 (2020)."). In addition to scintillator crystals, advancements have been made in photodetector technologies. Silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) are commonly used in TOF-PET detectors due to their high photon detection efficiency and fast response times[17](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR17 "Amini, M. et al. Inter-layer compton scatter recovery in provision-PET: A prostate dedicated PET scanner with four layered dual-readout PET Detector modules. Soc. Nucl. Med. (2024)."),[18](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR18 "Manesh, A. S. et al. Conceptual Design of a Dual-Panel Dedicated Prostate PET Scanner: A Monte Carlo Simulation Study. in IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC) (IEEE, 2022)."). Ongoing research aims to develop SiPMs with even lower dark count rates and improved single photon time resolution (SPTR) to further enhance the overall performance of TOF-PET scanners. One future direction involves developing SiPMs using metamaterials with unique photodetection efficiency and time resolution. By combining nano-photonics with modern microelectronics and 3D electronic integration, researchers are exploring the potential of quantum silicon detectors (QSDs) to achieve breakthroughs in time resolution and photon detection efficiency[19](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR19 "Lamprou, E. et al. Exploring TOF capabilities of PET detector blocks based on large monolithic crystals and analog SiPMs. Phys. Med. 70, 10–18 (2020)."),[20](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR20 "Gundacker, S. et al. Experimental time resolution limits of modern SiPMs and TOF-PET detectors exploring different scintillators and Cherenkov emission. Phys. Med. Biol. 65(2), 025001 (2020).").

One approach to improving the time resolution is using scintillator crystals with fast decay times. Lutetium-based scintillators, such as LSO (lutetium oxyorthosilicate), LYSO (lutetium-yttrium oxyorthosilicate), and LGSO (lutetium gadolinium oxyorthosilicate), have shown excellent timing performance. Co-doping these crystals with other elements, such as calcium and cerium, further enhances their timing capabilities[21](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR21 "Terragni, G. et al. Time resolution studies of thallium based Cherenkov semiconductors. Front. Phys. 10, 785627 (2022)."). These elements enhance the energy transfer process, resulting in higher light yield and improved time resolution. Researchers are exploring the use of hybrid and composite scintillator materials, combining different elements to achieve synergistic properties that may outperform traditional materials[22](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR22 "Xie, S. et al. Evaluation of various scintillator materials in radiation detector design for positron emission tomography (PET). Crystals 10(10), 869 (2020)."),[23](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR23 "Kratochwil, N. et al. Pushing Cherenkov PET with BGO via coincidence time resolution classification and correction. Phys. Med. Biol. 65(11), 115004 (2020).").

Designing TOF-PET detectors that can achieve excellent CTR while considering various factors, such as cost, sensitivity, and readout circuit performance, presents several challenges. One challenge is balancing the crystal size and timing performance. Smaller crystal volumes generally result in better timing performance, but they also increase the complexity and cost of the PET scanner[18](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR18 "Manesh, A. S. et al. Conceptual Design of a Dual-Panel Dedicated Prostate PET Scanner: A Monte Carlo Simulation Study. in IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC) (IEEE, 2022)."). On the other hand, longer crystals tend to have worse timing performance, although they offer higher sensitivity. Longer crystals tend to experience a degradation in coincidence time resolution due to multiple reflections, loss of a portion of scintillation photons and the introduction of transit time dispersion. Finding the optimal crystal size and length is crucial for achieving the desired CTR without compromising other aspects of the scanner’s performance[24](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR24 "Gundacker, S. et al. Time resolution deterioration with increasing crystal length in a TOF-PET system. Nucl. Instrum. Methods Phys. Res. Sect. A: Accel. Spectrom. Detect. Assoc. Equip. 737 92–100. (2014)."),[25](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR25 "Gonzalez-Montoro, A. et al. Study of optical reflectors for a 100ps coincidence time resolution TOF-PET detector design. Biomed. Phys. Eng. Express 7(6), 065008 (2021).").

Another challenge is minimizing the impact of detector cross-talk and electronic noise. Cross-talk can occur between adjacent detector elements and degrade the time resolution. It is essential to optimize the design and readout electronics to minimize cross-talk and reduce electronic noise, ensuring accurate timing measurements[26](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR26 "Mehranian, A. & Zaidi, H. Joint estimation of activity and attenuation in whole-body TOF PET/MRI using constrained Gaussian mixture models. IEEE Trans. Med. Imaging 34(9), 1808–1821 (2015)."). Additionally, the integration of depth-of-interaction (DOI) capabilities in PET detectors holds promise for further improving the spatial resolution and accuracy of TOF-PET images. Capturing the DOI information, results in more precise localization of the annihilation events and enhanced image quality. The depth information allows for a more accurate determination of the time of interaction[27](#ref-CR27 "Surti, S. & Karp, J. S. Update on latest advances in time-of-flight PET. Phys. Med. 80, 251–258 (2020)."),[28](#ref-CR28 "Zhang, X. et al. Development and evaluation of a dual-layer-offset PET detector constructed with different reflectors. Crystals 12(1), 93 (2022)."),[29](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR29 "Kang, H. G., Nishikido, F. & Yamaya, T. A staggered 3-layer DOI PET detector using BaSO4 reflector for enhanced crystal identification and inter-crystal scattering event discrimination capability. Biomed. Phys. Eng. Express 7(3), 035018 (2021)."). In addition, surface treatments and reflective materials have been investigated to enhance the optical properties of scintillation crystals. Mechanical polishing and roughening of the entrance surface, combined with optical isolation techniques, have been found to improve light collection efficiency and minimize the reabsorption of emitted light[30](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR30 "Kang, H. G. et al. Crystal surface and reflector optimization for the SiPM-based dual-ended readout TOF-DOI PET detector. Biomed. Phys. Eng. Express. 6 (6), 065028 (2020)."),[31](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR31 "Choghadi, M. A. et al. Evaluation of dual-ended readout GAGG‐based DOI‐PET detectors with different surface treatments. Med. Phys. 48(7), 3470–3478 (2021)."). Reflectors enhance the efficiency of light transmission within the scintillator crystals by redirecting photons that might otherwise escape. On the other hand, they are used to improve the light collection efficiency and the uniformity of light distribution within the crystal array[32](#ref-CR32 "Berg, E., Roncali, E. & Cherry, S. R. Optimizing light transport in scintillation crystals for time-of-flight PET: An experimental and optical Monte Carlo simulation study. Biomedical Opt. Express  6(6), 2220–2230 (2015)."),[33](#ref-CR33 "He, X. et al. Potential of depth-of-interaction-based detection time correction in Cherenkov emitter crystals for tof-pet. IEEE Trans. Radiat. Plasma Med. Sci. 7(3), 233–240 (2022)."),[34](#ref-CR34 "Stockhoff, M. et al. Advanced optical simulation of scintillation detectors in GATE V8. 0: First implementation of a reflectance model based on measured data. Phys. Med. Biol. 62(12), L1 (2017)."),[35](#ref-CR35 "Roncali, E. & Cherry, S. R. Simulation of light transport in scintillators based on 3D characterization of crystal surfaces. Phys. Med. Biol. 58(7), 2185 (2013)."),[36](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR36 "Roncali, E., Stockhoff, M. & Cherry, S. R. An integrated model of scintillator-reflector properties for advanced simulations of optical transport. Phys. Med. Biol. 62(12), 4811 (2017).").

Improving PET scanner sensitivity can be achieved through three methods: increasing detector efficiency, enhancing the geometrical acceptance of the imaging device, and optimizing the timing characteristics of the detectors[37](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR37 "Surti, S. Update on time-of-flight PET imaging. J. Nucl. Med. 56(1), 98–105 (2015)."). It’s important to note that improving timing performance does not directly enhance detection sensitivity; instead, it contributes to improving the SNR in the reconstructed image. This improvement is often marketed by vendors as sensitivity gain.

Ongoing research aims to address some of the remaining challenges and push the boundaries of TOF-PET imaging. The development of detectors for PET imaging involves parameters such as the crystal material and size, crystal surface treatment with diffuse or specular reflective materials, photodetector characteristics, and electronic readout. In this work, the parameters related to the crystal were investigated. The results of this research aim to develop a detector design for a dedicated experimental brainPET system of the University of Manitoba, Canada with a CTR of approximately 235 ps FWHM. This advancement in timing performance can have a positive impact on the overall image quality and contribute to the goals of detecting smaller tumors and improving patient staging. By modifying the optical reflector and surface treatment, and incorporating dual-layer offset scintillator crystal technology, the time resolution of the TOF-brain PET system can be improved. These technological innovations not only optimize photon detection efficiency but also reduce timing uncertainties, ultimately leading to more accurate and detailed images of brain activity and enabling researchers to pinpoint the exact location of gamma-ray interactions within the crystal, enhancing the overall precision of the imaging process.

## Materials and methods

Various factors affect the time resolution of PET detector modules, including detector structure, scintillator crystal properties (decay time and luminosity), optical properties of coupling materials and light guides, surface treatments (polished or roughened), optical reflectance properties (diffuse or specular), reflector types (ESR films, Teflon tapes, etc.), and the electrical and optical characteristics of photon detectors and readout electronics.

In this research, the parameters related to the crystal such as size, scintillation materials, reflectors, surface treatments, and dual-layer offset scintillators were investigated. To take into account photodetector noise, photon detection efficiency, and electronic readout effects, deteriorating factors and time offset corrections are considered in the simulations based on the timing pick-off detector setup. The timing pick-off detector is a 3 × 3 ×  5  mm3 LYSO-Ce crystal. This detector has < 11% energy resolution at 511 keV and CTR < 250 ps FWHM when set up for coincidence detection with another detector of its kind[31](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#ref-CR31 "Choghadi, M. A. et al. Evaluation of dual-ended readout GAGG‐based DOI‐PET detectors with different surface treatments. Med. Phys. 48(7), 3470–3478 (2021)."). Regarding this detector, the base simulation model consisted of two 3 × 3 × 5 mm3 LYSO crystal with roughened surface treatment and wrapped with Teflon reflector which showed a CTR of approximately 235 ps FWHM.

### TOF-brain PET scanner and detector design

This research aims to develop a detector for the experimental brainPET scanner at the University of Manitoba, Winnipeg, Canada (Fig. [1](/articles/s41598-025-98892-2#Fig1)). This brainPET geometry has 4 rings of 16 detectors per ring having a 35 cm ring diameter. It is a pixelated DLO LYSO-Ce scintillator whose light output is read out by an array of SiPMs. One of these detector blocks has a front face area of 4.9 × 6.3 cm2, and a total depth of roughly 3 cm, with the LYSO portion of the detector depth being 2 cm.
