## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333)Abstract

The leading edge timing pick-off technique is the simplest timing extraction method for PET detectors. Due to the inherent time-walk of the leading edge technique, corrections should be made to improve timing resolution, especially for time-of-flight PET. Time-walk correction can be done by utilizing the relationship between the threshold crossing time and the event energy on an event by event basis. In this paper, a time-walk correction method is proposed and evaluated using timing information from two identical detectors both using leading edge discriminators. This differs from other techniques that use an external dedicated reference detector, such as a fast PMT-based detector using constant fraction techniques to pick-off timing information. In our proposed method, one detector was used as reference detector to correct the time-walk of the other detector. Time-walk in the reference detector was minimized by using events within a small energy window (508.5 – 513.5 keV). To validate this method, a coincidence detector pair was assembled using two SensL MicroFB SiPMs and two 2.5 mm × 2.5 mm × 20 mm polished LYSO crystals. Coincidence timing resolutions using different time pick-off techniques were obtained at a bias voltage of 27.5 V and a fixed temperature of 20 °C. The coincidence timing resolution without time-walk correction were 389.0 ± 12.0 ps (425 –650 keV energy window) and 670.2 ± 16.2 ps (250–750 keV energy window). The timing resolution with time-walk correction improved to 367.3 ± 0.5 ps (425 – 650 keV) and 413.7 ± 0.9 ps (250 – 750 keV). For comparison, timing resolutions were 442.8 ± 12.8 ps (425 – 650 keV) and 476.0 ± 13.0 ps (250 – 750 keV) using constant fraction techniques, and 367.3 ± 0.4 ps (425 – 650 keV) and 413.4 ± 0.9 ps (250 – 750 keV) using a reference detector based on the constant fraction technique. These results show that the proposed leading edge based time-walk correction method works well. Timing resolution obtained using this method was equivalent to that obtained using a reference detector and was better than that obtained using constant fraction discriminators.

**Index Terms:**Leading edge discriminator, Time-walk correction, Timing resolution, PET, Time of Flight

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333)I. Introduction

Different algorithms and techniques have been proposed to estimate the gamma photon arrival times in PET to achieve an optimized coincidence timing resolution (CTR) [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R1)]–[[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R10)]. Among these methods, digital methods and statistical methods have advantages over the two traditional analog methods, the leading edge discriminator (LED) and the constant fraction discriminator (CFD) [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R11)], but are also more complicated, computational intense, and difficult to be implemented in hardware, such as within application-specific integrated circuits (ASIC) or field-programmable gate arrays (FPGA). CFD has been considered as a gold standard for obtaining timing information in PET application for many years, but it needs more components to implement, especially the delay line, which is difficult to incorporate in compact integrated circuit (IC) chips. Non-delay line CFDs also have been proposed, however, this requires more components to replace the delay line [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R12)]. The variable delay that is necessary for different pulse shapes to obtain the best timing resolution makes its use even more difficult [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R13)]–[[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R14)]. Although digital CFDs can be implemented inside an FPGA and can use variable delay lengths, this implementation needs a very fast analog-to-digital converter (ADC), which is power hungry and expensive [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R6)], [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R15)]. An LED with a low-level threshold applied to the leading edge of the signal is the simplest time pick-off method. The time for crossing the threshold suffers time-walk, but can be corrected by using the relationship between the threshold crossing time, and the energy, on an event-by-event basis [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R11)], [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R16)]. Recent work has shown that the timing resolution obtained using a LED is better than that obtained using a CFD, when a lower threshold (several photons) is used and a narrow energy window (with a width of tens of keV) was applied to select events [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R17)].

For clinical PET scanners, the energy window is typically 425 keV – 650 keV, and it can be as wide as ~250 – 750 keV for small-animal PET scanners. For such wide energy windows, time-walk correction is required to improve timing resolution. This is critical for applications requiring good timing resolution to lower the random coincidence event rate and obtain time-of-flight information, and imaging applications that use wide energy windows with a large range of pulse amplitudes to improve sensitivity, such as high-resolution, small-animal PET. The relationship between the event energy and the time to cross a pre-set threshold can be obtained by using a precision reference detector; data from the coincidence detector pair can be used to correct the detector of interest. In a real scanner, a calibration probe can be used as a reference detector [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R18)]. In this case, the electronics either needs to be modified during the time-walk correction process, or requires provision for spare connections for the external probe. Also, the calibration process must be performed with some frequency due to changes in the characteristics of the detector, such as aging effects and change of temperature or bias voltage for SiPM- or APD-based detectors. For detectors with readout electronics already incorporated, such as SensL’s Matrix9 and Hamamatsu’s MPPC modules [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R19)]–[[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R20)], reading out the timing and energy signals in coincidence with a calibration reference detector cannot be done without modifying the electronics. Hence, the time-walk correction needs to be done using the timing information generated by the detector itself.

In this work, we proposed and evaluated a time-walk correction method based on two detectors both using LEDs to generate timing information. This method is self-calibrated, as no extra reference detectors are needed to generate the relationship between threshold crossing time and event energy. The timing resolution obtained using our proposed method was also compared with results obtained using CFD and CFD-based correction methods at four different energy thresholds (15 keV, 100 keV, 200 keV and 300 keV).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333)II. Materials and Methods

### A. SiPM and LYSO-based detector

Two detectors were assembled using two MicroFB SiPM evaluation boards (MicroFB-SMTPA-30035, SensL Ltd., Cork, Ireland) and two 2.5 mm × 2.5 mm × 20 mm LYSO crystals (Crystal Photonics, Inc., FL). Each evaluation board contains one MicroFB SiPM pixel (as shown in [Fig.1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#F1) (top)), which has an active area of 3.0 × 3.0 mm 2 with 4774 microcells, each 35 × 35 µ m 2 in size with a fill factor of 64%. The MicroFB SiPMs are UV/blue enhanced light sensors with peak sensitivity at 420 nm [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R21)], well matching the emission spectrum of LYSO [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R22)]. Their photon detection efficiency (PDE) is 31% at a bias voltage of 27.0 V and a temperature of 21 °C.

The two LYSO crystals were wrapped using several layers of Teflon to maximize the light output and coupled to the SiPM using optical grease (Saint Gobain BC-630). With a view to real application in a PET scanner, 20 mm long crystals were used in these experiments, although it is well known that better timing resolution can be obtained using shorter crystals [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R23)].

### B. Coincidence timing measurement

Each MicroFB SiPM evaluation board was mounted on a custom front-end board as shown in [Fig. 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#F1) (top), and a schematic of the experiment setup is shown in [Fig. 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#F1) (bottom). The two LYSO crystals were placed head on to mimic the situation in real scanner. To easily align the two crystals and the radiation source, a 3D printed holder was fabricated to hold the detectors, crystals and the radiation source.

The MicroFB SiPM has both a fast and a standard output. In our experiments, the standard output was used to simplify the readout, as the signal from the fast output is 2 – 4% of that from the standard output and the fast output requires extra transformers and amplifiers with ultra-high bandwidth [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R21)]. This can be a drawback in terms of the electronics complexity, cost and power consumption at the scanner level.

The signal from the standard output was amplified by an AD8045-based (1 GHz bandwidth, Analog Devices, Inc.) transimpedance amplifier with a feedback resistor of 130 Ohms. The amplified signal was split and one arm was fed into a CAEN spectroscopy amplifier (N568B) for energy information, and the other arm was fed into an LED/CFD (ORTEC 584) for timing information. The ORTEC 584 can work in either LED mode or CFD mode. The outputs of the ORTEC 584s were sent to a time-to-amplitude converter (TAC, ORTEC 566). The output of the N568B and TAC were digitized by a power DAQ board, with 14-bit ADCs [[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R24)].

### C. Time walk correction method

It is impossible to correct the time-walk of one detector using another detector as a reference detector, when both detectors utilize LEDs to generate time information and events occur over a wide energy range. Our approach was to use events from one detector within a very narrow energy range (which we referred to as “bin size”) around the 511 keV photopeak and treat this detector as a reference detector to correct the time-walk of another detector.

[Fig. 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#F2) (top) (black line) shows the energy spectra of detector 1. The low energy cut of the energy spectra is ~ 15 keV, which is limited by the LED module used. If detector 1 is used as a reference detector, the 2D histogram of energy and threshold crossing time of events obtained from detector 2 is shown in [Fig. 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#F2) (middle). It is obvious, for events with a given energy, the threshold crossing times varies over a wide range, hence, the relationship between the two cannot be found. [Fig. 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#F2) (bottom) shows the relationship between energy and threshold crossing time of detector 2 when detector 1 was used as a reference detector and a 5 keV energy window (511 ± 2.5 keV) was used to select events from detector 1. An obvious relationship between energy and threshold crossing time can now be observed.

Instead of a directly fitting the data shown in [Fig.2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#F2) (bottom), which is difficult as the data is distributed in two dimensions, the events were rebinned according to their energy and an energy bin size. Gaussian fits were applied to the timing spectra of the events belonging to each energy bin; the center of the energy bin and the peak position of the timing spectra were calculated. A piecewise cubic hermite interpolating polynomial fit (pchip, Matlab 2012) was applied to the center of the energy bin and the peak position of the timing spectra data to find the relationship between event energy and threshold crossing time, as shown in [Fig. 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#F2) (bottom) blue line. The fitted function was then applied to the acquired data to correct the time-walk on an event by event basis. The use of a linear fit was also studied, but the performance was not as good, hence, the results using the linear fit are not presented.

For the CFD-based time-walk correction, one detector used the CFD technique and the other used the LED technique to generate timing information. The CFD based detector was used as a reference detector and a 5 keV energy window around the 511 keV photopeak was also applied to select events from the reference detector. A relationship between the energy and threshold crossing time similar to the one shown in [Fig. 2 (c)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#F2) was obtained (not shown). To reduce the statistical error, 50M events were collected for each study.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333)III. Results

### A. Effect of energy threshold on the relationship between event energy and threshold crossing time

[Fig. 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#F3) shows the relationship between event energy and threshold crossing time for detector 1. The four lines, obtained at different thresholds, cross at an energy of 511 keV which was set to 0. The threshold crossing time of events with lower (higher) energy was earlier (later) than that of events with an energy of 511 keV, due to the nature of LED technique [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R11)]. The relationships between event energy and threshold crossing time obtained for detector 2 was similar to those of detector 1 and are not shown.

It is expected that the higher the threshold, the steeper the slope of the relationship, because the time-walk of the LED is increased at higher thresholds. The relationship between energy and threshold, obtained at a threshold of 15 keV was fairly flat over a small energy range around 511 keV. It is likely to be even flatter using a lower energy threshold. To get better timing resolution without time-walk correction, a lower threshold should be used and a narrow energy window should be applied to select data, as has been previously presented in many publications [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R13)], [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R17)], [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R25)]–[[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R27)].

### B. Effect of energy windows on timing resolution

[Figure 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#F4) shows the timing resolution versus the energy window width obtained using CFD and LED methods for time pick-off with a threshold of 15 keV. The center of the energy windows was at 511 keV. The timing resolution increases with increasing width of the energy window, both for the CFD and LED. The timing resolution obtained using the LED (without time-walk correction) degrades faster than that obtained using CFD technique, especially above 300 keV energy window width due to the contribution of the strong time-walk effects (see [Fig 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#F2)). The timing resolution obtained using the LED technique was better than that obtained using CFD when the energy window width was narrower than 350 keV, corresponding to an energy window of 336 – 686 keV, which is consistent with other published data [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R17)].

### C. Effect of energy bin size

[Figure 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#F5) shows the obtained coincidence timing resolution using different energy bin sizes. The energy bin size (energy window) was used to select events with energy around the 511 keV photopeak for the reference detector and then rebin the events for the detector being corrected for finding the relationship between the event energy and threshold crossing time.

The coincidence timing resolution increases slightly with increasing bin size, due to 1) time-walk of the events from the reference detector, 2) decrease in precision of the pchip fit to the relationship between event energy and threshold crossing time. The timing resolution obtained using a bin size of 0.5 keV and 1 keV is also poorer due to the poor counting statistics and increased statistical error, which leads to difficulties in fitting the data. However, the timing resolution only varied between 365 ps and 370 ps, confirming that the result is quite insensitive to the bin size and large energy bins can be used.

### D. Timing resolution

Timing spectra obtained at an energy threshold of 15 keV and for two different energy windows using the LED technique are shown in [Fig. 6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#F6) (top). The red and blue lines are the results without time-walk correction, while the black and green lines are the results with time-walk correction respectively. Clearly, the results with time-walk correction are better and the time-walk correction provides a more significant improvement when the energy window was wider. The timing spectrum without time-walk correction and using 250 – 750 keV energy window to select data (blue line) has a broad tail, which was caused by Compton events. The broad tail made the timing spectra non-Gaussian in shape and disappeared after time-walk correction was applied to the data.

[Figure 6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#F6) (bottom) shows the timing resolution obtained using different time pick-off methods and different time-walk correction methods. The legends are explained in [Table I](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#T1). The threshold of the LED was 15 keV and two different energy windows (425 – 650 keV and 250 – 750 keV) were applied to select events. When a narrow energy window was used, the timing resolution obtained using the LED was better than that obtained using the CFD, even without time-walk correction. The timing resolution obtained using LED technique and with time-walk correction was better than that obtained using the CFD using both energy windows, and the timing resolution obtained using the two different time-walk correction methods, LED based self-correction method and reference detector based correction method, were similar.

[Table II](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#T2) lists the timing resolution versus threshold of the LED. The timing resolution obtained using the LED technique increases with increasing threshold [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R17)], [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R26)], while that obtained using the CFD was nearly constant at different thresholds. Timing resolutions obtained using LED_Cor and CFD_Cor are the same. This demonstrates that our proposed LED based time-walk correction method works as well as using a dedicated reference detector based on the CFD technique to generate timing information.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333)IV. Conclusion and Discussion

A self-correction time-walk method was proposed and evaluated for PET detectors using the LED technique to generate the timing information. The timing resolution obtained using our proposed method was the same as that obtained using a dedicated reference detector based on CFD technique, but our method has the advantage that it does not need an external reference detector, electronics modification nor a dedicated calibration process.

The coincidence timing resolution obtained was 389.0 ± 12.0 ps (425 – 650 keV) and 670.2 ± 16.2 ps (250 – 750 keV) without time-walk correction using a 15 keV threshold. The timing resolution was improved to 367.3 ± 0.5 ps (425 – 650 keV) and 413.7 ± 0.9 ps (250 – 750 keV) with time-walk correction. Timing resolutions were 442.8 ± 12.8 ps (425 – 650 keV) and 476.0 ± 13.0 ps (250 – 750 keV) using a CFD, and 367.3 ± 0.4 ps (425 – 650 keV) and 413.4 ± 0.9 ps (250 – 750 keV) using a reference detector based on a CFD.

The timing resolution degraded with increasing energy threshold for the LED, consistent with other results [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R17)], [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R26)]. The best timing resolution was obtained at a threshold of 15 keV among the four tested thresholds (15 keV, 100 keV, 200 keV, and 300 keV). We believe even better timing resolution can be obtained using lower threshold, but this was not tested in this paper. A threshold of 15 keV can be implemented in most state-of-the-art PET scanners, such as SiPM-based PET scanners. The timing resolutions obtained using the LED with time-walk correction were better than those obtained using a CFD by using a 15 keV threshold, which is consistent with other results [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R17)].

The best timing resolution we obtained was 367.3 ± 0.5 ps (425 – 650 keV energy window and 15 keV energy threshold for LED). Better results have been obtained with similar SiPMs and crystals, however we did not optimize the bias voltage for timing performance and our measurement were carried out at a temperature of 20 ° C. For SiPMs, the timing resolution varies with bias voltage and better timing resolution can be obtained at lower temperature, as the noise of SiPMs is decreased [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R28)]–[[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R29)].

We also have used our proposed method to correct the timing resolution of two PET detector modules based on large-area SiPM arrays and crystal arrays [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R19)], [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R30)]. Our proposed method worked well and the timing resolution was improved to 4.2 ± 0.1 ns from 11.2 ± 0.2 ns [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R19)].

With the dramatic improvements in data transfer speed that have occurred in recent years (such as USB 3.1 which has a transfer rate up to 1.25 GB/s), and improvements in date storage speeds using solid state drives (SSD), it is feasible to collect single events from the PET scanner [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R31)]–[[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333#R32)]. As the event time-stamps are included in the event data, our proposed LED-based time-walk correction method can be applied to these data to improve the timing resolution without any additional measurements from the PET scanner.

args.summary:
This scientific paper by Du et al. (2017) presents and evaluates a self-calibrating time-walk correction method for PET detectors that use leading edge discriminators (LEDs) to generate timing information. The leading edge technique is the simplest timing extraction method but suffers from "time-walk" (a timing error that depends on pulse amplitude/energy), which degrades timing resolution, especially for time-of-flight PET and when using wide energy windows.

The proposed method corrects time-walk without requiring an external reference detector (e.g., a fast PMT with constant fraction discrimination). Instead, it uses one detector as a reference by selecting events within a very narrow energy window (508.5–513.5 keV) around the 511 keV photopeak, then uses the relationship between threshold crossing time and event energy to correct the other detector's timing on an event-by-event basis. A piecewise cubic Hermite interpolating polynomial (pchip) fit was applied to binned energy/timing data.

Experimental validation used two SensL MicroFB SiPMs coupled to 2.5×2.5×20 mm polished LYSO crystals at 27.5V bias and 20°C. Key results:
- Without correction: 389.0±12.0 ps (425–650 keV window) and 670.2±16.2 ps (250–750 keV)
- With LED-based self-correction: 367.3±0.5 ps (425–650 keV) and 413.7±0.9 ps (250–750 keV)
- With CFD (constant fraction discriminator): 442.8±12.8 ps (425–650 keV) and 476.0±13.0 ps (250–750 keV)
- With CFD-based reference detector correction: 367.3±0.4 ps (425–650 keV) and 413.4±0.9 ps (250–750 keV)

The LED-based self-correction method matched the performance of a dedicated CFD reference detector and outperformed standard CFD. The method was also successfully applied to large-area SiPM arrays, improving timing from 11.2±0.2 ns to 4.2±0.1 ns. The authors note that with modern high-speed data transfer and storage, single-event data collection with timestamps is feasible, allowing this correction to be applied in software without additional hardware modifications.

args.key_excerpts: R&D on gaseous detectors achieved MIP timing with 24ps precision! J. Bortfeldt et. al. (RD51-PICOSEC collaboration), NIM A 903 (2018) 317-325
args.summary:
This presentation by I. Manthos et al. (HEP 2021, Thessaloniki) investigates signal processing techniques for precise timing with novel gaseous detectors, specifically the PICOSEC detector, to achieve ~20-30 ps timing resolution for HL-LHC pileup mitigation and particle identification.

**Motivation:** High Luminosity LHC produces >140 pile-up vertices per clock cycle within ±45mm. 3D tracking is insufficient; precise timing (~20-30 ps/MIP) adds a separation dimension for vertex association and PID (Pion/Kaon/Kaon-Proton separation).

**Methods tested on PICOSEC MIP data:**
- **Constant Fraction Discrimination (CFD):** Reference method. Achieved 50.5 ps (full dataset) and 24.4 ps (events fully embedded in detector area).
- **Leading Edge - multi Time-over-Threshold (mToT):** Used 7 thresholds (10-200 mV). Best thresholds: 10mV (73.5 ps), 100mV (29.2 ps). Combined: 48.8 ps overall.
- **Leading Edge - multi Charge-over-Threshold (mCoT):** Used pulse integral above threshold. Best thresholds: 10mV (54.8 ps), 100mV (26.7 ps). Combined: 44.9 ps overall; 23.2 ps for fully embedded events — **better than CFD**.
- **Neural Network (MLP):** Inputs from ToT at 10/50/100 mV thresholds. Achieved 46.0 ps overall; 25.2 ps for fully embedded events.

**Sub-picosecond domain test (70 p.e. dataset):** Both CFD (5.50 ps) and mCoT (5.52 ps) methods performed comparably.

**Conclusions:**
- mToT achieves CFD-level resolution using only 6 values (3 threshold crossings).
- mCoT outperforms CFD when charge info is available from front-end electronics (e.g., NINO chip).
- Neural networks yield results comparable to analytical methods.
- Leading edge-CoT method is adequate at one order of magnitude lower timing resolution (~5 ps).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018)Abstract

Positron emission tomography (PET) detectors suffer from time-walk when the leading edge discriminator is employed for timing pick-off as well as a timing-shift when thick crystals are utilized due to the depth-of-interaction (DOI) effect. In this study, a combined time-walk and timing-shift correction method was proposed for dual-ended readout PET detectors. To evaluate the proposed method, a pair of dual-ended readout PET detectors was constructed. Each detector was based on two Hamamatsu S14161-3050-08 silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) arrays coupled to both ends of an $8 \times 8$ arrays of $3 . 1 \times 3 . 1 \times 20 \left( m m\right)^{3}$ LYSO crystals with a 3.2 mm pitch. By employing the relationship between the energies and detected time differences of events, the time-walk and timing-shift were effectively corrected. The coincidence time resolution of the two detectors improved from $260 . 7 \pm 1 . 0 \text{ps}$ to $229 . 4 \pm 1 . 0 \text{ps}$ when a 400–650 keV energy window was used to select events. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed time-walk and timing-shift correction method.

**Index Terms—:**PET, DOI, Dual-Ended Readout, Time-Walk Correction, Timing-Shift Correction

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018)INTRODUCTION

I.
Time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET) can enhance the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the reconstructed images by estimating the interaction position of annihilation photons along the line-of-response (LOR) [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R1)], [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R2)]. Compared to non-TOF-PET, the TOF gain factor for the SNR of the reconstructed image roughly follows the formula $\sqrt{\frac{2 L}{c \delta_{t}}}$, where L is the size of the object (such as the human body or brain), c is the speed of light, and $\delta_{t}$ is the coincidence time resolution (CTR) of the PET system. This is equivalent to an effective gain increase of $\frac{2 L}{c \delta_{t}}$ for the system sensitivity [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R3)], [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R4)].

However, due to state-of-the-art whole-body TOF-PET systems utilizing $\sim 20 \text{mm}$ thick lutetium oxyorthosilicate (LSO) or lutetium yttrium oxyorthosilicate (LYSO) crystals for high sensitivity, depth-of-interaction (DOI), which is the interaction position of annihilation photons along the radial direction of the crystal elements, deteriorates CTR [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R5)], as DOI affects the travel time of annihilation photons in the crystal and the time of scintillation light reaching the photodetector, which is one of the major contributions to the timing-shift [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R6)], [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R7)], [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R8)]. Another major contribution to the timing-shift is the readout electronics (such as the different lengths of the signal traces) [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R9)], [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R10)]. Additionally, the parallax effect, resulting from DOI variability, adversely affects the radial spatial resolution, particularly in the radial and axial directions of a scanner with a long axial field-of-view (FOV) [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R11)], [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R12)], [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R13)], [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R14)]. Therefore, obtaining DOI information can enhance image quality, as evidenced in small-animal PET and human brain PET [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R15)], [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R16)], [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R17)], [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R18)].

Various methods for extracting DOI information from PET detectors have been proposed, including the dual-ended readout method, multi-layer crystals, monolithic or semi-monolithic crystals, and reflectors with complex shapes [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R19)], [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R20)], [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R21)], [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R22)], [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R23)], [[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R24)], [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R25)], [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R26)]. Among these, the dual-ended readout method, which uses the ratio of signals detected by the photodetectors coupled to both ends of the crystal or crystal array to extract DOI information, stands out for simultaneously providing good timing and DOI resolution. Typically, a DOI resolution of $\sim 2 – 3 \text{mm}$ has been obtained from 20 mm thick LYSO crystals [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R19)], [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R27)]. Moreover, previous studies on single crystals have demonstrated that the timing resolution can be improved by correcting the DOI effect [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R28)], [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R29)], [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R30)], [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R31)], [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R32)], [[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R33)], [[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R34)].

Besides the DOI effect, the method used for timing pick-off also significantly affects timing resolution. Leading-edge discrimination (LED) and constant fraction discrimination (CFD) are the two commonly used methods for extracting timing information. Compared to the CFD method, the LED method is much simpler and can achieve better timing resolution when applying a low threshold [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R35)]. However, the LED method is susceptible to time-walk due to the finite rise time and variable amplitudes of the signals. The time-walk is related to the signal amplitude and can be corrected by leveraging the relationship between the threshold crossing time and the signal amplitude on an event-by-event basis [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R35)], [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R36)].

In dual-ended readout detectors, to obtain DOI information, a fraction of the scintillation photons is expected to be lost before reaching the photodetectors, either through absorption by the crystal itself or by the reflectors, or escape from the crystal’s lateral surfaces. The ratio of lost scintillation photons is related to the interaction position of the annihilation photons. Hence, when a crystal detects an annihilation photon, the arrival timing of the scintillation photons at the photodetectors coupled to the two ends of the crystal and the signals detected by these photodetectors vary with the depth interaction location of the annihilation photon, or the DOI [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R36)], [[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R37)]. Generally speaking, the photodetector closer to the annihilation photon interaction position detects the photon earlier and generates a larger signal than the other photodetectors. For example, in detector A, as depicted in [Fig. 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F1)(top), when an annihilation photon is detected, and its interaction position is closer to silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) 2, SiPM 2 will detect more scintillation photons and generate a larger signal than SiPM 1, also producing a timestamp earlier than SiPM 1 ([Fig. 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F1)(middle)). Therefore, correcting time-walk is more crucial for enhancing timing resolution in dual-ended readout detectors than in non-DOI single-ended readout detectors. In the latter, the reflectors and crystal surface treatments are optimized such that the detected signal amplitudes do not vary much with the annihilation photon interaction position.

Hence, to achieve optimal timing resolution from a dual-ended readout detector, it is essential to correct both time-walk and timing-shift. However, most previous studies on time-walk correction focused on detectors based on single-ended readout. This paper introduced a novel method to correct both time-walk and timing-shift for dual-ended readout detectors. The effectiveness of the proposed method was evaluated using two dual-ended readout detectors based on Hamamatsu S14161-3050-08 SiPMs and $8 \times 8$ LYSO arrays with a 3.2 mm pitch and 20 mm thickness. Additionally, this paper also investigated the effect of the number of DOI layers on timing resolution.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018)Materials and Methods

II.
### Time Correction Method

A.
[Fig. 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F1) shows the proposed procedure for correcting time-walk and timing-shift in dual-ended readout detectors utilizing the LED method for timing pick-off. For simplicity, each detector consists of two SiPMs coupled to a single crystal. The timing information for each dual-ended readout detector is calculated by averaging the timing information generated by the two SiPMs coupled to both ends of the crystal using the formula [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R28)] (1) 

$$
t_{A} = \left(t_{1} + t_{2}\right) / 2
$$

 (2) 

$$
t_{B} = \left(t_{3} + t_{4}\right) / 2
$$

 where $t_{i} \left(\right. i = 1 \ldots 4 \left.\right)$ represents the threshold crossing time generated by the four SiPMs of the two detectors, $t_{A}$ and $t_{B}$ denote the timing information for detector A and detector B, respectively. Then, the timing difference of two annihilation photons from a positron decay detected by the two detectors is (3) 

$$
\Delta t = t_{A} - t_{B} = \left(t_{1} + t_{2} - t_{3} - t_{4}\right) / 2
$$

 Since the threshold crossing times $t_{i}$ suffer from both time-walk and timing-shift (as shown in [Fig. 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F1)(middle)), $\Delta t$ is influenced, too. To enhance timing resolution for better image quality, corrections for both time-walk and timing-shift are necessary.

For a pair of annihilation photons arriving at two identical scintillation detectors simultaneously, the same threshold is applied to both detectors, the relationship between the difference in threshold crossing time $\left(T_{1} - T_{2}\right)$, representing the time-walk, and the two detected energies ($E_{d 1}$ and $E_{d 2}$) can be expressed as [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R36)], [[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R37)] (4) 

$$
T_{1} - T_{2} = c \text{ln} \left(\frac{E_{d 1}}{E_{d 2}}\right) + b
$$

 where $c$ and $b$ are a constant value, and $c \text{ln} \left(\frac{E_{d 1}}{E_{d 2}}\right)$ and $b$ are used for correction of the time-walk and timing-shift, respectively. Therefore, for dual-ended readout detectors with four SiPMs, as is the case shown in [Fig. 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F1), the timing difference of threshold crossing time can be estimated using the formula: (5) 

$$
\left{\right. t_{1} - t_{4} = c_{14} \text{In} \left(\right. \frac{E_{1}}{E_{4}} \left.\right) + b_{14} \\ t_{2} - t_{3} = c_{23} \text{In} \left(\right. \frac{E_{2}}{E_{3}} \left.\right) + b_{23}
$$

 or (6) 

$$
\left{\right. t_{1} - t_{3} = c_{13} \text{In} \left(\right. \frac{E_{1}}{E_{3}} \left.\right) + b_{13} \\ t_{2} - t_{4} = c_{24} \text{In} \left(\right. \frac{E_{2}}{E_{4}} \left.\right) + b_{24}
$$

 where $c_{14} \text{ln} \left(\frac{E_{1}}{E_{4}}\right) , c_{23} \text{ln} \left(\frac{E_{2}}{E_{3}}\right) , c_{13} \text{ln} \left(\frac{E_{1}}{E_{3}}\right)$, and $c_{24} \text{ln} \left(\frac{E_{2}}{E_{4}}\right)$ are used for time-walk correction, and $b_{14} , b_{23} , b_{13}$, and $b_{24}$ are for timing-shift correction. $b_{14} , b_{23} , b_{13}$, and $b_{24}$ are different for events with different DOI information. Our study also compared results using both formulas, finding them equivalent. Thus, we will employ formula 5 to introduce our correction method and present our results.

Using formulas 3 and 5, the corrected time difference, $\Delta t_{\textit{corrected}}$, of the two dual-ended readout detectors, can be expressed as (7) 

$$
\Delta t_{\textit{corrected}} = \Delta t - \frac{1}{2} \left(\right. c_{23} \text{ln} \left(\frac{E_{2}}{E_{3}}\right) + b_{23} \left.\right) - \frac{1}{2} \left(\right. c_{14} \text{ln} \left(\frac{E_{1}}{E_{4}}\right) + b_{14} \left.\right)
$$

Due to the timing-shift being different for events with different DOI information, to correct the timing-shift, events need to be first categorized into different DOI layers based on the DOI information, which can be done using the ratio of the two energies detected by the two SiPM arrays coupled to both ends of the crystal array [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R27)]. If a crystal is divided into $N$ DOI layers (all layers had the same thickness), then the two crystals in coincidence comprise $N^{2}$ DOI layer pairs. We also studied the impact of the number of DOI layers on the timing resolution (refer to [Fig. 7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F7)).

### CTR Measurement

B.
To assess the proposed time-walk and timing-shift correction method, two dual-ended readout detectors were constructed. Each detector consisted of two Hamamatsu S14161-3050-08 SiPM arrays (Hamamatsu Photonics K.K., Japan) coupled to both ends of an $8 \times 8$ array of $3 . 1 \times 3 . 1 \times 20 \left(m m\right)^{3}$ polished lutetium–yttrium oxyorthosilicate (LYSO) crystals with a 3.2 mm pitch. Optical grease BC-630 (Luxium Solutions, USA) was used as the coupling material between the SiPM arrays and the LYSO arrays. Barium sulfate $\left(\left(\text{BaS} O\right)_{4}\right)$ with 100 um thickness was used as the inter-crystal reflector in the LYSO array. Each S14161-3050-08 SiPM array comprises $8 \times 8$ SiPM elements, also with a 3.2 mm pitch. The matching 3.2 mm pitch across the SiPM arrays and LYSO arrays ensured each LYSO element was aligned with two SiPM elements (one at each end of the crystal), achieving the best timing resolution. Additionally, the detector had a DOI resolution of 2.6 mm.

The block diagram of the experimental setup used to obtain the experimental data is shown in [Fig. 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F2). The outputs of the S14161-3050-08 SiPM arrays were processed using the PETsys TOFPET2 readout system (PETsys Electronics S.A., Portugal) [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#R38)]. The 128 SiPM signals from each dual-ended readout detector were fed into a PETsys FEM128 module, which was equipped with two 64-channel application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) and could process each SiPM signal individually, including energy measurement and timing pick-off. The outputs from the two FEM128 modules were then routed to a PETsys FEB/D-1k module for further data processing. This module also provided the bias voltage for the SiPM arrays, and the power and the clock for the FEM128 modules. The FEB/D-1k module was connected to a Linux-based workstation via an ethernet cable, which ran the data acquisition software to store the data and control the PETsys readout system.

All measurements were conducted at 18 °C inside a temperature-controlled, light-tight box. The face-to-face distance between the two detectors was 150 mm. A 22 Na source, with an activity of 925 kBq $\left(\right. 25 \mu \text{Ci} \left.\right)$ and an active diameter of 0.25 mm, was positioned centrally between the two detectors to irradiate them. The SiPM arrays were biased at 42.0 V, and a low threshold of 5 digital-to-analog converter (DAC) least significant bit (LSB) was used for timing pick-off.

Due to the use of a point source centrally located between the two detectors, only crystal pairs of $C_{i}^{A} C_{65 - i}^{B} \left(\right. i = 1 \ldots 64 \left.\right)$ were capable of detecting coincidence events. Here, $C_{i}^{A}$ and $C_{65 - i}^{B}$ denotes the order of the crystals in detectors A and B, respectively. At the edges of the LYSO arrays, events are primarily detected towards the front of the detectors, due to the oblique angles of the annihilation photons at these locations. Hence, to accurately investigate the DOI effect on the timing resolution, four central crystals of each crystal array were selected for our study, as annihilation photons can interact at all depths in these crystals. To select the events detected by the central four crystals of one detector, the center-of-gravity method was used to calculate the gamma interaction position of all detected events, and look-up tables generated from the flood histogram of all events were used to assigned events to corresponding crystal. This selection resulted in four crystal pairs: $C_{27}^{A} C_{38}^{B} , C_{28}^{A} C_{37}^{B} , C_{37}^{A} C_{28}^{B}$, and $C_{38}^{A} C_{27}^{B}$, which allowed us to more accurately assess the impact of DOI on the timing resolution, and were used as a measure the CTR of the two detectors.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018)Results

III.
### Combined time-walk and timing-shift correction

A.
[Fig. 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F3) shows scatter plots of the threshold crossing time difference, $t_{2} - t_{3}$ and $t_{1} - t_{4}$, versus the natural logarithm of the energy ratio, $\text{ln} \left(\frac{E_{2}}{E_{3}}\right)$ and $\text{ln} \left(\frac{E_{1}}{E_{4}}\right)$, respectively, for one crystal pair. The events detected by both crystals were categorized into four DOI layers following the application of a 400–650 keV energy window to select events. The red lines in each subfigure represent fitting lines based on the formula $c_{23} \text{ln} \left(\frac{E_{2}}{E_{3}}\right) + b_{23}$ for [Fig. 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F3)(left) and $c_{14} \text{ln} \left(\frac{E_{1}}{E_{4}}\right) + b_{14}$ for [Fig. 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F3)(right). The time-walk and timing-shift pattern can be clearly visualized: the slope of the fitting lines signifies the presence of time-walk, whereas the displacement of the center of the distribution from 0 ns indicates timing-shift. The values of timing-shift ($b_{23}$ and $b_{14}$) along with $c_{23}$ and $c_{14}$ for each DOI layer pair are listed in [Tables I](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#T1) and [II](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#T2), demonstrating that a greater layer difference corresponds to a larger timing-shift and the existence of a timing offset among different channels of the readout electronics. Particularly, the $b_{23}$ and $b_{14}$ for layer pairs of Layer 1–1, Layer 2–2, Layer 3–3, and Layer 4–4 were similar, due to for these layer pairs, the timing-shift were primarily caused by the time-offset among readout electronic channels, due to the time-offset caused by the DOI effect were the same.

[Fig. 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F4) presents scatter plots of the corrected threshold crossing time difference after time-walk and timing-shift corrections versus the energy difference, which clearly shows that the time-walk has been corrected. From [Tables I](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#T1) and [II](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#T2), we can see that the values used for timing-shift, $b_{23}$ and $b_{14}$, are almost identical for each DOI layer pair, thus verifying the timing-shift can be corrected when using formula 7 to calculate the timing difference of the annihilation photons.

[Fig. 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F5) shows the timing spectra of one crystal pair (the same crystal pair analyzed in [Fig. 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F3) and [Fig. 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F4)) with and without the time-walk and timing-shift corrections. [Fig. 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F5)(left) clearly shows the unaligned peak positions of the timing spectra for events from different DOI layers: the relative peak position differences were caused by the DOI effect and the deviations from 0 ns were caused by the timing-offset of the readout electronics. [Fig. 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F5)(middle) shows the results following the proposed time-walk and timing-shift correction method, all timing spectra align perfectly to 0 ps, and the timing resolution was improved by $\sim 30$ ps ([Fig. 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F5)(right)). Correcting the timing-shift that was caused by the DOI effect aligned the peak position of the timing spectra, thereby improving the timing resolution. Correcting the timing-offset that was caused by the readout electronics aligned the peak position of the timing spectra to 0 ns, however, it did not affect the timing resolution shown in this paper, which was the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the timing spectra. Nonetheless, correcting the timing-offset caused by the readout electronics does enhance the localization accuracy of the annihilation photon interaction position along the LOR, improving image quality.

### CTR with and without time-walk and timing-shift corrections

B.
[Fig. 6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F6) displays the CTR for the four selected central crystal pairs from the two detectors in coincidence ([Fig. 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F2)). The events were categorized into four DOI layers. The CTR values of the four crystal pairs, both for those with and without time-walk and timing-shift calibration, were comparable. After applying time-walk and timing-shift corrections, the average CTR value across the 4 selected crystal pairs improved to $229 . 4 \pm 1 . 0 \text{ps}$ from $260 . 7 \pm 1 . 0 \text{ps}$ when using a $400 - 650 \text{keV}$ energy window for event selection.

### Effect of number of DOI layer on CTR

C.
[Fig. 7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F7) shows the relationship between the average CTR across the four central crystal pairs and the number of DOI layers, where 0 DOI layer implies that no proposed time-walk and timing-shift correction was performed, which serves as a baseline for comparison. The 1 DOI layer implies that only the time-walk correction was performed. Owing to the dual-ended readout approach that enables continuous DOI information, all results were derived from the same dataset but events were categorized into different number of DOI layers. It was observed that the CTR improved with an increasing number of DOI layers, however, the CTR improvement became marginal when the number of DOI layers exceeded four. The CTR improved from $248 . 1 \pm 1 . 0 \text{ps}$ to $229 . 4 \pm 1 . 0 \text{ps}$ as the number of DOI layers increased from 1 to 4, whereas the CTR was 228.8 ps when 8 DOI layers were used. A higher number of DOI layers necessitates more computation. Therefore, the optimal number of DOI layers for our detector was determined to be four, which was also the selected number of layers used to process the results shown in [Fig. 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F3) to [Fig. 6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F6).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018)Discussion

IV.
Correcting time-walk and timing-shift is crucial for enhancing the timing resolution in detectors that utilize thick crystals for high detection efficiency and employ the LED method for timing pick-off. We proposed and evaluated a combined time-walk and timing-shift correction method in this paper. Our findings showed that 1) correcting time-walk only enhanced the timing resolution by 12.6 ps, and 2) correcting the DOI of annihilation photons further improved the timing resolution by $\sim 20 \text{ps}$ ([Fig. 7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F7)). These results demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed method.

It is important to recognize that DOI is just one factor influencing timing-shift, variations between electronic channels also significantly impact timing accuracy ([Tables I](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#T1) and [II](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#T2), [Fig. 6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F6)). While the timing-shift induced by readout electronics did not affect the timing resolution reported in this paper, it did impact the localization accuracy of positron decay along the LOR. Our proposed correction method effectively addresses both the influences of DOI and the readout electronics simultaneously ([Fig. 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F5)).

Additionally, our study explored how the number of DOI layers affects the corrected timing resolution ([Fig. 7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018#F7)). We observed that timing resolution improves with increasing DOI layers; however, the benefits plateaued when the number of DOI layers exceeds four. To ensure uniform spatial resolution across the FOV, eight DOI layers will be utilized in our image reconstruction. This suggests that the demands for timing resolution correction are less stringent than those for spatial resolution. Employing eight DOI layers provides a balanced approach that optimizes both timing and spatial resolutions. For dual-ended readout detectors with 20 mm thick LYSO or LSO arrays and better DOI resolution, the number of DOI layers used can be increased, but we expect that the optimal number of DOI layers will not exceed 10, as the DOI resolution is $\sim 2 \text{mm}$.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018)Conclusion

V.
A combined time-walk and timing-shift correction method for dual-ended readout PET detectors was proposed and evaluated using two dual-ended readout PET detectors based on Hamamatsu S14161-3050-08 SiPM arrays and LYSO arrays with a 3.2 mm pitch. By correcting the time-walk and timing-shift, the average CTR of the detectors was improved by $\sim 31 \text{ps}$, from $260 . 7 \pm 1 . 0 \text{ps}$ to $229 . 4 \pm 1 . 0 \text{ps}$ when a $400 - 650 \text{keV}$ energy window was used to select events. These improvements suggest that the proposed time-walk and timing-shift correction method can be used to enhance the timing resolution of PET scanners to improve image quality.

args.summary:
This scientific paper, published in IEEE Transactions on Radiation and Plasma Medical Sciences (Nov 2024), presents a novel combined time-walk and timing-shift correction method for dual-ended readout time-of-flight (TOF) PET detectors that use depth-of-interaction (DOI) information.

Key points:
- PET detectors suffer from time-walk (when using leading-edge discriminator for timing pick-off) and timing-shift (due to DOI effect in thick crystals and readout electronics)
- The proposed method uses the relationship between detected energies and time differences to correct both effects simultaneously
- Two dual-ended readout detectors were built using Hamamatsu S14161-3050-08 SiPM arrays coupled to both ends of 8×8 arrays of 3.1×3.1×20 mm³ LYSO crystals with 3.2 mm pitch
- Experimental setup: ²²Na source (925 kBq), 150 mm detector distance, 18°C, PETsys TOFPET2 readout system
- Using a 400-650 keV energy window, the coincidence time resolution (CTR) improved from 260.7 ± 1.0 ps to 229.4 ± 1.0 ps after correction
- The study also investigated the effect of DOI layer count on timing resolution, finding that CTR improved with more layers but plateaued beyond 4 layers (optimal for this detector)
- Time-walk correction alone improved CTR by 12.6 ps; DOI correction added another ~20 ps improvement
- The correction also addresses timing offsets from readout electronics, improving localization accuracy along the line-of-response
- Authors: Haibo Wang, Jiahao Xie, Jinyi Qi (Fellow, IEEE), Simon R. Cherry (Fellow, IEEE), Junwei Du (Senior Member, IEEE) - all from UC Davis Department of Biomedical Engineering
- Funded by NIH grants R01 EB028806 and R01 EB031961

### **Abstract deadline extended to 27 AprilNew submissions will be considered for poster, or oral if space is available**

The objective of this conference is to bring together researchers interested in the development of unconventional imaging, sensing, and adaptive-optics technologies. Therefore, we seek papers that:

1. use unconventional means of data collection, data processing, and interpretation;
2. leverage artificial intelligence and machine learning for efficient data and image processing;
3. address laboratory-, space-, airborne-, sea-, and ground-based systems;
4. deal with distributed-volume aberrations, high-speed aberrations, scattering media, speckle phenomena, etc.;
5. seek to design effective and efficient algorithms for processing different kinds of available data; and
6. obtain solutions to many kinds of imaging, sensing, and adaptive-optics applications.

  
 Papers from industry, academia, government, and other research organizations are welcome on the topics listed below. Note that papers related to atmospheric measurement and characterization will be included in a joint session coordinated with the *OP430 Laser Communication and Propagation through the Atmosphere and Oceans*  conference.   
   
 Topics of interest include, but are not limited to:

* modeling, simulation, and experimental efforts in imaging and/or sensing for biomedical, environmental, astronomy, industrial, communication, security, and defense applications
* novel algorithms or hardware for traditional as well as unconventional imaging and/or sensing systems
* modeling and characterization of optical systems operating in the atmosphere or underwater
* imaging using ultrafast pulses, active/passive illumination, synthetic apertures, coded apertures, THz and mm wave imaging
* information retrieval exploiting diversity in measurements (such as image plane/pupil plane measurements; phase/wavelength/polarization/aperture diversity)
* inversion problems in imaging and/or sensing
* coherent and direct detection techniques
* developments in emerging technologies such as autonomous vehicles, plenoptic cameras, and event-based cameras
* developments in wavefront sensing, wavefront reconstruction, and adaptive optics technologies
* characterization and developments in tracking technologies
* modeling, simulation, and experimental efforts in characterizing aero optics, deep turbulence, jitter, turbulence, wind, extinction and/or their effects on optical systems
* advances in deformable mirrors, fast-steering mirrors, phase modulators, spatial-light modulator technologies.

  
 Of particular interest to this conference are imaging, sensing, and adaptive optics techniques that employ machine learning or those that promote sustainability.;

14229-1

[The Starfire Optical Range SCIDAR](/optics-photonics/presentation/The-Starfire-Optical-Range-SCIDAR/14229-1)

Author(s): Denis W. Oesch, Leidos, Inc. (United States); Colton M. Bigler, Robert L. Johnson, Air Force Research Lab. (United States)

24 August 2026 • 8:40 AM - 9:00 AM PDT | Conv. Ctr. Room 6D

Show Abstract + Hide Abstract – 

Characterizing the turbulence encountered by the adaptive optical systems at the Air Force Research Laboratory’s Starfire Optical Range (SOR) is critical to understanding the performance of those systems. A stereo Scintillation Detection And Ranging (SCIDAR) system has begun collecting data from one of the 1.0 m telescopes at SOR. This stereo SCIDAR system captures the light from a binary star pair onto two cameras and uses cross-correlations of the images to estimate the index of refraction structure function C2n(z). Results from the initial period of testing are presented and compared with measurement of the turbulence taken with the Starfire Atmospheric Monitor (SAM).

14229-2

[Wave optics analysis of the Interferometric Refractive Index Sensor (IRIS)](/optics-photonics/presentation/Wave-optics-analysis-of-the-Interferometric-Refractive-Index-Sensor-IRIS/14229-2)

Author(s): Thomas J. Miletich, Naval Surface Warfare Ctr. Dahlgren Div. (United States), ASRI (United States); Matthew T. Kalensky, Naval Surface Warfare Ctr. Dahlgren Div. (United States); Daniel Whitley, The Univ. of Alabama in Huntsville (United States); Evan M. Bates, Naval Surface Warfare Ctr. Dahlgren Div. (United States)

24 August 2026 • 9:00 AM - 9:20 AM PDT | Conv. Ctr. Room 6D

Show Abstract + Hide Abstract – 

The Interferometric Refractive Index Sensor (IRIS) is a prototype sensor that utilizes a pair of Michelson interferometers to make high frequency optical phase measurements over a short optical path. Optical turbulence statistics are subsequently derived from the differential phase measurements or through the use of a second-order structure function calculated from the time series of the phase measurements. Making a direct nodal optical measurement of turbulence is beneficial because it inherently accommodates all components of optical turbulence, unlike traditional nodal turbulence sensors which infer turbulence strength from atmospheric structure parameters. This paper simulates and evaluates IRIS's measurement methodology through a wave-optics analysis. Using the simulation model that we develop, we conduct a sensitivity study to understand the accuracy of the phase retrieval algorithm and how it is impacted by both system as well as environmental parameters. These results and future simulations will help to optimize future design iterations of the IRIS system. We feel that this paper will be of interest to researchers exploring optical-turbulence measurement techniques.

14227-2

[Comparison of turbulence height profiles in the surface layer in different environments](/optics-photonics/presentation/Comparison-of-turbulence-height-profiles-in-the-surface-layer-in/14227-2)

Author(s): Thalia Sanqui, David Voelz, Miranda van Iersel, New Mexico State Univ. (United States)

24 August 2026 • 9:20 AM - 9:40 AM PDT | Conv. Ctr. Room 6D

Show Abstract + Hide Abstract – 

The strength of turbulence varies with height above the ground, and this variation is reasonably well understood for altitudes ranging from approximately 0.5 km to over 20 km, However, these variations are not well understood in the surface layer (ranging from 0 m to 50 m), i.e., close to the ground. It is known that turbulence develops differently depending on the surface roughness of the ground, meaning the environment (on the ground) influences the turbulence and its development. Turbulence height profiles are measured in the surface layer in two different environments within the city of Las Cruces, New Mexico: a flat, desert environment and a mountain environment located between a city and a mountain range. A system consisting of a series of boxes containing two horizontally spaced LEDs is mounted on a tower at both locations. Video footage of these LEDs is recorded using a UAV flying at the same altitude as the LEDs and processed to obtain the turbulence height profiles. These measured turbulence height profiles are compared with predictions from different models, which do not contain any information about the environment.

14229-71

[Jitter coupling and uplink scintillation characterization for active tracking](/optics-photonics/presentation/Jitter-coupling-and-uplink-scintillation-characterization-for-active-tracking/14229-71)

Author(s): Ian Kingsolver, Mark F. Spencer, The Univ. of Arizona (United States)

24 August 2026 • 9:40 AM - 10:00 AM PDT | Conv. Ctr. Room 6D

Show Abstract + Hide Abstract – 

When jitter is present in the uplink propagation path, an active tracking system mistakenly interprets the associated movement of non-uniform illumination as object motion, leading to a significant track error referred to as jitter coupling. While Riker [Proc. SPIE 8052, 805202 (2011)] summarizes analytical expressions for jitter coupling based on the ratio between beam size and object size, his expressions do not account for additional phenomena like uplink scintillation present in real-world active tracking scenarios. Using wave optics simulations, this paper demonstrates that Riker’s analytical expressions accurately estimate the track error due to jitter coupling in an ideal case but inaccurately estimate the track error due to jitter coupling when uplink scintillation is present. These results will inform the development of future scaling laws, as they demonstrate the need for further analytical work to better quantify the effects of jitter coupling in real-world active tracking scenarios.

Show Abstract + Hide Abstract – 

This study investigates the impact of particle size distribution on laser propagation effectiveness. By integrating particle counters with a weather monitoring system, real-time assessment of atmospheric particulate matter can be achieved, allowing for prediction of energy transmission efficiency. Experimental data, collected in diverse atmospheric environments, characterized the distribution of both nano- and micro-sized particles. These particle sizes range from 5nm to 500 nm for nano-particles and 0.5μm to 10μm for micro-particles. This data was correlated with atmospheric parameters and modeled energy propagation to assess the relative contribution of different particle size ranges to energy attenuation. An effective transmission metric is introduced that incorporates turbulence effects into the power received in the target “bucket” calculation and diagnostic evaluation. Results indicate that in short range engagements (3 km and less) near the surface with low turbulence quantifying micro-particles is critically important.

[Precise timing architectures for intensity interferometry: avoiding cross-talk with synchronized Time Taggers](/optics-photonics/presentation/Precise-timing-architectures-for-intensity-interferometry--avoiding-cross-talk/14229-7)

Author(s): Mare Sutphen, Swabian Instruments USA Inc. (United States)

24 August 2026 • 1:30 PM - 1:50 PM PDT | Conv. Ctr. Room 6D

Show Abstract + Hide Abstract – 

Intensity interferometry relies on sub-nanosecond timing correlations between photon detection events across spatially separated telescopes. A key challenge in these measurements is electronic channel crosstalk, which produces false coincidence peaks that can obscure weak astrophysical signals. Conventional mitigation strategies use fixed temporal delays to shift true correlations away from the zero-delay region, but this adds system complexity and can degrade timing performance. This presentation introduces two alternative synchronization architectures that eliminate the need for artificial delays while maintaining high timing resolution. For co-located systems, synchronized dual time-tagger operation using a shared reference clock enables crosstalk-free correlation without added jitter. For distributed observatories, precision timing protocols such as White Rabbit provide sub-nanosecond synchronization over fiber networks. Experimental results demonstrate improved resolution and reduced integration times, supporting scalable, next-generation intensity interferometry experiments.

Triaxial optomechanical inertial sensors offer compact, ground-testable alternatives to electrostatic sensors for applications in satellite geodesy, seismometry, and other areas. We demonstrate a low-CSWaP triaxial sensor using monolithic fused-silica resonators with dual heterodyne interferometric readout. Steady state thermal blooming results in path-integrated phase distortions (caused by local atmospheric heating) that reshape and deflect the high energy laser beam into a crescent or half-moon irradiance pattern. Polymer-embedded magnetic nanoparticle (MNP) composites in fiber-optic multimode-interference (MMI) sensors provide an electrically insulating, EMI-immune approach to magnetic field sensing. We present a mechanism-based model connecting the AC field to the resulting optical readout, combining a dielectric baseline, magnetization dynamics, and optical transduction. Thermal annealing switches the dominant readout harmonic from the fundamental (1f) to the second harmonic (2f). We attribute this switch to the collapse of a magnetically blocked nanoparticle fraction. Its directly measured remanent moment had been biasing an intrinsically even (2f) mechanism into an apparent 1f response. Surface oxidation and particle redispersion are both kinetically plausible causes of this collapse, and models of either reproduce the AC data comparably well. The measured drop in total saturation magnetization matches surface oxidation's predicted range, whereas redispersion predicts no measurable change.

Digital holographic wavefront sensors in the on-axis phase-shifting recording geometry (PSRG) can estimate the complex optical field while using a strong local oscillator (LO) to boost weak received signals above the focal-plane-array noise floor. Here, we experimentally demonstrate the measurement of tilt, while boosting the received signal with an LO, using a temporal four-step on-axis PSRG at 1550 nm. A spatial light modulator (SLM) applies a known tilt ramp, and the reconstructed phase along the pupil diameter is unwrapped and linearly fitted to recover the tilt. With a weak signal power of 8.3 nW, the 100 μrad tilt error RMS decreases from 360 μrad in the unboosted case of PLO = Psig to 46 μrad at the optimum LO power of 1.7 μW. This result is benchmarked against a high visibility reconstruction test where tilt error RMS is 7.1 μrad. These results show that LO boosting can improve low-order angular-mode sensing with on-axis PSRG, providing an experimental step toward weak-signal adaptive-optics wavefront sensing for free-space optical links.

Conventional astronomical spectrographs are seeing-limited and commonly use multi-mode fibers (MMFs) to inject starlight and illuminate downstream optics. Future Doppler radial-velocity instruments will increasingly rely on adaptive optics and smaller, single mode fibers (SMFs), whose mode-field diameters enable higher spectral resolution while improving stabilization of the spectrograph point-spread function. However, coupling starlight into SMFs with characteristic diameters of only ~5–10 μm is technically demanding, requiring automated alignment procedures that are both efficient and stable throughout the duration of an observation. In this poster, we describe a SMF coupling control program being developed for diffraction-limited radial-velocity spectrographs.

Author(s): Arlene J. Aleman, Justin R. Crepp, Caleb Abbott, Denise A. Huerta, Univ. of Notre Dame (United States)

24 August 2026 • 5:30 PM - 7:30 PM PDT | Conv. Ctr. Exhibit Hall B1

Show Abstract + Hide Abstract – 

Strong turbulence conditions induce phase-to-amplitude conversion creating scintillation patterns that present a challenge for phase retrieval methods. For multi-plane wavefront sensors, the Gerchberg-Saxton (GS) algorithm is often used, due to its simplicity and compatibility with forward/backward Fresnel propagations; however, GS has a tendency to stagnate in local minima and fail in the presence of branch points and/or large aberrations. To overcome these limitations, we are developing nonlinear least-squares (NLLS) methods as a robust alternative to the GS algorithm by directly minimizing the difference between measured and model-predicted multi-plane intensities. We present on-going work in developing regularized, branch-point-tolerant reconstruction algorithms that are candidates for next-generation phase retrieval pipelines.

The Shack–Hartmann wavefront sensor (SH-WFS) is a proven and reliable wavefront sensor. In this paper, we formulate the phase reconstruction matrix by calculating its pseudoinverse through singular value decomposition for the SH-WFS using the Fried recording geometry. We progress in a tutorial approach so that future research efforts can leverage this step-by-step formulation. Throughout, we use linear algebra to recover phase information from the calculated slope measurements obtained by the SH-WFS. Additionally, we test a waffle mitigation algorithm in simulation to measure its performance as the SH-WFS reconstructs increasingly aberrated phase errors after propagation through atmospheric turbulence. The results show that the performance of the SH-WFS decreases as the strength of atmospheric turbulence increases, even when mitigating the waffle mode. These results will help future computational and experimental efforts that need to implement a SH-WFS.

Author(s): Trevor L. Owens, Mark F. Spencer, Ronald Driggers, The Univ. of Arizona (United States)

25 August 2026 • 10:30 AM - 10:50 AM PDT | Conv. Ctr. Room 6D

Show Abstract + Hide Abstract – 

Uniform laser illumination is critical in active-imaging applications like active tracking. In practice, atmospheric turbulence causes uplink scintillation that degrades the uniformity of the laser illumination. In this paper, it is proposed that by spatially distributing multiple laser beams or “beamlets” in the source plane, the effects of uplink scintillation can be mitigated in the target plane via incoherent beam combination, leading to more uniform laser illumination. Thus, the research in this paper includes the creation of two wave-optics models to (1) describe the correlation of the uplink scintillation between two spatially separated beams and (2) describe the diminishing returns associated with increasing the number of spatially distributed beamlets. In support of (1), the results show that the Fresnel zone and the scattering disk appropriately predict the correlation length of the uplink scintillation between two beamlets. Similarly, in support of (2), the results show that when more than three beamlets are incoherently combined, there are diminishing returns in mitigating the effects of uplink scintillation.

The phase extracted from the interferometry carried a systematic error, and a correction procedure was provided.

14229-25

[Digital holography sensing beyond coherent source coherence length](/optics-photonics/presentation/Digital-holography-sensing-beyond-coherent-source-coherence-length/14229-25)

Author(s): Weston Jenkins, Tyler J. Hardy, Casey Pellizzari, U.S. Air Force Academy (United States)

25 August 2026 • 11:10 AM - 11:30 AM PDT | Conv. Ctr. Room 6D

Show Abstract + Hide Abstract – 

Interferometry is commonly considered limited by the coherence length of the laser source, which constrains the allowable optical path difference (OPD) between interfering beams. This work examines how sensor integration time affects interference fringe visibility at OPDs exceeding the coherence length of the laser using numerical simulation and laboratory Michelson interferometry. A simulation is developed to model laser phase drift as a Gaussian random walk governed by the laser linewidth, enabling calculation of fringe visibility as a function of OPD, coherence length, and integration time. Results show that short integration times preserve significant fringe visibility well beyond one coherence length, while long integration times do not. These predictions are validated experimentally using a Michelson interferometer, where measured fringe visibility increases as the camera integration time is reduced. These results demonstrate that sensor integration time, rather than coherence length alone, is a primary factor limiting observable interference and that effective interferometry beyond the conventional coherence-length limit is achievable.

14229-26

[Compact interferometers with differential wavefront sensing for precision segment sensing in space telescopes](/optics-photonics/presentation/Compact-interferometers-with-differential-wavefront-sensing-for-precision-segment-sensing/14229-26)

Author(s): Ramses Miranda Espino, Jose D. Rivero, Don George, Pengzhuo Wang, The Univ. of Arizona (United States); Miguel Dovale, Wyant College of Optical Sciences, The Univ. of Arizona (United States); Moritz Mehmet, Jose Sanjuan Munoz, Felipe Guzman, The Univ. of Arizona (United States)

25 August 2026 • 11:30 AM - 11:50 AM PDT | Conv. Ctr. Room 6D

Show Abstract + Hide Abstract – 

We present the development of compact heterodyne interferometric sensors that combine longitudinal displacement readout with differential wavefront sensing (DWS). The sensors employ a dual heterodyne detection scheme with beat-note frequencies in the kHz–MHz range, enabling phase extraction and rejection of common-mode noise. By implementing quadrant photodetectors, differential phase across the interfering wavefronts are measured, allowing simultaneous estimation of mirror tip and tilt alongside picometer-level displacement sensitivity, as demonstrated in related implementations. The long-term objectives of this work include fully integrating quadrant photodiodes and low-noise readout electronics together with our quasi-monolithic interferometer and demonstrating picometer-level (rms) displacement sensitivity together with nanoradian-level (rms) angular sensitivity over timescales from 0.1 to 100 seconds. Demonstrating compact, scalable heterodyne interferometric sensors with integrated DWS capability is relevant to ongoing efforts in high-stability wavefront control and optical metrology.

This webpage is for the SPIE Optics + Photonics 2026 conference, specifically Conference 14229: "Unconventional Imaging, Sensing, and Adaptive Optics 2026," taking place August 24-27, 2026, in San Diego, California at the Convention Center Room 6D. The abstract deadline was extended to April 27, 2026.

The conference brings together researchers developing unconventional imaging, sensing, and adaptive-optics technologies, with papers leveraging AI/ML, addressing various system platforms (laboratory, space, airborne, sea, ground-based), and dealing with distributed-volume aberrations, scattering media, and speckle phenomena.

The conference program spans 15 sessions including:
- **Sessions 1-2** (Aug 24): Atmospheric Characterization I & II (joint sessions with Conference 14227) — topics include SCIDAR turbulence characterization, wave optics analysis of IRIS sensor, turbulence height profiles, jitter coupling, estimating Cn2 from global datasets, particle quantification for laser propagation, and effects of extreme smoke events on optical turbulence.
- **Sessions 3-4** (Aug 24): Unconventional Sensing I & II — topics include intensity interferometry timing architectures, branch points, optomechanical inertial sensors, fiber optic pH sensing for marine applications, inflatable primary reflectors, thermal blooming modeling, magnetic field sensing, wavefront sensing with extended beacons, and digital holographic wavefront sensing.
- **Poster Session** (Aug 24, 5:30-7:30 PM): Including automated single-mode fiber coupling for spectrographs and branch-point-tolerant reconstruction algorithms.
- **Sessions 5-6** (Aug 25): Unconventional Sensing III & IV — phase diversity super-resolution, phase-retrieval wavefront sensors, Shack-Hartmann wavefront sensor tutorial, uplink scintillation mitigation via incoherent beam combination, dual-frame interferometry, digital holography beyond coherence length, and compact interferometers for space telescopes.
- **Sessions 7-15** (Aug 25-27): Unconventional Adaptive Optics I & II, Aero Optics I & II, Unconventional Sensing V, Unconventional Imaging I-III, Event-Based Imaging, and an Artificial Intelligence Plenary.

Key topics include: modeling/simulation for imaging and sensing, novel algorithms/hardware, atmospheric and underwater optical systems, ultrafast/THz/mm wave imaging, wavefront sensing and reconstruction, adaptive optics, deformable mirrors, autonomous vehicles, plenoptic cameras, event-based cameras, aero optics, deep turbulence, and machine learning applications.
