# Rethinking Timing Residuals: Advancing PET Detectors with Explicit TOF Corrections

###### Abstract

PET is a functional imaging method that can visualize metabolic processes and relies on the coincidence detection of emitted annihilation quanta. From the signals recorded by coincident detectors, TOF information can be derived, usually represented as the difference in detection timestamps. Incorporating the TOF information into the reconstruction can enhance the image’s SNR. Typically, PET detectors are assessed based on the coincidence time resolution (CTR) they can achieve. However, the detection process is affected by factors that degrade the timing performance of PET detectors. Research on timing calibrations develops and evaluates concepts aimed at mitigating these degradations to restore the unaffected timing information. While many calibration methods rely on analytical approaches, machine learning techniques have recently gained interest due to their flexibility. We developed a residual physics-based calibration approach, which combines prior domain knowledge with the flexibility and power of machine learning models. This concept revolves around an initial analytical calibration step addressing first-order skews. In the subsequent step, any deviation from a defined expectation is regarded as a residual effect, which we leverage to train machine learning models to eliminate higher-order skews. The main advantage of this idea is that the experimenter can guide the learning process through the definition of the timing residuals. In earlier studies, we developed models that directly predicted the expected time difference, which offered corrections only implicitly (implicit correction models). In this study, we introduce a new definition for timing residuals, enabling us to train models that directly predict correction values (explicit correction models). We demonstrate that the explicit correction approach allows for a massive simplification of the data acquisition procedure, offers exceptionally high linearity, and provides corrections able to improve the timing performance from 371±±6 ps371\pm\pm 6\text{\,}\mathrm{ps} to 281±±5 ps281\pm\pm 5\text{\,}\mathrm{ps} for coincidences from 430 keV to 590 keV430\text{\,}\mathrm{keV}590\text{\,}\mathrm{keV}. Furthermore, the novel definition makes it possible to exponentially reduce the models in size, making it suitable for applications with high data throughput, such as PET scanners. All experiments are performed with two detector stacks comprised of 4×44\text{\times}4 LYSO:Ce,Ca crystals (each 3.8×3.8×20 mm3.8\text{\times}3.8\text{\times}20\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}), which are coupled to 4×44\text{\times}4 Broadcom NUV-MT SiPMs and digitized with the TOFPET2 ASIC.

Keywords: TOF, PET, CTR, Machine Learning, TOFPET2

## 1 Introduction

The introduction of precise [TOF](#id3) ([TOF](#id3)) information in [PET](#id28) ([PET](#id28)) leads to a significant improvement in the [SNR](#id4) ([SNR](#id4)) of the reconstructed images, which could aid physicians in diagnosis [[1](#bib.bibx1), [2](#bib.bibx2)]. For this reason, in recent years, there has been increased research into various approaches that have the potential to further improve [TOF](#id3)-[PET](#id28), with the ultimate goal of eventually achieving a timing resolution in the order of 10 ps10\text{\,}\mathrm{ps} [[3](#bib.bibx3)].
  
The [PET](#id28) data acquisition begins with the detection of the emitted γ\gamma-photons using dedicated detectors consisting of a scintillation volume and attached readout technology. Recent research demonstrated the potential of co-doping approaches [[4](#bib.bibx4), [5](#bib.bibx5)], Cherenkov emitters [[6](#bib.bibx6), [7](#bib.bibx7)] like [BGO](#id34) ([BGO](#id34)) [[8](#bib.bibx8), [9](#bib.bibx9), [10](#bib.bibx10), [11](#bib.bibx11), [12](#bib.bibx12)] or composite materials like metascintillators [[13](#bib.bibx13), [14](#bib.bibx14)]. Furthermore, the research community investigates double-sided readout techniques [[15](#bib.bibx15), [16](#bib.bibx16), [17](#bib.bibx17), [18](#bib.bibx18)] and waveform sampling approaches [[19](#bib.bibx19), [20](#bib.bibx20), [21](#bib.bibx21), [22](#bib.bibx22)], both providing rich signal information but posing hardware-related challenges regarding the usage in full scanner configurations.
  
Besides previously mentioned research lines, a considerable number of studies are conducted on the development and improvement of calibration techniques aiming to minimize any deteriorating effects impacting the [TOF](#id3) measurement by estimating unaffected timestamps or providing corrections to them. Mathematically, one can describe a timestamp tdt\_{d} reported by the detection system as a superposition of unaffected, true timestamp Θ\Theta and a time offset Δ​ts\Delta t\_{s} often called skew,

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | td=Θ+Δ​ts,t\_{d}=\Theta+\Delta t\_{s}, |  | (1) |

with the offset value being a composition of different deteriorating sub-offset sis\_{i} parameterized by pi→\vec{p\_{i}},

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Δ​ts=∑isi​(pi→).\Delta t\_{s}=\sum\limits\_{i}s\_{i}(\vec{p\_{i}}). |  | (2) |

In reality, the sub-offset {si}\{s\_{i}\} might change from γ\gamma-interaction to γ\gamma-interaction (e.g., due to different energy depositions affecting the signal steepness, baseline shifts, [DOI](#id10) ([DOI](#id10))-related effects, etc. [[23](#bib.bibx23), [24](#bib.bibx24)]) leading to different magnitudes and constitutions of Δ​ts\Delta t\_{s}.
  
While in former times, primarily analytical calibration approaches were studied, [AI](#id37) ([AI](#id37)) methods gained interest in recent years, so that machine learning approaches are also an active area of research. Classical [PET](#id28) timing calibration methods in the literature rely on solving matrix equations [[25](#bib.bibx25), [26](#bib.bibx26), [27](#bib.bibx27)] or use timing alignment probes [[28](#bib.bibx28), [29](#bib.bibx29)]. Also, data-driven approaches without requiring specialized data acquisition setups have been investigated, e.g., using consistency conditions [[30](#bib.bibx30), [31](#bib.bibx31), [32](#bib.bibx32), [33](#bib.bibx33)] or detector-intrinsic characteristics [[34](#bib.bibx34), [35](#bib.bibx35)]. Other approaches use statistical modeling under the premise of a maximum-likelihood approach [[36](#bib.bibx36), [37](#bib.bibx37)].
  
Many machine learning-based timing calibrations utilize supervised learning and, therefore, generate labeled data by measuring radiation sources at multiple positions [[38](#bib.bibx38), [39](#bib.bibx39), [40](#bib.bibx40), [41](#bib.bibx41), [42](#bib.bibx42)] or at a single position [[43](#bib.bibx43)]. Nearly all of the existing approaches work with the signal waveforms. Although this kind of data represents a rich source of information, it often requires dedicated measurement hardware capable of high sampling rates, e.g., oscilloscopes, that might be challenging to implement in a full scanner setting.
  
In recent studies, we developed and demonstrated the functionality of a machine learning-based timing calibration for clinically relevant detectors (coupled to digital [SiPM](#id35) [[44](#bib.bibx44), [45](#bib.bibx45)] and analog [SiPM](#id35) [[46](#bib.bibx46)]) without the need of waveform information. Instead, we utilized detector blocks coupled to matrices of [SiPM](#id35), as is done in pre-clinical and clinical settings. Furthermore, we proposed to follow a residual physics-based calibration concept, which separates the calibration effort into two parts.
  
In the first part, an analytical calibration procedure is conducted, which addresses so-called skews of first order that do not change during measurement and are similar for each event. After correction for those skews, each deviation from an expectation can be interpreted as a residual effect caused by higher-order skews that might change on an event basis. To address these higher-order skews in the second part, we endeavor to use machine learning techniques since they offer high flexibility and are suitable for finding characteristic patterns in the calibration data. The strength of the residual physics concept is the underlying idea that the experimenter can incorporate prior domain knowledge in the way the residual effects are defined.
  
When applying machine learning techniques in physical problems, one should ensure that the trained models produce results that are in alignment with physical laws. Therefore, we proposed in prior works, to use a three-folded evaluation scheme. In the first instance, models are assessed regarding their [MAE](#id17) ([MAE](#id17)) performance. How well the models are with physics is tested in the second instance. Finally, models that passed the first two evaluation levels are tested in the third instance regarding the improvement in [CTR](#id6) ([CTR](#id6)).
  
In our proof-of-concept study [[44](#bib.bibx44)], we used a similar label generation like Berg and Cherry [[38](#bib.bibx38)], which demands the collection of multiple source positions between two detectors in order to label the data for supervised training of the model. Successfully trained regression models are able to predict the expected time difference for a given input sample, e.g., consisting of information about the measured time difference, the detected timestamps, the detected energy signals, and the estimated γ\gamma-interaction position. In this sense, the trained models provide implicit corrections by directly predicting the corrected time difference.
  
Although this procedure demonstrated that significant improvements in [CTR](#id6) are possible, the acquisition of the labeled data was time-consuming considering future applications in a fully equipped [PET](#id28) scanner. In a follow-up work [[46](#bib.bibx46)], we demonstrated that the acquisition time can be significantly reduced without losing the calibration quality making the approach more practical. However, the study also revealed a strong dependence of the trained regression models on the used training step width given as the distance between subsequent source positions. As soon as this stepping distance becomes too large, the regression model showed on finer sampled test data a kind of collapse towards a classification model for positions present in the training data set. This resulted in a worse prediction quality for radiation sources located at positions being not present in the training data. Even though the overall prediction quality of the collapsing models was in an acceptable range regarding the [MAE](#id17), it also led to a substantial loss of linearity. The linearity property of a calibration model, namely that a source shift in the spatial domain translates linearly to shift of the time difference distribution in the time domain, is especially for [TOF](#id3)-[PET](#id28) one of the most important attributes, since it ensures a correct interpretation of the [TOF](#id3) information. The precise value of the maximum training stepping width at which the model remains functional might depend on the spatial sampling of the training dataset and on the timing resolution that can be achieved with the detectors being calibrated. While the precise derivation of the dependence on the measurement parameters is out of the scope of this work, one can safely assume that a training step width being large compared to either the testing step width or/and the timing resolution will likely result in a model collapse. The implication of this observation leads to the conclusion that the smaller the [CTR](#id6) value and/or testing step width is, the smaller the training step width used has to be, resulting potentially in an elaborate data acquisition.
  
In this work, we provide a new definition of the timing residuals (oriented on the work of Onishi et al. [[43](#bib.bibx43)]), which allows us to train [TOF](#id3)-correction models explicitly, providing correction values instead of expected time differences.
  
In the first part, we compare the novel residual formulation (explicit corrections) with the already established one (implicit corrections) regarding a three-folded evaluation scheme. The analyses use real measurement data and demonstrate that by using the explicit correction approach, the strong dependence on the step width is removed, the biased prediction distributions are suppressed, and the linearity property is preserved. Considering a typical [PET](#id28) scanner geometry, we will refer to this study as the transaxial performance study.
  
In the second part, we analyze how the in-plane distribution of sources for a given location between the detectors affects the calibration quality, minding a later in-system application with, e.g., dedicated phantoms or a point source located at a single position between the detectors. In the following, this study is called the in-plane distribution study.

## 2 Materials

### 2.1 PET Detectors

Two clinically relevant [PET](#id28) detectors of identical design are used for the experiments. The scintillator topology is given by 4×44\text{\times}4 LYSO:Ce,Ca crystals manufactured by Taiwan Applied Crystals (TAC), which have shown promising performance in previous studies [[5](#bib.bibx5)]. Each crystal element is separated by ESR-OCA-ESR sheets with a thickness of 155 µ​m155\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m} and a volume of 3.8×3.8×20 mm3.8\text{\times}3.8\text{\times}20\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} with polished top and bottom faces and depolished lateral faces [[47](#bib.bibx47), [48](#bib.bibx48)]. The crystals are coupled to a 4×44\text{\times}4 array of Broadcom NUV-MT SiPMs (AFBR-S4N44P164M) having a pitch of 3.8 mm3.8\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} and 40 µ​m40\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m} SPAD size. Each SiPM is coupled to one channel of the TOFPET2 ASIC (version 2c) [[49](#bib.bibx49), [50](#bib.bibx50)]. A timestamp in picoseconds and an energy value in arbitrary units is reported if an SiPM is triggered. The trigger and validation settings can be found in [Table 7](#Sx3.T7 "In Additional Tables ‣ Rethinking Timing Residuals: Advancing PET Detectors with Explicit TOF Corrections").

### 2.2 Experimental Setup & Settings

The measurement setup is located in a light-protected climate chamber, which is controlled at a temperature of 16 °C16\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolCelsius}. The sensor tiles are mounted at a distance of 565 mm565\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}. In between the detectors, a 22Na point source with an active diameter of 0.5 mm0.5\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} is used. The source holder is connected to a custom-manufactured translation stage system, allowing movement along all three spatial axes with a precision of <1 µ​m<$1\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m}$. The activity of the source was given to 1.4 MBq1.4\text{\,}\mathrm{MBq}. The ASIC board temperatures are kept constant while operation and are measured to be 33.9±±0.1 °C33.9\pm\pm 0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolCelsius} and 36.3±±0.1 °C36.3\pm\pm 0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolCelsius}, respectively. For all data acquisitions, the same measurement settings (listed in [Table 7](#Sx3.T7 "In Additional Tables ‣ Rethinking Timing Residuals: Advancing PET Detectors with Explicit TOF Corrections")) are used.

## 3 Methods

### 3.1 Defining Timing Residuals: Implicit & Explicit Corrections

Labeling the acquired measurement data is essential to make it applicable for supervised learning algorithms. The labels represent a kind of ground truth since they guide the training procedure of machine learning models. However, for [PET](#id28) timing calibrations, the underlying ground truth is not accessible since the time skews can vary on an event basis, and the only information available to the experimenter is the measured time difference given as the difference between the timestamps reported by two coincident detectors. Nevertheless, it is possible to obtain a certain level of ground truth by connecting the spatial location of a radiation source with the expected time difference, assuming that no systematic skews are present. By shifting the radiator to a different spatial location zz, one can anticipate that also the expected time difference Δ​t𝔼\Delta t\_{\mathbb{E}} will shift. Both quantities are related to each other via,

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Δt𝔼(z)=−2c⋅z,\Delta t\_{\mathbb{E}}(z)=-\frac{2}{c}\cdot z, |  | (3) |

with cc denoting the speed of light. In our proof-of-concept work [[44](#bib.bibx44)], we used [Eq. 3](#S3.E3 "In 3.1 Defining Timing Residuals: Implicit & Explicit Corrections ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Rethinking Timing Residuals: Advancing PET Detectors with Explicit TOF Corrections") to generate labels lil\_{i} by shifting a radiation source between the detectors,

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | li≔Δ​t𝔼,i​(zi).l\_{i}\coloneq\Delta t\_{\mathbb{E},i}(z\_{i}). |  | (4) |

Models that have been trained with this definition of the timing residuals correct the measured timestamps ta/bt\_{a/b} of detector aa and bb intrinsically by directly predicting the corrected time difference value Δ​tmcorr\Delta t\_{m}^{\text{corr}}. Following this approach, it becomes apparent that a certain number of source positions is needed to generate a sufficient label variability (or class cardinality for classifier problems), otherwise it will lead to poor generalization, as shown in [[46](#bib.bibx46)].
  
To remove the need for measuring multiple source positions along the zz-axis in order to have sufficient label variability, we propose to redefine the residuals in a way which significantly enlarges the label space even when using only one source position at the zz-axis. This can be achieved by using the correction distribution {ri}\{r\_{i}\}, where each correction rir\_{i} is defined as

|  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | li≔ri​(Δ​tm,i,zi)\displaystyle l\_{i}\coloneq r\_{i}(\Delta t\_{m,i},z\_{i}) | =Δ​tm,i−Δ​t𝔼​(zi)2\displaystyle=\frac{\Delta t\_{m,i}-\Delta t\_{\mathbb{E}}(z\_{i})}{2} |  | (5) |
|  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | =Δ​tm,i+2c⋅zi2,\displaystyle=\frac{\Delta t\_{m,i}+\frac{2}{c}\cdot z\_{i}}{2}, |  | (6) |

with Δ​tm,i\Delta t\_{m,i} denoting the ii-th measured time difference and Δ​t𝔼\Delta t\_{\mathbb{E}} the expected time difference defined in [Eq. 3](#S3.E3 "In 3.1 Defining Timing Residuals: Implicit & Explicit Corrections ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Rethinking Timing Residuals: Advancing PET Detectors with Explicit TOF Corrections"). From [Eq. 6](#S3.E6 "In 3.1 Defining Timing Residuals: Implicit & Explicit Corrections ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Rethinking Timing Residuals: Advancing PET Detectors with Explicit TOF Corrections") it becomes clear, that models trained on these labels are able to provide explicit corrections, namely that the corrected timestamps are given as

|  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | ta,icorr\displaystyle t\_{a,i}^{\text{corr}} | =ta,i−ri,\displaystyle=t\_{a,i}-r\_{i}, |  | (7) |
|  | tb,icorr\displaystyle t\_{b,i}^{\text{corr}} | =tb,i+ri.\displaystyle=t\_{b,i}+r\_{i}. |  |

Furthermore, the novel formulation of [Eq. 6](#S3.E6 "In 3.1 Defining Timing Residuals: Implicit & Explicit Corrections ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Rethinking Timing Residuals: Advancing PET Detectors with Explicit TOF Corrections") does not pose any restriction on the number of sources along the zz-axis. The experimenter can decide if it is wanted to include a spatial sampling along zz during the acquisition process or if a few or even one source position is sufficient regarding practicability. Mathematical considerations about the explicit correction formulation can be found in the appendix.
  
When comparing both label definitions (see [Fig. 1](#S3.F1 "In 3.1 Defining Timing Residuals: Implicit & Explicit Corrections ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Rethinking Timing Residuals: Advancing PET Detectors with Explicit TOF Corrections")), one can see that the label distribution is discrete for the implicit approach. Precisely, the number of unique labels (unique expected time differences) is equal to the number of used source positions, which might result a sparse coverage of the label domain. Contrary to this, the explicit correction approach generates a continuous spectrum of labels, which is independent from the number of measured source positions due to translational symmetry of the formulation resulting in a high coverade of the label domain. The various label approaches also lead to differences in terms of label balance or imbalance. In the implicit approach, it is very easy to generate a high balance of labels by using the same measurement time per source position. This promotes that all labels can be trained equally well. In comparison, the explicit approach leads to a label imbalance independent of the selected measurement time. This is because the labels are based, among other things, on the measured time difference spectrum, which is Gaussian-like distributed. As a result, corrections with a large magnitude are less often represented in the training data set than corrections with a smaller magnitude.

![Refer to caption](2502.07630v1/LabelScheme.png)

### 3.2 Evaluation Metrics

In recent works, we proposed to use a three-fold evaluation scheme [[45](#bib.bibx45), [46](#bib.bibx46), [51](#bib.bibx51)] for any kind of machine learning-based [TOF](#id3) correction or calibration. The scheme consists of a data scientific, physics-based and [PET](#id28)-based evaluation approach. Only models that pass the first two evaluation criteria are evaluated in a subsequent step regarding their application in [PET](#id28).

#### 3.2.1 Data Scientific Evaluation

The data scientific evaluation approach assesses the models based on typical metrics known from machine learning. In this work, we calculate the [MAE](#id17) for all distinct NN label classes {l1,…,lN}\{l\_{1},\dots,l\_{N}\} separately,

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | MAEk=1nk​∑i=1nk‖pk,i−lk,i‖1,\text{MAE}\_{k}=\frac{1}{n\_{k}}\sum\limits\_{i=1}^{n\_{k}}||p\_{k,i}-l\_{k,i}||\_{1}, |  | (8) |

with nkn\_{k} denoting the number of test sampled for the label class lkl\_{k}, and pk,ip\_{k,i} describing the prediction associated to the ii-th sample with ground truth lkl\_{k}, respectively. Although the [MAE](#id17) provides a numerical value, we use it rather as a qualitative metric to check if a model’s performance is stable for large portions of the test data. While for the first part of this work, the progression of the [MAE](#id17) is analyzed, the second part relies on the mean [MAE](#id17) and weighted mean [MAE](#id17) for visualization and comparability reasons. The mean [MAE](#id17) is defined by the sample mean over the NN label classes,

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | mean MAE=1N​∑k=1NMAEk.\text{mean MAE}=\frac{1}{N}\sum\limits\_{k=1}^{N}\text{MAE}\_{k}. |  | (9) |

The weighted mean [MAE](#id17) takes the label distribution into account by weighting the [MAE](#id17) with the number of occurrences nkn\_{k} of the label class lkl\_{k},

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | weighted mean MAE=(∑k=1Nnk)−1​(∑k=1NMAEk⋅nk)\text{weighted mean MAE}=\left(\sum\limits\_{k=1}^{N}n\_{k}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum\limits\_{k=1}^{N}\text{MAE}\_{k}\cdot n\_{k}\right) |  | (10) |

We perform the data scientific evaluation without posing any restrictions on the estimated energy of the input data.

#### 3.2.2 Physics-based Evaluation

The next evaluation part considers aspects from physics, which are the linearity and a so-called ε\varepsilon-value indicating the agreement with fundamental quantities like the speed of light. For this test, data stemming from different source positions along the zz-axis are fed into the model. The directly (implicit) or indirectly (explicit) predicted time differences are histogrammed for each source position, and the means of the corresponding prediction distributions are estimated by fitting [[52](#bib.bibx52)] over a 3​σ3\sigma-range a Gaussian function assuming Poissonian uncertainties on the time differences. The obtained means {μi}\{\mu\_{i}\} and the corresponding source positions {zi}\{z\_{i}\} are finally used to perform a linear regression using

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Δt𝔼≈μ(z;ε,b)=−2c⋅ε⋅z+b,\Delta t\_{\mathbb{E}}\approx\mu(z;\varepsilon,b)=-\frac{2}{c}\cdot\varepsilon\cdot z+b, |  | (11) |

where we assume that the mean μ\mu matches in good approximation the expected time difference Δ​t𝔼\Delta t\_{\mathbb{E}}. For the linear regression, the uncertainty σz\sigma\_{z} on the source position zz is dominated by the active source diameter and estimated by assuming a uniform distribution of activity within this diameter (σz=0.5 mm/12\sigma\_{z}=$0.5\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}$/\sqrt{12}). In a similar fashion, the uncertainty σμ\sigma\_{\mu} on the estimation of mean time difference μ\mu is given by assuming an uniform distribution within the histogram bin width (σμ=10 ps/12\sigma\_{\mu}=$10\text{\,}\mathrm{ps}$/\sqrt{12}).
  
[Equation 11](#S3.E11 "In 3.2.2 Physics-based Evaluation ‣ 3.2 Evaluation Metrics ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Rethinking Timing Residuals: Advancing PET Detectors with Explicit TOF Corrections") closely resembles the fundamental [Eq. 3](#S3.E3 "In 3.1 Defining Timing Residuals: Implicit & Explicit Corrections ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Rethinking Timing Residuals: Advancing PET Detectors with Explicit TOF Corrections"), with both describing a linear dependence between the expected time difference and the source position. We evaluate qualitatively if this assumption is fulfilled by the predictions of our models using reduced χ2\chi^{2}-values, which should be in the optimal case closely distributed around one. For the sake of easier comparability of many models, in the second part of this work, we compress the χ2\chi^{2}-distribution information into a single value sχ2s\_{\chi^{2}} measuring the spread of the χ2\chi^{2}-value from the optimal value of 1 in units of the standard deviation σχ2\sigma\_{\chi^{2}},

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | sχ2=|χ2¯−1|σχ2,s\_{\chi^{2}}=\frac{|\overline{\chi^{2}}-1|}{\sigma\_{\chi^{2}}}, |  | (12) |

with χ2¯\overline{\chi^{2}} denoting the mean.
  
As a quantitative measure, we use the number of σ\sigma-environments nϵ¯n\_{\overline{\epsilon}} of the ε\varepsilon-value minding the theory value of εtheo=1\varepsilon\_{\text{theo}}=1,

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | nε¯=|ε¯−εtheo|σε¯.n\_{\overline{\varepsilon}}=\frac{|\overline{\varepsilon}-\varepsilon\_{\text{theo}}|}{\sigma\_{\overline{\varepsilon}}}. |  | (13) |

In order to suppress any deteriorating effects coming from time walk, events are selected to be in an energy window from 430 keV to 590 keV430\text{\,}\mathrm{keV}590\text{\,}\mathrm{keV} for the physics-based evaluation.
A model passes the physics-based evaluation, if the χ2\chi^{2}-values are closely distributed around 1, or the spread sχ2s\_{\chi^{2}} in units of the standard deviation is smaller than 3. Furthermore, the models must demonstrate their agreement with physics by having ε¯\overline{\varepsilon}-values being compatible with the theory in a 3​σ3\sigma-range.

#### 3.2.3 PET-based Evaluation

If the data scientific and physics-based evaluations are positive, finally, the performance of the model is tested assessing the achievable [CTR](#id6). For this, data from the isocenter of the test dataset is fed into the models and the resulting predictions are filled into a histogram. The [FWHM](#id29) ([FWHM](#id29)) of this distribution is estimated by fitting a Gaussian function assuming Poissonian uncertainties on the time differences.

### 3.3 Model Architecture

We use [GBDT](#id38) as model architecture for the second part of the residual physics-based timing calibration. [GBDT](#id38) are a classical machine learning approach with the advantage that they can handle missing values and allow the implementation in a [FPGA](#id39) ([FPGA](#id39)) [[53](#bib.bibx53)]. This makes it especially suitable for the application in [PET](#id28) scanners minding edge-[AI](#id37) approaches [[54](#bib.bibx54), [55](#bib.bibx55)]. The model is based on an ensemble of binary decision trees, which uses boosting as a learning procedure. Each tree that is added to the ensemble during the training process attempts to minimize the errors of the predecessor model. In this study, we worked with the implementation of XGBoost [[56](#bib.bibx56)], which has proven it’s predictive power [[57](#bib.bibx57)] in our prior studies [[44](#bib.bibx44), [46](#bib.bibx46)].
  
Like in many other machine learning algorithms, several hyperparameters can be set before training a model. The maximum tree depth dd describes the maximum number of decisions inside a single tree. The learning rate l​rlr works as a smoothing parameter and controls the contribution of each new tree to the overall model. Another hyperparameter is the maximum number of trees within the ensemble, which is often used in combination with an early stopping criterion that stops the training procedure as soon as the validation loss has not improved for a certain amount of boosting rounds. The [MR](#id40) ([MR](#id40)) [[58](#bib.bibx58)] of a single decision tree is given to be

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | MR​(d)=(2d−1)⋅11 B+2d⋅6 B.\text{MR}(d)=\left(2^{d}-1\right)\cdot$11\text{\,}\mathrm{B}$+2^{d}\cdot$6\text{\,}\mathrm{B}$. |  | (14) |

### 3.4 Study Design

Several datasets were recorded in order to realize the different study designs for evaluating the implicit and explicit correction approach. In the following text, we will often refer to the coordinate system defined in [Fig. 1](#S3.F1 "In 3.1 Defining Timing Residuals: Implicit & Explicit Corrections ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Rethinking Timing Residuals: Advancing PET Detectors with Explicit TOF Corrections").

![Refer to caption](2502.07630v1/comp_merged.png)

#### 3.4.1 The Transaxial Performance Study

This study aims to compare both calibration approaches regarding their performance along the axis connecting both detector stacks. To acquire data for training, validation and testing 3535 positions along the zz-axis were utilized, while at each zz-position, a grid of 4×44\text{\times}4 in-plane positions are measured. The in-plane positions were chosen so that each crystal segmented was centrally irradiated. The step width (sw) between two subsequent planes was set to sw=10 mm10\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}, with the maximum zz-positions given to be zmin/max=±170 mmz\_{\text{min/max}}=\pm$170\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}$. The distribution of the source positions is shown in [Fig. 2](#S3.F2 "In 3.4 Study Design ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Rethinking Timing Residuals: Advancing PET Detectors with Explicit TOF Corrections"). For each source position a measurement time of 45 min45\text{\,}\mathrm{min} was used.
  
From the acquired dataset, 26 391 00926\,391\,009 and 8 797 0038\,797\,003 samples are used to form the training and validation dataset (66/33 split), respectively. The remaining data of the measurement run, namely 105 252 579105\,252\,579 samples, is used to build the test dataset.
  
In addition to the experiment, where each zz-position is present in the training data, we removed data along the zz-axis to artificially create new training and validation datasets with different step widths (sw=50 mm50\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} and sw=100 mm100\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}) between the grid planes. Although this results in a lower number of training samples, we follow this approach to analyze how implicit and explicit correction models perform at unknown zz-position. Therefore, new models are trained on these datasets but tested on the finely sampled and unseen test dataset comprising 3535 zz-positions.
  
For both kinds of training approaches (implicit and explicit), the same amount of training and validation samples are used, and a big parameter space of the maximum tree depth dd is sampled, ranging from very narrow to very deep trees (d∈{4,8,12,16,20}d\in\{4,8,12,16,20\}). The learning rate is always set to l​r=0.1lr=0.1, the maximum number of trees in an ensemble is set to 10001000, and we use 1010 early stopping rounds.
  
All models are evaluated regarding their [MAE](#id17) performance and linearity behavior.
In prior studies [[44](#bib.bibx44), [46](#bib.bibx46)], we demonstrated that this results in edge effects leading to non-Gaussian distribution (see [Fig. 3](#S3.F3 "In 3.4.1 The Transaxial Performance Study ‣ 3.4 Study Design ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Rethinking Timing Residuals: Advancing PET Detectors with Explicit TOF Corrections")). For this reason, the linearity analysis of the implicit correction models is performed for a large central region (−100 mm to 100 mm-100\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}100\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}), while the explicit correction approach allows an analysis over the complete zz-range (−170 mm to 170 mm-170\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}170\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}). Models that pass the data scientific and physics-based quality control are finally evaluated regarding their [CTR](#id6) improvement on input data from one zz-position (z=0 mmz=$0\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}$). We denote an implicit model that has been trained with data utilizing a step width of sw and a maximum tree depth of d as IM(sw,d){}\_{(\text{sw},\text{d})}, while the corresponding explicit model is called EM(sw,d){}\_{(\text{sw},\text{d})}.

#### 3.4.2 The In-Plane Distribution Study

This study aims to evaluate how the in-plane source distribution affects the performance of explicit correction models. Data is acquired at only one zz-position (z=0 mmz=$0\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}$), but with an extended source distribution of 33×3333\text{\times}33 source positions in the xx-yy-plane. At each source position a measurement time of 5 min5\text{\,}\mathrm{min} is to obtain the same number of training and validation samples as in the transaxial performance study. Six distinct new datasets for the training of explicit correction models are formed from the data, by removing sources in a regular pattern until only one source located at the iso-center remains. The in-plane distributions (IPD) are quadratic

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | IPD∈{(1×1),(3×3),(5×5),(9×9),(17×17),(33×33)},\text{IPD}\in\{($1\text{\times}1$),($3\text{\times}3$),($5\text{\times}5$),($9\text{\times}9$),($17\text{\times}17$),($33\text{\times}33$)\}, |  | (15) |

which also can be seen [Fig. 4](#S3.F4 "In 3.4.2 The In-Plane Distribution Study ‣ 3.4 Study Design ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Rethinking Timing Residuals: Advancing PET Detectors with Explicit TOF Corrections"). Identical to the transaxial performance study, five explicit correction models were trained for each dataset with the maximum tree depth dd being d∈{4,8,12,16,20}d\in\{4,8,12,16,20\}. The models are tested on the transaxial test dataset comprising 35 zz-positions. The same evaluation scheme like in the transaxial performance study is used, which incorporates data scientific, physics-based and PET-based metrics.

### 3.5 Data Pre-Processing

Hits corresponding to a single γ\gamma-interaction must be grouped into clusters by analyzing their initial timestamps. This clustering approach enables the aggregation of all relevant information linked to a specific γ\gamma-interaction. Following this step, clusters are further grouped into coincidences by applying a coincidence window, which considers the time differences between two clusters using their main [SiPM](#id35). Hits with energy values (in arbitrary units) below 2.52.5 or above 100100 were excluded from the clustering process. A cluster window of 8 ns8\text{\,}\mathrm{ns} was empirically chosen by analysis of the temporal distribution. Furthermore, a coincidence window of 50 ns50\text{\,}\mathrm{ns} was applied to significantly reduce the proportion of random events and minimize the risk of excluding true coincidences.
  
To each cluster, a γ\gamma-interaction position was assigned based on the coordinates of the SiPM with the highest energy value. The energy signals were saturation corrected using the 511 keV511\text{\,}\mathrm{keV} and 1275 keV1275\text{\,}\mathrm{keV} energy peak of the 22Na source. An energy value derived from the deposited energy on the main SiPM was assigned to each cluster.
  
Following our proposed residual physics-based calibration scheme, a conventional time skew calibration [[59](#bib.bibx59)] is conducted in order to remove the major skews of the first order.

### 3.6 Input Features

The input features for both models are derived from the detection information of coincident clusters and can be separated into a set with information from detector aa, and a set with information about detector bb. Since both sets are similar content-wise, we describe in a general way the information a sample is made up of.
  
The na/bn\_{a/b} first relative timestamp values and their [SiPM](#id35) ID represent the temporal information. Furthermore, we use the magnitude of the detected energy signal on these [SiPM](#id35), and the ID, energy signal, and coordinates of the main [SiPM](#id35) ([SiPM](#id35) detecting the highest number of photons) as additional information. In addition to this, the row and column energy sums are used. Furthermore, the number of triggered [SiPM](#id35), and the difference between the first and last timestamp of a cluster are fed to the model. Finally, the first ( [COG](#id5) ([COG](#id5))) and second moment of the light distribution are also included.
  
While these quantities represent the input for the explicit correction models, the implicit correction models use one additional feature: the measured time difference. Based on a prior statistical analysis on how many triggered [SiPM](#id35) are contained in a cluster, na/bn\_{a/b} is set to twelve and nine.

## 4 Results

### 4.1 The Transaxial Performance Study

#### 4.1.1 Data Scientific Evaluation

Prior to assessing the models with the three-fold evaluation scheme, we checked that the models were trained successfully by analyzing the training and validation curves. All models showed a smoothing training progression and were fully trained out.
  
The [MAE](#id17) progression of the explicit and implicit correction models for different training step width is displayed in [Fig. 5](#S3.F5 "In 3.6 Input Features ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Rethinking Timing Residuals: Advancing PET Detectors with Explicit TOF Corrections"), [Fig. 6](#S4.F6 "In 4.1.1 Data Scientific Evaluation ‣ 4.1 The Transaxial Performance Study ‣ 4 Results ‣ Rethinking Timing Residuals: Advancing PET Detectors with Explicit TOF Corrections"), and [Fig. 7](#S4.F7 "In 4.1.1 Data Scientific Evaluation ‣ 4.1 The Transaxial Performance Study ‣ 4 Results ‣ Rethinking Timing Residuals: Advancing PET Detectors with Explicit TOF Corrections"). For the models trained on data with a step width of 10 mm10\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}, both correction models show a smooth [MAE](#id17) progression without any outliers. While most of the [MAE](#id17) values of the implicit correction models are located in a region between 100 ps to 200 ps100\text{\,}\mathrm{ps}200\text{\,}\mathrm{ps}, the [MAE](#id17) rises towards the edges of the testing data. The labels of the training dataset for implicit correction models are, in good approximation, uniformly distributed. The [MAE](#id17) progression of the explicit correction models resembles a U-form, with the lowest [MAE](#id17) of sub-100 ps100\text{\,}\mathrm{ps} being achieved at labels of small magnitude. When moving to higher label magnitudes, and therefore, also to higher correction magnitudes, the [MAE](#id17) strongly rises. The explicit label distribution follows, in good approximation, a Gaussian shape with non-Gaussian tails.
  
For both correction approaches trained on 10 mm10\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} step width data, no significant performance differences for different maximum depths of the trees can be observed, except for the implicit correction model with maximum depth 2020 providing by far the worst [MAE](#id17) performance ([MAE](#id17) >> 400 ps400\text{\,}\mathrm{ps}).

The [MAE](#id17) performances of models trained on data with fewer source positions on the zz-axis compared to the test data are shown in [Fig. 6](#S4.F6 "In 4.1.1 Data Scientific Evaluation ‣ 4.1 The Transaxial Performance Study ‣ 4 Results ‣ Rethinking Timing Residuals: Advancing PET Detectors with Explicit TOF Corrections") and [Fig. 7](#S4.F7 "In 4.1.1 Data Scientific Evaluation ‣ 4.1 The Transaxial Performance Study ‣ 4 Results ‣ Rethinking Timing Residuals: Advancing PET Detectors with Explicit TOF Corrections"). While the spatial undersampling has no big impact on the performance of the explicit models, it does have a strong effect on implicit correction models. It can be observed that for the explicit approach the label distributions between spatially full-sampled and undersampled training data does not differ. Thus, the overall [MAE](#id17) progression of the models trained on 50 mm50\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} and 100 mm100\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} data is strongly similar to the finely sampled training data with 10 mm10\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} stepping. It can be stated that there is a tendency for models with small maximum tree depth to provide slightly better results for spatially undersampled data.

The implicit correction models are strongly affected by spatial undersampling, which can also be seen in the corresponding label distribution of the training data. Oscillation effects in the [MAE](#id17) progression can be seen, and become more dominant the bigger the spatial undersampling is, which was first observed and studied in [[46](#bib.bibx46)]. In addition, implicit correction models with low maximum tree depth show a more robust behavior against the spatial undersampling than models with higher complexity. This can especially be seen in [Fig. 6](#S4.F6 "In 4.1.1 Data Scientific Evaluation ‣ 4.1 The Transaxial Performance Study ‣ 4 Results ‣ Rethinking Timing Residuals: Advancing PET Detectors with Explicit TOF Corrections")a, where the zoom-in window clearly reveals oscillation effects for the implicit models starting from a maximum tree depth of 1212. Furthermore, the figure also suggests that the model with a maximum tree depth of 88 shows very minor oscillation behavior, being in a transition zone between non-oscillation (d=4d=4) and oscillation behavior (d=12d=12).
  
The observations show that all explicit correction models meet the data scientific quality check. All implicit correction models pass the quality check for a training step width of 10 mm10\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}, except for IM10,20. For a stepping of 50 mm50\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}, this reduces to the implicit correction models with a maximum tree depth of 44 and 88, while for a step width of 100 mm100\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} only the model with maximum tree depth 44 passes the evaluation, although minor oscillation tendencies are visible.

#### 4.1.2 Physics-based Evaluation

The estimated χ2\chi^{2}-analysis and ε\varepsilon-values are depicted in [Fig. 8](#S4.F8 "In 4.1.1 Data Scientific Evaluation ‣ 4.1 The Transaxial Performance Study ‣ 4 Results ‣ Rethinking Timing Residuals: Advancing PET Detectors with Explicit TOF Corrections"). Models that show a high compatibility with our physical expectations can be identified by χ2\chi^{2}/ndf-values near to one, and an ε\varepsilon-value that matches within 3​σ3\sigma the theoretical value of εtheo=1\varepsilon\_{\text{theo}}=1. The explicit correction models show good agreement with linearity and high compatibility with the theoretical ε\varepsilon-value of εtheo=1\varepsilon\_{\text{theo}}=1 across all tested step widths and tree depths. Contrary to this, there is the trend that implicit correction models lose their linearity property with increasing step width. While for the smallest step width of 10 mm10\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}, IM10,12 and IM10,16 meet the physics-based quality criteria, it remains only IM50,8 and IM50,12 for a training step width of 50 mm50\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} and for the highest step width no implicit model passes the physics-based quality check.

args.summary:
This paper presents a novel machine learning-based timing calibration approach for PET (Positron Emission Tomography) detectors that improves time-of-flight (TOF) performance. The authors introduce a new definition of timing residuals that enables "explicit correction models" (directly predicting correction values) rather than the previous "implicit correction models" (directly predicting expected time differences).

Key aspects:
- The method uses a residual physics-based calibration approach combining analytical calibration (for first-order skews) with machine learning (for higher-order skews).
- The explicit correction formulation redefines timing residuals as ri = (Δtm,i - ΔtE(zi))/2, allowing models to predict correction values directly.
- This approach eliminates the need for multiple source positions along the z-axis, dramatically simplifying data acquisition.
- Experiments used two detector stacks with 4×4 LYSO:Ce,Ca crystals coupled to Broadcom NUV-MT SiPMs and digitized with TOFPET2 ASIC.
- The explicit correction approach improved CTR from 371±6 ps to 281±5 ps for coincidences from 430 keV to 590 keV.
- GBDT (Gradient Boosted Decision Trees) with XGBoost implementation was used as the model architecture.
- The new approach removes the strong dependence on training step width, suppresses biased prediction distributions, and preserves linearity.
- Models can be exponentially reduced in size, making them suitable for high-throughput PET scanner applications.
- Two studies were conducted: a transaxial performance study (comparing implicit vs explicit approaches) and an in-plane distribution study (evaluating how source distribution affects explicit correction models).

The explicit correction approach demonstrated superior performance: all models passed physics-based quality checks regardless of training step width, while implicit models failed at larger step widths. The explicit approach also showed compatibility with calibration using only a single source position at the isocenter.

Otarid𝑎 𝑎EP-DT-TP, CERN, Esplanade des Particules, Meyrin, Switzerland 𝑏Department of Detector Development and Data Processing, Institute of Physics of the Czech Academy of Sciences, Na Slovance, Prague, Czech Republic 𝑐School of Physics and Astronomy, University of Glasgow, Glasgow, United Kingdom 𝑑Physics Department, BNL, Upton, NY, United States of America 𝑒Radiation Detectors Group, IMB-CNM-CSIC, Carrer dels Til·lers, Barcelona, Spain E-mail: peter.svihra@cern.ch Abstract: This contribution reports on characterisation results of a large-area (2 cm2) small pitch (55 µm) inverse Low-Gain Avalanche Detector (iLGAD), bonded to a Timepix3 readout chip. The ilGAD sensors were produced by Micron Semiconductor Ltd with the goal to obtain good gain uniformity and maximise the fill-factor – an issue present with standard small-pitch LGAD designs.
We have conducted detailed performance evaluations using both X-ray calibrations and beam tests.
An X-ray fluorescence setup has been used to obtain energy calibration and to identify the optimal operating settings of the new devices, whereas the extensive beam tests allowed for a detailed evaluation of the detector performance. The beam-tests were performed at the CERN SPS North Area H6 beamline, using a 120 GeV/c pion beam. The reference tracking and time-stamping is achieved by a Timepix3-based beam telescope setup.
The results show a gain of around 5 with very good uniformity, measured across the whole gain area, as well as a hit time resolution down to 1.3 ns without correcting for the time-walk effects.
Furthermore, it is shown that the gain opens the possibility of a good X-ray energy resolution down to 4.5 keV.

The gain is achieved by implanting high concentrations of p- and n- type dopants in the silicon bulk, resulting in strong electric fields O(1 × 1015 V cm−1) within the sensor that triggers impact ionisation of free charge carriers [2]. Such an approach enables the sensors to be thin (about 50 µm), lowering the material budget and at the same time decreasing the distance required for the charge collection thus improving the timing for minimum ionising particles (MIPs) down to below 50 ps [3]. The High-Luminosity upgrades of the ATLAS and CMS experiments at CERN will contain LGAD-based MIP timing layers with O(1 mm2) pixel sizes for improving the separation of tracks in time [4, 5] but charge multiplication can enable the detection of low-energy X-rays below the readout threshold [6].
For many high-energy physics applications the most commonly used type of silicon sensor bulk is p-type which is targets electron collection in the readout pixels. These sensors are often produced with multiplication layers directly underneath each pixel, with the added requirement of proper termination of the strong electric fields using either Junction Termination (JTE), shown in fig. 1a, or trenches filled with oxide. A downside of this approach is seen when decreasing the pixel pitch, where the no-gain pixel area starts to affect the signal formation. This effect can be approximated by a geometrical fill factor 𝐹described as 𝐹= 𝐴gain 𝐴total , (1.1) – 1 – (a) LGAD – multiplication in each pixel, need of field separation using JTE.
(b) iLGAD – flat multiplication layer at the back-side.
Figure 1: Visual comparison of the standard and inverse LGAD design.
Figure 2: Comparison of geometrical fill factor 𝐹for different widths of junction terminations (JTE). The red dotted line indicates the 55 µm pixel pitch matching the Timepix3 readout.
where 𝐴represents gain and total areas covered by a pixel. The dependency on the size of the no-gain region caused by the JTE is known [7], demonstrated in fig. 2. There are different approaches that aim to mitigate this effect - this work focuses on the characterisation of iLGAD sensors [8].
1.1 Sensor design The sensor has been produced by Micron Semiconductor Ltd as part of R&D efforts by Universities of Manchester, Glasgow and Edinburgh. Compared to the standard LGAD design, an iLGAD sensor uses the same p-type bulk, but the multiplication layer is at the backside (schematic shown in fig. 1b). This design results in a uniform multiplication across the full sensor at the cost of double-sided processing, hole collection at the pixels and need for full depletion.
The produced sensors are 300 µm thick with 256x256 pixels with 55 µm pitch and have been bump-bonded to Timepix3 readout chips. In order to simplify the gain and no-gain performance evaluation, an outer rim 4 pixels wide has been included without multiplication layer, followed by a pixel-wide rim containing JTE and finally an area of 246x246 pixels with multiplication.
– 2 – 1.2 Timepix3 readout chip The Timepix3 versatile readout chip [9] has a pixel matrix of 256x256 pixels with 55 µm pitch.
The zero-suppressed data-driven readout provides access to a Time over Threshold (ToT) and Time of Arrival (ToA) information. While ToT provides a measurement of the deposited charge, ToA measures the time of the signal crossing the threshold with a binning of 1.5625 ns – making the chip suitable for evaluating the charge collection of the new sensor designs and for performing an initial characterisation of the timing performance.
The chip is read out using the SPIDR DAQ system [10]. Apart from the raw Timepix3 data, the readout also provides a Time-to-digital converter (TDC) input with binning of 260 ps.
2 Laboratory characterisation As part of evaluating the performance of the device, a set of laboratory tests has been performed.
The testing presented here was done after bump-bonding the sensor to an ASIC. Both parts were confirmed to be of good quality based on wafer-level examinations. Results from a single iLGAD sensor bonded to a Timepix3 chip (ID W0068_I11) are presented.
The tests included a current vs voltage scan to establish the operating points of the device, approximating depletion voltage of the gain layer 𝑉gain = 25 V and about 𝑉dep = 150 V for the full sensor. The threshold response of the pixels in the Timepix3 chip has been then equalised based on the electronic noise, resulting in 114 masked pixels (0.2 %) due to increased noise. The average noise baseline was estimated to (1088.5 ± 2.4) DAC units with an average electronic noise of (11.5 ± 1.4) DAC units. The default operational threshold has been set to noise-free operation at 1000 DAC and was used for all main measurements. Furthermore the device has been calibrated using the on-chip available test-pulse injection and finally an energy calibration using X-rays.
2.1 Test-pulse energy calibration The Timepix3 chip also has the capability of injecting analogue and digital pulses to each pixel.
Using this approach, the signal amplification, shaping and digitisation can be tested without the need of radioactive sources, resulting in measurements of ToT and ToA at arbitrary input energies.
The injected energy 𝐸′ = 𝐶𝑉is obtained by charging the built-in capacitor 𝐶≈3.2 fF to different voltages 𝑉. The value of the test-pulse capacitor is constrained by design, but cannot be measured directly. An uncertainty of ±20 % is assumed caused by variations in the semiconductor manufacturing processes. By discharging the capacitor and measuring the ToT response in every pixel, a dependency in the form 𝑇𝑜𝑇= 𝐴′𝐸′ + 𝑏′ − 𝑐′ 𝐸′ −𝑡′ (2.1) is observed, where 𝐴′ and 𝑏′ correspond to the gain and offset of the linear part and 𝑐′ and 𝑡′ describe the curvature and asymptote of the non-linear part observed at small amplitudes.
2.2 X-ray energy calibration Following the initial test-pulse energy calibration, X-rays of known energy are used for two purposes: providing conversion from threshold DAC units to energy as well as obtaining the per-pixel ToT – 3 – Figure 3: Example of the detector single-pixel XRF response for pixels without and with gain.
Gain of around 5 as well as improved low-energy resolution is clearly seen.

(b) Pixel energy calibration.
Figure 4: Charge calibration results done at 200 V.

Materials used for the targets were titanium (4.51 keV), iron (6.40 keV), copper (8.05 keV), molybdenum (17.48 keV), silver (22.16 keV) and tin (25.27 keV). The pointing resolution at the centre of the telescope in the device under test (DUT) location is about 1.5 µm and the track timing resolution is about 300 ps. Reconstruction and analysis of the data was performed using the Corryvreckan framework [12].

Firstly, we have evaluated the signal response and in-pixel efficiency of signal detection at the operational point of 300 V and 983 e−, as shown in fig. 5 and fig. 6, respectively. Excellent multiplication and detection performance is visible in both plots, overall efficiency is above 99.94 %.
The outer rim in cluster charge matches with the region with pixels without multiplication layer.

Comparison plots of pixels without and with multiplication are in figs. 7 to 9. An impact of the gain can be seen, increasing the efficiency, charge and cluster size. This paper presents the characterisation results of a 55 µm pitch inverse Low-Gain Avalanche Detector (iLGAD) bonded to a Timepix3 readout chip, produced by Micron Semiconductor Ltd. The sensor is 300 µm thick with 256x256 pixels and a 2 cm² area. Unlike standard LGADs, the iLGAD has a uniform multiplication layer at the backside, improving fill-factor and gain uniformity.

Key results from laboratory and beam-test evaluations:

- **Gain**: Measured gain of approximately 4.86 with very good uniformity across the gain region.
- **Timing**: Hit time resolution down to 1.3 ns (without time-walk correction).
- **X-ray energy resolution**: Down to 4.5 keV.
- **Efficiency**: Overall tracking efficiency above 99.94% at 300 V bias and 1 ke⁻ threshold.
- **Beam tests**: Conducted at CERN SPS H6 beamline with 120 GeV/c pions, using a Timepix3-based telescope for tracking (~1.5 µm pointing resolution, ~300 ps timing resolution).
- **Charge screening**: Observed at near-perpendicular angles, consistent with standard LGAD behaviour.
- **Optimal bias voltage**: Around 200 V for peak gain, with full depletion at ~150 V.

The iLGAD design shows excellent multiplication uniformity and improved detection of low-energy X-rays (e.g., 4.86 keV titanium peak detectable only with gain). The study was performed as part of CERN EP R&D, with contributions from University of Manchester, Glasgow, and Edinburgh.
