This webpage is an open-access scientific article published in *Particles* (MDPI, 2025) titled "Development and Explainability of Models for Machine-Learning-Based Reconstruction of Signals in Particle Detectors" by Kalina Dimitrova, Venelin Kozhuharov, and Peicho Petkov from Sofia University "St. Kliment Ohridski," Bulgaria. The article presents convolutional neural networks with modified autoencoder (MAC) architectures for reconstructing pulse arrival times and amplitudes in scintillating crystal calorimeters used in high-energy physics experiments. The models are trained on simulated waveforms (1024 values, 1 ns bins) matching CAEN V17XX digitizer output, with up to five pulses per event. Key methodological points include:

- **Architecture**: The MAC uses an encoder with three convolutional layers (128, 64, 32 filters with kernel sizes 18, 12, 6) and a decoder with three mirrored transposed convolution layers, with dropout layers (rate 0.2) for regularization. The output preserves input dimensions but reconstructs only pulse arrival time positions with amplitude values.
- **xAI Application**: Occlusion Sensitivity (a mask-based explainable AI method) was applied to understand which waveform regions are most important for signal recognition. Results show that the signal rise (front) and the region around the signal maximum are both critical for pulse identification. A modified version (revealing values one by one) revealed two distinct loss patterns depending on whether the predicted arrival time falls before or after the rounded label position.
- **Key Finding**: The model is sensitive to sub-bin timing — it can distinguish arrival times with higher precision than the 1 ns time bin width. This is demonstrated by the correlation between true arrival time offset and predicted offset.
- **UMAC Development**: A new upsampling version (UMAC) was developed with 4096-length labels (0.25 ns precision), achieved by adding two upsampling layers (factor of 2) in the decoder. The UMAC significantly improves time resolution: the MAC showed a mean difference of 0.7 ns between true and predicted arrival time, while the UMAC reduced this to −0.003 ns with a narrower distribution. Both time and amplitude reconstruction accuracy improved.
- **Performance Metrics**: The article compares MAC and UMAC using MAE and MSE for both arrival time and amplitude, with clear improvements from the upsampling approach.
- **Real Data Application**: The MAC model was tested on real data from a fixed-target experiment's electromagnetic calorimeter, showing a higher number of recognized low-energy events and better time resolution compared to conventional peak-finding methods, though requiring additional calibration.

The work demonstrates that explainable AI techniques can guide architectural improvements (e.g., the UMAC development) and that ML-based signal reconstruction offers superior time resolution in particle detectors.

# Learning by machines, for machines: Artificial Intelligence in the world's largest particle detector

5 June 2024 | By

In today’s age, you can't do much without interfacing with artificial intelligence and [machine learning](https://atlas.cern/tags/machine-learning) (AI/ML). This technology lets you unlock your phone via face recognition, helps curate your social media feed and powers internet search. In the future, it promises to automate tasks as mundane as driving a car and as cerebral as scientific outreach. Its clear transformative capability has captured our collective attention, sparking dialogue across scientific communities, governments and the general public, alike. But long before ChatGPT or DALL-E, the basic statistical principles that underpin the world's most sophisticated ML tools were hard at work in the field of high-energy collider physics. Today, they are enabling unprecedented progress in understanding the nature of our fundamental universe.

High-energy physics (HEP) can trace its relationship with ML back many decades, with the earliest neural networks coming into play in the 1990s. ML algorithms improved Higgs-boson searches at CERN’s LEP collider, powered CP-violation measurements at the B factories at KEK and SLAC, and enabled the observation of single top-quark production at Fermilab's Tevatron collider. They were also key for the discovery and study of the Higgs boson as well as the observation of the ultra rare two-muon decay of the Bs meson at the LHC.

But it wasn't until the 2010s that modern computational power and methodological innovation enabled deep learning, and let AI-based research methods like ML really shine. In many ways, the relationship between particle physics and ML is a natural and symbiotic one. High energy particle collisions offer a means to study fundamental interactions under conditions similar to the early universe, allowing a window into potential particles or processes that are “frozen out” in the current universe. In this way, finding optimal and intelligent ways to sift through the trove of data from experiments at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is crucial, as it enables researchers to precisely characterise the Standard Model (SM) and understand mysteries like dark matter and matter-antimatter asymmetry that motivate new physics beyond the Standard Model (BSM).

Collider-based experiments led to some of the original “big data” problems. Experiments like ATLAS at the LHC operate with staggering data rates, producing over 60 terabytes per second, yet only some of these proton collision events may contain processes of interest. What's more, these experiments offer a dataset that is unique in its complexity and statistical power, in which new ML architectures or problems such as systematic biases or hardware optimization can be studied.

### High-energy physics can trace its relationship with machine learning back many decades, with the earliest neural networks coming into play in the 1990s.

The task of operating the ATLAS experiment and extracting results from its vast datasets is a computational labyrinth. From its inception in the 1990s, the ATLAS experiment was designed to process every proton collision digitally. Within seconds of a collision the data from millions of sensors have been filtered through a web of custom electronics and analysed on a computing farm with tens of thousands of CPUs. Collisions of interest are recorded and reanalysed countless times by physicists looking to better understand the nature of the universe. In all cases the goal of this analysis is to discover precisely what happened at the interaction point, where two protons travelling at 99.999999% the speed of light collide in the accelerator, producing a plethora of new particles.

Unfortunately, the physics at the interaction point can be elusive. Many of the most interesting SM or BSM particles produced in the proton collision will decay in less than one trillionth of one trillionth of a second! Physicists can only pick up on hints of SM or BSM physics by looking for the decay products of the most interesting particles, which may themselves decay before reaching any sensors in ATLAS. From a single collision the ATLAS experiment may record thousands of individual particles, and to make matters worse, it typically has to deal with dozens of simultaneous collisions. To understand what happened at the interaction point, physicists must carefully reconstruct, identify and measure each of these particles. These are then used to reconstruct the entire collision event, which are scoured for processes of interest that may lead to a better understanding of known particles, or shed light on the existence of never-before-observed ones.

ML methods are designed to harness large amounts of data in order to infer new information, making them naturally suited to various data processing tasks in ATLAS, from the moment a particle hits the detector all the way to the final published results. The examples that follow give a representative idea of how extensively this technology has pervaded the experiment, but merely scratch the surface of the full picture and potential of ML in HEP.

### Machine learning at work in ATLAS

During regular operation of the ATLAS experiment, the first challenge is what to do with the data that is created. With multiple subsystems, an LHC collision frequency of 40 million per second and millions of individual channels of data to read out, the ATLAS experiment produces a data rate far greater than can possibly be written to disk. A complex *trigger system* implements algorithms that rapidly evaluate incoming data events to determine if they are interesting enough to keep, rejecting the overwhelming majority of events produced.

![Physics,ATLAS](//cds.cern.ch/images/ATLAS-PHOTO-2024-020-1/file?size=large)

This task requires sophisticated inference that can be done very quickly, introducing the use of “fast ML” to accelerate ML algorithms traditionally run in software for use in hardware such as field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). This process allows for greater intelligence closer to the source of the data, leading to more accurate reconstruction and better trigger decisions. For example, the energy and timing of signals in the ATLAS electromagnetic calorimeter subsystem can now be estimated by convolutional and recurrent ML architectures in real time of LHC operation, [outperforming existing signal filters](https://cds.cern.ch/record/2775033/) (Figure 1). This capability of ML to perform fast and accurate regression of key physical quantities can also be used for more accurate [calibrations of detector signals](http://cds.cern.ch/record/2866591).

AI/ML also comes into play in the *reconstruction* algorithms that turn detector signals into physics objects. Well before ATLAS recorded its first data, physicists had developed hundreds of algorithms to reconstruct specific particle types based on the signatures they leave in the different ATLAS sub-detectors. Some particles, like b-hadrons, will decay before reaching any of the ATLAS sub-detectors, and are discerned by triangulating the trajectories of the decay products back to a displaced vertex that is separated from the proton collision point by just a few millimetres. ML has proved essential in identifying this distinctive signature. The [latest tools to identify b-hadrons](https://cds.cern.ch/record/2860610) in the detector make use of cutting-edge architectures, such as *transformers* with attention mechanisms that carefully study simulated b-hadron decays and learn to reject vertices from regular light quark processes at the best rate achieved in ATLAS to date. Transformers have [also been used](https://atlas.web.cern.ch/Atlas/GROUPS/PHYSICS/PUBNOTES/ATL-PHYS-PUB-2023-021/) to learn the complex signature of a particle decaying to two b-hadrons when the decay is collimated and the b-hadron tracks are overlapping.

### Machine-learning methods are designed to harness large amounts of data in order to infer new information, making them naturally suited to various data processing tasks in ATLAS.

Once the data have been recorded and the events are reconstructed, it's time to study the underlying physics mechanism that produced the event. ATLAS physics analyses are predicated on effective solutions to classic signal-to-noise problems. Many processes of interest are incredibly rare and can be challenging to distinguish among the billions of ordinary proton collisions. Here is where ML can shine: its broad ability to exploit subtle features within a complex and high-statistics dataset make it a primary workhorse for isolating interesting signal processes.

![Physics,ATLAS](//cds.cern.ch/images/ATLAS-PHOTO-2024-020-3/file?size=large)

No particle has held more interest in the past decade than the Higgs boson, discovered in 2012 by the ATLAS and CMS experiments and met with great fanfare and excitement. Understanding and characterising the Higgs boson and the underlying mechanism of mass generation remains an essential goal of high-energy physics today, and ML is in use throughout Higgs-boson analyses. The [2018 observation](https://atlas.cern/updates/briefing/higgs-observed-decaying-b-quarks) of the Higgs boson in its most common, but trickiest, decay channel, H→bb, made use of a classic *boosted decision tree (BDT)* architecture to classify the Higgs-boson signal from the overwhelming background of multijet processes to make observation possible (Figure 2).

ML has also enabled unprecedented study of the top quark, the heaviest known particle and one with a particularly interesting connection to the Higgs boson. In 2023, researchers adapted a *graph neural network* to model collisions in a geometrical way using the particles produced during the collision and their relationship to one another in the detector space. Training this model to separate the rare four-top-quark-production process from SM backgrounds allowed ATLAS to make its first statistically confident [observation](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1140/epjc/s10052-023-11573-0) of such events, along with a measurement of its production rate and constraints on key possible extensions of the SM.

While these examples of ML to isolate a specific signal demonstrate the depth of its effectiveness, another implementation of ML can reveal its breadth. A growing interest in the LHC community in *anomaly detection* has led to the proliferation of ML methods that can isolate unusual phenomena from a well-known background model. Such an approach lowers the need to rely on a specific signal model, making these search techniques very broad and sensitive to new physics that may have been missed by previous analysis approaches. In recent years, ATLAS published its first use cases of anomaly detection, implemented via ML algorithms without complete labelling information of training inputs, all in the [context](https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.125.131801) [of searches](https://journals.aps.org/prd/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevD.108.052009) [for new heavy particles](https://atlas.cern/Updates/Briefing/Anomaly-Detection) decaying to two-object final states (Figure 3). These analyses leveraged the power of data-driven ML training through a mix of conventional and novel architectures to perform model-independent searches for new particles with a variety of mass and decay hypotheses, providing an invaluable new approach for extracting the most from the ATLAS dataset.

![Physics,ATLAS](//cds.cern.ch/images/ATLAS-PHOTO-2024-020-2/file?size=large)

### Subtleties and challenges

Despite these successes, there's no such thing as a flawless solution. While ML can offer incredible benefits to ATLAS throughout all stages of the analysis chain, its usage has to be closely coupled with continuous monitoring. Models can inherit unintended biases in the course of training, leading it to make spurious or, even worse, incorrect inferences. The risk of such biases is so significant that it has spawned a broader subfield of AI alignment and safety, and must be carefully considered when applying ML tools to produce physics results.

Luckily there are many ways ATLAS physicists can tackle this challenge. One potential source of such bias emerges from the use of simulated collision events to develop ML tools. While physicists have invested decades into generating accurate and fast simulations, there are still some known ways in which their predictive capabilities can break down. Furthermore, the development of a tool using a particular selection of data with limited statistical power can often require the intentional decorrelation of the model's learned conclusions from certain sensitive properties that should not be considered. To address these issues, physicists make use of dedicated de-biasing or decorrelation techniques from the HEP-ML research community, such as moment decomposition or distance correlation. The limitations of statistical power in simulation samples used for training can also be mitigated through the use of fast simulation methods, which use ML to circumvent the costly full Monte Carlo simulation chain by making [fast estimations](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s41781-023-00106-9) of key collision and detector properties.

### While machine learning can offer incredible benefits to ATLAS throughout all stages of the analysis chain, its usage has to be closely coupled with continuous monitoring.

On top of it all, developing, training and running these advanced algorithms takes a staggering amount of power. To run and adequately cool the mainframes and supercomputers of the CERN Data Centre takes about [37 gigawatt-hours per year](https://home.cern/news/news/cern/environmental-awareness-challenges-cerns-it-infrastructure), about 3% of [CERN's total annual electrical consumption](https://www.lhc-closer.es/taking_a_closer_look_at_lhc/0.energy_consumption) when the LHC operates. While this computing covers all CERN operations, including many applications beyond AI/ML development, producing this quantity of electricity has a significant carbon footprint. The growing role of AI/ML, combined with the uptake of larger and larger models, means that [associated power consumption](https://www.newyorker.com/news/daily-comment/the-obscene-energy-demands-of-ai) will likely increase as well; ​​for context, Open AI’s ChatGPT uses half a gigawatt-hour daily! Greener approaches are being investigated to continue these operations at CERN in an increasingly climate-focused society. Through dedicated sustainability initiatives, CERN is [working with experts](https://home.cern/tags/sustainability) across areas of research to find environmentally friendly data management solutions and greener ways to run collider experiments.

### A new AI era of scientific research

With this striking history of success, and expectations for computational power to continue its tremendous rise, the future of ML in high-energy physics is bright. ATLAS researchers are collaborative by nature, and much of the work described here wouldn't be possible without close ties to the computer science and AI/ML research communities. Maintaining and expanding these relationships means that physics experimentation will continue to benefit from the latest and greatest in ML algorithms and software capabilities. A recent push across CERN to provide more "[open data](https://opendata.cern.ch/)" recorded by the experiments will further engage researchers outside of HEP who can benefit from the uniquely complex and high-statistics LHC datasets to design and optimise their tools.

Beyond the horizons of ATLAS, AI/ML techniques are similarly impacting the broader landscape in physics. Within theoretical physics, ML offers the promise of dramatically reducing computation cost/time of challenging calculations and simulations, among other things. Further, ML is being studied to perform comprehensive optimizations of future detector designs, which comes at an exciting time for the strategic planning of next-generation colliders.

The long-term future of AI will have an impact on our world that is exciting, transformative and yet unimaginable – and things are no different for particle physics. Through continued collaboration and thoughtful planning for the potential ethical and environmental consequences, researchers can properly harness AI/ML to usher in a new era of precision understanding (and potentially groundbreaking discoveries) in particle physics.

*The author would like to thank Katarina Anthony, Dan Guest, Andreas Hoecker, Walter Hopkins, Michael Kagan, Zach Marshall, Benjamin Nachman, and Manuella Vincter for their input and feedback.*

### About the Author

**Julia Gonski** is a Panofsky Fellow (associate staff scientist) working on the energy frontier at SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. Her research focuses on novel approaches to searching for beyond the Standard Model physics with the ATLAS experiment, particularly incorporating machine learning (ML) and anomaly detection. She also works on fast ML for electronics in advanced trigger and readout systems, and planning for next-generation global collider facilities.

args.summary:
This article from the ATLAS Experiment at CERN explores the extensive use of artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) in high-energy particle physics, particularly within the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The relationship between high-energy physics and ML dates back decades, with neural networks first used in the 1990s for Higgs-boson searches and other measurements. Modern deep learning has become essential for handling the LHC's enormous data rates—ATLAS produces over 60 terabytes per second from 40 million collisions per second. ML is used throughout the data processing chain:

1. **Trigger System**: "Fast ML" implemented on FPGAs enables real-time data filtering, with convolutional and recurrent architectures outperforming traditional signal filters for calorimeter signals.

2. **Reconstruction**: ML algorithms identify particles like b-hadrons using transformer architectures with attention mechanisms. Graph neural networks have been used to reconstruct complex collision events.

3. **Physics Analysis**: Boosted decision trees (BDTs) enabled the 2018 observation of the Higgs boson decaying to b-quarks. In 2023, graph neural networks helped achieve the first statistically confident observation of four-top-quark production. Anomaly detection methods using ML are being deployed for model-independent searches for new physics.

The article also addresses challenges: ML models can inherit biases from simulated training data, requiring dedicated de-biasing techniques. The computational power required is significant—CERN's data center consumes about 37 gigawatt-hours per year (approximately 3% of CERN's total consumption). The article concludes that continued collaboration between physics and computer science communities, along with open data initiatives, will drive future advances in particle physics research.

SUMMARY:

This paper, published in *Computer Science* on December 10, 2023, investigates using deep neural networks to improve the precision of fast-sampled particle timing detectors, specifically the CMS-TOTEM Precision Proton Spectrometer (PPS) diamond timing detectors. The authors evaluated various neural network architectures using data acquired at the DESY-II synchrotron test beam facility, where a precise MCP detector was installed alongside PPS diamond detectors. A UNet-based model outperformed classical convolutional networks and multilayer perceptrons in improving timing precision. The paper has 2 citations and 32 references, and is associated with authors including Mateusz Kocot, K. Misan, Valentina Avati, Edoardo Bossini, Leszek Grzanka, and Nicola Minafra. DOI: 10.7494/csci.2024.25.1.5784.

--- SOURCE 2: A Time-Walk and Timing-Shift Correction Method for Dual-Ended Readout TOF-DOI PET Detectors ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12493018

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents a combined time-walk and timing-shift correction method for dual-ended readout time-of-flight (TOF) PET detectors with depth-of-interaction (DOI) capability. The research was conducted by Haibo Wang, Jiahao Xie, Jinyi Qi (Fellow, IEEE), Simon R. Cherry (Fellow, IEEE), and Junwei Du (Senior Member, IEEE) from the Department of Biomedical Engineering, University of California at Davis, and published in IEEE Transactions on Radiation and Plasma Medical Sciences (2024).

**Background:** TOF-PET detectors using leading-edge discriminators (LED) suffer from time-walk (due to signal amplitude variations) and timing-shift (due to DOI effects from thick crystals and electronics channel offsets). Dual-ended readout detectors, which use SiPMs at both ends of crystals, can provide DOI information but are particularly susceptible to these effects.

**Methods:** Two dual-ended readout detectors were constructed using Hamamatsu S14161-3050-08 SiPM arrays coupled to 8×8 arrays of 3.1×3.1×20 mm³ LYSO crystals (3.2 mm pitch). The PETsys TOFPET2 readout system was used for data acquisition. Events were categorized into DOI layers based on the ratio of energies detected by the two SiPM arrays. The correction method uses the relationship between threshold crossing time differences and the natural logarithm of energy ratios (e.g., t₂-t₃ vs. ln(E₂/E₃)) to derive correction parameters (c for time-walk, b for timing-shift) for each DOI layer pair.

**Key Results:**
- CTR improved from 260.7 ± 1.0 ps to 229.4 ± 1.0 ps (an improvement of ~31 ps) using a 400–650 keV energy window.
- Correcting time-walk alone improved CTR by 12.6 ps; DOI correction added ~20 ps further improvement.
- The optimal number of DOI layers was determined to be 4; beyond 4 layers, improvement plateaued (228.8 ps at 8 layers).
- The detector had a DOI resolution of 2.6 mm.
- The method also corrects timing offsets from readout electronics, improving localization accuracy along the LOR.

**Conclusion:** The proposed method effectively corrects both time-walk and timing-shift in dual-ended readout PET detectors, enhancing timing resolution and image quality. The work was supported by NIH grants R01 EB028806 and R01 EB031961.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The coincidence time resolution of the two detectors improved from 260.7 ± 1.0 ps to 229.4 ± 1.0 ps when a 400–650 keV energy window was used to select events., The CTR improved from 248.1 ± 1.0 ps to 229.4 ± 1.0 ps as the number of DOI layers increased from 1 to 4, whereas the CTR was 228.8 ps when 8 DOI layers were used., Correcting time-walk only enhanced the timing resolution by 12.6 ps, and correcting the DOI of annihilation photons further improved the timing resolution by ~20 ps., After applying time-walk and timing-shift corrections, the average CTR value across the 4 selected crystal pairs improved to 229.4 ± 1.0 ps from 260.7 ± 1.0 ps., The detector had a DOI resolution of 2.6 mm.
</key_excerpts>



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


--- SOURCE 3: Using deep neural networks to improve the precision of fast ... ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.05883

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This research paper (accepted for publication in Computer Science journal) investigates using deep neural networks to improve the timing precision of particle detectors, specifically for the CMS-PPS (Precision Proton Spectrometer) subsystem at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. The key problem addressed is the "time walk effect" — statistical fluctuations in charge deposited by particles that cause errors in arrival time measurements. The standard method, the Constant Fraction Discriminator (CFD) algorithm, is simple and effective but does not utilize all voltage samples in a time series.

**Methodology:** The researchers used data from the DESY-II synchrotron test beam facility (2020), where both PPS diamond timing detectors and a high-precision MCP-PMT (Microchannel Plate Photomultiplier Tube) detector were installed. The MCP served as the ground-truth reference (precision ~10 ps, compared to diamond sensors' 50-100 ps). The SAMPIC readout chip sampled signals every 156.25 ps, producing 64-sample waveforms within a 10 ns window. After preprocessing (inversion, filtering of noisy/saturated events, trimming to 48 samples, baseline subtraction, and amplitude normalization), the final dataset contained approximately 500,000 waveform entries (reduced from 5.5 GB to 126 MB).

**Network Architectures Tested:** Three architectures were evaluated using hyperparameter tuning with KerasTuner and Bayesian optimization: (1) Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) — 2,737 parameters, (2) Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) — 36,865 parameters, (3) UNet-based model — 456,965 parameters. The UNet architecture, which uses an encoder-decoder structure with skip connections, performed best.

**Results:** The UNet-based model achieved the best timing precision (60.71 ps in cross-validation) compared to CNN (62.83 ps) and MLP (63.90 ps). Against the baseline CFD algorithm, improvements ranged from 8% to 23% across different detector readout channels. In the base experiment, precision improved by 17% (from 71.6 ps with CFD to 58.4 ps with UNet). Under LHC-like conditions (24-sample time series instead of 48), precision improved from 73.3 ps to 62.1 ps (15% improvement). The networks generally required training on specific channels to achieve optimal results; training on one channel and testing on another could perform worse than CFD.

**Conclusion:** Deep neural networks, particularly UNet-based architectures, can significantly improve particle timing precision over the CFD method without modifying the detector setup. The inference requires only ~10 milliseconds of CPU time, making it suitable for online processing. The authors note that the absence of an MCP reference detector in the LHC setup poses a challenge for training data acquisition, and recurrent networks were not tested but are suggested for future research.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We improved the timing precision by 8% to 23%, depending on the detector's readout channel. The best results were obtained using a UNet-based model, which outperformed classical convolutional networks and the multilayer perceptron.", "The network's histogram is visibly narrower, indicating better precision.", "Neural networks have a wide range of applications in high energy physics.", "The inference from the neural network has a very low demand for the CPU time (order of 10 milliseconds), making it well-suited for online processing, such as in the high-level trigger reconstruction chain."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Reconstruction of charged tracks with Timepix4 ASICs ---
URL: https://cds.cern.ch/record/2837841/files/2210.01442.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper (arXiv:2210.01442v2, submitted to JINST) reports on the characterization of a four-plane tracking telescope system based on Timepix4 ASICs, tested with a 180 GeV/c mixed hadron beam at the CERN SPS H8 beam line. The system consists of two 100 μm thick silicon sensors placed perpendicular to the beam and two 300 μm thick sensors angled at 9°, all bump-bonded to Timepix4 readout ASICs (55×55 μm² pixel pitch, 195 ps TDC bin width). 

Key findings:
- Spatial resolution: (15.5±0.5) μm for 100 μm sensors, (4.5±0.3) μm for 300 μm tilted sensors.
- Single-plane time resolution: (452±10) ps and (420±10) ps for the two 100 μm sensors; (639±10) ps and (631±10) ps for the two 300 μm sensors (at 1000 e⁻ threshold, 50 V bias for thin sensors, 130 V for thick sensors).
- Combined track time resolution: (340±5) ps.
- Single-plane efficiencies: 92.0% (N30, limited by malfunctioning columns), 99.4% (N29), 99.1% (N23), 98.2% (N28).

The hardware uses a custom SPIDR4 readout system based on Xilinx Zynq 7000 FPGA, with 10 Gbit Ethernet data transmission. The readout ASIC (Timepix4v1, first submission) had a VCO design flaw causing ~25% faster oscillation and unstabilized frequency, degrading time resolution. Timewalk corrections were applied using ToT-based lookup tables, with different methods for perpendicular vs. tilted sensors. Per-pixel time offset corrections were also implemented. The system includes cooling (3D printed titanium blocks with liquid glycol), scintillators for reference timing, and a WinCC OA-based experiment control system. The Kepler software framework (based on Gaudi) was used for reconstruction and analysis.

--- SOURCE 1: Real-time Surface-Code Error Correction Using an FPGA-based Neural-Network Decoder ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2605.04892v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper reports a hardware-integrated control architecture featuring an FPGA-based neural-network (NN) decoder for real-time surface-code quantum error correction (QEC) on a superconducting quantum processor. The system uses a 17-qubit distance-3 surface-code logical qubit on a 66-qubit processor. The NN decoder, comprising an LSTM layer with 32 hidden units and a dense output layer, achieves a deterministic latency of 124 ns with a throughput period of 184 ns. The complete closed-loop latency is 550 ns, enabling feedback within a 1.25 μs QEC cycle.

Key results include: (1) Real-time decoding achieving logical error rates of 0.072(1) and 0.097(2) per round for |1L⟩ and |+L⟩ states, closely matching offline MWPM decoding (0.073(2) and 0.095(2)). (2) The NN decoder achieves logical error rate ϵL=6.9(2)% compared to 7.2(2)% for offline MWPM in logical memory experiments. (3) Successful demonstration of mid-circuit feedback correction in non-Clifford logical circuits (logical rotation about XL axis), where Pauli-frame updating alone is insufficient.

The architecture uses a Central Feedback Module (CFM) with an AMD Kintex-7 FPGA for syndrome decoding, integrated with arbitrary waveform generators and data acquisition modules. The authors demonstrate repeated multi-round feedback and robustness under varying error conditions. They discuss scaling to larger code distances (up to distance-13 with current FPGAs) and multi-logical-qubit systems, noting that larger distances will require more advanced hardware such as RFSoC platforms, higher-end FPGAs or ASICs, and multi-FPGA partitioning.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: A Time-Walk Correction Method for PET Detectors Based on ... ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper by Du et al. (2017) presents and evaluates a self-calibrating time-walk correction method for PET detectors that use leading edge discriminators (LEDs) to generate timing information. The leading edge technique is the simplest timing extraction method but suffers from "time-walk" (a timing error that depends on pulse amplitude/energy), which degrades timing resolution, especially for time-of-flight PET and when using wide energy windows.

The proposed method corrects time-walk without requiring an external reference detector (e.g., a fast PMT with constant fraction discrimination). Instead, it uses one detector as a reference by selecting events within a very narrow energy window (508.5–513.5 keV) around the 511 keV photopeak, then uses the relationship between threshold crossing time and event energy to correct the other detector's timing on an event-by-event basis. A piecewise cubic Hermite interpolating polynomial (pchip) fit was applied to binned energy/timing data.

Experimental validation used two SensL MicroFB SiPMs coupled to 2.5×2.5×20 mm polished LYSO crystals at 27.5V bias and 20°C. Key results:
- Without correction: 389.0±12.0 ps (425–650 keV window) and 670.2±16.2 ps (250–750 keV)
- With LED-based self-correction: 367.3±0.5 ps (425–650 keV) and 413.7±0.9 ps (250–750 keV)
- With CFD (constant fraction discriminator): 442.8±12.8 ps (425–650 keV) and 476.0±13.0 ps (250–750 keV)
- With CFD-based reference detector correction: 367.3±0.4 ps (425–650 keV) and 413.4±0.9 ps (250–750 keV)

The LED-based self-correction method matched the performance of a dedicated CFD reference detector and outperformed standard CFD. The method was also successfully applied to large-area SiPM arrays, improving timing from 11.2±0.2 ns to 4.2±0.1 ns. The authors note that with modern high-speed data transfer and storage, single-event data collection with timestamps is feasible, allowing this correction to be applied in software without additional hardware modifications.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>

Due to the inherent time-walk of the leading edge technique, corrections should be made to improve timing resolution, especially for time-of-flight PET., The timing resolution obtained using the LED technique was better than that obtained using CFD when the energy window width was narrower than 350 keV, These results show that the proposed leading edge based time-walk correction method works well. Timing resolution obtained using this method was equivalent to that obtained using a reference detector and was better than that obtained using constant fraction discriminators., The method is self-calibrated, as no extra reference detectors are needed to generate the relationship between threshold crossing time and event energy., With the dramatic improvements in data transfer speed that have occurred in recent years... it is feasible to collect single events from the PET scanner. As the event time-stamps are included in the event data, our proposed LED-based time-walk correction method can be applied to these data to improve the timing resolution without any additional measurements from the PET scanner.

--- SOURCE 2: Signal processing techniques for precise timing with novel ... ---
URL: https://indico.cern.ch/event/1047066/contributions/4399272/attachments/2265836/3847074/Manthos_timing_hep21.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This presentation by I. Manthos et al. (HEP 2021, Thessaloniki) investigates signal processing techniques for precise timing with novel gaseous detectors, specifically the PICOSEC detector, to achieve ~20-30 ps timing resolution for HL-LHC pileup mitigation and particle identification.

**Motivation:** High Luminosity LHC produces >140 pile-up vertices per clock cycle within ±45mm. 3D tracking is insufficient; precise timing (~20-30 ps/MIP) adds a separation dimension for vertex association and PID (Pion/Kaon/Kaon-Proton separation).

**Methods tested on PICOSEC MIP data:**
- **Constant Fraction Discrimination (CFD):** Reference method. Achieved 50.5 ps (full dataset) and 24.4 ps (events fully embedded in detector area).
- **Leading Edge - multi Time-over-Threshold (mToT):** Used 7 thresholds (10-200 mV). Best thresholds: 10mV (73.5 ps), 100mV (29.2 ps). Combined: 48.8 ps overall.
- **Leading Edge - multi Charge-over-Threshold (mCoT):** Used pulse integral above threshold. Best thresholds: 10mV (54.8 ps), 100mV (26.7 ps). Combined: 44.9 ps overall; 23.2 ps for fully embedded events — **better than CFD**.
- **Neural Network (MLP):** Inputs from ToT at 10/50/100 mV thresholds. Achieved 46.0 ps overall; 25.2 ps for fully embedded events.

**Sub-picosecond domain test (70 p.e. dataset):** Both CFD (5.50 ps) and mCoT (5.52 ps) methods performed comparably.

**Conclusions:**
- mToT achieves CFD-level resolution using only 6 values (3 threshold crossings).
- mCoT outperforms CFD when charge info is available from front-end electronics (e.g., NINO chip).
- Neural networks yield results comparable to analytical methods.
- Leading edge-CoT method is adequate at one order of magnitude lower timing resolution (~5 ps).
</summary>

- **Detection limits and resolution**: Fluctuations (both from the sensor signal and electronic noise) determine the minimum detectable signal. The noise level affects energy, timing, and position measurements.

- **Acquiring the sensor signal**: Methods of integrating the current pulse (on sensor capacitance, via charge-sensitive amplifiers, or with integrating ADCs). The charge-sensitive amplifier uses feedback to make charge calibration independent of sensor capacitance. Input impedance is critical, especially in position-sensitive detectors.

- **Electronic noise**: Two main mechanisms — thermal (Johnson) noise from velocity fluctuations (white spectrum, proportional to 4kT/R) and shot noise from number fluctuations (white spectrum, proportional to 2eI). The noise amplitude distribution is Gaussian.

- **Signal-to-noise ratio vs. sensor capacitance**: SNR is inversely proportional to total capacitance at the input node, a fundamental relationship independent of amplifier type.

- **Pulse shaping**: Balances bandwidth limitation (to reduce noise) and pulse duration constraint (to avoid pile-up). The CR–RC shaper is the basic model, with differentiation and integration time constants. More sophisticated shapers use multiple integrators or correlated double sampling.

- **Noise analysis**: A detailed methodology for calculating equivalent noise charge (ENC) considering sensor leakage current, bias resistor noise, series resistance noise, and amplifier noise (both white and 1/f). The ENC formula shows contributions from current noise (increases with shaping time), voltage noise (decreases with shaping time, increases with capacitance), and 1/f noise (independent of shaping time).

- **Practical noise levels**: Range from <1 electron for CCDs at long shaping times to ~10^4 electrons in high-capacitance liquid-Ar calorimeters. Silicon strip detectors operate at ~10^3 electrons, pixel detectors at 100–200 electrons.

- **Timing measurements**: Depend on slope-to-noise ratio rather than signal-to-noise ratio.

- **Digital electronics**: Brief coverage of logic elements, propagation delays, logic arrays, analog-to-digital converters (ADCs), time-to-digital converters (TDCs), signal transmission, and interference/pickup remediation.

The chapter emphasizes that in practice, compromises are necessary between noise, power dissipation, speed, and cost.

--- SOURCE 7: Constant fraction discriminator - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constant_fraction_discriminator

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A constant fraction discriminator (CFD) is an electronic signal processing device that mimics finding the maximum of a pulse by detecting the zero of its slope. It is designed to overcome the problem of "time walk" in threshold triggering, where the trigger time depends on the signal's peak height when signals have identical rise times but varying amplitudes. CFDs are used with input signals from plastic scintillation counters, such as those in electron-positron annihilation experiments for lifetime measurement. By triggering on a constant fraction of the total peak height rather than a fixed threshold, the CFD yields trigger times independent of peak heights.

**Principle of operation:** The incoming signal is split into three components. One is delayed and connected to the noninverting input of a comparator. Another is connected to the inverting input of that comparator. The third is connected to a second comparator with a threshold. The outputs of both comparators are fed through an AND gate.

**Applications:** When combined with a sampler and comparator, it is called a single channel analyzer (SCA). When an analog-to-digital converter is used, it is called a multi channel analyzer (MCA).
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
**Technical Document Summary: Constant Fraction Discriminators (CFDs) — JRM Lab**

This document, authored by Kevin Carnes (January 2003), catalogs the various Constant Fraction Discriminators used at the James R. Macdonald Laboratory (Kansas State University) and explains their operating principles, circuit details, and configuration notes.

**Available CFD Models:** The lab uses multiple types: Tennelec TC453 single CFDs, Ortec 453/473 singles, Ortec 934/935 quad CFDs, homemade CF4000 quad CFDs, and an EG&G ESN CF8000 octal CFD. The 935 units are faster versions of the 934s. Pulse pair resolutions vary significantly: TC453 (10 ns), Ortec 934 (7-10 ns), Ortec 935 (5 ns), CF4000 (15-20 ns), and CF8000 (30 ns).

**Operating Principle:** CFDs produce accurate timing from analog signals of varying amplitudes but identical rise times by splitting the input signal, attenuating one half and delaying the other, then feeding both into a fast comparator with the delayed input inverted. This triggers a timing signal at a constant fraction (typically ~20%) of the input amplitude. The technique virtually eliminates timing "walk" for signals with the same rise time but different amplitudes.

**Key Circuit Details (CF4000):** The input splits three ways: to a threshold comparator, an attenuated path, and a delayed path. The outputs of the fast comparator halves form a NAND gate. A 10130 latch handles output width and deadtime, adjustable via a width pot (R39) providing 0.2 to 8.8 mA bias current. Outputs are shifted from ECL to NIM levels. RG174 delay cable provides ~1.8 ns/ft of delay.

**Configuration Guidance:** 
- Walk/ZC Adjust: For 934/935 units, set the walk adjust so bipolar monitor signals cross zero simultaneously. For CF4000/TC453, set DC noise level midway between ECL high and low.
- Update vs. Blocking Mode: Update mode (934/935 internal switch) gives best pulse pair resolution; blocking mode prevents ringing.
- For noisy signals, a 40% fraction may be needed instead of 20%.
- The threshold setting affects pulse width and pulse pair resolution.
- A conversation with Ortec's Dale Gedcke (May 2000) notes that the optimal fraction concept is for scintillation detectors; for channel plates or SBDs, minimizing amplitude walk is the primary concern, and time resolution is relatively insensitive to the actual fraction.

**Mathematical Background:** For a linear ramp input, the CFD crossing time is independent of slope (rise time). The fraction F equals the attenuation factor f, and the delay should be set to the product f × rise time for proper operation.
</summary>

For work with channel plates or SBD's, we care only about minimizing amplitude walk. Time resolution is relatively insensitive to the actual fraction set on the constant fraction.

URL: https://liquidinstruments.com/application-notes/understanding-jitter-and-interpolation-in-the-moku-time-frequency-analyzer

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This application note from Liquid Instruments explains how to optimize time measurements using the Moku Time & Frequency Analyzer, focusing on understanding jitter, interpolation, and achieving the best measurement accuracy.

**Key Concepts:**
- The Time & Frequency Analyzer functions as a time tagger, frequency counter, event counter, and event timer, recording the time of arrival of signal edges using a sampled ADC front end rather than dedicated time-to-digital converters.
- **Jitter** measures variation in repeated edge arrival time measurements (standard deviation). **Accuracy** measures how close a single measurement is to the true value. **Digital resolution** is the smallest reportable difference between measurements.
- The analyzer has a digital resolution ~20x finer than jitter, making resolution not a performance limitation.

**Interpolation:**
- Moku:Pro samples at 1.25 GSa/s (800 ps period). Without interpolation, this would be the performance-limiting resolution.
- Linear interpolation improves timing performance by ~100x, but assumes the rising edge is linear between sample points around the threshold crossing.
- Faster edge rates cause interpolation bias (distribution biases toward multiples of sample period), degrading accuracy and jitter.

**Optimization:**
- Two competing requirements exist: edges must be fast to minimize amplitude noise coupling into timing, but slow enough to preserve linear interpolation assumptions.
- The "goldilocks" edge rate is characterized for each Moku platform. Moku:Pro has an optimum rise time of **6 ns** (~7.5 sample periods).
- If direct control isn't possible, a low-pass filter can condition the signal. For Moku:Pro's 6 ns optimum rise time, a **60 MHz low-pass filter** is recommended (using BW = 0.35/rise).
- The filter introduces group delay equally for all edges, so timing measurements remain unaffected (absolute timing shifts cancel out).

**Conclusion:** Optimal Time & Frequency Analyzer performance requires conditioning the signal edge to meet specified rise times, achievable by adding a low-pass filter in series with the signal.
</summary>

URL: https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/2477571

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific paper authored by researchers at Brookhaven National Laboratory (L. Gerlach, W. Gu, N. Nayak, X. Qian, B. Viren) and Princeton University, to be published in the Journal of Instrumentation (JINST) in October 2024. The paper presents the LMN method for waveform resampling, an optimized technique based on Fast Fourier Transformation (FFT) for digital signal processing.

**Key Context and Motivation:** The work is motivated by the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE), which uses Liquid Argon Time Projection Chambers (LArTPCs) as its primary detector technology. DUNE's far detector modules (FD1-HD and FD2-VD) employ different readout electronics with different sampling periods (500 ns and 512 ns), creating a need to resample waveforms to a common period before applying the large software suite for data processing.

**The LMN Method:** The LMN method is a variant of trigonometric interpolation that implements optimized resampling in the frequency domain. It avoids the computational inflation of naive algorithms that require integer upsampling followed by integer downsampling. The method works by finding a special case where the resampling ratio allows the net number of frequency-domain samples to be changed directly (ΔN = Nr - Ns), avoiding the need to inflate to a large intermediate size. The method requires a rationality condition: the ratio of the sampling periods must be rational. The minimal sequence size Nmin is determined by δN = (Ts - Tr) / gcd(Tr, Ts - Tr).

**Performance Comparisons:** The LMN method was compared against linear interpolation, polyphase filtering, cardinal cubic B-spline, and a naive resampler. Key findings:
- For noiseless signals, the LMN method achieves mean squared error (MSE) very close to or identical to zero across all signal frequencies, while other methods show increasing MSE with higher signal frequencies.
- The LMN method preserves spectral features accurately, while interval-domain methods (linear, spline) introduce spectral artifacts.
- In terms of processing time, the LMN method is competitive with linear interpolation (depending on the exact resampled size) and typically two orders of magnitude faster than the naive approach.
- DFT processing time depends heavily on the prime factors of the sequence length.

**Normalization Considerations:** The paper discusses three interpretations of signal samples and corresponding normalization:
1. Interpolation (preserve local amplitude): additional normalization of A0 = Nr/Ns
2. Integral (preserve sum of samples): nominal DFT normalization is appropriate
3. Energy (preserve sum-of-squares): additional normalization of A2 = √(Nr/Ns)

**LArTPC Application:** The method was demonstrated on simulated LArTPC waveforms from the Wire-Cell Toolkit. The field responses originally sampled at 100 ns were resampled to 64 ns using LMN, then downsampled by integer factors to achieve the desired 512 ns ADC sampling period. Results show very good alignment between native 500 ns waveforms and 512 ns→500 ns LMN-resampled waveforms, with discrepancies being small and attributable to the differential downsampling of the response rather than the LMN method itself.

**Potential Artifacts:** The method can produce ringing artifacts from endpoint discontinuities (non-periodic signals) and from the sharp low-pass filter effect of frequency-domain sample removal. Mitigation strategies include padding with linear interpolation between endpoints or applying low-pass filters in the frequency domain.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 23: Chapter 4: Sampling Theory and Signal Fidelity ---
URL: https://www.berkeleynucleonics.com/books/arbitrary-waveform/html/04-sampling-theory-and-fidelity.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This chapter from an arbitrary waveform generator (AWG) guide covers sampling theory and signal fidelity, focusing on five key concepts that determine waveform quality.

**1. Nyquist-Shannon Sampling Theorem:** To represent a signal without loss, sample at a rate strictly greater than twice the highest frequency component. The AWG's sample clock (Fs) sets the Nyquist frequency at Fs/2. The practical limit is lower than the theoretical limit; engineers recommend keeping highest frequencies at or under Fs/2.5 to Fs/3 for spectral purity.

**2. Aliasing, Images, and Nyquist Zones:** The DAC produces mirror images of the spectrum around multiples of the sample rate. Frequencies above Fs/2 fold back (alias) into lower frequencies, masquerading as legitimate signals. Defenses include reconstruction filters (analog low-pass filters) and frequency planning.

**3. Sin(x)/x Roll-off:** The zero-order hold of a DAC creates a sinc function envelope that attenuates signals. At Nyquist frequency, attenuation is approximately -3.9 dB (36% amplitude loss). The fix is sinc correction (inverse-sinc pre-emphasis filtering).

**4. Interpolation and Oversampling:** Running the DAC faster than required moves Nyquist higher, reducing filter demands, lowering roll-off penalties, and spreading quantization noise. Digital interpolation computes intermediate samples. Tradeoffs include increased memory, compute, and power consumption.

**5. Quantization Noise and Dither:** Finite DAC resolution (N bits) creates quantization error. Ideal SNR is approximately 6.02 dB per bit plus 1.76 dB. Periodic signals can create discrete spurs rather than broadband noise. Dither (adding small random noise before quantization) breaks correlation and spreads spur energy into a smooth noise floor.

The chapter concludes with a practical checklist: keep frequencies well under Fs/2, plan spectrum for image/alias rejection, correct sin(x)/x roll-off, oversample appropriately, and choose resolution/dither based on application needs.
</summary>

To represent a signal without loss, you must sample at a rate strictly greater than twice the highest frequency component present in that signal.,The number to remember is -3.9 dB. At the Nyquist frequency, Fs/2, the zero-order hold has attenuated your signal by about 3.9 dB relative to DC.,The familiar rule of thumb is that an ideal converter delivers roughly 6.02 dB of signal-to-noise ratio per bit, plus about 1.76 dB.,When a spur appears at a frequency you cannot explain, check whether it is an alias before you chase it through the hardware.,Dither and sinc correction pull in different directions, so set them with intent.

--- SOURCE 1: [PDF] Limitations of t he Pulse-Shape Technique for Particle ... - HZDR ---
URL: https://www.hzdr.de/publications/000732/732.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific paper (FZR-157, November 1996) from Forschungszentrum Rossendorf investigates limitations of the pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) technique for identifying charged particles stopped in planar Si detectors. The research was conducted in the context of the EuroSiB project—a 4π Si-detector array for charged-particle detection inside the European γ-ray facility EUROBALL, consisting of hexagonal and pentagonal Si slices (500 μm thick, ~1300 mm² active area) forming a 42-element polyhedron.

Key findings:

1. **Primary limitation: Resistivity fluctuations in bulk silicon.** The particle resolution is fundamentally determined by inhomogeneities in the silicon material, which cause the charge-collection time to depend on the point of impact. Detector maps revealed concentric ring structures (correlated with impurity distributions from the floating-zone crystal growth process) and a radial trend of slower charge collection toward the wafer center.

2. **Detector bias optimization is critical.** Best p/α separation is achieved with bias slightly below depletion voltage. The quality parameter Q = δtₓₓ/⟨tₓₓ⟩ was developed to measure detector performance using mixed α sources (²³⁹Pu-²⁴¹Am-²⁴⁴Cm).

3. **Finite energy threshold for particle identification.** A critical range R<sub>c</sub> ≈ 50 μm (for 500 μm detectors) and R<sub>c</sub> ≈ 25 μm (for 50 μm detectors) was observed, below which the charge-collection time unexpectedly decreases, causing overlapping particle lines. This effect is not fully understood but limits discrimination at low energies.

4. **Practical test method developed.** Detectors can be characterized without beam experiments by exposing both front and rear sides simultaneously to α sources, measuring zero-crossing time shifts, energy resolution, and energy deficit.

5. **Beam experiments** using 150 MeV ³⁶Ar on a 2 mg/cm² target at the VICKSI accelerator in Berlin confirmed the source test results and demonstrated that spot irradiation (~2 mm diameter) yields much sharper particle lines than full-area exposure.

The paper concludes that PSD is not only a promising method for particle identification but also a powerful tool for investigating semiconductor material properties and charge-collection processes in radiation detectors.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Limitations of the pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) technique - a promising method to identify the charged particles stopped in planar Si-detectors - have been investigated. The particle resolution turned out to be basically determined by resistivity fluctuations in the bulk silicon which cause the charge-collection time to depend on the point of impact.", "We conclude that the homogeneity of the dopand concentration (resistivity) in the silicon crystals used for detector production is a key parameter for the quality of particle discrimination based on PSD.", "The finite energy threshold for particle discrimination is due to an unexpected decrease of the charge-collection time for ionization tracks which are shorter than a critical range Rc. This effect results in overlapping particle lines.", "We found values of Rc ≈ 50μm and Rc ≈ 25μm for detectors of 500μm and 50μm thickness, respectively.", "In summary, we conclude that pulse-shape discrimination is not only a promising method for particle identification, but also a simple and powerful tool to investigate properties of semiconductor materials and to study details of the charge-collection process in radiation detectors."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Wireless Pi explains the Gardner Timing Error Detector (TED), a non-data-aided version of zero-crossing timing error detectors used for symbol timing synchronization in digital communication systems.

**Key Concepts:**
- The Gardner TED is based on a zero-crossing philosophy where the algorithm targets zero crossings of the waveform rather than symbol peaks. It uses three samples per symbol (at 2 samples/symbol rate) and converges such that the middle sample aligns with the zero crossing.
- The Gardner TED formula is: e_D[m] = z(mT_M - T_M/2 + ε̂_Δ) × {z((m-1)T_M + ε̂_Δ) - z(mT_M + ε̂_Δ)}
- Data-aided and decision-directed variants (Zero Crossing TEDs) replace the matched filter outputs with known data symbols or symbol decisions.

**Key Points:**
- The Gardner TED was invented by F. M. Gardner and is based on ideas from wave difference method and Digital Data Transition Tracking Loop (DTTL).
- Like derivative and early-late TEDs, its performance suffers when excess bandwidth α is small.
- The article demonstrates that Gardner TED's carrier-independent operation is not unique to it—any TED using conjugate products between complex samples with the same phase rotation is carrier independent.
- The non-data-aided version of early-late TED exhibits the same carrier phase independence property.
- A simulation example is provided: 2-PAM, L=2 samples/symbol, α=0.4, B_n T_M=1/200, ζ=1/√2, ε_Δ=0.25T_M, showing convergence in approximately 800 symbols.
- For QAM, the zero crossing TED combines inphase and quadrature components.
- The receiver structure uses a matched filter, interpolator, and timing locked loop operating at 2 samples/symbol.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: Comparison Between Digital and Analog Pulse Shape ... ---
URL: https://inldigitallibrary.inl.gov/sites/sti/sti/3394890.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This preprint (INL/CON-05-00284) presented at the 2005 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium by researchers from Idaho National Laboratory (Rahmat Aryaeinejad, John K. Hartwell, David F. Spencer) investigates digital signal processing (DSP) techniques for neutron/gamma ray pulse shape discrimination (PSD) in a BC501 liquid scintillator detector, comparing results with analog methods.

**Key Points:**
- **Methodology:** The study used a CAMAC DGF-4C DSP module (XIA Corp.) with 40 MHz digitization rate (25 ns sampling). The PSD approach integrated the tail region (PID window: 0.25-0.4 μs) divided by the total waveform integral to create a particle identification index.
- **Setup:** A 2"x2" BC501 liquid scintillator coupled to a Phillips XP2020 PMT, with a Cf-252 source (neutrons + gamma rays) at 4 inches distance, plus Cs-137 and Co-60 sources for calibration. Energy calibration used Compton edge energies.
- **Results:** The digital method achieved good neutron/gamma separation at energy thresholds above 100 keVee, with Figure of Merit (FOM) values increasing from 0.85 (50 keVee) to 1.04 (600 keVee).
- **Comparison:** The analog zero crossing method outperformed the digital method at all thresholds (FOM: 1.19 at 50 keVee to 1.65 at 600 keVee), by a factor of 1.4-1.6x. The authors attribute this to the slow 40 MHz digitization rate of the DGF-4C module.
- **Conclusion:** The authors conclude that using faster DSP chips (e.g., ACTEL 350 MHz or XILINX 450 MHz with 2 ns resolution) would substantially improve digital PSD performance, potentially exceeding analog methods.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
In digital signal processing (DSP) technique, the detector preamplifier outputs are directly digitized without any analog signal shaping and then, according to specific application, processed to deduce desired results. The major difference between analog and digital signal processing is that with the digital method after signal conditioning, the preamplifier pulse is digitized immediately and all operations are carried out in digital filters. With the analog signal processing method, the filtering must be completed in relatively slower analog circuits. The DSP system offers significant advantages over the analog system in the areas of cost, accuracy, and efficiency by eliminating a need for extra electronic modules. At first glance one can clearly see that the zero crossing method is better for all threshold values from 50 keVee to 600 keVee by a factor of 1.4 to 1.6, respectively. This is mainly because in digital processing the DGF-4C module we used was slow (40 MHz), which limited the sampling rate to 25 ns only. We believe using faster FPGA chips that are commercially available today, like ACTEL 350 MHz or XILINX 450 MHz devices, will substantially improve the separation between gamma-ray and neutron peaks.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a presentation on Techniques in Experimental Nuclear Physics by K.A. Chipps, presented at ORNL (UT-Battelle for the US Department of Energy). The talk covers the fundamentals of nuclear physics detectors and experimental setups.

**Key Topics Covered:**

1. **What We Want to Measure vs. What We Actually Measure:** Physicists aim to infer energy, velocity, momentum, mass, time, position, cross section, and correlations to derive spin/parity, angular momentum transfer, and spectroscopic factors. They primarily measure charge/light pulses, time, segment ID, and logic gates.

2. **Detector Basics:** Three main detector types:
   - **Semiconductor Detectors** (Silicon, Germanium): Ionization creates electron-hole pairs (~3 eV/pair). Use p-n junctions with reverse bias to create depletion regions. Require charge-sensitive preamps. Segmentation provides position information.
   - **Scintillator Detectors:** Inorganic (NaI(Tl), BGO, BaF₂) and organic (plastics, liquid). Light converted to electrons via photocathodes, PMTs, or SiPMs. Pulse shape discrimination (PSD) possible via singlet/triplet state differences.
   - **Gas-Filled Detectors:** Ionization with W-value ~30 eV/ion pair. Can use Frisch grids, segmentation for 3D position tracking (TPC principle). Include MUSIC, FMA focal plane PGAC.

3. **Common Detector Attributes:** Pulse mode vs. current mode, pulse height spectra (differential vs. integrated), energy resolution (R = FWHM/H₀), detection efficiency (absolute vs. intrinsic vs. peak), and dead time (paralyzable vs. nonparalyzable models).

4. **Analog DAQ Flow:** Signal → Shaping (CR-RC circuits, pole-zero cancellation) → Discrimination (leading edge, CFD) → Logic (coincidences, anticoincidences, triggers) → Event recording.

5. **Digital DAQ:** Signal sent directly to digitizer, self-triggering, traces digitized, virtual filtering and logic instead of physical modules. Useful for pulse shape analysis but can be rate-limited.

6. **Analysis Techniques:** Branching ratios, pulse shape discrimination (n/γ separation, beam/reaction γ separation), combination detector systems.

7. **Sample Experiment:** Measuring ¹⁰⁰Sn(d,p) at 10 MeV/u requires: charged particle detection (silicon detector array like ORRUBA or HELIOS), heavy recoil detection (ionization chamber, solid state, or scintillator/phoswich), and gamma detection for level energies.

**Closing Thought:** "Know thy detector! Know thy system! Think outside the box to solve analysis problems! READ KNOLL!"
</summary>

5. For a typical SCA-based digitizer (like SAMPIC), the total timing variance combines voltage noise components (with correlation from noise spectrum), sampling/quantization/digitization noise, master clock jitter (correlated), and delay step jitter (uncorrelated).

**Conclusion:** dCFD and dLED methods improve timing by only up to 20% compared to basic analog methods, and this improvement decreases when consecutive samples are correlated.

--- SOURCE 15: Constant fraction discriminator ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constant_fraction_discriminator

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A constant fraction discriminator (CFD) is an electronic signal processing device that mimics finding the maximum of a pulse by detecting the zero of its slope. It is designed to overcome the problem of "time walk" in threshold triggering, where the trigger time depends on the signal's peak height when signals have identical rise times but varying amplitudes. CFDs are used with input signals from plastic scintillation counters, such as those in electron-positron annihilation experiments for lifetime measurement. By triggering on a constant fraction of the total peak height rather than a fixed threshold, the CFD yields trigger times independent of peak heights.

**Principle of operation:** The incoming signal is split into three components. One is delayed and connected to the noninverting input of a comparator. Another is connected to the inverting input of that comparator. The third is connected to a second comparator with a threshold. The outputs of both comparators are fed through an AND gate.

**Applications:** When combined with a sampler and comparator, it is called a single channel analyzer (SCA). When an analog-to-digital converter is used, it is called a multi channel analyzer (MCA).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 24: [PDF] PET Systems ---
URL: https://bme.unc.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/917/2022/03/Background_PET_Systems.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive chapter on PET (Positron Emission Tomography) systems from the textbook "Emission Tomography" (2004), authored by Thomas Lewellen and Joel Karp. The chapter covers the fundamental principles, detector designs, system geometry, scintillators, electronics, and correction methods for PET imaging.

**I. Basic Principles:** PET images the distribution of positron emitters in vivo by detecting annihilation gamma rays (511 keV) in coincidence. Spatial resolution is limited by three factors: (1) positron range (travel distance before annihilation, e.g., 18F: 1.2 mm, 82Rb: 12.4 mm in water), (2) noncolinearity (approximately 0.23° angular uncertainty, leading to resolution loss proportional to ring diameter), and (3) detector intrinsic spatial resolution (FWHM ≈ half the crystal size). Parallax error from depth-of-interaction uncertainty also degrades resolution at oblique angles. Three types of coincidence events exist: true, scattered, and random coincidences. Increasing sensitivity can be achieved by increasing patient dose, using more efficient scintillators, accepting more of the energy spectrum, or increasing solid angle (most useful approach).

**II. Detector Designs:** Two major approaches are used: (1) Anger-logic continuous detectors (large NaI(Tl) crystals viewed by PMT arrays, used in C-PET) and (2) block detectors (discrete crystal arrays viewed by 4 PMTs, used with BGO, LSO, GSO). Block designs include standard block (16:1 crystal/PMT ratio) and quadrant-sharing block (49:1 ratio). Pulse shortening, local centroid positioning, and multiple trigger channels enable high count-rate capability.

**III. System Geometry:** Systems can be full-ring or partial-ring with rotation. Full-ring NaI(Tl) systems have 25 cm axial extent; discrete crystal systems use BGO (25-30 mm thick), LSO (25 mm), or GSO (20 mm). Systems operate in 2D mode (with axial collimation/septa) or 3D/PVI mode (without septa). 3D mode offers up to 5x sensitivity increase but increases scatter fraction (3-4x) and randoms rates. LLED settings vary: BGO 300-375 keV, LSO 350-400 keV, GSO 420 keV, NaI(Tl) 435 keV.

**IV. Scintillators:** Key properties compared: NaI(Tl) has highest light yield (100% relative) but 230 ns decay; BGO has high stopping power (0.92 cm⁻¹ attenuation) but low light (15%); LSO offers 75% light yield with 40 ns fast decay; GSO has 30% light yield with 65 ns decay. No single scintillator has all ideal properties.

**V. Electronics:** Basic components include amplifiers, pulse-height analyzers, timing discriminators, and coincidence circuits. Randoms correction uses either a delayed-window approach or calculation from singles rates (R = 2τ·S₁·S₂). Dead time in BGO block systems is dominated by integrating amplifiers; in large-area detectors, by pulse pile-up.

**VI. Attenuation Correction:** A key advantage of PET is that attenuation correction depends only on the total path length through the object, not on the source position along the LOR. Transmission scans use rotating rod sources (⁶⁸Ge) in coincidence mode, or singles mode with ¹³⁷Cs (662 keV, requiring 10% scaling). CT-based attenuation correction is also used in PET/CT systems.

**VII. Scatter Correction:** Techniques include integral transform, function fitting, energy-based subtraction, and analytic calculation. Accuracy depends on operating mode (2D vs. 3D), scanner design, scintillator, and object size.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: Using deep neural networks to improve the precision of fast ... ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.05883

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This research paper (accepted for publication in Computer Science journal) investigates using deep neural networks to improve the timing precision of particle detectors, specifically for the CMS-PPS (Precision Proton Spectrometer) subsystem at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. The key problem addressed is the "time walk effect" — statistical fluctuations in charge deposited by particles that cause errors in arrival time measurements. The standard method, the Constant Fraction Discriminator (CFD) algorithm, is simple and effective but does not utilize all voltage samples in a time series.

**Methodology:** The researchers used data from the DESY-II synchrotron test beam facility (2020), where both PPS diamond timing detectors and a high-precision MCP-PMT (Microchannel Plate Photomultiplier Tube) detector were installed. The MCP served as the ground-truth reference (precision ~10 ps, compared to diamond sensors' 50-100 ps). The SAMPIC readout chip sampled signals every 156.25 ps, producing 64-sample waveforms within a 10 ns window. After preprocessing (inversion, filtering of noisy/saturated events, trimming to 48 samples, baseline subtraction, and amplitude normalization), the final dataset contained approximately 500,000 waveform entries (reduced from 5.5 GB to 126 MB).

**Network Architectures Tested:** Three architectures were evaluated using hyperparameter tuning with KerasTuner and Bayesian optimization: (1) Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) — 2,737 parameters, (2) Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) — 36,865 parameters, (3) UNet-based model — 456,965 parameters. The UNet architecture, which uses an encoder-decoder structure with skip connections, performed best.

**Results:** The UNet-based model achieved the best timing precision (60.71 ps in cross-validation) compared to CNN (62.83 ps) and MLP (63.90 ps). Against the baseline CFD algorithm, improvements ranged from 8% to 23% across different detector readout channels. In the base experiment, precision improved by 17% (from 71.6 ps with CFD to 58.4 ps with UNet). Under LHC-like conditions (24-sample time series instead of 48), precision improved from 73.3 ps to 62.1 ps (15% improvement). The networks generally required training on specific channels to achieve optimal results; training on one channel and testing on another could perform worse than CFD.

**Conclusion:** Deep neural networks, particularly UNet-based architectures, can significantly improve particle timing precision over the CFD method without modifying the detector setup. The inference requires only ~10 milliseconds of CPU time, making it suitable for online processing. The authors note that the absence of an MCP reference detector in the LHC setup poses a challenge for training data acquisition, and recurrent networks were not tested but are suggested for future research.
</summary>

URL: https://cos.colorado.edu/COS_publications/cos_spie4139Vallerga.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper by Vallerga and McPhate (UC Berkeley Space Science Laboratory) reviews the optimization of readout electronics for microchannel plate (MCP) detectors with delay line anodes, used in space missions such as FUSE, GALEX, and the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph (COS) on the Hubble Space Telescope. The delay line anode measures the position of charge clouds exiting MCP detectors by timing the difference between pulse arrival at both ends of the delay line.

**Key Topics:**
- **Delay Line Types:** Serpentine (planar zig-zag) and Helical (multi-planar) delay lines, plus Double Delay Line (DDL) and Cross Delay Line (XDL) anode patterns. These affect pulse shape due to dispersion, capacitive/inductive coupling, and reflections from unterminated strips.
- **Timing Electronics:** Pulses (~10 mV, 5ns wide) are amplified, filtered, and sent to Constant Fraction Discriminators (CFDs) which generate logic pulses for a Time-to-Amplitude Converter (TAC). Spatial resolution <25 µm FWHM over 85 mm is achievable at >100 kHz count rates.
- **CFD Optimization:** The optimum fraction F for minimizing timing error is the ratio of slopes at the zero crossing (F = -dV(T)/dt / dV(T-t0)/dt). For a symmetric Gaussian pulse, the optimum delay is t0 = 2σ (slightly shorter than FWHM), corresponding to the inflection points where slope is greatest.
- **Real-World Complications:** Pulse dispersion (pulses widen and lose amplitude as they traverse the delay line), reflections causing baseline disturbances and non-linearity, and amplifier non-linearity (which causes amplitude-dependent timing errors, especially at anode ends where start and stop amplitudes differ). Bandpass filtering helps make pulses more uniform across the anode.
- **Mitigation Strategies:** Use low dispersion anodes, linear amplifiers, narrow MCP pulse height distributions, and careful empirical optimization of filters and CFD settings (especially for large anodes like COS, GALEX, and FUSE).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Real-time Surface-Code Error Correction Using an FPGA-based Neural-Network Decoder ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2605.04892v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper reports a hardware-integrated control architecture featuring an FPGA-based neural-network (NN) decoder for real-time surface-code quantum error correction (QEC) on a superconducting quantum processor. The system uses a 17-qubit distance-3 surface-code logical qubit on a 66-qubit processor. The NN decoder, comprising an LSTM layer with 32 hidden units and a dense output layer, achieves a deterministic latency of 124 ns with a throughput period of 184 ns. The complete closed-loop latency is 550 ns, enabling feedback within a 1.25 μs QEC cycle.

Key results include: (1) Real-time decoding achieving logical error rates of 0.072(1) and 0.097(2) per round for |1L⟩ and |+L⟩ states, closely matching offline MWPM decoding (0.073(2) and 0.095(2)). (2) The NN decoder achieves logical error rate ϵL=6.9(2)% compared to 7.2(2)% for offline MWPM in logical memory experiments. (3) Successful demonstration of mid-circuit feedback correction in non-Clifford logical circuits (logical rotation about XL axis), where Pauli-frame updating alone is insufficient.

The architecture uses a Central Feedback Module (CFM) with an AMD Kintex-7 FPGA for syndrome decoding, integrated with arbitrary waveform generators and data acquisition modules. The authors demonstrate repeated multi-round feedback and robustness under varying error conditions. They discuss scaling to larger code distances (up to distance-13 with current FPGAs) and multi-logical-qubit systems, noting that larger distances will require more advanced hardware such as RFSoC platforms, higher-end FPGAs or ASICs, and multi-FPGA partitioning.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The system achieves a deterministic closed-loop latency of 550 ns, including 124 ns for NN decoding, enabling feedback corrections within a 1.25 us QEC cycle.,We show that real-time decoding and feedback correction achieve logical performance comparable to offline decoding while maintaining robustness against varying error conditions.,We further demonstrate mid-circuit feedback correction in non-Clifford logical circuits, where Pauli-frame updating alone becomes insufficient.,The NN decoder achieves a latency of 124 ns with a throughput period of 184 ns, and the complete system realizes a deterministic closed-loop latency of 550 ns, enabling feedback within a sub-microsecond QEC cycle.,These results establish a deterministic hardware-integrated feedback architecture for low-latency QEC, supporting future implementations of universal fault-tolerant quantum computation.
</key_excerpts>
