args.summary:
This presentation by R. Arcidiacono (Università del Piemonte Orientale & INFN Torino) at the XXXIII Bonaudi-Chiavassa International School on Particle Detectors covers a decade of developments in 4D-tracking with silicon detectors, focusing on measuring both position (3D) and time (4th dimension) of charged particles.

**Key Sections:**

1. **3D Tracking Basics**: Silicon sensors have been the preferred technology for particle tracking for over 40 years due to excellent spatial resolution, flexibility, and reliability. Traditional silicon sensors are ~300 µm thick diodes operated under reverse bias, functioning as solid-state ionization chambers. Key characteristics: small band gap (1.12 eV), 3.6 eV per e-h pair, ~106 e-h/µm, high carrier mobility allowing fast charge collection (<10 ns).

2. **The 4th Dimension (Time)**: Traditionally, time measurement used MRPCs, scintillators, and Cherenkov detectors. The feasibility of silicon sensors for precision timing was demonstrated through Low-Gain Avalanche Diode (LGAD) technology, enabling 4D-tracking detectors that measure both position and time.

3. **Applications of Timing**: Time information can be used at each point along the track, at track level, or at trigger level. Benefits include massive simplification of pattern recognition, distinguishing overlapping events, and trigger rate reduction.

4. **Future Collider Requirements**: Next-generation facilities (FCC-ee, ILC, CLIC) demand spatial resolution of 3-5 µm, time resolution of tens of ps, very thin material (~100 µm Si), and pixel sizes of 25×25 µm².

5. **LGAD Technology**: The key innovation is an internal moderate gain layer (thin p+ doping) that provides large signals with short rise time and low noise, ideal for timing. State-of-the-art LGADs achieve 25-40 ps time resolution with 1.3×1.3 mm² pixels. The time resolution equation is: σ²t = σ²Jitter + σ²TimeWalk + σ²LandauNoise + σ²Distortion + σ²TDC.

6. **Radiation Hardness**: LGADs face acceptor removal effects under irradiation, with active acceptor density evolving as NA(Φ) = geffΦ + NA(0)e^(-c·NA(0)·Φ/Φ0). Pre-irradiated devices achieve ~30 ps timing; after irradiation to 1.5×10¹⁵ neq/cm², resolution degrades to ~50-60 ps.

7. **Resistive AC-Coupled LGADs (RSD/AC-LGAD)**: To overcome the inter-pad dead area problem in standard LGADs, resistive AC-coupled readout was developed. This design uses a continuous gain layer with resistive n+ layer and AC-coupled readout pads, achieving 100% fill factor. Spatial resolution of ~3% of pitch size was demonstrated (e.g., ~40 µm for 1300 µm pitch, ~15 µm for 450 µm pitch). Time jitter of ~20 ps was achieved at gain ~30.

8. **Testbeam Results**: RSD2-450 µm pitch devices at gain ~50 demonstrated ~19 µm spatial resolution (with tracker resolution to be deconvolved). Using FAST2 ASIC readout, spatial resolution of ~3-4% of pitch was measured, with a constant term of ~13 µm dominating at higher amplitudes.

9. **DC-RSD Evolution**: The next generation (DC-coupled Resistive Silicon Detectors) removes the oxide layer for AC-coupling, implants readout electrodes directly on the resistive layer, and adds charge containment structures (isolating trenches). Advantages include: no signal dispersion (predetermined number of pads), no bipolar signals (~1 ns pulses), no baseline fluctuations, improved SNR, and feasibility of O(cm²) active surface devices.

10. **DC-RSD1 Production**: First proof-of-concept production completed at FBK in November 2024, implementing square and triangular pixel matrices with isolating trenches, multiple pitch options, and various test structures. Preliminary testbeam results at DESY with 5 GeV electrons show clear signal separation, fast unipolar signals matching standard LGAD shape, and perfect isolation with signals seen only in electrodes belonging to the hit pixel.

## Abstract

Various digital methods were examined for determining the relative arrival times of [pulses](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/immunology-and-microbiology/pulse-rate) from to 5.08×2.54 cm BaF 2[scintillators](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/physics-and-astronomy/scintillation-counter). In this study, pulses from the [photomultiplier tubes](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/photomultiplier-tubes) were digitized by a 1 Gs/s analog-to-digital converter and post processed with multiple techniques. These techniques include: (1) [leading edge](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/engineering/leading-edge) discrimination, (2) moment-analysis, (3) constant-fraction discrimination, (4) digital constant-fraction discrimination, (5) triangular pulse shaping with a leading edge linear regression, and (6) pulse-shape fitting. Average timing resolutions of 456±8 ps were obtained with constant-fraction discrimination, which is slightly higher than the analog average resolution of 419±7 ps. This study explores the application of these digital techniques for pulse-timing applications and their potential advantages and limitations.

## Introduction

Digital methods are being used more often to analyze detector signals. Advantages include: reduced drift, archiving of data for later analysis, and better control over analysis parameters. Analog methods also have advantages since they are not limited, as digital methods are, by quantization in time and amplitude.

This paper compares various digital and analog methods of determining the difference in arrival time of two coincident 60 Co gamma rays detected by two BaF 2 detectors. The analog method used the constant-fraction-zero-crossing technique. The digital techniques included: (1) leading-edge discrimination [1], (2) moment-analysis [1], (3) constant-fraction-zero-crossing [1], (4) digital constant-fraction discrimination (DCFD) [2], (5) triangular pulse shaping with a leading-edge linear-regression analysis [3], and (6) pulse-shape fitting. Each technique was repeated multiple times to optimize the parameters for the best resolution and accuracy.

The difference of the calculated arrival times were plotted as a histogram and fit with a Gaussian distribution. The full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) of the fit was used as the resolution.

The simplest digital method was leading-edge discrimination. The first 200 samples of each waveform were averaged and subtracted from the rest of the waveform to compensate for any DC offset. The signal was then filtered with a rank-3 median filter [4]. A median filter was chosen because of its ability to filter out low amplitude, high frequency noise and still maintain the leading edge of a digitized signal. If the threshold-crossing time occurs between time samples, linear interpolation is used to estimate the actual time.

Moment analysis involved determining the first moment of the pulse centered on the maximum digitized value (MDV) of the pulse. The numbers of points used in the analysis before and after the MDV were varied in order to optimize the resolution and the accuracy. These are referred to as pre-MDV and post-MDV, respectively.

The next method is a digital version of the analog constant-fraction discrimination zero-crossing technique. The original signal is delayed from 1 to 5 time steps, amplified, inverted, and then added to the original signal. This process, when optimized, transforms the unipolar signal into a bipolar pulse. The bipolar pulse crosses the time-axis at a constant fraction of the height of the original pulse. The crossing time was linearly interpolated if it occurred between time-steps. The amplification of the delayed signal is later referred to as ‘delayamp’.

The constant-fraction-zero-crossing method is used by many analog systems to determine pulse arrival times. However, in the digital regime it is easy to implement constant-fraction discrimination without modifying the original signal. The DCFD method searched for the MDV and then set a threshold based on a predefined fraction of the MDV. The pulse was then analyzed to determine when it initially crossed this threshold. The time pick off was linearly interpolated if the crossing of the threshold fell between two time-steps.

The triangular-shaping leading-edge discrimination routine converted the pulses into a triangular pulse [5] and performed a linear regression on its leading edge. The slope and intercept from the regression were used to determine the time when the pulse crosses the axis. The variable parameters in this method are _K_, which corresponds to the number of time steps in the leading edge, and _T_ _clk_/_τ_, which corresponds to the shaping of the pulse.

The most complicated routine implemented fit the digitized pulse to the Gaussian equation. The pulse was first corrected for any DC offset by subtracting the average of the first 200 samples from the waveform. The number of points before the MDV (pre-MDV) varied from 1 to 10 points and after the MDV (post-MDV) from 1 to 6 points. The Gaussian equation was fit to these data points and the mean of the fit was used as the pulse arrival time.

This research article (published June 1, 2003, in Nuclear Instruments and Methods in Physics Research Section A) examines various digital timing methods for determining relative arrival times of pulses from BaF₂ scintillators. The study used two 5.08×2.54 cm BaF₂ detectors with quartz-window Hamamatsu PMTs, digitized by a 1 Gs/s ADC, and compared six digital techniques against analog constant-fraction discrimination.

**Methods tested:** (1) leading edge discrimination, (2) moment-analysis, (3) constant-fraction discrimination, (4) digital constant-fraction discrimination (DCFD), (5) triangular pulse shaping with leading edge linear regression, and (6) pulse-shape fitting (Gaussian fitting).

**Experimental setup:** Two BaF₂ scintillators placed 20 cm apart with a ⁶⁰Co source moved between them in 1 cm increments.

**Key results:** The best average timing resolution (456±8 ps) was obtained with constant-fraction discrimination, slightly higher than the analog average resolution of 419±7 ps. The most complicated method (pulse-shape fitting) was also the most time-consuming. The study concluded that simpler methods may suffice depending on required resolution and accuracy, and that advantages of digital methods include reduced drift, data archiving, and better control over analysis parameters, while limitations include quantization in time and amplitude.

Spencer October 2005 1 Abstract-- Recent advancements in digital signal processing (DSP) using fast processors and a computer allows one to envision using it in pulse shape discrimination. In this study, we have investigated the feasibility of using a DSP to distinguish between neutrons and gamma rays by the shape of their pulses in a liquid scintillator detector (BC501). For neutron/gamma discrimination, the advantage of using a DSP over the analog method is that in an analog system, two separate charge-sensitive ADCs are required. One ADC is used to integrate the beginning of the pulse rise time while the second ADC is for integrating the tail part. In DSP techniques the incoming pulses coming directly from the detector are immediately digitized and can be decomposed into individual pulses waveforms. This eliminates the need for separate ADCs as one can easily get the integration of two parts of the pulse from the digital waveforms. This work describes the performance of these DSP techniques and compares the results with the analog method. Index terms- Digital signal processing, gamma ray/neutron pulse shape discrimination. I. This technique captures the detailed shape of the preamplifier signals using the fast analog-to-digital converters (ADCs), decomposes the inputs into their individual signals, and processes captured waveforms in real time using field-programmable gate arrays (FPGA) and fast digital signal processors to perform all necessary data processing functions digitally. The digital real time processing is now possible because computer CPUs are not only becoming faster and faster, they also have larger and faster memories. In addition, front-end ADCs and FPGAs are currently available at speeds up to 500 MHz and up to 16-bit resolution. The major difference between analog and digital signal processing is that with the digital method after signal conditioning, the preamplifier pulse is digitized immediately and all operations are carried out in digital filters. With the analog signal processing method, the filtering must be completed in relatively slower analog circuits. The DSP system offers significant advantages over the analog system in the areas of cost, accuracy, and efficiency by eliminating a need for extra electronic modules. DSP techniques have been used for pulse shape discrimination to simultaneously measure multiple radiation types such as beta, gamma, and alpha using a single CSI detector [6] or a phoswich detector [7] in which several different scintillators are coupled to a common photomultiplier tube. These techniques were also compared with the analog methods [8,9]. However, this technique has not been fully studied using a liquid scintillator detector (e.g. BC501) to distinguish neutrons from gamma rays by the shape of their pulses produced in the detector. In our past work, we used two analog methods of the pulse shape discrimination (PSD) of charge integration and zero crossing and performed the comparisons between the two. The results of these studies were presented at the IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium in 2001 and published in the Transactions on Nuclear Science journal [10]. They showed that the zero crossing method gives much better PSD for 100 keV electron equivalent (keVee) and lower, whereas the charge integration method leads to better separation above 100 keVee. In this study, we investigated the feasibility of using the digital signal processing to separate neutron from the gamma ray events in a liquid scintillator. II. EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURE Fig. 1 shows the experimental setup with a detector to source distance of 4 inches. The liquid scintillator used in this work was made of the organic scintillator BC501 manufactured by Saint-Gobain, Inc. This is the same detector that we used for the analog signal processing measurements. This detector is 2" in diameter and 2" long coupled to the Phillips XP2020 photomultiplier. Comparison Between Digital and Analog Pulse Shape Discrimination Techniques For Neutron and Gamma Ray Separation Rahmat Aryaeinejad, John K. Hartwell, and David F. Spencer I The pulse shape discrimination techniques are based on the fact that neutrons and gamma rays give different pulse shapes when interacting with the neutron sensitive organic scintillators. The neutron interaction results in a slower timing signal than the gamma-ray interaction. This means that a gamma-ray pulse rises and decays faster from and to the baseline, respectively, than a neutron pulse generated by the recoiled protons. The major difference between these two signals occurs in the tail. A neutron creates a large ionization density by producing a recoil proton resulting in a long tail. A gamma ray, on the other hand, produces scattered electrons with a very small ionization density, and as a result, decays much faster. In analog signal processing two separate charge-sensitive ADCs are needed: one ADC to integrate the beginning of the pulse rise time; and the second ADC for integrating the tail part. Using a DSP eliminates the need for separate ADCs as one can easily get the integration of two parts of the pulse from the digital waveforms. We used the CAMAC digital signal processing module model DGF-4C made by the XIA Corporation [11]. It is a 4-channel module with waveform digitization capable of on-line pulse shape analysis (PSA). It can store waveforms of up to 100 μs long and process 50,000 counts per second per channel into 32K spectra. Unfortunately, its digitization rate is only 40MHz, which means the minimum sampling time is limited to 25 ns. This is not the ideal rate that one would like to use for fast output pulses of the organic liquid scintillator. However, it was the only commercially available DSP module at the time of our investigation. The digitization rate is important for two reasons: 1) the rise of the pulses is slightly different for the gamma rays and neutrons on a 0-10 ns time scale. With a faster ADC (>100MHz), one can easily see this difference and then use it to help distinguish between two events. On the other hand, one can only look at the long component part of the signal and get even a better separation. 2) In this case, the difference in the long component could be examined more accurately if a faster ADC were to be used. Basically, one would be able to optimize the point where the "tail" begins to distinguish between gamma and neutron events. III. MEASUREMENTS AND SUMMARY OF THE RESULTS Table I summarizes the list of parameters used in our measurements. Because the anode signal of the liquid scintillator detector has a fast rise time, we used 0.05 μs for the trigger filter and 0.8 μs for the energy filter, respectively. For pulse shape analysis, a total trace length of 1.0 μs and a delay time of 0.1 μ were used. The latter was necessary for defining the background before the start of the pulse and comparing it with the background in the last 0.1 μs of the end of the trace. The DGF-4C data acquisition system can be operated in two modes - multi-channel analyzer (MCA) mode and list mode. In the MCA mode, the system acts like a typical singles spectrum in which data are collected for a defined period of time and stored in the internal memory. The spectrum can then be saved into a file. In the list mode, however, all the waveforms, energies, and time stamps are collected on an event-by-event basis. In this mode the data can be stored in various formats. In our measurements we used a "0x100" list mode to store full event data plus waveforms into a binary file for later off-line data analysis. Fig. 2 shows the energy spectra Fig. 2. Spectra taken with Cs-137, Co-60 and Cf-252. Fig. 1. Experimental setup showing the 2"x2" liquid scintillator detector and Cf-252 source. Table I. Filtering and PSA parameters used in this study. Filter Parameters Pulse Shape Analysis Trigger Filter Energy Filter Trace Length (μs) 1.0 RiseTime (μs) 0.05 0.8 Delay (μs) 0.1 Flat Top (μs) 0.0 1.2 PSA Start (μs) 0 PSA End (μs) 1 taken with the Cs-137, Co-60, and Cf-252 sources. As we mentioned in our previous work [10], due to the low Z-value of the liquid scintillator, photopeak efficiency is low and an energy calibration using photopeaks is not viable. Consequently, the Compton edge energies of 447 keV for the 662 keV Cs-137 emission and 1041 keV for the average energy of Co-60 1173 and 1333 keV emissions were used to perform the energy calibration [12]. This calibration was used to correlate equivalent electron energy (keVee) corresponding to each threshold setting. A data-sorting program was developed to read the binary event-by-event data file for generating waveforms and sorting the data according to specific configuration parameters defined by the user in the configuration file. This file establishes the default values for the particle identification range, the total normalization range, the background range, and waveform start and end indexes to be displayed. In addition, the energy threshold value can be set in the configuration file. This value will be used to ignore any data that falls below this threshold in the sorting process. The user can modify any or all of these values via an options pop-up dialog shown in Fig. 3. The user has the option to either define a region to determine the average background, or supply a fixed background value in the “Fixed Background Value” edit box. After the program is started and the configuration file parameters are loaded, the screen displays a list of current file and associated waveform values. The program determines overall file length, buffer length (in bytes), the number of words in an event, the number of events in a buffer, and the total number of events for the binary input file. After the threshold-qualified data is stored into internal arrays, it is sorted in ascending order and then compacted. The compacting reduces the input arrays to a list of values and the count of the number of occurrences of the associated values. The output file is then written to disk with header information indicating the range of the optional selections followed by the compacted output values. The configuration parameters determine how the pulse shape analysis will be processed. IV. PSD ANALYSIS RESULTS AND COMPARISON WITH ANALOG METHOD Fig. 4 shows typical waveform traces obtained in our measurements using a Cf-252 source. The total waveform trace length was set to 1.0 μs as shown in table I. The delay region of 0.0-0.1 μs at the beginning of the trace was used to deduce the average background to be subtracted from each data point. In this work we only looked at the long tail component of the traces to distinguish between gamma rays and neutrons. This is because the ADC digitization of the DGF-4C is only 40 MHz and therefore is not fast enough to distinguish between fast rise time components of the traces. The pulse shape analysis can be achieved by properly selecting a region of the tail called the particle identification (PID) window as shown in Fig. 4. The insert in this figure shows the expanded plot of this region. There are three distinct groups of traces labeled 1, 2, and 3. Groups 1 and 3 represent pure gamma ray and pure neutron events, respectively. In group 2 the gamma ray and neutron events are mixed. This is the area that determines how well the low-energy neutrons are separated from the gamma rays, which consequently depends on the energy threshold. It is very important to optimize where the PID window starts and ends Fig. 4. This plot shows the first 50 waveform traces, which were extracted from the data file. Fig. 3. An example of configuration parameters set in the options pop-up dialog box. in order to achieve the largest separation between the traces. In our case, we found that the best discrimination between gamma rays and neutrons was achieved when this PID window is from 0.25 μs to 0.4 μs. We also found the position of the start is substantially more important than the end. In addition, selecting the background at the beginning or the trace led to a slightly better discrimination than the end of the trace.
For PSD analysis, each waveform was integrated in the PID region and then divided by the integral of the whole trace. This ratio is called the particle identification index and is between 0 and 1. It was then plotted versus the number of events or counts. Fig. 5 shows the results of the PSD analysis obtained for the Cs-137, Co-60, and Cf-252 sources. The blue and red plots are for the Cs-137 and Co-60 sources, respectively, that emit only gamma rays, the black plot is for Cf-252, which emits both neutrons and gamma rays. Clearly, for Cf-252, the neutron peak is separated and distinguishable from the gamma-ray peak. Fig. 6 shows the results of the spectra produced with energy threshold cuts of 50, 100, 300, and 600 keVee from the top. To quantify the separation of the peaks corresponding to the neutrons and gamma rays, a figure of merit (FOM) was used: n FWHM FWHM separation peak FOM + = γ _ The peak_separation is the number of channels between the gamma ray peak and neutron peak centroids and the FWHM γ and FWHM n are the full width at half maximum (channels) of the gamma and neutron peaks, respectively. FOM values increase from the top to the bottom spectra as expected. The FOM is shown for each energy threshold. At 50 keVee, the peaks are not completely separated which doesn’t allow the discrimination between all the neutrons and gamma rays. However one can easily separate neutrons from gamma rays with energies above 100 keVee. A comparison with the analog pulse shape discrimination of the zero crossing technique was done using previous measurements performed at the same threshold settings between 50 to 600 keVee [10]. The same detector and Cf-252 source were used. The detector signal was sent to a γ/n discrimination module (Canberra 2160A), which contains an RC-shaping amplifier. This signal was also sent through to a CFD (Tennelec TC454), which produced the start trigger for the time-to-amplitude converter, TAC (Canberra 2143). The γ/n discrimination module sent a pulse corresponding to the zero crossing point of the signal. This signal was then delayed before it was sent to stop the TAC. Finally the TAC signal was sent to an MCA (Canberra Series 20) and the time spectra were recorded. Plots of the MCA spectra are shown in Fig. 7. Table II summarizes the comparison between the two methods of PSD at different electron energy thresholds. A figure of merit was used to compare the results of the two methods. Here, the FOM values for Fig. 5. Digital pulse shape discrimination using Cs-137, Co-60, and Cf-252 sources. No energy thresholds were applied to these spectra. Figure 6. Digital pulse shape analysis showing gamma ray and neutron separation at various electron energy thresholds. Table II. Comparison between digital and analog zero crossing methods versus threshold energy. Threshold (keVee) Digital Method (FOM) Analog Zero Crossing method (FOM) 50 0.850 1.19 100 0.89 1.30 300 0.96 1.45 600 1.04 1.65 both digital and analog methods increases as a function of energy threshold setting. At first glance one can clearly see that the zero crossing method is better for all threshold values from 50 keVee to 600 keVee by a factor of 1.4 to 1.6, respectively. This is mainly because in digital processing the DGF-4C module we used was slow (40 MHz), which limited the sampling rate to 25 ns only. We believe using faster FPGA chips that are commercially available today, like ACTEL 350 MHz or XILINX 450 MHz devices, will substantially improve the separation between gamma-ray and neutron peaks. A 500 MHz chip, for example, gives us a 2 ns resolution as compared to 25 ns sampling rate. With this resolution we can get much better separation, even better than the analog PSD technique, between gamma rays and neutrons. V. CONCLUSIONS In this work, we have investigated the feasibility of using the digital signal processing technique to distinguish neutrons from gamma rays by the shape of their pulses in a liquid scintillator detector (BC501). The results based on FOM values for energy thresholds of 50 to 600 keVee show that a good γ/n discrimination can be achieved using this technique. Comparison with the analog zero crossing method shows that the zero crossing technique gives higher FOM values and therefore a better separation. This is because of the digital processing rate limitation of 40 MHz. Using a faster DSP chip, like a XILINX 450 MHz device with a 2 ns sample rate, will result in much better discrimination. VI. args.summary:
This paper (INL/CON-05-00284) by Rahmat Aryaeinejad, John K. Hartwell, and David F. Spencer from Idaho National Laboratory, presented at the 2005 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium, investigates the feasibility of using digital signal processing (DSP) to distinguish neutrons from gamma rays via pulse shape discrimination (PSD) in a BC501 liquid scintillator detector. The study compares DSP techniques with the analog zero-crossing method.

**Key Methodology:**
- Used a 2"x2" BC501 liquid scintillator detector coupled to a Phillips XP2020 photomultiplier
- Employed a CAMAC DGF-4C module (XIA Corporation) with 40 MHz digitization rate (25 ns sampling)
- Neutron pulses have longer tails due to recoil protons; gamma-ray pulses decay faster
- PSD performed by integrating the tail region (PID window from 0.25 μs to 0.4 μs) divided by total trace integral
- Sources used: Cs-137 (gamma only), Co-60 (gamma only), Cf-252 (neutrons and gamma rays)

**Results:**
- Digital method achieved good neutron/gamma separation at energy thresholds of 50-600 keVee
- Figure of Merit (FOM) values for digital method: 0.850 (50 keVee), 0.89 (100 keVee), 0.96 (300 keVee), 1.04 (600 keVee)
- Analog zero-crossing method outperformed digital by factor of 1.4-1.6x (FOM: 1.19 at 50 keVee to 1.65 at 600 keVee)
- The limitation was attributed to the 40 MHz digitization rate of the DGF-4C module

**Conclusion:**
The authors conclude that with faster DSP chips (e.g., XILINX 450 MHz devices with 2 ns sample rate), digital PSD could achieve better separation than analog methods. The DSP approach eliminates the need for separate charge-sensitive ADCs required in analog systems.

• input signal decreases with increasing input capacitance, so signal-to-noise ratio depends on detector capacitance.
In a charge-sensitive preamplifier, the signal at the amplifier output is independent of detector capacitance (if Ci >>Cdet ).
What is the noise behavior?
• Noise appearing at the output of the preamplifier is fed back to the input, decreasing the output noise from the open-loop value vno= vni Av0.
• The magnitude of the feedback depends on the shunt impedance at the input, i.e. the detector capacitance.
Note, that although specified as an equivalent input noise, the dominant noise sources are typically internal to the amplifier.
Only in a fed-back configuration is some of this noise actually present at the input. In other words, the primary noise signal is not a physical charge (or voltage) at the amplifier input, to which the loop responds in the same manner as to a detector signal.
⇒ S/N at the amplifier output depends on feedback.

In the time domain this result is more intuitive. Since every shaper also acts as an integrator, one can view the total shot noise as the result of “counting electrons”.
Assume an ideal integrator that records all charge uniformly within a time T. The number of electron charges measured is The associated noise is the fluctuation in the number of electron charges recorded Does this also apply to an AC-coupled system, where no DC current flows, so no electrons are “counted”?
Since shot noise is a fluctuation, the current undergoes both positive and negative excursions. Although the DC component is not passed through an AC coupled system, the excursions are.
Since, on the average, each fluctuation requires a positive and a negative zero crossing, the process of “counting electrons” is actually the counting of zero crossings, which in a detailed analysis yields the same result.

args.summary:
This is a technical course note from the 1999 IEEE NPSS Short Course on Radiation Detection and Measurement, presented by Helmuth Spieler of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The document covers pulse processing and analysis for radiation detector systems, organized into 8 sections:

1. **Acquiring the Detector Signal**: Detector signals are short current pulses proportional to deposited energy. The total charge must be integrated. Methods include integration on input capacitance (which depends on detector capacitance) or using a charge-sensitive preamplifier. The charge-sensitive amplifier uses feedback to make the output signal independent of detector capacitance, with effective input capacitance Ci = Cf(A+1). Realistic amplifiers have finite bandwidth, and rise time increases with detector capacitance.

2. **Resolution and Signal-to-Noise Ratio**: Two resolution regimes: (1) signal variance >> baseline variance (e.g., high-gain PMTs), where electronic noise is unimportant; (2) signal variance << baseline variance (e.g., semiconductor detectors), where electronic noise is critical. Basic noise mechanisms include thermal noise (4kTR spectral density), shot noise (2qeI spectral density), and 1/f noise. Noise bandwidth differs from signal bandwidth. Signal-to-noise ratio depends on detector capacitance.

3. **Pulse Shaping**: Balances two conflicting objectives: (a) improve S/N by restricting bandwidth (increasing pulse width), and (b) improve pulse pair resolution (decreasing pulse width). CR-RC shaping is a simple example. Equivalent Noise Charge (ENC) is the input charge yielding S/N=1. ENC depends on shaping time constants, with current noise ∝ τ, voltage noise ∝ 1/τ, and 1/f noise independent of τ. Optimal shaping time occurs when voltage and current noise contributions are equal.

4. **Noise Analysis**: Includes analytical methods, experimental determination (using pulse generators and spectrum analyzers), and numerical simulation (SPICE). The equivalent circuit includes detector bias resistor, coupling capacitor, series resistance, and amplifier noise sources. A numerical expression for CR-RC shaper ENC is provided.

5. **Time-Variant Shapers**: Correlated double sampling and gated integrators are analyzed. The weighting function approach allows noise analysis in the time domain. For current noise, the weighting function is the shaper's step response; for voltage noise, it's the derivative. Time-variant shapers can achieve different noise trade-offs (e.g., less voltage noise but more current noise).

6. **Shaper Comparison**: Multi-integrator shapers (up to n=8) provide more symmetrical pulses with faster return to baseline. Time-invariant vs. time-variant trapezoidal shapers show different noise characteristics.

The key takeaway is that optimum shaping depends on the application, and practical considerations often lead to non-textbook compromises. The fundamental noise limit is electronic noise, and S/N cannot be improved by feedback alone.

# Analog vs digital simulation: advanced real-time guide

04 / 25 / 2025

![Analog vs digital simulation: advanced real-time guide](https://www.opal-rt.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Hero-Image-2-1024x538.png?format=auto)

Organizations in automotive, aerospace, and [power systems](https://www.opal-rt.com/power-systems-overview/) often face high-stakes decisions when replicating complex signals. The right simulation strategy can reduce design risk, protect budgets, and unify technical teams across the organization. Senior engineers, R&D managers, and technical leads who need reliable, real-time data on circuit performance or embedded software behavior can gain an advantage by selecting the most effective simulation approach for their goals. This overview compares analog and digital simulation methods, offers concrete examples of how each is used, and clarifies the value of integrating both in a unified [hardware-in-the-loop (HIL)](https://www.opal-rt.com/hardware-in-the-loop/) platform.

## Why simulation strategies matter for advanced engineering

High-fidelity simulation is critical for professionals who build advanced power systems, [automotive electronics](https://www.opal-rt.com/automotive-overview/), aerospace controls, and beyond. A robust simulation platform can validate hardware and software under realistic boundary conditions, reveal hidden design flaws, and support rapid iteration without risking physical equipment. By focusing on real-time performance and open integration with standard modeling tools, engineers and technical leaders can streamline testing, meet stringent safety requirements, and stay ahead of unexpected changes.

Real-time simulation aligns with product deadlines and mitigates the need for expensive prototypes. It also clarifies system behavior for cross-functional teams—from software developers verifying code to hardware specialists optimizing circuit topologies. Thorough exploration of analog and digital simulation ensures projects leverage the right mix of continuous signal analysis and discrete logic checks.

## The fundamentals of analog simulation

Analog simulation uses continuous signal models to represent varying voltages and currents in real time. Rather than looking at on/off or binary states, analog methods treat signals as uninterrupted waveforms, providing a direct view of physical phenomena.

Senior engineers working on power conversion, sensor feedback loops, or control circuitry often prefer analog methods because these techniques capture small voltage shifts, noise, and temperature effects that can alter performance. Accurate waveforms matter when verifying stability in operational amplifiers, analyzing electromagnetic interference, or confirming that filtering components function properly under load.

Development cycles benefit when teams can exercise an analog simulation model with different operating conditions and boundary parameters. This deeper visibility fosters confidence that a design will respond properly to variations in load, temperature, or supply voltage. Engineers can then reduce guesswork during prototyping and deliver more reliable hardware for subsequent testing phases.

> ***Some combine both methods through hybrid simulation to capture continuous elements alongside discrete ones.***

## Key applications of analog simulation

Analog methods suit scenarios where continuous signals play a major role. Examples include:

* **Power generation & transmission:** Utilities often replicate grid fluctuations in high-voltage networks to confirm that converters and other equipment can withstand fault conditions. Analog simulation supports investigations of harmonic distortion and grid stability when integrating renewable sources.
* **Aerospace controls:** Flight control engineers test inertial guidance boards or sensor feedback loops to confirm that outputs remain stable across a range of stress factors. Analog waveforms show real voltage responses, allowing precise design improvements.
* **Industrial automation:** Production lines and robotic arms rely on constant signaling for actuators, drives, and sensors. Analog simulation helps validate motor drivers, reduce power consumption, and maintain consistent performance.
* **Automotive electronics:** Hybrid and [electric vehicles](https://www.opal-rt.com/automotive-overview/) often incorporate complex powertrains. Analog simulation assists with evaluating converter topologies, sensor interfaces, and battery management circuits under varying loads.
* **Research & academia:** Labs focused on electromagnetic interactions, high-frequency applications, or advanced control algorithms often require analog simulations to verify ideas before building physical prototypes.
* **Consumer electronics:** Engineers designing wearables, smartphones, or gaming devices use analog techniques to check amplifier performance, battery management, and thermal behavior.

These activities target real signal integrity at every stage. Precisely modeling operational amplifiers, feedback circuits, and filters removes guesswork. Engineers can anticipate design challenges ahead of production, cutting down on multiple prototyping rounds.

## The fundamentals of digital simulation

[Digital simulation](https://www.opal-rt.com/simulation-acceleration/) deals with discrete states—often represented as binary logic or multi-level signals. Instead of examining continuous voltage waveforms, this method tracks changes at defined time steps, which suits software-driven operations, microcontrollers, or digital signal processing tasks.

R&D and test engineers favor digital simulation to verify firmware logic, communication protocols, and timing across large systems. Code-level issues can be identified before final hardware arrives, sparing teams from rework. By replicating on/off states, engineers can confirm that software triggers happen at precise intervals, data formatting is correct, and clock signals align with design requirements.

Digital simulations tend to run faster because they skip the detailed math of continuous waveforms, making it easier to apply automation in regression testing. This reduces the chance of missing corner cases in logic flows. Many industries rely on digital simulation to confirm reliability in devices that handle data transmission, user interfaces, or sensor sampling.

> ***At OPAL-RT, decades of expertise and a commitment to excellence guide our delivery of open, scalable, and high-performance solutions for hardware-in-the-loop, software-in-the-loop, and beyond.***

## Key applications of digital simulation

Projects involving digital logic or large codebases often benefit from digital methods:

* **Microprocessor design:** Semiconductor firms run register-transfer-level checks to confirm timing for signals that move between functional blocks. Early detection of errors avoids costly chip re-spins.
* **Networking & communications:** Engineers validate protocols to confirm proper handshakes, error checking, and packet transfers. This approach detects cryptic bugs in advanced data routing and industrial IoT systems.
* **Automotive control units:** Complex firmware in battery management, ADAS (Advanced Driver Assistance Systems), and body electronics requires thorough verification. Digital simulation flags concurrency issues or missed interrupts that jeopardize safety.
* **Industrial robotics:** Controller software drives motion planning, sensor fusion, and operational checks. Digital simulations of these logic flows foster consistent performance in manufacturing environments.
* **Medical devices:** Regulatory standards demand that implantable devices and patient monitors go through rigorous testing. Digital simulation confirms code reliability under boundary conditions before clinical trials.
* **Consumer device firmware:** Features like touchscreen response, battery optimization, and data encryption can be modeled with discrete logic to reduce firmware rollbacks and ensure a stable user experience.

A careful digital testing approach saves time and budget by avoiding multiple hardware prototype runs. It also encourages collaboration between embedded software teams and hardware designers.

## Core differences between analog and digital simulation

The main distinction lies in signal representation. Analog models continuous waveforms, capturing every fractional change in current or voltage. Digital methods rely on discrete states or steps. The choice depends on the system’s primary nature:

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Aspect** | **Analog Simulation** | **Digital Simulation** |
| **Signal Representation** | Continuous waveforms, varying over time | Discrete states (often binary or multi-level) |
| **Typical Use Cases** | Circuit stability, noise, sensors | Firmware logic, communication protocols |
| **Accuracy vs. Speed** | High precision, potentially slower execution | Faster execution, less granularity in analog detail |
| **Tools/Methodologies** | SPICE-like solvers, real-time analog platforms | HDL-based verification, logic analyzers |
| **Industry Examples** | Power grids, sensor feedback loops | Microprocessor design, ADAS firmware |

Some organizations combine both. A hybrid approach allows analog waveforms to coexist with discrete logic states. This can be essential for large systems—consider an automotive powertrain with both analog sensor signals and digital microcontrollers. Engineers benefit from the ability to evaluate everything in one place, especially when real-time hardware-in-the-loop test setups bring these processes closer to actual operating conditions.

## Selecting the right method

Senior engineers and technical leads often weigh the following factors when deciding on analog or digital simulation:

* **Nature of the signals:** Systems based on continuous voltages or currents often favor analog methods. Digital logic or state-based design calls for binary-style modeling.
* **Scope and complexity:** Large systems with multiple microcontrollers could benefit from digital simulation, while subsystems that include intricate circuits need analog detail.  
   **Time and cost constraints:** Digital simulations usually run faster and may allow more tests per hour. Analog simulations can be more computationally intense, yet reveal subtle phenomena missed by discrete modeling.
* **Stage of development:** Early conceptual work might focus on high-level digital checks. Later refinement might need analog detail for final fine-tuning of power electronics or sensor loops.
* **Integration with Hardware-in-the-Loop:** Real-time HIL often combines analog [I/O channels](https://www.opal-rt.com/io-and-communication-interfaces/) with digital interfaces to represent every aspect of the design. One consolidated platform saves time and fosters more meaningful collaboration among mechanical, electrical, and software teams.

In many cases, an organization will pair both methods to cover all design layers. Digital checks can validate logic flow and firmware timing, while analog checks confirm that real signals stay within safe margins.

## Emerging methods and tools in simulation

Technical leaders see new avenues in simulation through cloud-based resources, machine learning-assisted modeling, and unified real-time platforms that handle both analog and digital signals. Parallel processing on FPGAs (Field-Programmable Gate Arrays) expands the potential to run high-fidelity simulations at a rate that keeps up with real hardware. This is particularly valuable for testing power electronics, advanced battery systems, and complex microgrids.

Multi-domain models bring mechanical, electrical, and software elements together so engineers don’t have to bounce between separate tools. This creates a single source of truth, reducing manual alignment across teams. Open software architectures also let smaller teams adopt real-time simulation without major up-front investment in proprietary solutions.

By selecting modern real-time simulation platforms, engineers gain:

* **Scalable performance:** Configure processing capability based on project scope.
* **Open toolchains:** Use industry-standard modeling environments (MATLAB/Simulink, FMI/FMU, Python) without vendor lock-in.
* **High-fidelity results:** Benefit from specialized modules for power electronics, automotive control, or aerospace.
* **Collaboration across locations:** Work with colleagues in remote labs or different departments by sharing the same validated models.

Organizations that integrate these solutions often discover quicker time-to-market cycles and a sharper ability to handle late-stage changes or new requirements.

## Real-time simulation

OPAL-RT provides real-time solutions that match the needs of senior simulation engineers, R&D managers, and system architects looking to validate complex designs. Our platforms combine analog precision and digital scalability, making them ideal for automotive powertrains, grid emulation, flight controls, and other demanding applications.

* **Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) test:** Verify hardware interactions early by connecting physical components or control units to real-time simulators. This reveals system-level behavior, bridging analog signals and digital logic in a single setup.
* **Open architecture:** Seamlessly integrate with MATLAB/Simulink, Python, and established toolchains. Our solutions address specific industry standards, including communication protocols for automotive, utilities, and aerospace.
* **Scalable performance:** Start with a smaller configuration for initial testing and ramp up as projects grow more complex. This accommodates emerging technologies like autonomy or wide-bandgap semiconductors.
* **High-fidelity FPGA capabilities:** Capture fast transients and microsecond-scale events with [FPGA-based simulators](https://www.opal-rt.com/solver-ehs/). This approach is essential for power electronics, propulsion systems, and advanced sensor modeling.
* **Ease of collaboration:** Let cross-functional teams validate designs from a common interface, share data, and align on real test outcomes. This cuts iteration time and clarifies technical debates.

# Analog vs Digital Systems The Ultimate 2026 Comparison Guide

08 May 2026 3713

Analog and digital systems are two fundamental technologies in electronics, communication, and control systems.

Analog systems process continuous signals, while digital systems use binary data to process information.

Understanding their differences, similarities, applications, and limitations is essential for choosing the right system for modern electronic and industrial applications.

This guide explores analog vs digital systems in detail, including common misconceptions and which system is best suited for different needs in 2026.

## What Is an Analog System?

An analog system uses continuous signals  to process and transmit information.

These signals vary smoothly over time and can represent real-world physical quantities such as temperature, sound, pressure, light, or speed.

Unlike digital systems use binary values (0s and 1s), analog systems can handle an infinite range of values within a specific range.

Analog systems are commonly used in devices that interact directly with natural signals because most real-world phenomena are naturally analog.

For example, the sound captured by a microphone or the temperature measured by a thermometer changes continuously rather than in fixed steps.

In electronics and control applications, analog systems use components such as resistors, capacitors, inductors, and transistors to process signals.

These systems are favored for their smooth signal representation, fast real-time response, and simplicity in certain applications.

Common examples of analog systems include traditional radios, vinyl record players, analog clocks, and mercury thermometers.

## Common Examples of Analog Devices

Analog Clock: One of the most familiar analog devices. Analog clocks use continuously moving hands to display time.

Mercury Thermometer: A mercury thermometer measures temperature through the continuous expansion and contraction of mercury inside a glass tube.

Vinyl Record Player: Record players use continuous analog audio signals engraved on vinyl discs to store and reproduce sound.

Analog Radio: AM and FM radios receive and process continuously varying radio frequency signals for audio broadcasting.

Microphone: Traditional microphones convert sound waves into continuous electrical signals for audio transmission and recording.

Analog Voltmeter: Analog voltmeters use a moving needle to display electrical voltage levels in real time.

CRT Television: Older cathode-ray tube televisions process analog broadcast signals to display images and sound.

Tape Recorder: Cassette tape recorders store audio as continuous magnetic signals on magnetic tape.

Analog Camera: Film cameras capture images using chemical reactions on photographic film rather than digital sensors.

Oscilloscope (Analog Type): Analog oscilloscopes display continuously changing electrical waveforms for signal analysis and testing.

## What Is a Digital System?

A digital system uses discrete signals to process, store, and transmit information, typically represented by binary numbers such as 0s and 1s.

Unlike analog systems use continuously varying signals, digital systems use fixed values, making them more accurate, reliable, and easier to process.

Digital systems convert real-world analog signals into digital data through devices such as analog-to-digital converters (ADCs).

Once converted, computers, microcontrollers, and digital circuits process the data with high precision and minimal signal loss.

These systems are widely used in modern technology because they support fast computation, efficient data storage, automation, and advanced communication.

Digital systems are also less affected by electrical noise and can easily integrate with software and intelligent control systems.

Common examples of digital systems include computers, smartphones, digital watches, calculators, smart TVs, and modern automotive control systems.

## Common Examples of Digital Control

Computer Numerical Control (CNC) Machines: CNC machines use digital controllers to automate cutting, drilling, and manufacturing processes with high precision.

Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs): PLCs are widely used in factories and industrial automation to control machines, conveyors, and production systems.

Smart Thermostats: Digital thermostats automatically control heating and cooling systems using programmed temperature settings and sensors.

Automotive Engine Control Units (ECUs): Modern vehicles use digital control systems to manage fuel injection, ignition timing, braking, and engine performance.

Robotics Systems: Industrial and service robots rely on digital controllers for movement, positioning, and task automation.

Traffic Light Control Systems: Digital control systems manage traffic signals by analyzing timing, traffic flow, and sensor data.

Washing Machines: Modern washing machines use digital controllers to regulate washing cycles, water levels, and spin speeds.

Drone Flight Controllers: Drones use digital control systems to stabilize flight, process sensor data, and manage navigation.

Elevator Control Systems: Digital controllers coordinate elevator movement, door operation, and floor selection efficiently and safely.

Smart Home Automation Systems: Devices such as smart lighting, security systems, and voice-controlled assistants use digital control for automation and remote operation.

## Similarities Between Digital and Analog Systems

Process Information: Analog and digital systems process, transmit, and control information in electronic and communication systems.

Use Electrical Signals: Both systems rely on electrical signals to perform operations, but the signal formats are different.

In Control Systems: Analog and digital technologies are commonly used in automation, industrial control, and monitoring applications.

Require Input and Output Devices: Each system uses sensors, transducers, and output devices to interact with real-world environments.

Used for Communication: Analog and digital systems can transmit audio, video, and data signals through communication networks.

Use Electronic Components: Both analog and digital systems contain electronic components such as resistors, capacitors, transistors, and integrated circuits.

Can Work Together: Many modern devices combine analog and digital technologies to form hybrid systems for better performance and efficiency.

Improve Accuracy and Efficiency: Although they operate differently, both systems provide reliable operation, signal processing, and effective control.

## Main Difference between Analog and Digital Systems

The main difference between analog and digital systems lies in how they represent and process information.

Analog systems use continuous signals that vary smoothly over time, while digital systems use discrete signals represented in binary form (0s and 1s).

### Signal Type

Analog signals are continuous and smoothly varying (such as sinusoidal waves), while digital signals are discrete and represented in binary form (such as square waves and bits).

### Data Representation

* Analog systems represent information using continuously varying physical quantities (such as voltage, sound waves, or temperature changes).

* Digital systems represent information using discrete binary values (0s and 1s).

### Accuracy and Precision

Analog systems can represent values in a continuous range, but they are more susceptible to noise and signal distortion, and their accuracy decreases over time.

Digital systems provide higher accuracy and consistent precision by representing data in exact binary values (0s and 1s) with minimal error.

### Noise Sensitivity

Analog systems are highly sensitive to noise and external interference, which can distort or degrade the signal quality during transmission or processing,

Digital systems are much more resistant to noise because they use binary signals (0s and 1s) and can easily regenerate without losing original information.

### Storage and Processing

Analog systems store and process information in continuous form, leading to difficult long-term storage and gradual signal degradation.

Digital systems store and process data in binary format (0s and 1s), allowing for easy, accurate, and lossless storage, copying, and fast computational processing.

### Flexibility

Analog systems have limited flexibility because their behavior is directly dependent on physical signal variations and hardware constraints.

Digital systems are highly flexible, allowing easy modification, software-based control, and integration with modern technologies like AI, automation, and IoT.

In simple terms, analog systems deal with continuous real-world signals, while digital systems convert those signals into binary data for more accurate, efficient, and scalable processing.

## Analog vs Digital Systems Applications

### Analog System Applications

#### Audio Systems

Analog technology is used in audio devices such as microphones, amplifiers, speakers, and record players. In these devices, the sound is captured and reproduced as continuous wave signals.

#### Radio Communication

AM and FM radio broadcasting rely on analog signals and use varying frequencies and amplitudes to transmit audio information over long distances.

#### Measurement and Instrumentation

Analog devices like voltmeters, ammeters, thermometers, and pressure gauges measure physical quantities in real time.

#### Medical Equipment

Many medical instruments, such as ECG machines and traditional blood pressure monitors, use analog signals to capture and display continuous physiological data.

#### Industrial Sensors and Control

In industries, analog sensors measure temperature, pressure, flow, and speed in processes that require real-time monitoring.

#### Television Systems (Older Models)

Older CRT televisions used analog signals to transmit and display video and audio content before the shift to digital broadcasting.

#### Analog Photography

Film cameras use chemical processes on photographic film to capture continuous light information and create images.

#### Signal Processing Equipment

Oscilloscopes and signal generators often use analog circuits to analyze and display waveforms in electronics testing and development.

### Digital System Applications

#### Computing Devices

Digital systems are the foundation of computers, laptops, and servers, enabling fast data processing, storage, and complex computations.

#### Mobile Devices

Smartphones and tablets use digital systems for communication, internet browsing, applications, gaming, and multimedia processing.

#### Industrial Automation

Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) and robotics systems use digital control for manufacturing, assembly lines, and process automation.

#### Automotive Electronics

Modern vehicles rely on digital systems for engine control units (ECUs), navigation systems, anti-lock braking systems (ABS), and driver assistance features.

#### Communication Networks

Digital systems power the internet, Wi-Fi, 4G/5G networks, and satellite communication, ensuring fast and reliable data transmission.

#### Smart Home Technology

Devices like smart thermostats, lighting systems, security cameras, and voice assistants use digital control for automation and remote access.

#### Healthcare Technology

Digital systems are used in MRI machines, CT scanners, patient monitoring systems, and digital diagnostic equipment for accurate medical analysis.

#### Entertainment and Media

Streaming platforms, digital cameras, video editing tools, and gaming consoles rely on digital processing for high-quality media creation and delivery.

#### Hybrid Applications in Modern Systems

Many modern devices combine analog and digital technologies. For example, smartphones use analog sensors (like microphones and cameras) but convert the signals into digital data for processing, storage, and transmission.

## Analog or Digital Which Is More Accurate?

![Digital Signal and Their Devices](https://static.ventronchip.com/static/thumbnail/placeholder.gif)Digital Signal and Their Devices

In most practical applications, digital systems are more accurate than analog systems.

Because digital systems represent information using fixed binary values (0s and 1s). This reduces uncertainty and minimizes the impact of noise or signal degradation during processing and transmission.

On the other hand, analog systems represent data as continuous signals, which can capture fine variations in real-world phenomena.

However, these signals are more susceptible to interference, distortion, and environmental noise, reducing overall accuracy over time.

![Analog Signal and Their Devices](https://static.ventronchip.com/static/thumbnail/placeholder.gif)Analog Signal and Their Devices

Digital systems also allow for error detection and correction techniques, making them highly reliable for long-distance communication, data storage, and complex computations.

Once analog signals are converted into digital form using analog-to-digital converters (ADCs), the data can be processed with high precision and consistency.

Nevertheless, analog systems can still be more “naturally precise” in certain real-time measurements, such as audio or sensor signals, where continuous variation is important.

In modern engineering, the most accurate solutions often combine both systems, capturing real-world analog signals and processing them digitally for maximum precision.

## Common Misconceptions About Analog and Digital Systems

### “Digital Is Always Better”

* Many people assume digital systems are superior in every case.

* In reality, while digital systems offer higher precision and reliability, analog systems can still outperform in real-time response and natural signal representation in certain applications.

### “Analog Is Obsolete”

* It is often believed that analog technology is outdated.

* However, analog systems are still widely used in sensors, audio equipment, communication hardware, and as the first stage of almost all digital systems (signal acquisition).

### “Digital Signals Have No Noise”

* Digital systems are completely unaffected by noise.

* While they are more resistant, noise can still affect digital signals, especially during analog-to-digital conversion or in poor transmission environments.

### “Analog Systems Are Simpler in All Situations”

Although analog circuits are simple for basic tasks, complex analog systems are very difficult to design, calibrate, and maintain compared to modern digital systems.

### “Digital Means Perfect Accuracy”

-Digital systems are highly accurate, but they are still limited by sampling rates, quantization errors, and conversion processes.

-They do not represent reality perfectly but rather approximate it with high precision.

Analog and digital systems have strengths and limitations. Misunderstanding them lead to incorrect design choices. Therefore, many modern technologies combine them for optimal performance.

## Which System Should You Choose?

Choosing between analog and digital systems depends on the specific application, performance requirements, and operating environment.

### Choose Analog Systems When:

#### Real-Time Signal Response Is Critical

Analog systems are best when you need immediate, continuous response without delay, such as in live audio amplification or real-time sensor monitoring.

#### Working with Natural Signals

Choose analog when dealing directly with physical phenomena like sound, temperature, pressure, or light, because these signals are naturally continuous.

#### Simpler Circuit Design Is Preferred

For basic applications where high-level processing is not required, analog circuits can provide a simpler and more cost-effective solution.

#### Requiring High Sensitivity Measurement

Analog systems are useful in applications that require detecting small changes in signals, such as precision measurement instruments and scientific sensors.

#### Requiring Low-Latency Performance

In systems where minimal processing delay is undesirable, analog control can provide faster response compared to digital processing.

#### Basic Industrial and Audio Applications

Analog systems are still commonly used in audio equipment, RF communication, and industrial control systems where smooth and continuous signal handling is essential.

### Choose Digital Systems When:

#### Requiring High Accuracy and Precision

Digital systems are the best choice when you need consistent, repeatable results with minimal error, such as in computing, measurements, and data processing.

#### Data Storage and Processing Are Important

Choose digital systems when large amounts of information need to store, copy, or process efficiently without signal degradation.

#### Noise Resistance Is Essential

Digital systems are ideal in environments with electrical interference because binary signals (0s and 1s) are less affected by noise than analog signals.

#### Needing Complex Computation

When tasks involve advanced calculations, algorithms, or automation, digital systems provide the processing power needed for complex operations.

#### Requiring Integration with Software and AI

Digital systems are necessary when working with modern technologies like artificial intelligence, machine learning, IoT, and cloud computing.

#### Scalability and Flexibility Matter

Choose digital systems when you need easy upgrades, system expansion, and flexible control through software rather than hardware changes.

#### Modern Communication and Control Systems

Digital systems are preferred in internet communication, mobile devices, robotics, and automotive electronics due to their speed, reliability, and efficiency.

### Hybrid Systems Best Modern Solution

-In most modern technologies, the best solution is combining analog and digital systems.

-Analog signals are often used to capture real-world information, then converted it into digital form for processing, storage, and control.

-The hybrid approach is used in smartphones, medical devices, automotive systems, and industrial automation.

### Factors to Consider

Accuracy Requirements: Determine the accuracy your application requires the system to achieve.

Speed and Response Time: Consider whether continuous real-time response or computational processing is more important.

Noise Environment: Evaluate the amount of electrical interference the system may experience.

Complexity: Analog systems are simpler for basic tasks, while digital systems handle complex operations more efficiently.

Cost: Compare hardware, maintenance, and long-term scalability costs.

Scalability and Flexibility: Digital systems are generally easier to upgrade and integrate with software-based technologies.

Application Type: The intended use, such as audio, communication, automation, sensing, or computing, greatly influences the best system choice.

Analog and digital systems play a vital role in modern technology. They offer unique strengths and are suitable for different applications.

Analog systems excel in representing real-world, continuously varying signals and provide fast, natural responses in areas like audio processing, sensing, and basic control.

Digital systems, on the other hand, deliver higher accuracy, better noise resistance, and powerful data processing capabilities. They are essential for computing, communication, and automation.

In today’s technology, combinating analog and digital systems are key to building efficient, reliable, and high-performing systems.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is 4 20mA analog or digital?

4-20 mA is an analog current loop signal. It uses a continuous range of current (4mA = 0% to 20mA = 100%) to represent process variables.

### What are 5 examples of analog devices?

Common examples of analog devices include mercury thermometer, analog clock (watch), speedometer, microphone, and voltmeter.

### Is Wi-Fi analog or digital?

Wi-Fi uses digital signals to transmit data (0s and 1s) between devices, but it uses analog radio waves to broadcast these signals.

### Is Gen Z going analog?

Yes, Gen Z is actively embracing an "analog renaissance" in 2026. It is a deliberate shift to foster deeper focus and disconnect from oversaturated, algorithm-driven feeds.

### How to tell if a device is analog or digital?

Check if the device uses continuous signals/physical movement (analog) or discrete, sampled data (digital). Analog devices have smooth, variable, or physical movement; digital devices operate on a binary 0s/1s system to store or transmit data.

### Why use analog instead of digital?

Because analog signal has superior, continuous representation of real-world phenomena (e.g., sound and light), and offers higher, infinite, resolution without the sampling errors in digital data.

### Which is better, 4/20ma or 0 10v?

4-20mA is better for long-distance, noise-resistant industrial applications due to high noise immunity and fault detection. 0-10V is ideal for short-distance, cost-sensitive, or local devices.

### Are CDs analog or digital?

CDs (Compact Discs) are a digital audio format. They store sound as microscopic pits on a reflective surface, which represent binary code (0s and 1s).

### What are the 4 types of digital computers?

Based on size, speed, and processing power, the four main types of digital computers are Microcomputers, Minicomputers, Mainframe Computers, and Supercomputers.

### Is analog always better than digital?

No, analog is not always better than digital, depending personal preference, application, and intended aesthetic. Analog excels in capturing continuous signals naturally, while digital offers precision, noise resistance, and easier processing for most modern applications.

### What industries use analog devices?

Industries including automotive, industrial automation, communications, healthcare, and consumer electronics use analog devices for precise, continuous measurements (e.g., pressure sensors, thermometers, ECG machines).

Abstract

Analog computers can be revived as a feasible technology platform for low precision, energy efficient and fast computing. We justify this statement by measuring the performance of a modern analog computer and comparing it with that of traditional digital processors. General statements are made about the solution of ordinary and partial differential equations. Computational fluid dynamics are discussed as an example of large scale scientific computing applications. Several models are proposed which demonstrate the benefits of analog and digital-analog hybrid computing.

1 Introduction

Digital computing has transformed many — if not close to all — aspects of industry, humanities and science. Turing completeness allows statements to be made about the computability and decidability of problems and *computational power* of machines. Digital storage has undergone numerous technological advances and is available in increasingly vast amounts. Nevertheless, contemporary digital computing is possibly not the last word in computing, despite its dominance in the consumer market for the last 40+ years.

Fundamental research about non-traditional (also referred to as *unconventional* or *exotic*) computing is taking place in material sciences, chemistry but also in more exotic branches such as biology and life sciences. Amongst others, beyond-Turing computing ([Siegelmann](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx39), [1995](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx39)), natural computing ([Calude et al.](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx6), [1999](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx6)), neuromorphic computing ([Schuman et al.](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx37), [2017](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx37); [Ziegler](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx55), [2020](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx55)) or quantum computing ([Zhou et al.](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx54), [2020](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx54); [Georgescu et al.](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx18), [2014](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx18); [Kendon et al.](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx26), [2010](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx26)) are fields of active investigation. Being fundamental research at heart, these disciplines come with technological challenges. For instance, computing with DNA still requires the use of large scale laboratory equipment and machinery ([Deaton et al.](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx12), [1998](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx12)). Currently, not only the low-temperature laboratory conditions but also the necessary error correction schemes challenge practical quantum computers ([Wilhelm et al.](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx53), [2017](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx53)). This currently negates any practical advantage over silicon based digital computing. Furthermore, all of these alternative (or *exotic*) computer architectures share the characteristic that they are fundamentally *non-portable*. This means they will have to be located at large facilities and dedicated special-purpose computing centers for a long time, if not forever. This is not necessarily a practical drawback, since the internet allows for delocalization of systems.

In contrast to this, silicon based *electronic analog computing* is a technology with a rich history, which operates in a normal workplace environment (non-laboratory conditions;  [Ulmann](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx47), [2020](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx47)). Digital computers overtook their analog counterparts in the last century, primarily due to their ever-increasing digital clock speeds and their flexibility that comes from their algorithmic approach and the possibility of using these machines in a time-shared environment. However, today Moore's law is coming to a hard stop and processor clock speeds have not significantly increased in the past decade. Manycore architectures and vectorization come with their own share of problems, given their fundamental limits as described, for instance, by Amdahl's law ([Rodgers](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx34), [1985](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx34)). GPGPUs and specialized digital computing chips concentrate on vectorized, and even data flow-oriented programming paradigms but are still limited by parasitic capacitances which determine the maximum possible clock frequency and provide a noticeable *energy barrier*.

Thanks to their properties, analog computers have attracted the interest of many research groups. For surveys of theory and applications, see for instance [Bournez and Pouly](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx3) ([2021](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx3)) or the works of [MacLennan](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx28) ([2004](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx28), [2012](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx29), [2019](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx30)). In this paper, we study the usability of analog computers for applications in science. The fundamental properties of analog computers are low power requirements, low resolution computation and intrinsic parallelism. Two very different uses cases/scenarios can be identified: High performance computing (HPC) and low energy portable computing. The energy and computational demands for both scenarios are diametrically-opposed and this paper is primarily focused on HPC.

The paper is structured as follows: In Sect. [2](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#Ch1.S2), we review the general assumptions about digital and analog computing. In Sect. [3](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#Ch1.S3), small scale benchmark results are presented for a simple ordinary differential equation. In Sect. [4](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#Ch1.S4), a typical partial differential equation is considered as an example for a large scale problem. Spatial discretization effects and computer architecture design choices are discussed. Finally, Sect. [5](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#Ch1.S5) summarizes the findings.

2 A Simple (Linear) Model for Comparing Analog and Digital Performance

In this paper, we study different techniques for solving differential equations computationally. Due to the different conventions in algorithmic and analog approaches, a common language had to be found and is described in this section. Here, the term *algorithmic approach* addresses the classical Euler method or classical quasi-linear techniques in ordinary or partial differential equations (ODEs/PDEs), *i.e.*, general methods of numerical mathematics. The term *analog approach* addresses the continuous time integration with an operational amplifier having a capacitor in the feedback loop. The fundamental measures of computer performance under consideration are the time-to-solution *T*, the power consumption *P* and the energy demand *E*.

It should be emphasized that, in the general case, this estimate for the digital computer is a most optimistic (best) estimate, using today's numerical methods. It does not take into account hypothetical algorithmic “shortcuts” which could archive solutions faster than 𝒪(*M*), because they imply some knowledge about the internal structure of *f*(*y*) which could probably also be exploited in analog implementations.

## 2.3 Criticism and outlook

Given that the digital and analog technology (electric representation of information, transistor-based computation) is quite similar, the model prediction of a similarly growing energy demand is useful. Differences are of course hidden in the constants (prefactors) of the asymptotic notation 𝒪(*M*). Quantitative studies in the next sections examine this prefactor in 𝒪(*M*).

The linear model is already limited in the case of serial digital processors when the computation gets *memory bound* (instead of *CPU-bound*). Having to wait for data leads to a performance drop and might result in a worsened superlinear .

*Parallel digital* computing as well as *serial analog* computing has not yet been subject of the previous discussion. While the first one is a widespread standard technique, the second one refers to analog-digital hybrid computing which, inter alia, allows a small analog computer to be used repeatedly on a large problem, effectively rendering the analog part as an analog accelerator or co-processor for the digital part. Parallel digital computing suffers from a theoretical speedup limited due to the non-parallel parts of the algorithm (see also [Gustafson](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx20), [1988](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#bib1.bibx20)), which has exponential impact on . This is where the intrinsically parallel analog computer exhibits its biggest advantages. Section [4](https://ars.copernicus.org/articles/19/105/2021/#Ch1.S4) discusses this aspect of analog computing.
