[The International School for Advanced Studies (SISSA)](https://www.sissa.it/) was founded in 1978 and was the first institution in Italy to promote post-graduate courses leading to a Doctor Philosophiae (or PhD) degree. A centre of excellence among Italian and international universities, the school has around 65 teachers, 100 post docs and 245 PhD students, and is located in Trieste, in a campus of more than 10 hectares with wonderful views over the Gulf of Trieste.

SISSA hosts a very high-ranking, large and multidisciplinary scientific research output. The scientific papers produced by its researchers are published in high impact factor, well-known international journals, and in many cases in the world's most prestigious scientific journals such as Nature and Science. Over 900 students have so far started their careers in the field of mathematics, physics and neuroscience research at SISSA.

# Topical Workshop on Electronics for Particle Physics

## 30 September - 4 October 2024

University of Glasgow, Scotland, UK

The workshop covers all aspects of electronic systems, components and instrumentation for particle and astro-particle physics such as: electronics for particle detection, triggering, data-acquisition systems, accelerator and beam instrumentation.
Operational experience in electronic systems and R&D in electronics for LHC, High Luminosity LHC, FAIR, neutrino facilities and other present or future accelerator projects are the major focus of the workshop.

## Participating Journals

Michael Wiebusch 2024 *JINST* **19** C12009

This work presents a custom analog front-end card designed for the read-out of PMTs
coupled to lanthanum bromide scintillators. It integrates 16 discrete analog constant fraction
discriminators (CFDs) on a compact 12×10 cm board, providing precise timing information for
nuclear lifetime measurements. The design emphasizes cost-effectiveness, utilizing off-the-shelf
discrete components, as well as compactness, achieved by using miniature coaxial connectors and
cables as delay elements. The focus of this paper lies on the unusual and extremely minimalist
analog shaper/discriminator design which is devised without operational amplifiers, making use of
only a handful of RF transistors and LVDS receivers in place of comparators.

M. Caselle *et al* 2024 *JINST* **19** C12015

The Micro-Vertex Detector (MVD) is the innermost subdetector of the PANDA (anti-Proton ANnihilations at DArmstadt) detector at FAIR. Its microstrip sensors are read out by custom front-end electronics called ToASt (Torino ASIC for Strip readout) [1]. The ToASt chips are locally managed by an MDC (Module Data Concentrator) [2]. The MDC processes incoming event data and forwards them to the off-detector readout cards based on the AMC (Advanced Mezzanine Card) standard. Both the MDC and the AMC readout card are currently under development at KIT [3].
The complete readout chain, including the double-sided microstrip sensor read by the ToASt chips and the FPGA implementation of the MDC, was successfully tested during a 2023 beam test at COSY (Forschungszentrum Jülich). This proof-of-concept validation of the MDC logic paves the way for the forthcoming ASIC version of the MDC, which is planned for submission in February 2025.
Extensive performance characterization of the current readout chain has been achieved with the MDC-FPGA optically connected to an AMD-Xilinx ZCU102 evaluation card [4], which emulates the AMC off-detector card, through a Versatile Link+ Demo Board (VLDB+) [5].
This contribution presents the MDC-ASIC design, its integration with both the front-end and back-end electronics and the performance results of the complete readout chain.

Zhenwu Ge *et al* 2024 *JINST* **19** C12012

To mitigate the effects of pileup resulting from increased luminosity during the ATLAS Phase-II upgrade, the High Granularity Timing Detector (HGTD) was proposed to accurately measure the timing of tracks. The Peripheral Electronics Board (PEB) serves as a critical component of the HGTD, functioning as an intermediary between the front-end modules and off-detector electronics. A prototype PEB, designated 1F, was designed and produced by the end of 2023. Extensive evaluations of PEB 1F were conducted in 2024, encompassing both single board tests and collaborative tests with the demonstrator. These assessments well determined the quality of PEB 1F.

K. Stachon *et al* 2024 *JINST* **19** C12016

Efforts aiming at consolidating the powering for the CMS detector have led to the development of a Low Voltage Power Supply (LVPS). The LVPS converts 380 V DC to 12 V DC, suitable for powering the widely used bPOL12V point-of-load DC-DC converter. To limit cable size, the LVPS must be hosted in the CMS experimental cavern, being exposed to ionizing radiation and stray magnetic field of up to 120 mT. The device is made of Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) components, therefore, thorough qualifications at various design stages were performed to ensure its reliable operation in the harsh environmental conditions for the HL-LHC era.

L. Gaioni *et al* 2024 *JINST* **19** C12011

This work describes the design, in a 28 nm CMOS technology, of a front-end channel for the readout of pixel sensors in future particle accelerators. The channel being developed leverages the Time-Over-Threshold technique for the numerical conversion of the detector signal amplitude, and includes a low-noise charge sensitive amplifier featuring a compact gain stage architecture. The front-end circuit features an equivalent noise charge not exceeding 70 electrons r.m.s. for a detector capacitance of 50 fF, with a threshold dispersion of the order of 20 electrons r.m.s. A prototype chip including a matrix of 8x32 readout channels has been submitted for fabrication. The design of the front-end channel, together with the main simulation results, is discussed in the paper.

P. Hazell *et al* 2024 *JINST* **19** C12019

The LHC RF and Timing Distribution Backbone is being upgraded for the HL-LHC. A White Rabbit technology solution for the generation and the distribution of the RF, similar to the system currently employed in SPS, is being considered. To verify its suitability from a phase stability perspective, an investigation was conducted on a proof-of-concept system. The requirement for the end-nodes is ± 1 degree of the 200 MHz SPS RF frequency. The key figure of merit to check compliancy is peak-peak phase variation which must be < 28 ps. The compliance tests campaign will be described and results presented.

Nils H. van der Blij *et al* 2024 *JINST* **19** C12018

The development of 48 V compatible DC/DC converters that are tolerant to high magnetic fields and radiation helps to reduce the cost and weight of the cabling, power supplies and cooling of High Energy Physics (HEP) experiments.
In this paper, a new, optimized and compact bPOL48V module is presented aimed at 48 V to 5–12 V power conversion.
This new module, which is available for purchase and as a reference design, reduces the size by 93% compared to previous designs while exhibiting similar efficiency.
Furthermore, a framework for optimizing and comparing converter topologies is also introduced, which identifies the 3-level buck topology as a promising topology for future research and development.
Moreover, experimental validation of different optimized converters is also provided.
The experimental results show that the 3-level buck topology is promising for 48 V to 5 V conversion stages, and that the Berkeley buck topology is promising for the development of 48 V to 1 V conversion stages.

S. Emiliani *et al* 2024 *JINST* **19** C12021

The MOSS wafer-scale monolithic sensor, designed for the vertex detector (ITS3) of the ALICE experiment, features a pixel input capacitance of ∼ 5 fF. Such a small input capacitance is needed to reach a satisfactory SNR with a low-power analog front-end (36 nW/pixel). This makes the design of the pulsing circuitry needed to characterize the front-end performance particularly challenging. As an example, measurements of the front-end of MOSS are presented, showing that even a parasitic capacitance less than 5 aF can significantly alter the charge injection from the pulsing circuit. In this contribution, design methods and solutions to address these challenges are detailed.

F. Giordano *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C01005

Next-generation high-energy physics experiments will employ high-granularity detectors with thousands of readout channels, necessitating the use of low-power, compact ASICs. The CAEN FrontEnd Readout System (FERS) 5200 integrates these ASICs within small, synchronizable, and distributable systems featuring both Front and Back Ends. The A5203 FERS module incorporates the recently released CERN picoTDC ASIC, enabling high-resolution timing measurements for Time of Arrival (ToA) and Time over Threshold (ToT).
In this work, we analyze the performance of the A5203 unit, which has a 3.125 ps least significant bit (LSB), delivering ToA measurements with an RMS resolution of approximately 7 ps for signals of fixed amplitude, and approximately 20 ps RMS for input signals with variable amplitude over a 50 dB dynamic range over a single board. The amplitude-dependent walk effect is corrected using ToT, which, in addition to walk correction, is also utilised for signal amplitude reconstruction and background reduction.
The A5203 has been successfully applied across various experimental and industrial contexts. In the concluding section of this paper, we will discuss its application within the ProVision project: a PET scanner specialised in imaging aggressive prostate cancer at an early-stage.

E. Orzes *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C01003

Picosecond-level phase determinism in timing distribution systems is a requirement for future detectors in High Energy Physics. FPGA transceivers traditionally used to propagate timing signals generally do not meet this stringent requirement, suffering from phase jumps at startup and from drifts due to temperature variations. While *ad hoc* solutions have been developed using FPGA features to measure and correct for phase shifts, they remain FPGA specific and therefore cannot be generalized to all types of timing links. This paper presents a study using discrete components to monitor and correct for phase drift, allowing for an implementation of a generic deterministic link.

M.M. Patil *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C01006

Designed for accelerator beam diagnostics and photon science applications, KALYPSO is a line array camera that stands out for its high-speed performance with the ability to operate at rates up to 12 Mfps in continuous readout mode while maintaining full occupancy. In this contribution, the KALYPSO system with sensor based on TI-LGAD is presented. The latest version of this system is employed as a beam diagnostic imaging sensor to measure radiation profiles of the particle beam at the KIT accelerator, KARA. The system's key features will be presented, including its linearity, sensitivity, and dynamic range.

Patryk Prus *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C01009

The design and simulation results of an ultra-low power, fast 10-bit Successive Approximation Register (SAR) Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) in CMOS 130 nm technology are presented. This ADC is an extension of an experimentally verified 10-bit SAR ADC (INL, DNL < 0.5 LSB, ENOB > 9.5), working up to 50 MSps and consuming 680 μW at 40 MSps. The goal of the present work was to add a programmable threshold for the processed input signal, to stop the conversion and thus greatly reduce power consumption in case the signal is below the threshold. The new ADC works up to around 40 MSps and consumes around 350 μW at 40 MSps for low particle occupancy.

C. Zhang *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C01008

A monolithic High Voltage CMOS (HV-CMOS) prototype, UKRI-MPW1, has been developed to further improve the radiation tolerance of this technology, which is a promising candidate for future high-energy physics experiments. UKRI-MPW1 addresses the issues of high leakage current and parasitic channels identified in its predecessor, UKRI-MPW0, by incorporating an improved chip ring structure and a custom p-shield layer. Additionally, a new pixel flavour with an NMOS-only trimming Digital-to-Analogue Converter (DAC) further improves pixel performance. This chip has demonstrated a radiation tolerance of up to 3 × 1015 neq/cm2.

P. Antoszczuk *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C01007

An on-detector power distribution scheme for the High Granularity Calorimeter (HGCAL) Phase-2 upgrade of CMS is under development. This scheme is based on a heavy-copper flexible printed circuit board (FPC), allowing for an efficient use of the tight integration space, with minimal insulation overhead, excellent electrical and thermal performance and simplified integration, when compared with a wired solution. This work introduces the technology, how it allows the HGCAL challenges to be overcome, and the characterization studies. Prototypes testing are presented to validate the concept and quantify the manufacturability, electrical performance, and safety of the proposed solution.

Mirosław Firlej *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C01013

The design and measurement results of a prototype Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC) fabricated in 130 nm CMOS
technology are presented. The TDC architecture with analog interpolators was chosen, which
was motivated by previous experience in Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) design [1]. The measured time
difference between the event and the trigger signal is converted to the amplitude and then
digitised by a 10-bit ADC. The TDC prototype is functional and achieved good Differential Non-Linearity (DNL)
and jitter (below 1 LSB), slightly dependent of the selected time precision. The obtained
Integral Non-Linearity (INL) is significantly higher than simulated and should be still improved. The prototype
Application-Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC) has configurable time resolution from 15 ps to 140 ps, which gives the total possible
time measure range from ±9.5 ns to ±70 ns. In this paper the architecture of the developed
TDC is described, comprising the implementation of the Time-to-Analog Converter (TAC) and 10-bit ADC. The
measurements of the prototype 8 channel TDC ASIC, showing its linearity and timing
resolution are also shown.

A. Zografos *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C01012

For the high-luminosity upgrade of the ATLAS Inner Tracking detector, a new pixel detector will be installed to increase bandwidth and to cope with higher radiation, among other challenges. In this contribution, the design aspects and qualification of the data transmission from pixel modules to optical readout are presented. A focus is put on the data cable bundles and their performance for one of the Pixel sub-systems, the Outer Barrel. The development of a custom system for production testing of the bundles is discussed. Finally, in preparation of the detector integration, developments regarding functionality and connectivity testing are analyzed.

I. Redondo
on behalf of the CMS collaboration 2025 *JINST* **20** C01011

The electronics of the CMS Drift Tubes (DT) chambers will be replaced to operate during High Luminosity (HL-LHC). In the upgraded architecture, optical links (lpGBT, VTRX+) send all signals to the backend, where complex logic running on FPGAs will process the data within trigger latency with precision enough to profit from the full chamber resolution, which in the present system is only possible offline. One of the sixty sectors of the detector was instrumented with the final version of the front-end boards (OBDTs, in two types) during the Winter stop 2022–23. After commissioning and integrating this setup in CMS operations during 2023, its stability has been tested in 2024 LHC collisions. Performance during 2024 campaign is summarized.

Davide Falchieri *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C01014

This work describes a custom electronics card named PicoTDC board developed at INFN Bologna, whose goal is to provide fast timing measurements to generic detectors. The board is able to connect to different front-end electronics using a common FMC (FPGA Mezzanine Connector) interface. The fast timing measurements are provided by 2 PicoTDC ASICs from CERN, which supply 128 channels with 3.05 ps LSB. Design choices and performance of the card are discussed. We are also designing a family of front-end cards compatible with the PicoTDC board to improve the flexibility of the board itself and ease the connection to generic detectors and their front end electronics. We then measured the timing resolution achievable with this board, which is compatible with the PicoTDC expected performances.

D. Panchal and T. Andeen 2025 *JINST* **20** C01018

The COLUTA (COLumbia-University of Texas at Austin) ASIC is an 8-channel, 15-bit, 40 million samples per second (MSPS), analog-to-digital (ADC) converter designed for the high-luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) upgrade of the Liquid Argon (LAr) calorimeter readout electronics. The production version of the ADC meets and exceeds the specifications for the analog performance and the HL-LHC radiation tolerance.
Radiation tolerance test procedure and the results of the irradiation test on pre-production lot chips will be discussed. The production testing will be performed by a custom-designed robotic test setup which will test 80,000 chips required for the upgrade. The chip performance results, and the chip quality information are stored in a local and centralized database.
Results from robotic chip-testing of the production lots will be described, along with the yields of the chips which meet the specifications for the upgrade.

Francisco Piernas Diaz *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C01017

Particle tracking and imaging detectors are becoming increasingly complex, driven by demands for densely integrated functionality and maximal sensitive area. These challenging requirements can be met using 3D interconnect techniques widely used in industry. In this paper, we present the results of an evaluation of the 3D Through-Silicon-Via (TSV) technology, using the Timepix4 integrated circuit as a test-vehicle. We will present the concepts for 3D integration and test results from TSV-processed chips bonded to custom-designed circuit boards conceived as proofs-of-principle for future detector modules.

D. Ecker *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C01020

The Embedded Monitoring and Control Interface (EMCI) and Embedded Monitoring Processor (EMP) system is a state-of-the-art solution developed for the Detector Control System (DCS) upgrade in the ATLAS experiment. The EMCI serves as a radiation-tolerant interface for control and monitoring data of the detector Front-End electronics. The EMP, a multi-processing System on Chip (MPSoC) platform, serves as the interface between the EMCIs and the Back-End of the DCS, providing centralized data handling and monitoring capabilities. The firmware and software ecosystem includes the EMP operating system (*epos*), dedicated firmware IP blocks, associated software libraries, and OPC UA based middleware applications. This paper focuses on the ongoing hardware verification and development of the firmware and software infrastructure for the EMCI-EMP system.

D. Panchal
on behalf of the ATLAS Liquid Argon Calorimeter group 2025 *JINST* **20** C01016

The High-Luminosity LHC will start operations for physics in 2029 and aims to record 3000 fb-1 of proton collision data. This expansion of the dataset will be achieved by a
four-fold increase in the number of collisions per bunch crossing, leading to
∼ 10× higher radiation doses and busier events. To cope with those harsher
conditions and to be compatible with the new ATLAS data acquisition paradigm, the ATLAS Liquid
Argon Calorimeter on-detector electronics will have to be replaced. The presentation will cover
the validation of the performance of the new boards, a critical step before launching the
full production of about 1500 boards and their installation which is planned to start in 2027.

F. Hummer
on behalf of the CMS collaboration 2025 *JINST* **20** C01015

For the upcoming high-luminosity LHC, the endcap calorimeters of the CMS experiment will be replaced by the high granularity calorimeter (HGCAL), a sampling calorimeter using both silicon and scintillator as active materials in different regions depending on the radiation dose. This contribution describes the integration details of the scintillator-based front-end into the readout chain of HGCAL.
A prototype of the SiPM-on-tile readout chain was successfully operated in two recent beam tests at CERN SPS, demonstrating stable operation in a 3 T magnetic field and synchronization of sensor modules across different optical links.
For the first time, both the silicon and SiPM-on-tile sensors of HGCAL are integrated into a single system utilizing a Serenity-Z FPGA card. Coarse event data which would be used for trigger logic are read out synchronously for both sensor types and across multiple layers.

P. Casolaro *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C01023

This work reports on Total Ionizing Dose (TID) assessment on off-the-shelf LVDS links that will be used for the new trigger and readout system of the ATLAS muon barrel spectrometer within the HL-LHC program. We developed an experimental setup that allows to investigate TID effects on the currents drawn by the devices under test and on their signal integrity, including variations in amplitude, rise/fall time, and bit error rate. No significant variations of these quantities has been observed after integrating the ATLAS target dose of 84.6 Gy. In order to investigate high-dose effects, the irradiation has been extended up to 15.4 kGy. No post-annealing effects were observed. These results complement existing literature, proving the robustness of off-the-shelf LVDS links for the ATLAS environment.

Jakub Moroń *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C01026

The design and qualification results of a System on Chip (SoC) Application-Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC), called FLAXE, fabricated in 130 nm CMOS technology are presented. FLAXE is a readout ASIC designed for ECAL-p, a compact electromagnetic calorimeter being a part of a detector system for Laser Und XFEL Experiment (LUXE) proposed at DESY, Hamburg, as an extension to the European X-ray Free Electron Laser (XFEL) facility. ECAL-p is a sampling calorimeter with a very compact design targeting small Molière radius, comprising 16 (up to 20) layers composed of 3.5 mm (1 X0) thick tungsten absorber plates interspersed with silicon sensors. Sensor signal is read and shaped by the analogue readout channel, comprising a Charge Sensitive Amplifier (CSA) and a fully differential CR-RC shaper with 50 ns peaking time, which output is digitized in each channel by a 10-bit Successive Approximation Register (SAR) Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC). Data from ADC are collected into the ASIC internal memory and read out by the Data Acquisition (DAQ) system between Bunch Crossings (BXs). Around 1000 ASICs have been fabricated and a first batch of 142 ASICs has been packaged and tested. The results of the qualification procedure, as well as measurement result of a single ASIC are presented and discussed.

Carlo Di Fraia
on behalf of the CMS Muon group 2025 *JINST* **20** C01025

Part of the muon upgrade of the CMS Experiment for the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider consists of three new GEM stations, GE1/1, GE2/1 and ME0. The purpose of these stations is to increase the redundancy of the CMS muon spectrometer in the forward endcap regions and to extend the acceptance of the detector up to a pseudorapidity |*η*| ∼ 2.8 with the ME0 station. To achieve this result, these detectors must be able to withstand the background radiation of the installation environment, with a rate capability of up to 150 kHz/cm2.
The first station, GE1/1, was installed during the Long Shutdown 2. Since the start of Run 3 in 2022, GE1/1 has been active in CMS operations and data acquisition; this will be the focus of this work. The presence of high radiation in the area where the detector operates is a challenge for the High-Voltage system, since a large charge has to be handled without reducing the effective gain of the detector. This phenomenon leads to a drop in the effective voltage applied and therefore voltage compensation must be applied to have a stable gain. We quantify this effect by measuring the currents flowing in the High-Voltage system of GE1/1 detectors and comparing them with the observed particle hit-rate measured in the same chambers, as a function of LHC beam luminosity. This study, based on data provided by detectors already installed in CMS, aims to test the performance of detectors in terms of rate capability in order to help the development of the GE1/1 station and to support the development and to highlight the operational needs of the next two stations to be built, GE2/1 and ME0.

A. Navarro-Tobar and J. León Holgado 2025 *JINST* **20** C01024

The High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) has motivated a generalized upgrade in electronic systems across all experiments. In the new electronics architecture for the CMS (Compact Muon Solenoid) Drift Tubes detector, the trigger generation moves from on-detector ASICs to the back-end, to be carried out by top-range FPGAs. The new algorithm aims to deliver full-resolution, offline-grade performance in the reconstruction of muon segments. To achieve this objective, meeting the latency and data rate requirements, a high-speed, highly-pipelined FPGA design with several optimizations has been developed. This work describes the architecture and performance of this algorithm, as well as the challenges encountered during implementation and the solutions adopted.

Abhijeet Ghodgaonkar *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C01045

The high luminosity operation of the LHC will deliver collisions with a luminosity about 10 times the original design value. This poses a big challenge for trigger and data acquisition due to nearly 200 overlapping collisions, called pile up, within the same bunch crossing. Disentanglement of the pileup particles from those of interesting physics processes is achieved by implementing the *Pile-Up Per Particle Identification* (PUPPI) algorithm. We present the strategy for implementation of PUPPI at the *Level-1* (L1) trigger, focusing on the *Hadron Forward* (HF) Calorimeter detector of the CMS experiment. The main features of the custom firmware developed for this purpose is discussed.

M.J. Basso
on behalf of the ATLAS ITk collaboration 2025 *JINST* **20** C01044

For the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider, the ATLAS experiment will replace its current Inner Detector with an all-silicon Inner Tracker (ITk), consisting of pixel and strip systems. In the end-cap, silicon sensor modules of the strip system are mounted onto support structures called “petals”. To facilitate the assembly of petals, an automated system has been developed which streamlines the production process and ensures uniformity. This paper presents the latest results from the assembly of the first ITk pre-production petals, including characterization of their electrical performance and studies of their robustness at temperatures ≤ -35 ∘C.

L. Giannessi *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C01043

T2K is a long baseline neutrino experiment, entering Phase II with a Near Detector upgrade. The T2K near detector (ND280) upgrade consists of the installation of three new detector systems: a plastic scintillator neutrino active target (Super-FGD), two time projection chambers (HA-TPC) and a time of flight detector (TOF). The Super-FGD is composed of 2-million 1 cm3 scintillating cubes read by almost 60 thousand wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers coupled to an MPPC on one end. Given the large number of channels, the limited space inside magnetic environment, and the limited time from production to installation, the development and testing of the Front-end electronics boards (FEB) for the read-out of the Super-FGD channels represented a challenging task for the success of the upgrade.
This work presents the performance tests confirming that the FEB aligns with detector requirements, and the hardware qualification of 240 FEBs through a custom QC test bench designed to detect and locate hardware failures to speed up the repairing process. Installation of the electronics in the detector took place in March 2024, one year after the beginning of the FEB mass production, and the first successful neutrino beam run took place in June of the same year.

G. Mazza *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C01034

The Cleopatra ASIC is a 12-channel prototype ASIC for the readout of hydrogenated
amorphous silicon sensors used for real-time dosimetry in radiation diagnostic and radiation
therapy. The architecture is based on a current to frequency conversion based on the recycling
integrator principle in order to cover a dynamic range of four orders of magnitude with high
linearity. Three different input amplifier configurations have been implemented in order to check
the trade-off between detector capacitance and maximum output frequency. Cleopatra has been
designed in CMOS 28 nm technology and succesfully tested in laboratory.

Y. Khwaira
on behalf of the ATLAS ITK Pixel group 2025 *JINST* **20** C01048

A demonstrator for each slice of the ATLAS pixel detector was built to replicate the real detector and provide early solutions for operating and maintaining its components. This system-level testing of the all-silicon Inner Tracker (ITk) pixel detector for the ATLAS experiment at CERN's HL-LHC encompasses a wide array of system components, which is essential for managing the increased luminosity and radiation levels expected at HL-LHC, thereby enhancing tracking performance. Utilizing advanced silicon sensor technologies, serial powering, and lightweight carbon fiber structures, the demonstrator and assembled components on the support structure will undergo several studies for verification and commissioning. Extensive tests on serial powering, monitoring, and data acquisition were conducted, ensuring the system's robustness and reliability for future high-energy physics experiments. Additionally, three different sub-components will be introduced for the novel ITk pixel detector, specifically designed for the outer barrel (OB), outer end caps (OEC), and inner system (IS) sections.

A. Weidberg
on behalf of the ATLAS ITk strips collaboration 2025 *JINST* **20** C01047

This paper reviews the bus tapes used for the barrel and end cap detectors for the ATLAS
ITk strip detector. The long copper/polyimide tapes with narrow track and gap are very challenging
to produce with an acceptable yield. Two different technologies for these tapes are
compared. After several iterations, barrel and end cap tapes are in production at two different
manufacturers. Results from the electrical and dimensional QC show that both approaches meet the
tight specifications. Tests of the radiation tolerance are also discussed.

M. Lupi *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C02002

Verification is a critical aspect of designing front-end (FE) readout ASICs for
High-Energy Physics (HEP) experiments. These ASICs share several similar functional features,
resulting in similar verification objectives, which can be addressed using comparable verification
strategies. This contribution presents a set of re-usable verification components for addressing
common verification tasks, such as clock generation, reset handling, configuration, as well as hit
and fault injections. The components were developed as part of the CHIPS initiative and they have
been successfully used in the verification of multiple HEP ASICs.

D. Hashimoto *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C02001

Results are presented for reliability tests of the SFP+ transceivers and the readout board of Thin Gap Chambers (TGC) for the ATLAS experiment at HL-LHC. The radiation tolerance was evaluated for the SFP+ transceivers from Broadcom and FS and the TGC frontend board with gamma ray irradiation up to *𝒪*(100) Gy at the Cobalt-60 facility of Nagoya University. An accelerated aging test was also performed for the SFP+ transceivers with the Kintex-7 evaluation board integrated in the temperature chamber.

Jaafar Alawieh *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C02005

For the Phase-2 upgrade of the CMS experiment, the CMS
central DAQ group designed and developed two custom ATCA
boards. These boards provide the interfaces between the sub-detector
electronics and the central CMS systems. This paper describes our
experience with the chosen prototyping strategy, with a focus on the
design modification choices made along the way. It concludes with a
brief overview of recent firmware developments, and a look at the
transition towards the full board production.

Gabriela Cabrera *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C02009

The Beam Gas Ionisation (BGI) profile monitor, located in the Proton Synchrotron (PS) and
Super Proton Synchrotron (SPS) at CERN, requires a radiation-tolerant readout system to transfer
data from the challenging accelerator surroundings to the back-end for processing. The system
needs to control and acquire data from four Timepix3 Hybrid Pixel Detectors (HPDs) located
directly inside the beam pipe, a highly radioactive environment. It must ensure reliability given
limited hardware access and preserve signal integrity for the high-speed data (32 channels at 320 MHz). However, due to the unavailability of a suitable rad-hard Timepix3 readout, the Beam
Instrumentation PiXeL (BIPXL) readout system was designed to meet these requirements. This system
employs radiation-hardened components such as the GBTx and the FEASTMP, both developed at CERN. It
will be compatible with forthcoming hybrid pixel detector initiatives in similarly harsh radiation conditions.

M. Lupi *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C02004

The High-Granularity Calorimeter (HGCAL) will replace the current CMS
Endcap Calorimeter during Long-Shutdown 3. The Endcap Concentrator (ECON) ASICs represent key
elements in the readout chain, processing trigger (ECON-T) and data (ECON-D) streams from the
HGCROC to the lpGBT. The ECONs will operate in a radiation environment with a High-Energy Hadron
(E≥20 MeV) flux up to 2·107 cm-2s-1.
This contribution describes the Universal Verification Methodology (UVM)-based functional verification of the ECON ASICs focusing on the re-use of existing components to manage the complexity of the verification environment.

Zijie Zhou *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C02008

We present the design and preliminary test results of a MAPS sensor, MIC6\_Explorer1, based on a 55 nm Quad-well CMOS Image Sensor process for high-energy physics experiment vertex detector applications.
MIC6\_Explorer1 consists of three large matrices and is designed to investigate the charge collection properties of the 55 nm process with various MAPS design parameters, including pixel pitch, diode geometry, reset methods, and readout circuit structure. Preliminary test results demonstrate that the pixel array with a 24 μm × 24 μm pitch achieved a 93.5% charge collection efficiency when exposed to a 55Fe source.

V. Bobillier *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C02013

For nearly 20 years, the Power Supply and Crate Service at CERN has been responsible for
the maintenance tracking of power supplies and crates used by the CERN experiments. With this
experience, and with the imminent introduction of a new generation of power supplies for the
HL-LHC, the timing is ideal to conduct a statistical analysis to draw lessons from the past and
make recommendations for the future. This study aims to analyze failures, expose
the most vulnerable components, identify the improvement solutions, and highlight
the benefits of preventive maintenance campaigns to ensure reliable long-term operation.

Johann Christoph Voigt
on behalf of the ATLAS Liquid Argon Calorimeter group 2025 *JINST* **20** C02012

To deal with the higher pileup after the high-luminosity upgrade of the LHC, the ATLAS
liquid argon calorimeter readout electronics will be replaced. 556 Intel Agilex-7 FPGAs will be
installed as part of the off-detector electronics, enabling a more sophisticated digital energy
reconstruction. Instead of using a linear optimal filter like the current readout, we evaluated
the use of recurrent and convolutional neural networks. These artificial neural networks are
trained on signal-enriched simulated detector pulses for a set of representative cells. The
network size is limited to approximately 500 multiply-accumulate operations per detector
cell. They show improvements in energy reconstruction especially for the case of overlapping
signal pulses, as they will appear more often under high-luminosity conditions. An FPGA prototype
firmware has been developed for both RNNs and CNNs, that supports processing the required number
of 384 detector cells on one FPGA. This uses a low-level VHDL approach to minimize the resource
usage. The ANN architecture is fixed at compile time, but the weights are configurable per
cell. The compilation results show that such a neural network based readout is feasible with the
available hardware. This is possible through the use of time multiplexing, i.e. by running the
FPGA at a multiple of the 40 MHz input data frequency.

G. Aglieri Rinella *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C02015

For the LS3 ALICE ITS3 upgrade the detector material budget reduction has been pushed to the limit by proposing a system composed almost exclusively of silicon wafer thinned down to 50μm. This improves performance, but adds complexity to the ASIC design. It requires a wafer-scale module with embedded power delivery network and on-chip data transfer, which were usually done through flexible printed circuit cable.
This contribution covers different aspects of the power delivery network design for a wafer-scale detector. It describes the difficulties, shows possible solutions and presents the power scheme design of the full-size ITS3 sensor prototype MOSAIX.

F. Costanza *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C02018

The ATLAS ITk Pixel system requires large-scale flex circuits for low-voltage power, high-voltage sensor bias, and command/data transmission due to tight space constraints. This report focuses on the design and production of the services running from the modules to the first patch panel of the ITk Pixel Outer Barrel. The results from the quality control tests on the pre-production (10% of what is required to equip the final detector) will be discussed. In this report we also describe the procedure developed for the complex 3D bending needed to accommodate the routing and to respect the mechanical envelope.

Marco Andorno *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C02017

As front-end ASIC complexity in HEP experiments grows, there is a shift towards more modular, programmable, and cost-effective designs. This work introduces the SOCRATES platform, a radiation-tolerant SoC generator toolset, based on SoCMake, a hardware/software build system that automates SoC assembly and verification. Utilizing existing IP blocks, SoCMake generates the SoC hardware and the software framework to run application code. The platform includes radiation-tolerant IPs and fault-tolerant extensions supporting redundancy and error correction. A prototype ASIC based on the RISC-V Ibex processor, generated using SOCRATES in a 28nm CMOS process, will validate the toolset through SEE and TID testing.

T. Kishishita *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C02016

We have developed a prototype of the muon beam monitor (*μ*BM) for the COMET experiment
at J-PARC. The COMET aims to search for the neutrino-less muon-to-electron conversion event in
the field of the nucleus, as a charged lepton flavor violation process. The SiC-based *μ*BM
will be installed in a vacuum chamber and located in front of the muon-stopping target and the
main central drift chamber. The detector consists of SiC PN-diodes and dedicated readout
electronics. By tailing the 256 sensors in a matrix, the beam profile and bunch stability can be
extracted, and then, are utilized for the background estimation of the rare process. To validate
the *μ*BM concept, we implemented the SiC sensors on the prototype Kapton-flex sensor board and
conducted a beam test at J-PARC. The pulse height of *μ*-events in the SiC sensor was linearly
correlated with an averaged coincidence of the decayed electrons by scintillators. We thus
conclude that the number of incident muons can be estimated from the pulse height information from
the *μ*BM. The radiation tolerance of the sensor was also proven to be sufficient for the COMET
Phase-1 by irradiating fast neutrons with 1.7×1012/ cm2 fluence at research
nuclear reactor. The electronics designed in 65 nm CMOS is currently under testing. In the
lab.-testing, we confirmed the basic functionality as a required waveform digitizer and sufficient
signal-integrity to drive the 10 m cable length to the backend electronics.

L. Bauckhage *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C02020

The silicon tracker of the ATLAS experiment will be upgraded for the upcoming
High-Luminosity Upgrade of the LHC. The main building blocks of the new strip tracker are
modules that consist of silicon sensors and hybrid PCBs hosting the read-out ASICs. The modules
are mounted on rigid carbon-fiber substructures, known as staves in the central barrel region and
petals in the end-cap regions, that provide common services to all the modules. At the end of
each stave or petal side, a so-called End-of-Substructure (EoS) card facilitates the transfer of
data, power, and control signals between the modules and the off-detector systems. The EoS
connects up to 28 data lines to one or two lpGBT chips that provide data serialization and uses a
10 Gbit s-1 versatile optical link to transmit signals to the off-detector
systems. To meet the tight integration requirements in the detector, several different EoS card
designs are needed. The power to the EoS is provided by a dedicated dual-stage DC-DC package
providing 2.5 V and 1.2 V to the EoS cards. As the EoS production of almost 2000 EoS
cards and accompanying DC-DC converters is getting close to completion, the production experience
including detailed QC statistics and design validation (QA) results is reported on.

M. Schneider *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C02029

We report on characterization results for our new silicon photonic chip for high-speed data transmission, called COTTONTAIL (**C**hip f**o**r de**t**ector ins**t**rumentati**on** wi**t**h w**a**velength d**i**vision mu**l**tiplex). Modulation bandwidths of different travelling-wave Mach-Zehnder modulators and ring resonator modulators are sufficient for very high data transmission rates. Bit error rate measurements were conducted with a very low voltage swing of 1.1 V *pp* and error free transmissions could be established up to a data rate of 11.3 Gb/s with the ring modulators and up to 8.5 Gb/s with the Mach-Zehnder modulators. Wavelength filters for wavelength division multiplexing show a very low transmission loss of less than 2.3 dB with a slight wavelength shift of the filtering characteristics. Also included photodiodes are well suited for high speed downlinks with data rates in excess of 40 Gb/s or on-chip modulator monitoring.

Valentin Stümpert *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C02024

This work presents first results from a feasibility study to qualify commercial 100 Gb/s Ethernet as a readout link for future high-energy physics detectors. The motivation for this work is to examine the possibility of reading out future detector front-ends directly via commercial, high bandwidth, cost-optimized data centers, without the need of the intermediate custom-link/hardware layer used for this purpose thus far. In an attempt to determine how well 100 Gb/s Ethernet is adapted to the readout of such systems, this paper examines the protocol on aspects such as unidirectional operation and radiation hardness. Initial work towards a complete demonstrator system is also presented.

Yoshifumi Narukawa
on behalf of the ATLAS TDAQ collaboration 2025 *JINST* **20** C02023

Firmware testing on actual hardware is an optimal way to validate large-scale FPGA-based trigger/DAQ systems. For the Phase-II level-0 muon trigger system at the ATLAS experiment, a methodology using prototype ATCA-based Sector Logic (SL) boards was developed, featuring self-complete DAQ, high-statistics test patterns, and various nature of input test data. The design exploits Zynq SoC on the board for control, injection of BRAM-based test patterns data and flexible DAQ to probe the process. This success is thanks to the flexibility of the SL board design around the SoC device. This methodology facilitates precise firmware validation and systematic debugging.

A. Perro *et al* 2025 *JINST* **20** C02027

High Energy Physics (HEP) data acquisition systems are often built from high-end FPGAs. As such systems scale in the HL-LHC era, severe under-utilization of FPGA transceivers can occur because front-end links prioritize radiation hardness and power consumption over raw data bandwidth. This work evaluates recently introduced low-power, low-cost FPGA devices as an alternative building block for future readout architectures. This study presents the implementation of a readout back-End on FPGA where the front-end protocol is based on the Low-Power GigaBit Transceiver (lpGBT) and the readout protocol is based on 10 Gigabit Ethernet, using the LHCb Run 4 RICH detector as a practical case s

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents a combined time-walk and timing-shift correction method for dual-ended readout time-of-flight (TOF) PET detectors with depth-of-interaction (DOI) capability. The research was conducted by Haibo Wang, Jiahao Xie, Jinyi Qi (Fellow, IEEE), Simon R. Cherry (Fellow, IEEE), and Junwei Du (Senior Member, IEEE) from the Department of Biomedical Engineering, University of California at Davis, and published in IEEE Transactions on Radiation and Plasma Medical Sciences (2024).

**Background:** TOF-PET detectors using leading-edge discriminators (LED) suffer from time-walk (due to signal amplitude variations) and timing-shift (due to DOI effects from thick crystals and electronics channel offsets). Dual-ended readout detectors, which use SiPMs at both ends of crystals, can provide DOI information but are particularly susceptible to these effects.

**Methods:** Two dual-ended readout detectors were constructed using Hamamatsu S14161-3050-08 SiPM arrays coupled to 8×8 arrays of 3.1×3.1×20 mm³ LYSO crystals (3.2 mm pitch). The PETsys TOFPET2 readout system was used for data acquisition. Events were categorized into DOI layers based on the ratio of energies detected by the two SiPM arrays. The correction method uses the relationship between threshold crossing time differences and the natural logarithm of energy ratios (e.g., t₂-t₃ vs. ln(E₂/E₃)) to derive correction parameters (c for time-walk, b for timing-shift) for each DOI layer pair.

- CTR improved from 260.7 ± 1.0 ps to 229.4 ± 1.0 ps (an improvement of ~31 ps) using a 400–650 keV energy window.
- Correcting time-walk alone improved CTR by 12.6 ps; DOI correction added ~20 ps further improvement.
- The optimal number of DOI layers was determined to be 4; beyond 4 layers, improvement plateaued (228.8 ps at 8 layers).
- The detector had a DOI resolution of 2.6 mm.
- The method also corrects timing offsets from readout electronics, improving localization accuracy along the LOR.

**Conclusion:** The proposed method effectively corrects both time-walk and timing-shift in dual-ended readout PET detectors, enhancing timing resolution and image quality. The work was supported by NIH grants R01 EB028806 and R01 EB031961.
</summary>

URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.05883

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This research paper (accepted for publication in Computer Science journal) investigates using deep neural networks to improve the timing precision of particle detectors, specifically for the CMS-PPS (Precision Proton Spectrometer) subsystem at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. The key problem addressed is the "time walk effect" — statistical fluctuations in charge deposited by particles that cause errors in arrival time measurements. The standard method, the Constant Fraction Discriminator (CFD) algorithm, is simple and effective but does not utilize all voltage samples in a time series.

**Methodology:** The researchers used data from the DESY-II synchrotron test beam facility (2020), where both PPS diamond timing detectors and a high-precision MCP-PMT (Microchannel Plate Photomultiplier Tube) detector were installed. The MCP served as the ground-truth reference (precision ~10 ps, compared to diamond sensors' 50-100 ps). The SAMPIC readout chip sampled signals every 156.25 ps, producing 64-sample waveforms within a 10 ns window. After preprocessing (inversion, filtering of noisy/saturated events, trimming to 48 samples, baseline subtraction, and amplitude normalization), the final dataset contained approximately 500,000 waveform entries (reduced from 5.5 GB to 126 MB).

**Network Architectures Tested:** Three architectures were evaluated using hyperparameter tuning with KerasTuner and Bayesian optimization: (1) Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) — 2,737 parameters, (2) Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) — 36,865 parameters, (3) UNet-based model — 456,965 parameters. The UNet architecture, which uses an encoder-decoder structure with skip connections, performed best.

**Results:** The UNet-based model achieved the best timing precision (60.71 ps in cross-validation) compared to CNN (62.83 ps) and MLP (63.90 ps). Against the baseline CFD algorithm, improvements ranged from 8% to 23% across different detector readout channels. In the base experiment, precision improved by 17% (from 71.6 ps with CFD to 58.4 ps with UNet). Under LHC-like conditions (24-sample time series instead of 48), precision improved from 73.3 ps to 62.1 ps (15% improvement). The networks generally required training on specific channels to achieve optimal results; training on one channel and testing on another could perform worse than CFD.

**Conclusion:** Deep neural networks, particularly UNet-based architectures, can significantly improve particle timing precision over the CFD method without modifying the detector setup. The inference requires only ~10 milliseconds of CPU time, making it suitable for online processing. The authors note that the absence of an MCP reference detector in the LHC setup poses a challenge for training data acquisition, and recurrent networks were not tested but are suggested for future research.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper by Vallerga and McPhate (UC Berkeley Space Science Laboratory) reviews the optimization of readout electronics for microchannel plate (MCP) detectors with delay line anodes, used in space missions such as FUSE, GALEX, and the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph (COS) on the Hubble Space Telescope. The delay line anode measures the position of charge clouds exiting MCP detectors by timing the difference between pulse arrival at both ends of the delay line.

**Key Topics:**
- **Delay Line Types:** Serpentine (planar zig-zag) and Helical (multi-planar) delay lines, plus Double Delay Line (DDL) and Cross Delay Line (XDL) anode patterns. These affect pulse shape due to dispersion, capacitive/inductive coupling, and reflections from unterminated strips.
- **Timing Electronics:** Pulses (~10 mV, 5ns wide) are amplified, filtered, and sent to Constant Fraction Discriminators (CFDs) which generate logic pulses for a Time-to-Amplitude Converter (TAC). Spatial resolution <25 µm FWHM over 85 mm is achievable at >100 kHz count rates.
- **CFD Optimization:** The optimum fraction F for minimizing timing error is the ratio of slopes at the zero crossing (F = -dV(T)/dt / dV(T-t0)/dt). For a symmetric Gaussian pulse, the optimum delay is t0 = 2σ (slightly shorter than FWHM), corresponding to the inflection points where slope is greatest.
- **Real-World Complications:** Pulse dispersion (pulses widen and lose amplitude as they traverse the delay line), reflections causing baseline disturbances and non-linearity, and amplifier non-linearity (which causes amplitude-dependent timing errors, especially at anode ends where start and stop amplitudes differ). Bandpass filtering helps make pulses more uniform across the anode.
- **Mitigation Strategies:** Use low dispersion anodes, linear amplifiers, narrow MCP pulse height distributions, and careful empirical optimization of filters and CFD settings (especially for large anodes like COS, GALEX, and FUSE).
</summary>

Existing technologies struggle to achieve high-precision, low-latency real-time triggering decisions and adaptive, efficient data compression while ensuring the physical integrity of data in high-throughput particle physics experiments.

## Method
The invention introduces a fully connected neural network-based trigger decision model combined with an adaptive compression-quality feedback closed-loop mechanism into particle detector readout electronics. The method comprises four steps:

**S4: Real-time quality assessment and feedback** - Decompresses and reconstructs data, calculates Mean Square Error (MSE) and Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), and dynamically adjusts compression parameters via closed-loop control.

--- SOURCE 1: Real-time Surface-Code Error Correction Using an FPGA-based Neural-Network Decoder ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2605.04892v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper reports a hardware-integrated control architecture featuring an FPGA-based neural-network (NN) decoder for real-time surface-code quantum error correction (QEC) on a superconducting quantum processor. The system uses a 17-qubit distance-3 surface-code logical qubit on a 66-qubit processor. The NN decoder, comprising an LSTM layer with 32 hidden units and a dense output layer, achieves a deterministic latency of 124 ns with a throughput period of 184 ns. The complete closed-loop latency is 550 ns, enabling feedback within a 1.25 μs QEC cycle.

Key results include: (1) Real-time decoding achieving logical error rates of 0.072(1) and 0.097(2) per round for |1L⟩ and |+L⟩ states, closely matching offline MWPM decoding (0.073(2) and 0.095(2)). (2) The NN decoder achieves logical error rate ϵL=6.9(2)% compared to 7.2(2)% for offline MWPM in logical memory experiments. (3) Successful demonstration of mid-circuit feedback correction in non-Clifford logical circuits (logical rotation about XL axis), where Pauli-frame updating alone is insufficient.

The architecture uses a Central Feedback Module (CFM) with an AMD Kintex-7 FPGA for syndrome decoding, integrated with arbitrary waveform generators and data acquisition modules. The authors demonstrate repeated multi-round feedback and robustness under varying error conditions. They discuss scaling to larger code distances (up to distance-13 with current FPGAs) and multi-logical-qubit systems, noting that larger distances will require more advanced hardware such as RFSoC platforms, higher-end FPGAs or ASICs, and multi-FPGA partitioning.
</summary>

URL: https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/2632-2153/ae8218

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents an end-to-end demonstration of a viable, ultra-fast, radiation-hard machine learning (ML) application on FPGAs for future high-energy physics experiments, using the LHCb Upgrade II's PicoCal calorimeter as a test case. The authors make three contributions: (1) development of a lightweight autoencoder to compress a 32-sample timing readout into a 2D latent space; (2) a hardware-aware quantization strategy reducing the model to 10-bit weights with minimal performance loss; and (3) a new backend for the hls4ml library enabling automatic translation of ML models into high-level synthesis projects for Microchip PolarFire FPGAs, which are radiation-hard. The paper describes the high-luminosity LHC era challenges, with LHCb Upgrade II expected to produce data rates of 200 Tb/s at 40 MHz bunch crossing rate, requiring compression of 32 inputs into a maximum of two numbers on-detector. The autoencoder approach preserves pulse shape information (timing, rise-time) while meeting strict real-time constraints. The extension to hls4ml is positioned as a significant contribution enabling broader adoption of ML on FPGAs in high-radiation environments. Published in Machine Learning: Science and Technology, Volume 7, Number 4, on 15 July 2026. **Key Components:**

- A Euresys Coaxlink Octo frame grabber card with a Xilinx Kintex UltraScale KU035 FPGA for on-board processing

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Physics-Based Deep Learning (PBDL) Repository

This GitHub repository (thunil/Physics-Based-Deep-Learning) collects links to works on **deep learning algorithms for physics problems**, with a particular emphasis on **fluid flow** (Navier-Stokes related problems). It primarily collects links to the work of the I15 lab at TUM, as well as miscellaneous works from other groups.

## Core Concepts

The repository defines **Physics-Based Deep Learning** (PBDL) as the field combining physical modeling and deep learning techniques. Methods can be categorized by:

- **Forward vs. Inverse problems**: Forward simulations predict state/temporal evolution; inverse problems obtain parametrization from observations.
- **Integration tightness**: 
  - **Data-driven**: Data from physical systems, no further interaction.
  - **Loss-terms**: Physical dynamics encoded in loss functions (typically via differentiable operations).
  - **Interleaved**: Full physical simulation combined with DNN output, requiring fully differentiable simulators.

Approaches leveraging **differentiable physics** enable very tight integration of deep learning and numerical simulations.

## Major Sections

The repository contains extensive curated lists across multiple categories:

1. **I15 Physics-based Deep Learning Links** (primary focus) - 40+ projects including diffSPH, PDE-Transformer, PhiFlow, ConFIG, PRDP, and many others covering differentiable simulation, diffusion models for PDEs, turbulence modeling, and neural network-based solvers.

2. **Additional Links for Fluids** - 70+ references covering fluid dynamics applications including turbulence modeling, super-resolution, reduced-order modeling, CFD surrogate models, graph neural networks for fluids, and reinforcement learning for fluid control.

3. **Additional Links for General PDEs** - 40+ references covering neural PDE solvers, physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), neural operators, Koopman theory, and differentiable programming for PDEs.

4. **Additional Links for Other Physics Problems** - 60+ references covering climate modeling, molecular dynamics, soft-body physics, robotics, material science, and general scientific machine learning.

5. **Surveys and Overview Articles** - 5 key survey papers on physics-guided deep learning, ML for fluid mechanics, and reinforcement learning for fluids.

6. **Simulation and Deep Learning Frameworks** - 8 frameworks including PhiFlow, DiffTaichi, Jax-MD, Jax-CFD, and SciML.

## Key Facts

- **1.9k stars** on GitHub
- **317 forks**
- **131 watchers**
- **254 commits** on the master branch
- The digital PBDL book is available at https://www.physicsbaseddeeplearning.org/ (or as PDF on arXiv)
- Maintained by the I15 lab at TUM (Technical University of Munich)

## Concluding Remarks

The repository is intended as a dynamic, curated collection. The maintainers invite submissions of overlooked papers via email (i15ge at cs.tum.de).

<summary>
This is a GitHub repository page for a research project by Jithin Sasikumar, conducted between June 2020 and March 2021, comparing explainable AI (XAI) methods for explaining deep LSTM models used in anomaly detection for time-series data (specifically satellite telemetry data). The project was affiliated with the German Aerospace Center (DLR) and Hochschule Bonn-Rhein-Sieg.

**Problem:** Deep learning models lack transparency and interpretability ("black box" problem), which is critical for safety-critical applications like satellite anomaly detection.

**Methods Compared:**
- **LRP (Layer-wise Relevance Propagation):** A gradient-based attribution method. Implemented only for bi-directional LSTM models (due to tool limitations at the time).
- **LIME:** A perturbation-based method. Threw an exception because LIME expects a classifier (probability output), but the models were regression-based with ReLU activation.
- **SHAP:** A perturbation-based method. Worked for most LSTM architectures (vanilla, stacked, bi-directional) but failed on encoder-decoder LSTM due to flatten layers producing zero SHAP values. SHAP is slower than LRP.

**LSTM Architectures Tested:** Simple/vanilla LSTM, encoder-decoder LSTM, stacked LSTM, and bi-directional LSTM.

**Key Conclusions:**
- Gradient-based attribution methods (like LRP) are the best-fit approach for LSTM regression-based models (differentiable models).
- SHAP works but is not optimized for neural networks and is slower than LRP.
- LIME does not work for regression models (only classifiers).
- The research recommends gradient-based methods as the most suitable for explaining LSTM regression models for anomaly detection in time series.

**Future Work:** Implement integrated gradients and DeepLIFT; extend LRP to support more LSTM architectures; develop optimal evaluation metrics for explanations.

**Resources:** The repository contains Jupyter notebooks, models, result plots, and images. The code is not refactored and was based on tools/libraries available during the 2020-2021 timeframe.

--- SOURCE 17: PoS(Pixel2022)010 ---
URL: https://inspirehep.net/files/d00e37f98693ee30c1a6a31d0c7a00a8

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific paper presented at the 10th International Workshop on Semiconductor Pixel Detectors (Pixel2022) in December 2022 in Santa Fe, New Mexico, authored by Gregor Kramberger of the Jožef Stefan Institute, Slovenia. The paper discusses silicon detector technologies for precision track timing, motivated by the need for tens-of-picosecond time resolution in future particle physics experiments (HL-LHC, FCC-hh, etc.) where high collision rates require 4D tracking (position + time).

**Key technologies discussed:**

1. **Low Gain Avalanche Detectors (LGADs):** Planar sensors with a gain layer (p+) that provides avalanche multiplication (~10x gain). Achieve excellent time resolution (~30 ps) for large pads (~1 mm). Main drawbacks: radiation tolerance limited to ~few×10^15 cm^-2 due to acceptor removal in the gain layer (mitigated by carbon enrichment), and poor fill factor (large inter-pad gaps of ~50 μm). Several variants to improve fill factor: Inverse-LGAD, AC-LGAD, DC-Resistive-LGAD, and Trench-Isolated LGAD (few μm inter-pad gaps).

2. **Monolithic sensors:** Electronics and sensor on same wafer. Two designs: small-electrode (low capacitance, low noise, but large weighting field contribution) and large-electrode (similar to conventional planar). Novel PicoAD detector uses thin active layer (5 μm) with gain, aiming for ~10 ps resolution.

3. **3D sensors:** Electrodes (columns or trenches) extend through the sensor thickness, decoupling drift distance from signal generation. Column-3D (50×50 μm² cells) achieved ~20-30 ps resolution. Trench-3D (Time Spot project) reached ~20 ps with <10 ps weighting field contribution. Very radiation hard (up to 3×10^16 cm^-2). Drawbacks: larger capacitance, fill factor issues, complex production.

**Time resolution contributions:** Noise jitter (σ_j ~ t_p/(S/N)), time walk from Landau fluctuations (σ_lf), and weighting field effects (σ_wf). For 10 ps resolution, gain is necessary for planar detectors. 3D sensors minimize σ_lf due to short drift distances.

**Future directions:** Internal gain in CMOS and 3D detectors, improved DRIE for smaller electrodes, monolithic 3D sensors, and fast electronics with low power consumption.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 19: 4D-tracking with silicon detectors: ---
URL: https://agenda.infn.it/event/46193/contributions/268085/attachments/137563/206794/4Dtracking-CogneSchool.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This presentation by R. Arcidiacono (Università del Piemonte Orientale & INFN Torino) at the XXXIII Bonaudi-Chiavassa International School on Particle Detectors covers a decade of developments in 4D-tracking with silicon detectors, focusing on measuring both position (3D) and time (4th dimension) of charged particles.

**Key Sections:**

1. **3D Tracking Basics**: Silicon sensors have been the preferred technology for particle tracking for over 40 years due to excellent spatial resolution, flexibility, and reliability. Traditional silicon sensors are ~300 µm thick diodes operated under reverse bias, functioning as solid-state ionization chambers. Key characteristics: small band gap (1.12 eV), 3.6 eV per e-h pair, ~106 e-h/µm, high carrier mobility allowing fast charge collection (<10 ns).

2. **The 4th Dimension (Time)**: Traditionally, time measurement used MRPCs, scintillators, and Cherenkov detectors. The feasibility of silicon sensors for precision timing was demonstrated through Low-Gain Avalanche Diode (LGAD) technology, enabling 4D-tracking detectors that measure both position and time.

3. **Applications of Timing**: Time information can be used at each point along the track, at track level, or at trigger level. Benefits include massive simplification of pattern recognition, distinguishing overlapping events, and trigger rate reduction.

4. **Future Collider Requirements**: Next-generation facilities (FCC-ee, ILC, CLIC) demand spatial resolution of 3-5 µm, time resolution of tens of ps, very thin material (~100 µm Si), and pixel sizes of 25×25 µm².

5. **LGAD Technology**: The key innovation is an internal moderate gain layer (thin p+ doping) that provides large signals with short rise time and low noise, ideal for timing. State-of-the-art LGADs achieve 25-40 ps time resolution with 1.3×1.3 mm² pixels. The time resolution equation is: σ²t = σ²Jitter + σ²TimeWalk + σ²LandauNoise + σ²Distortion + σ²TDC.

6. **Radiation Hardness**: LGADs face acceptor removal effects under irradiation, with active acceptor density evolving as NA(Φ) = geffΦ + NA(0)e^(-c·NA(0)·Φ/Φ0). Pre-irradiated devices achieve ~30 ps timing; after irradiation to 1.5×10¹⁵ neq/cm², resolution degrades to ~50-60 ps.

7. **Resistive AC-Coupled LGADs (RSD/AC-LGAD)**: To overcome the inter-pad dead area problem in standard LGADs, resistive AC-coupled readout was developed. This design uses a continuous gain layer with resistive n+ layer and AC-coupled readout pads, achieving 100% fill factor. Spatial resolution of ~3% of pitch size was demonstrated (e.g., ~40 µm for 1300 µm pitch, ~15 µm for 450 µm pitch). Time jitter of ~20 ps was achieved at gain ~30.

8. **Testbeam Results**: RSD2-450 µm pitch devices at gain ~50 demonstrated ~19 µm spatial resolution (with tracker resolution to be deconvolved). Using FAST2 ASIC readout, spatial resolution of ~3-4% of pitch was measured, with a constant term of ~13 µm dominating at higher amplitudes.

9. **DC-RSD Evolution**: The next generation (DC-coupled Resistive Silicon Detectors) removes the oxide layer for AC-coupling, implants readout electrodes directly on the resistive layer, and adds charge containment structures (isolating trenches). Advantages include: no signal dispersion (predetermined number of pads), no bipolar signals (~1 ns pulses), no baseline fluctuations, improved SNR, and feasibility of O(cm²) active surface devices.

10. **DC-RSD1 Production**: First proof-of-concept production completed at FBK in November 2024, implementing square and triangular pixel matrices with isolating trenches, multiple pitch options, and various test structures. Preliminary testbeam results at DESY with 5 GeV electrons show clear signal separation, fast unipolar signals matching standard LGAD shape, and perfect isolation with signals seen only in electrodes belonging to the hit pixel.
</summary>

### 1. Appications in PET (Positron Emision Tomography) Detector Readout

#### 1.1 Time-Walk and Timing-Shift Correction for Dual-Ended Readout TOF-DOI PET
**Soure 2**: H. Wang, J. Xie, J. Qi, S. R. Cherry, and J. Du, "A Time-Walk and Timing-Sift Correction Method for Dual-Ended Readout TOF-DOI PET Detectors," *IEEE Transations on Radiation and Plasma Medical Sciences*, 2024.

This paper presents a combined time-walk and timing-shift correction method for dual-ended readout time-of-flight (TOF) PET detectors with depth-of-interaction (DOI) capability. Two dual-ended readout detectors were constructed using Hamamatsu S14161-3050-08 SiPM arrays coupled to 8×8 arrays of 3.1×3.1×20 mm³ LYSO crystals (3.2 mm pitch). The PETsys TOFPET2 readout system was used for data acquisition. Events were categorized into DOI layers based on the ratio of energies detected by the two SiPM arrays. The correction method uses the relationship between threshold crossing time differences and the natural logarithm of energy ratios (e.g., t₂-t₃ vs. ln(E₂/E₃)) to derive correction parameters (c for time-walk, b for timing-sift) for each DOI layer pair.
- CTR improved from 260.7 ± 1.0 ps to 229.4 ± 1.0 ps (improvement of ~31 ps) using a 400–650 keV energy window.
- Correcting time-walk alone improved CTR by 12.6 ps; DOI correction added ~20 ps further improvement.
- Optimal number of DOI layers was determined to be 4; beyond 4 layers, improvement plateaued (228.8 ps at 8 layers).
- Detector had a DOI resolution of 2.6 mm.
- Method also corrects timing offsets from readout electronics, improving localization accuracy along the LOR.
- Supported by NIH grants R01 EB028806 and R01 EB031961.

#### 1.2 Deep Learning-Based Positon and Non-Linearity Correction for PET Detectors Using TOT Readout
**Soure 11**: D. Baek, L. Sunwoo, I. Lee, S. Lee, J. Jung, J. H. Jung, and Y. Choi, "Deep Learning Based Position and Non-Linearity Correction for High-Performance PET Detector Using a Time-Over-Threshold Readout Method," *Journal of Nuclear Medicine*, Vol. 65, supplement 2, June 2024.

This study uses a pre-trained MLP (Multi-Layer Perceptron) with four hidden layers and ReLU activation functions to estimate gamma interaction positions in a PET detector module consisting of a 7×7 array of LYSO crystals (1.75×1.75×16 mm³) and a 4×4 array of SiPMs (3×3 mm²) with a 0.5 mm light guide. Training data (~1,000,000 counts) was acquired using both QDC and TOT modes of the ASIC (FEM128, PETsys electronics). The MLP was initially designed in Python, translated to HDL using HLS4ML, and implemented on a Xilinx Kintex-7 FPGA (XC7K325T-2FFG900C).

Key Results:
- GPU-processed PSNR: 25.92 dB, SSIM: 0.9197
- FPGA-implemented PSNR: 22.90 dB, SSIM: 0.9161
- Compared to uncorrected TOT data, MLP-corrected maps showed PSNR improvements of 86.21% (GPU) and 64.51% (FPGA), and SSIM improvements of 30.32% (GPU) and 29.81% (FPGA).
- Conclution: Feasibility of correctng TOT-acquired gamma interacion positions using an MLP model implemented on FPGA, achieving quailty similar to QDC while enabing real-time correction at the edge.

#### 1.3 Machine earning-Based Timing Calibration for PET Detectors (Gradient-Bosted Decision Trees)
**Soure 12**: S. Naunheim et al., "Holistic evaluation of a machine learning-based timing calibration method for PET detectors," *Physics in Medicine & Biology*, 2024. DOI: 10.1088/1361-6560/ad63ec.

This paper presents a holistic evaluation of a machine learning-based timing calibration method for PET detectors using gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDT) combined with residual physics. The study used two PET detectors with LSO scintillators and TOFPET2 ASIC readout. Coincidence data was colcted with a moving ²²Na radiation source at various positions. Two parameters were introduced: step width (sw, spatial sparsity) and undersamling factor (usf, statistical sparsity) to simlate reduced measurement time. 80 GBDT models were trained with varying sw (10-50mm) and usf (1-100,000) combinaions.

Key Resuts:
- CTR improved from 304±5 ps (conentional analytical calibation) to 216±1 ps (ML-based calibation) for the 450-550 keV energy window.
- Calibration time reduced from 43 hours to approximatey 3 minutes (acceleration factor of 1000) without sacrifiing quailty.
- Models trained with sw ≤ 20mm and usf ≤ 500 passed al quailty criteria.
- Method demonstated for the first time on analog readout technology, proving technology independence.

#### 1.4 Explicit TOF Corrections for PET Detectors Using Residual Physics-Based Machine earning
**Soure 13**: S. Naunheim et al., "Rethinking timing residuals: advancing PET detectors with explicit TOF corrections," *Frontiers in Physics*, 17 Apri 2025. DOI: 10.3389/fphy.2025.1570925. Also avaiable on arXiv: 2502.07630.

This paper introduces a novel "explicit correction" machine learning method that directy predicts correction values for timing residuals, as oppposed to their previous "implicit correction" approach that predicted expected time differences. The study used two detector stacks of 44 LYSO:Ce,Ca crystals (3.8mm × 3.8mm × 20mm each) coupled to 4×4 Broadcom NUV-MT SiPMs and digitized with TOFPET2 ASIC.

Key Findings:
- Explicit correction approach removes the strong dependence on training step width (distance between source positions)
- The new method preserves linearity even when training data is sparsely sampled
- Timing performance improved from (371 ± 6) ps to (281 ± 5) ps for coincidences in the 430-590 keV energy window
- Approach alows for massive simplifiation of data acquisition, potentially requiring only a single source position
- Models can be exponentially reduced in size, making them suitable for high-throughput PET scanner applications
- Uses gradient-boosted decision trees (XGBoost) as the model architecture, which can be implemented in FPGAs for edge-AI applications

#### 1.5 Review: Machine earning in PET from Photon Detection to Quantiative Image Reconstruction

URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739333

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper by Du et al. (2017) proposes and validates a self-calibrated time-walk correction method for PET detectors using leading edge discriminators (LEDs). The method uses one detector as a reference to correct the time-walk of another detector, without needing an external dedicated reference detector or electronics modifications. Events from the reference detector within a narrow 5 keV energy window around the 511 keV photopeak are used to establish the relationship between event energy and threshold crossing time. A piecewise cubic hermite interpolating polynomial fit is applied to the rebinned energy and timing data to correct time-walk on an event-by-event basis.

Key experimental details: Two detectors were assembled using SensL MicroFB SiPMs and 2.5 mm × 2.5 mm × 20 mm polished LYSO crystals. Tests were conducted at 27.5 V bias and 20 °C.

Key results:
- Coincidence timing resolution (CTR) without correction: 389.0 ± 12.0 ps (425–650 keV window) and 670.2 ± 16.2 ps (250–750 keV window)
- CTR with LED-based self-correction: 367.3 ± 0.5 ps (425–650 keV) and 413.7 ± 0.9 ps (250–750 keV)
- CTR using CFD: 442.8 ± 12.8 ps (425–650 keV) and 476.0 ± 13.0 ps (250–750 keV)
- CTR using CFD-based reference detector correction: 367.3 ± 0.4 ps (425–650 keV) and 413.4 ± 0.9 ps (250–750 keV)

The proposed LED-based time-walk correction method achieved timing resolution equivalent to the CFD-based reference detector method and better than using CFD alone. The method also successfully improved timing resolution of large-area SiPM array detector modules from 11.2 ± 0.2 ns to 4.2 ± 0.1 ns.

The authors conclude that this self-correction method is advantageous because it requires no external reference detector, electronics modification, or dedicated calibration process. It can be applied to single-event data from PET scanners with time-stamped events to improve timing resolution.
</summary>

SUMMARY:

This scientific article, published in IEEE Transactions on Radiation and Plasma Medical Sciences (2024), presents a novel method for correcting both time-walk and timing-shift in dual-ended readout time-of-flight (TOF) PET detectors. The method was developed and evaluated by researchers at the University of California, Davis.

The correction addresses two main issues: (1) time-walk caused by using leading-edge discrimination (LED) for timing pick-off, which is sensitive to signal amplitude variations, and (2) timing-shift caused by the depth-of-interaction (DOI) effect in thick scintillation crystals (~20 mm LYSO). The method uses the relationship between detected energies and threshold crossing times to correct both effects simultaneously.

Key aspects of the methodology: Two dual-ended readout PET detectors were constructed using Hamamatsu S14161-3050-08 SiPM arrays coupled to both ends of 8×8 arrays of 3.1×3.1×20 mm³ LYSO crystals (3.2 mm pitch). A PETsys TOFPET2 readout system was used for data acquisition. Events were categorized into DOI layers, with timing corrections applied per layer pair.

Results: The average coincidence time resolution (CTR) improved from 260.7 ± 1.0 ps to 229.4 ± 1.0 ps (a ~31 ps improvement) using a 400–650 keV energy window. Time-walk correction alone contributed ~12.6 ps improvement, while DOI-based timing-shift correction added another ~20 ps. The study also found that using 4 DOI layers provided near-optimal timing improvement (229.4 ps vs 228.8 ps for 8 layers), making it a practical choice for balancing performance and computational cost. The timing-shift caused by readout electronics (which doesn't affect FWHM CTR but impacts localization accuracy along the LOR) was also corrected.
