messages.content:
**List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

1. "AI neural network time-walk correction electronics readout timing resolution improvement over CFD leading edge"
2. "time-walk correction machine learning deep learning timing resolution picoseconds precision"
3. "FPGA neural network timing correction resource utilization LUT DSP BRAM inference latency"
4. "neural network FPGA time-walk correction readout electronic high-rate MHz"
5. "spiking neural network transformer timing correction particle detector electronics"
6. "hls4ml neural network timing correction FPGA resource utilization LUT DSP BRAM latency"
7. "radiation tolerance FPGA neural network particle detector LHC CERN"
8. "on-chip learning FPGA neural network particle detector timing calibration drift"

---

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

## (1) Time Resolution Improvement: AI Methods vs. Traditional Methods

### DNN-based Time-Walk Correction for CMS-PPS Diamond Timing Detectors (CERN)
A study published in *Computer Science* (2024) by researchers at CERN investigated using deep neural networks to replace the Constant Fraction Discriminator (CFD) algorithm for time-walk correction in the Precision Proton Spectrometer (PPS) subsystem of the CMS detector at the LHC. The neural networks used all voltage samples in a waveform time series. Three architectures were evaluated: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and a UNet-based model. The UNet-based model achieved the best results, improving timing precision by 8% to 23% depending on the detector's readout channel. The base experiment showed a 17% improvement over CFD, from 71.6 ps to 58.4 ps. The networks were also tested under LHC-like conditions with 24-sample time series, achieving a 15% improvement (73.3 ps to 62.1 ps). The study used data from DESY-II synchrotron test beam facilities, employing MCP-PMT detectors as a reference (10 ps precision) alongside PPS diamond timing detectors (50-100 ps precision). The dataset consisted of ~500,000 waveform entries. [Source 7, Source 12]

### LSTM-based Timing Correction for MRPC TOF Detectors (EIC)
A proposal (July 2022) for the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) described a sealed MRPC (sMRPC) with 32 gas gaps of 104 µm thickness achieving 16 ps intrinsic resolution in cosmic-ray tests using standard gas. A new analysis based on the deep learning method using a Long-Short-Term-Memory (LSTM) network further improved the time resolution to ~16.8 ps, compared to 23 ps with the traditional Time-Over-Threshold (ToT) method. This represents an improvement of approximately 27% over the conventional ToT method. At high rates (15 kHz/cm²), the resolution degrades to ~20 ps. [Source 6]

### MLP Neural Network for PICOSEC Gaseous Detector Timing (CERN RD51)
A presentation by I. Manthos et al. (HEP 2021, Thessaloniki) investigated signal processing techniques for precise timing with the PICOSEC detector, targeting ~20-30 ps timing resolution for HL-LHC pileup mitigation. Methods tested on PICOSEC MIP data included:
- **Constant Fraction Discrimination (CFD):** Reference method achieved 50.5 ps (full dataset) and 24.4 ps (events fully embedded in detector area).
- **Leading Edge - multi Time-over-Threshold (mToT):** Used 7 thresholds (10-200 mV). Best thresholds: 10mV (73.5 ps), 100mV (29.2 ps). Combined: 48.8 ps overall.
- **Leading Edge - multi Charge-over-Threshold (mCoT):** Best thresholds: 10mV (54.8 ps), 100mV (26.7 ps). Combined: 44.9 ps overall; 23.2 ps for fully embedded events — **better than CFD**.
- **Neural Network (MLP):** Inputs from ToT at 10/50/100 mV thresholds. Achieved 46.0 ps overall; 25.2 ps for fully embedded events.

In sub-picosecond domain tests (70 p.e. dataset), both CFD (5.50 ps) and mCoT (5.52 ps) performed comparably. The key conclusion was that mCoT outperforms CFD when charge info is available from front-end electronics, and neural networks yield results comparable to analytical methods. [Source 2]

### CNN-based Time-Walk Correction for BGO TOF-PET Scintillators
A study published in *EJNMMI Physics* (2025) compared different timing estimation methods for BGO scintillators in TOF-PET, comparing leading-edge discrimination (LED), time-walk correction (TWC) using two thresholds, and a convolutional neural network (CNN) approach. For 2×2×3 mm³ crystals:
- LED: 157±3 ps CTR
- TWC: 129±2 ps (18% improvement)
- CNN: 115±2 ps (26% improvement)

For 2×2×20 mm³ crystals:
- LED: 280±8 ps
- TWC: 241±7 ps (14% improvement)
- CNN: 239±7 ps (15% improvement), showing similar performance between TWC and CNN for longer crystals.

The CNN demonstrated better tail suppression in coincidence time distributions, particularly evident in the full-width tenth-maximum (FWTM) metrics. The study concluded that for longer BGO crystals, a simpler two-threshold TWC approach captures most essential information, while the CNN offers marginal additional benefits. [Source 9]

### LED-based Self-Correction for PET Detectors
A study by Du et al. (2017) presented a self-calibrating time-walk correction method for PET detectors using leading edge discriminators (LEDs). Experimental validation used two SensL MicroFB SiPMs coupled to 2.5×2.5×20 mm polished LYSO crystals. Key results:
- Without correction: 389.0±12.0 ps (425–650 keV window) and 670.2±16.2 ps (250–750 keV)
- With LED-based self-correction: 367.3±0.5 ps (425–650 keV) and 413.7±0.9 ps (250–750 keV)
- With CFD: 442.8±12.8 ps (425–650 keV) and 476.0±13.0 ps (250–750 keV)
- With CFD-based reference detector correction: 367.3±0.4 ps (425–650 keV) and 413.4±0.9 ps (250–750 keV)

The LED-based self-correction method matched the performance of a dedicated CFD reference detector and outperformed standard CFD. The method was also successfully applied to large-area SiPM arrays, improving timing from 11.2±0.2 ns to 4.2±0.1 ns. [Source 1]

### Combined Time-Walk and Timing-Shift Correction for Dual-Ended Readout TOF-PET
A paper published in *IEEE Transactions on Radiation and Plasma Medical Sciences* (November 2024) by researchers at UC Davis presented a combined correction method for dual-ended readout TOF-PET detectors with DOI capability. Using two Hamamatsu S14161-3050-08 SiPM arrays coupled to 8×8 arrays of 3.1×3.1×20 mm³ LYSO crystals with a 400-650 keV energy window:
- CTR improved from 260.7 ± 1.0 ps to 229.4 ± 1.0 ps after correction (~31 ps improvement)
- Time-walk correction alone improved CTR by 12.6 ps
- DOI correction added another ~20 ps improvement
- The optimal number of DOI layers was 4 (228.8 ps at 8 layers)
- The detector had a DOI resolution of 2.6 mm [Source 3, Source 6]

### MAC/UMAC Autoencoder Architectures for Timing Reconstruction
A study published in *Particles* (MDPI, 2025) by Sofia University researchers presented convolutional neural networks with modified autoencoder (MAC) architectures for reconstructing pulse arrival times in scintillating crystal calorimeters. The MAC model showed a mean difference of 0.7 ns between true and predicted arrival time, while the UMAC (upsampling version) reduced this to −0.003 ns with a narrower distribution. The model is sensitive to sub-bin timing — it can distinguish arrival times with higher precision than the 1 ns time bin width. The UMAC significantly improves time resolution by adding two upsampling layers (factor of 2) in the decoder, achieving 4096-length labels (0.25 ns precision). [Source 14]

### ML-Aided Self-Calibration for FPGA-Based Time-to-Digital Converters (TDC)
A paper published in *Intelligent Systems with Applications* (May 2026) presented a novel FPGA-based TDC using machine learning-aided self-calibration. Three ML models (NN, DNN, CNN) were trained on over 300,000 raw TDC samples to correct residual non-linearities. On a Kintex UltraScale FPGA, the ML-aided TDC achieved timing precision below 15 ps (13.6 ps standard deviation), improving precision by more than 10.5× over conventional encoder-based FPGA TDC, and reaching performance comparable to state-of-the-art ASIC TDCs. [Source 13]

---

## (2) Processing Speed: Inference Latency of Neural Networks vs. Traditional Digital CFD

### hls4ml Framework for Ultra-Low-Latency Inference
The hls4ml framework, originally presented in 2018 for CERN high-energy physics applications, enables FPGA-based ML inference with latencies ranging from 10 ns for small fully connected networks to microseconds for moderate CNNs and transformers. For the Level-1 trigger at the LHC, which requires sub-microsecond inference latencies (hundreds of nanoseconds) at 40 MHz collision rates, hls4ml demonstrated a fully-connected three-hidden-layer network (64, 32, 32 neurons) with latency of approximately 75-150 ns (10-35 clock cycles at 200 MHz) on a Xilinx Kintex Ultrascale FPGA. [Source 3, Source 4, Source 2, Source 3 (from second search)]

### Specific Inference Latency Examples

**FPGA-based Neural Network for NA62 Experiment (CERN):**
The FPGA-RICH system for the NA62 experiment combines classical online processing with a compact Neural Network algorithm (RiNNgs) to achieve efficient event classification while managing the ~10 MHz throughput requirement. The streaming pipeline achieves ~1 μs latency, comparable to that of the NA62 detectors. [Source 15]

**ML-on-FPGA for EIC (Jefferson Lab):**
A presentation by Sergey Furletov (Jefferson Lab, November 2022) reported specific FPGA inference latencies for ML algorithms implemented for the EIC:
- MLP neural network for PID (ionization counting): 65 ns latency, 3% DSP utilization
- RNN/LSTM for track fitting: 1 µs latency, 19% DSP resources after pruning
- Graph Neural Networks (GNN) for pattern recognition: 1.4 µs latency, 70% DSP usage, handling up to 21 hits/42 edges
- Convolutional VAE for calorimeter reconstruction: 1.3 µs latency, 71% DSP resources
- The test board was a Xilinx Virtex UltraScale+ (XCVU9P with 6,840 DSP slices, >1 Tera multiplications/second peak performance). [Source 11]

**hls4ml CNN for LHC Triggers:**
A paper published in *Machine Learning: Science and Technology* (2021) by Thea Aarrestad et al. demonstrated an inference latency of 5 µs using convolutional architectures for microsecond-latency applications at the LHC level-1 trigger system. Models were synthesized targeting a Xilinx Virtex UltraScale+ VU9P FPGA at 200 MHz, achieving ~5 µs latency regardless of bit width. [Source 1 (from second search)]

**CMS-PPS DNN Timing Inference:**
For the CMS-PPS diamond timing detectors, the neural network inference time was reported as ~10 ms per sample on CPU, making it suitable for online processing in the high-level trigger reconstruction chain. [Source 7]

**RNN (LSTM/GRU) on FPGA via hls4ml:**
A paper by Khoda et al. (2023, *Mach. Learn.: Sci. Technol.* 4 025004) presented RNN implementations within hls4ml for LHC applications. The non-static mode reduced initiation interval (II) from ~315 to 1, enabling up to 40 MHz operation rates. Benchmark models included:
- Top quark tagging (~3,500 parameters): latency 1.7 µs
- Jet flavor tagging (~67,500 parameters): latency 6.7–38.8 µs
- QuickDraw dataset (~134,000 parameters): latency 35.4–332 µs

For the QuickDraw LSTM model, FPGA throughput (4,300–9,700 events/sec at batch 1) significantly outperformed GPU inference (660 events/sec at batch 1). GRU models use approximately 1/4 less resources than LSTM models due to the 3:4 ratio of matrix multiplications. [Source 2 (from second search)]

**CNN for DUNE Neutrino Experiment:**
A Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence article (May 2022) presented a 2D CNN for real-time data selection in the DUNE experiment. On a Xilinx UltraScale+ (XCKU115) FPGA, the quantized network achieved an inference latency of 23.4 μs — well below the 2.25 ms per image exposure time. [Source 13]

**FPGA-Accelerated NIDS Anomaly Detection:**
Using the hls4ml framework on a PYNQ-Z2 FPGA (Xilinx Zynq-7020 SoC), the FCNN FPGA deployment achieved 193.50× faster inference and 170.56× higher throughput than CPU, and 898.50× faster inference and 792.07× higher throughput than GPU. The CNN FPGA deployment achieved 64.00× faster inference and 72.67× higher throughput than CPU, and 574.00× faster inference and 650.58× higher throughput than GPU. [Source 10]

**FPGA for PET Signal Processing:**
A paper published in *IEEE Trans.Nucl.Sci.* (2019) presented a real-time FPGA-based digital signal processing system for a marmoset brain PET scanner using a Xilinx Artix-7 FPGA. The pipeline logic works at 125 MHz with a signal processing capability exceeding 1,000,000 events/s/channel. [Source 8]

**Embedded FPGA (eFPGA) at SLAC:**
At SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, two eFPGAs (130nm and 28nm nodes) were designed and tested. The 28nm eFPGA successfully ran a toy ML algorithm for classifying high-momentum particle tracks from soft tracks, achieving 100% accuracy relative to simulation. The eFPGA has a central FPGA fabric that is flexible and configurable, but it's "embedded" into an ASIC design, combining the reconfigurability of an FPGA with the efficiency and robustness of an ASIC. [Source 7 (from second search)]

**Ultra-Small ML (1K LUTs) for On-Detector Processing:**
A presentation by Qibin LIU (SLAC) at IEEE Real-Time 2026, Elba, demonstrated an ultra-small ML model for cluster counting achieving ~1K LUTs utilization — 20× smaller than reference HLS models with no DSP usage — while delivering better performance than derivative-based peak-finding and comparable to reference ML models. The design was validated in system simulation with AXI-S interface. [Source 12]

---

## (3) Resource Consumption: FPGA Resource Utilization

### hls4ml Jet Substructure Classification Network
For the example jet substructure model (three-hidden-layer network: 64, 32, 32 neurons, 16 inputs, 5 outputs) on a Xilinx Kintex Ultrascale FPGA at 200 MHz:
- Latency: ~75 ns (15 clocks @ 200 MHz)
- DSPs: 954 (17%) — with pruning and quantization
- FFs: 53k (3%)
- LUTs: 36k (5%)
- With compression (pruning 70% of weights via L1 regularization) and quantization (fixed-point precision <16,6> bits), the design fit well within available resources. [Source 4 (from first search), Source 4 (from second search)]

### hls4ml CNN Resource Reduction
For the SVHN dataset benchmark using a CNN on a Xilinx Virtex UltraScale+ VU9P FPGA:
- The FPGA critical resource consumption (DSPs) can be reduced by 97% with zero loss in model accuracy, and by 99% when tolerating a 6% accuracy degradation
- The heterogeneously quantized AutoQ (AQ) model reduces DSP consumption by 99% while maintaining 88% accuracy
- Pruning and quantization-aware training (QAT) through QKERAS is the recommended workflow before FPGA deployment
- Inference latency: ~5 µs regardless of bit width [Source 1 (from second search)]

### DUNE 2D CNN on Xilinx UltraScale+ (XCKU115)
- Block RAM: 4%
- DSP units: 38%
- Flip flops: 10%
- Look-up tables: 20%
- Inference latency: 23.4 μs
- Classification accuracy: 95.2% in both floating-point and fixed-point implementations (with quantization-aware training)
- Without QAT, accuracy dropped to 72.4% [Source 13]

### FPGA-RICH for NA62 (AMD Xilinx Versal VCK190)
- Combines classical online processing with a compact Neural Network algorithm (RiNNgs)
- Streaming pipeline achieves ~1 μs latency
- Handles ~10 MHz throughput requirement
- Developed using HLS and hls4ml for software-hardware codesign [Source 15]

### ML-on-FPGA for EIC (Xilinx Virtex UltraScale+ XCVU9P)
- MLP for PID: 65 ns latency, 3% DSP utilization
- RNN/LSTM for track fitting: 1 µs latency, 19% DSP resources after pruning
- GNN for pattern recognition: 1.4 µs latency, 70% DSP usage, handles up to 21 hits/42 edges
- Convolutional VAE for calorimeter: 1.3 µs latency, 71% DSP resources
- The XCVU9P has 6,840 DSP slices and >1 Tera multiplications/second peak performance [Source 11]

### Ultra-Small ML (DA4ML) for On-Detector Processing
- Ultra-small ML model for cluster counting achieved ~1K LUTs utilization — 20× smaller than reference HLS models
- No DSP usage
- Better performance than derivative-based peak-finding
- Comparable performance to reference ML models
- Validated in system simulation with AXI-S interface [Source 12]

### SparseLUT Framework for LUT-Based DNNs on FPGAs
- Aggregates multiple PolyLUT sub-neurons via an adder, increasing neuron fan-in from F to F×A while reducing LUT complexity from O(2^(βFA)) to O(A×2^(βF) + 2^(A(β+1)))
- Achieves LUT reductions of 2.0×–13.9× and latency improvements of 1.2×–1.6× while maintaining accuracy
- At comparable accuracy, reduces LUT consumption by 4.8× and 13.9× on MNIST and Jet Substructure Classification tasks, respectively, while also decreasing latency by 1.2× to 1.6×
- Connectivity optimization (dynamic sparsification) achieves up to 2.13% accuracy gain on MNIST and 0.94% on Jet Substructure Classification without additional hardware overhead [Source 5 (from second search)]

### VGG16/VGG19 on Avnet Ultra96-V2 (Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC)
- VGG16: 89.54% Top-1 accuracy, 0.652 ms/frame latency (7.29× faster than CPU)
- VGG19: 87.46% Top-1 accuracy, 0.846 ms/frame latency (6.6× faster than CPU)
- Resource utilization: 90.6% DSP, 54.5% LUT, 58.3% BRAM, 41.7% FF
- Model file sizes reduced from 180 MB to 60.1 MB through quantization [Source 1 (from second search)]

### hls4ml Implementation Strategies
hls4ml implements three strategies for constant matrix-vector multiplication (CMVM):
- **Latency:** Fully unrolled, weights embedded into multiplier circuits; suitable for small models with very low latency requirements
- **Resource:** Stores weights in BRAM with explicit parallelism control; better for larger models
- **Distributed Arithmetic (DA):** Decomposes CMVM into shift-and-add operations via adder graph; no DSP usage; lowest fabric utilization

Users control parallelism via Reuse Factor (RF) and Parallelization Factor (PF) per layer. Low reuse factor achieves the lowest latency and highest throughput but uses the most resources, while high reuse factor saves resources at the expense of longer latency and lower throughput. [Source 3, Source 5 (from second search)]

### FPGA Power Consumption
- An FPGA-based accelerator (Xilinx Alveo U50) consumes 75W, significantly lower than GPU (300W for NVIDIA V100)
- FPGA multi-threading improves throughput nearly linearly
- The CERN Data Centre consumes about 37 gigawatt-hours per year, about 3% of CERN's total annual electrical consumption when the LHC operates [Source 8 (from second search), Source 15 (from first search)]

---

## (4) Technical Feasibility: Challenges in Training Data, Generalization, Radiation Tolerance, and Calibration Drift

### Training Data Requirements
- **CMS-PPS DNN study:** The dataset consisted of ~500,000 waveform entries, preprocessed to remove noisy and saturated events. The study used data from DESY-II synchrotron test beam facilities, employing MCP-PMT detectors as a reference (10 ps precision) alongside PPS diamond timing detectors (50-100 ps precision). A key limitation noted is the lack of MCP reference detectors in the actual LHC setup, though ongoing work aims to address this. [Source 7]
- **FPGA-based TDC ML calibration:** Trained on over 300,000 raw TDC samples to correct residual non-linearities. [Source 13]
- **NA62 FPGA-RICH:** Used a dataset of 3.13 million events for training and 3.50 million for testing from NA62 RUN 1 (2016-2018). [Source 15]
- **PETNet SNN:** Training was conducted on a multi-node GPU cluster (NVIDIA A100-40 GPUs) using data-parallel training with PyTorch DistributedDataParallel. [Source 11]

### Generalization to Different Detectors
- **CMS-PPS study:** Neural networks trained on specific channels perform best on those channels. Cross-channel training often yields worse results than CFD. The neural network approach works with both 48-sample and 24-sample time series. [Source 7]
- **BGO TOF-PET study:** For longer BGO crystals (20 mm), both CNN and TWC methods yield similar CTR (~240 ps FWHM), offering ~15% gain over LED. The simpler two-threshold TWC approach appears to capture most essential information for improving CTR in longer BGO crystals, suggesting that the additional complexity of CNNs may not always be justified. [Source 9]
- **MAC/UMAC study:** The MAC model was tested on real data from a fixed-target experiment's electromagnetic calorimeter, showing a higher number of recognized low-energy events than conventional peak-finding methods, as well as a better time resolution, though requiring additional calibration. [Source 14]
- **PICOSEC study:** The leading edge-CoT method was found to be adequate at one order of magnitude lower timing resolution (~5 ps). [Source 2]

### Radiation Tolerance of FPGA-based AI Implementations
- **Embedded FPGA (eFPGA) at SLAC:** The eFPGA combines the reconfigurability of an FPGA with the radiation-tolerance and efficiency of an ASIC. Two eFPGAs were designed and tested (130nm and 28nm nodes). The 28nm eFPGA successfully ran a toy ML algorithm for classifying high-momentum particle tracks from soft tracks. The findings demonstrate that open-source eFPGA design frameworks can be verified in silicon, and applications for future detectors (FCC, SuperKEKB, DUNE) are just beginning. The A3D3 Institute facilitates collaboration between academia and industry to advance these technologies. [Source 7 (from second search)]
- **CERN/AXOL1TL model:** The AXOL1TL model is a VAE (small MLP) trained with QAT. The weights are "hard-wired in the fabric" (shift-add operations instead of read-multiply-add cycles), but the chip can be reprogrammed. Everything runs in ≤2 clock cycles at 40MHz. The CICADA model is also a VAE but distilled with supervised loss on anomaly scores. Both models use ≤30K LUTs with low complexity. [Source 6 (from second search)]
- **ML-on-FPGA for EIC:** The presentation addressed reliability of methods through quantization aware training via QKeras, HLS C-simulation, C/RTL co-simulation, and Vivado test benches. [Source 11]

### Calibration Drift
- **PET LED-based self-correction:** The method is self-calibrated, as no extra reference detectors are needed to generate the relationship between threshold crossing time and event energy. With modern high-speed data transfer and storage, single-event data collection with timestamps is feasible, allowing this correction to be applied in software without additional hardware modifications. [Source 1]
- **Combined time-walk and timing-shift correction (UC Davis):** The method also corrects timing offsets from readout electronics, improving localization accuracy along the line-of-response. The correction uses the relationship between threshold crossing time differences and the natural logarithm of energy ratios to derive correction parameters for each DOI layer pair. [Source 3, Source 6 (from first search)]
- **ML-aided TDC self-calibration:** The approach significantly reduces design complexity, accelerates deployment, and eliminates lengthy manual calibration procedures. [Source 13]

### Other Feasibility Considerations
- **ATLAS ML challenges:** ML models can inherit biases from simulated training data, requiring dedicated de-biasing techniques. The usage of ML has to be closely coupled with continuous monitoring. [Source 15 (from first search)]
- **hls4ml limitations:** Very large models may exceed on-chip memory; primarily fixed-point precision; some vendor-specific pragmas remain; further sparsity support under development. Large/complex models may fail HLS compilation due to resource constraints; compression (quantization, pruning) is recommended. GNN support is still in development (no PyTorch Geometric). Transformer support is currently limited to Vitis back end via HGQ 2. [Source 3, Source 4 (from second search)]
- **FPGA-RICH for NA62:** The development leverages HLS and the open-source hls4ml package software-hardware codesign workflow, enabling fast and flexible reprogramming, debugging, and performance optimization. [Source 15]

---

## (5) Future Trends: On-Chip Learning, Spiking Neural Networks, Transformer Architectures, and Hybrid Analog-Neural Approaches

### On-Chip Learning and Runtime Reconfiguration
- Ongoing work in hls4ml targets extension to transformer variants, support for causal masking in attention, dynamic per-layer bit-width search, and runtime reconfiguration. [Source 2 (from second search)]
- Open-source toolchains and agentic workflows are boosting co-design for specialized algorithms on customized devices. Agentic EDA (electronic design automation) is becoming increasingly practical, with rapid progress from both vendors and open-source communities. [Source 12]
- The proposed co-design workflow includes: hardware-aware ML training using High Granularity Quantization (HGQ) for differentiable quantization and resource estimation; Direct-RTL conversion via the DA4ML open-source tool (HLS-free, bit-exact mapping); and system integration using agentic AI (LLM-based) frameworks like SciFi for automatic debugging, interface integration, and validation. [Source 12]

### Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) for PET
- **PETNet** (published by KIT researchers) presents a spiking neural network architecture for detecting photon coincidence pairs in PET data. A multi-objective loss function accounts for both spike count and spike timing.
- On the clinical PET dataset (240 crystals, low activity): PETNet achieved a maximum F1 score of 95.2%, outperforming the classical SCW algorithm (F1=93.3%).
- On the pre-clinical SAFIR dataset (2880 crystals, high activity): PETNet achieved F1=84.8% vs SCW's 90.1%, but inference was ~36× faster (30.64 min vs 880.41 min).
- On the clinical dataset, PETNet processed data ~20× faster than the classical approach.
- The multi-objective loss combining spike count loss (LΓ) and timing loss (L∆) significantly improved performance over count loss alone.
- The SNN used a single hidden layer LIF (Leaky Integrate and Fire) neuron architecture, trained with surrogate gradients and backpropagation through time using the snnTorch library.
- A comparison LSTM baseline failed to predict any coincidence pairs, driving all outputs to zero.
- The potential deployment of SNNs on low-power neuromorphic hardware enables integration of the algorithm directly into the detector ring for on-board prediction with minimal computational requirements. Current software implementations still operate on dense matrix operations, limiting efficiency gains. [Source 11]

### Transformer Architectures for Timing
- The ATLAS experiment at CERN uses ML algorithms to identify particles like b-hadrons using transformer architectures with attention mechanisms. Graph neural networks have been used to reconstruct complex collision events. [Source 15 (from first search)]
- hls4ml now supports transformers (multi-head attention via HGQ 2 front end), with sub-2 µs inference latency. Ongoing work targets extension to transformer variants, support for causal masking in attention, and dynamic per-layer bit-width search. [Source 2, Source 3 (from second search)]
- The HEP ML Living Review (frozen as of June 1, 2026) covers emerging areas including foundation models, LLMs, agents, and Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) as new neural network architectures being explored in HEP. [Source 14]

### Hybrid Analog-Neural Approaches
- The **PICOSEC study** demonstrated that the multi Charge-over-Threshold (mCoT) method outperforms CFD when charge info is available from front-end electronics (e.g., NINO chip). The mCoT method achieved 44.9 ps overall and 23.2 ps for fully embedded events — better than CFD. This represents a hybrid approach where analog front-end information is combined with digital processing. [Source 2]
- The **BGO TOF-PET study** concluded that the higher complexity of waveform digitization needed for CNNs could potentially be mitigated by adopting a simpler two-threshold TWC approach, which captures most essential information for improving CTR in longer BGO crystals. The authors note that deep learning methods may still contribute further as timing features in TOF-PET detector signals become more discernible. [Source 9]
- The **LED-based self-correction for PET** by Du et al. (2017) demonstrated that the method works without an external reference detector, using one detector as a reference by selecting events within a very narrow energy window (508.5–513.5 keV) around the 511 keV photopeak. This approach bridges analog thresholding with digital correction. [Source 1]

### Other Emerging Trends
- **hhs4ml Evolution:** The hls4ml platform supports inference times from 10 ns for small fully connected networks to microseconds for moderate CNNs and transformers. It is extensively validated in physics and commercial domains: LHC Level-1 triggers, QICK qubit readout (32 ns latency, 96% fidelity), real-time semantic segmentation at 3–4.9 ms/image for autonomous vehicles. [Source 2 (from second search)]
- **Ultra-small ML models** (<10K LUTs) are required for on-detector applications, and the DA4ML open-source toolchain enables Direct-RTL conversion without HLS, achieving bit-exact mapping. [Source 12]
- **Fast ML on FPGAs** at ATLAS uses convolutional and recurrent architectures outperforming traditional signal filters for calorimeter signals in the trigger system. [Source 15 (from first search)]
- **The HEP ML Living Review** provides a comprehensive, nearly exhaustive list of citations for ML applications in HEP, covering experimental, phenomenological, and theoretical analyses through June 2026. It includes sections on equivariant networks, physics-informed neural networks, generative models, anomaly detection, foundation models, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, and simulation-based inference. [Source 14]

---

Based on all the research conducted, create a comprehensive, well-structured answer to the overall research brief:
<Research Brief>
我是一名从事电子学读出系统（如高能物理探测器、核电子学或高速数据采集系统）的研究人员。我希望调研AI算法（特别是深度学习、机器学习方法）能否提升现有电子学读出系统中的时幅修正（time-amplitude correction / time-walk correction）方法。

具体来说，我需要调研以下内容：
1. 现有电子学读出时幅修正方法有哪些？包括传统方法（如恒定阈值甄别、过零甄别、CFD鉴别、波形采样+内插拟合等）及其局限性。
2. AI/ML算法在电子学读出时间修正中的应用现状：是否有已发表的研究将神经网络（如CNN、RNN、MLP）或回归模型用于时间-幅度关系的修正或时间恢复精度提升？
3. AI算法相比传统方法在时间分辨率、处理速度、资源消耗（FPGA实现可行性）等方面的优势与劣势。
4. 如果存在相关研究，请列出具体文献、数据集、开源代码或实际应用案例（如PET探测器、硅探测器、闪烁体探测器读出等）。
5. 该研究方向的技术可行性、潜在挑战以及未来发展趋势。

请优先调研中文和英文的学术文献，并尽量链接到原始论文、期刊文章或预印本（如arXiv）。如果可能，请提供可直接参考的官方或学术来源。调研范围不限时间，但优先关注近5年（2021-2026）的进展。
</Research Brief>

For more context, here is all of the messages so far. Focus on the research brief above, but consider these messages as well for more context.
<Messages>
Human: 为我调研AI算法能否提升现有电子学读出时幅修正方法
</Messages>
CRITICAL: Make sure the answer is written in the same language as the human messages!

### 1. LEADING EDGE DISCRIMINATION (CONSTANT THRESHOLD / LED)

#### 1.1 Operating Principle

The leading edge timing pick-off technique is the simplest timing extraction method for detector systems. In this method, a comparator triggers when the input signal crosses a fixed threshold voltage. The time of this crossing is recorded as the event time. The leading edge discriminator (LED) method introduces "time walk" errors because the threshold crossing time is signal-dependent: larger amplitude signals cross the fixed threshold earlier than smaller amplitude signals, even if their true arrival time is identical. As explained by the "Nuclear Physics 101" resource, "The time walk is due to a fixed trigger threshold for the various amplitude of signals. Larger the signal, the lesser the time walk." [14]

The signal amplitude must be recorded on an event-by-event basis to allow for offline correction of time walk, as described in the off-line correction method for CFD walk [6]. The correction is typically applied using a function of the form a/√(Q+b), which the Nuclear Physics 101 source found "fits the simulated data fairly well." [14] The Woods-Saxon type function only approximates the actual signal for a limited range of amplitude, and "the range of time walk from that can be infinity." [14]

#### 1.2 Typical Time Resolution Achieved

Time resolution for leading edge discriminators depends heavily on the application and correction method:

- **PET detectors (LYSO + SiPM, 2.5×2.5×20 mm³ crystals):** Without correction, coincidence timing resolution (CTR) was 389.0 ± 12.0 ps (425–650 keV energy window) and 670.2 ± 16.2 ps (250–750 keV energy window). With LED-based self-correction, CTR improved to 367.3 ± 0.5 ps (425–650 keV) and 413.7 ± 0.9 ps (250–750 keV). [1][11]

- **Dual-ended readout TOF-PET (LYSO + SiPM, 3.1×3.1×20 mm³):** CTR improved from 260.7 ± 1.0 ps to 229.4 ± 1.0 ps after time-walk correction using a 400–650 keV energy window. Correcting time-walk alone enhanced the timing resolution by 12.6 ps. [2][22]

- **Multi-ended readout TOF-PET (LYSO 6×6×25 mm³):** Compensated CTRs after fourth-order polynomial fitting time-walk correction: dual-ended readout 216.9 ps, side dual-ended readout 231.0 ps, and triple-ended readout 203.6 ps. The time-walk correction improved timing performance by approximately 10%, with maximum improvement of 25.2%. [3][21]

- **Large-area SiPM array detector modules:** Timing resolution improved from 11.2 ± 0.2 ns to 4.2 ± 0.1 ns using the LED-based self-correction method. [1][11]

- **PICOSEC gaseous detectors:** Using multi Time-over-Threshold (mToT), timing resolution of 48.8 ps was achieved for the complete dataset and 29.4 ps for events fully embedded in the detector area. [13]

#### 1.3 Limitations and Drawbacks

1. **Amplitude-Dependent Time Walk:** This is the fundamental limitation. The threshold crossing time depends on signal amplitude, causing timing errors that can be significant for signals with large dynamic range. As noted in the literature, "When the threshold of LED is set very low to achieve the best timing resolution, the energy walk depends on the emitted light in the first ns of scintillation, but not the total integrated number of photons." [12]

2. **Noise Sensitivity at Low Thresholds:** Setting the threshold very low to improve timing resolution increases susceptibility to electronic noise, as the threshold may be close to the baseline noise level.

3. **Limited Dynamic Range:** The LED method works best when signal amplitudes are relatively uniform. Large dynamic ranges (e.g., 100:1) require extensive correction or result in degraded timing.

4. **Requires Correction:** Unlike CFD, LED inherently requires time-walk correction post-processing to achieve good timing resolution, adding computational overhead. The correction typically uses the relationship between threshold crossing time and event energy on an event-by-event basis. [11]

5. **Rise Time Dependence:** The LED method also exhibits walk that depends on the rise time of the signal, which can vary with detector type and operating conditions.

6. **Count Rate Limitations:** At high count rates, baseline shifts can cause threshold-crossing time variations, further degrading timing accuracy.

### 2. ZERO-CROSSING DISCRIMINATION

#### 2.1 Operating Principle

The zero-crossing discrimination method determines timing information by detecting the zero-crossing point of a suitably shaped bipolar signal. The signal is converted from a unipolar pulse to a bipolar pulse (typically through differentiation or CR-RC shaping), and the timing pick-off occurs at the point where the shaped signal crosses zero. This zero-crossing point is independent of the signal amplitude, making it a form of amplitude-independent timing.

In the zero-crossing method, "information on the particle type is obtained from the zero-crossing time of the suitably shaped signal." [15][16] When used for pulse shape discrimination (PSD), the zero-crossing time differs for different particle types due to differences in the pulse shape (e.g., neutrons vs. gamma rays in liquid scintillators).

The Gardner Timing Error Detector, used in digital communication systems, is "a non-data-aided version of zero-crossing timing error detectors" where the algorithm targets zero crossings of the waveform rather than symbol peaks. [2]

For digital zero-crossing detection, the FPGA calculates the second derivative of the input signal, "whose zero crossing provides amplitude-independent timing with uncertainty equivalent to one sampling unit." [11]

#### 2.2 Typical Time Resolution Achieved

- **Analog zero-crossing for n/γ discrimination (BC501 liquid scintillator):** The analog zero-crossing method achieved Figure of Merit (FOM) values of 1.19 at 50 keVee to 1.65 at 600 keVee, outperforming the digital method by a factor of 1.4–1.6x. [4][17]

- **Digital zero-crossing (FPGA second derivative method):** Achieved intrinsic time resolution of 28 ps with a pulse generator using CAEN V1751 1 GS/s digitisers, and less than 500 ps total time dispersion with two LaBr₃(Ce) detectors and a ²²Na source. [11]

#### 2.3 Limitations and Drawbacks

1. **Requires Bipolar Shaping:** The signal must be converted to bipolar form, which requires additional analog circuitry (differentiator) or digital processing, adding complexity.

2. **Noise Sensitivity at Zero Crossing:** The zero-crossing point is sensitive to baseline noise, especially for low-amplitude signals where the slew rate near zero is small. As noted in the ILL FPGA implementation, the "zero crossing of the second derivative of the input signal" provides timing with uncertainty equivalent to one sampling unit, but this is limited by timing resolution of the digitizer. [11]

3. **Resistivity Fluctuations in Silicon Detectors:** For silicon detectors, the particle resolution is fundamentally determined by "resistivity fluctuations in the bulk silicon which cause the charge-collection time to depend on the point of impact." This creates a practical limitation because "the homogeneity of the dopand concentration (resistivity) in the silicon crystals used for detector production is a key parameter for the quality of particle discrimination based on PSD." [1]

4. **Finite Energy Threshold for Particle Identification:** A critical range Rc ≈ 50 μm (for 500 μm detectors) and Rc ≈ 25 μm (for 50 μm detectors) was observed, below which "the charge-collection time unexpectedly decreases, causing overlapping particle lines." This effect is not fully understood but limits discrimination at low energies. [1]

5. **Sampling Rate Limitation:** The analog zero-crossing method outperforms digital implementations primarily due to digitization rate limitations. As found in the INL study, "in digital processing the DGF-4C module we used was slow (40 MHz), which limited the sampling rate to 25 ns only." The authors concluded that "using faster FPGA chips that are commercially available today, like ACTEL 350 MHz or XILINX 450 MHz devices, will substantially improve the separation between gamma-ray and neutron peaks." [4][17]

6. **Complexity of Analog Circuitry:** Analog zero-crossing implementations require precision shaping amplifiers, baseline restoration circuits, and zero-crossing comparators, all of which contribute to system complexity, power consumption, and cost.

### 3. CONSTANT FRACTION DISCRIMINATION (CFD)

#### 3.1 Operating Principle

A constant fraction discriminator (CFD) is an electronic signal processing device that is designed to mimic the mathematical operation of finding a maximum of a pulse by finding the zero of its slope. "This forbids simple threshold triggering, which causes a dependence of the trigger time on the signal's peak height, an effect called time walk." [7][15] For signals with "identical rise times and peak shapes," triggering on "a constant fraction of the total peak height" yields trigger times independent from peak heights. [7][15]

The operating principle involves splitting the incoming signal into three components: "One component is delayed..., and connected to the noninverting input of a comparator. One component is connected to the inverting input of this comparator. One component is connected to the noninverting input of another comparator. A threshold value is connected to the inverting input of the other comparator. The output of both comparators is fed through an AND gate." [7][15]

In more detail, the CFD technique splits the input signal, attenuates one half and delays the other, then feeds both into a fast comparator with the delayed input inverted. This triggers a timing signal at a constant fraction (typically ~20%) of the input amplitude. The technique virtually eliminates timing "walk" for signals with the same rise time but different amplitudes. [8]

For a linear ramp input, the CFD crossing time is independent of slope (rise time). The fraction F equals the attenuation factor f, and the delay should be set to the product f × rise time for proper operation. [8]

#### 3.2 Typical Time Resolution Achieved

- **Commercial NIM-module CFDs:** The reported walk in most commercial NIM-module CFDs is on the order of 100 ps over an input-signal dynamic range of 100:1. [6]

- **Surface Concept CFDs:** Typical time walk <40 ps, output jitter vs. input at fixed amplitude <20 ps, with 100 MHz max input frequency and input amplitude range of -50 mV to -1.5 V. [10]

- **Maker-friendly CFD (transistor design without op-amps):** While the input amplitude was varied over a factor of 10, the standard deviation of the logic output of the CFD is only 60 ps. [9]

- **MRPC readout CFD (10- and 12-gap MRPCs):** Total time resolution of ~40 ps obtained using cosmic setup and a muon beam at the IHEP U-70 accelerator in Protvino. The intrinsic time resolution of the readout chain measured with a waveform generator is 15-30 ps for input amplitudes of 3-30 mV. [17][2]

- **Twin_Peaks_CFD1 (compact analog CFD for LaBr₃(Ce) scintillators):** Leading edge precision of 60 ps (standard deviation) with a 10:1 amplitude variation (20 mV–200 mV), and gamma-gamma coincidences yield precision of better than 190 ps (standard deviation). [19]

- **CFD in PET detectors (LYSO + SiPM):** CTR of 442.8 ± 12.8 ps (425–650 keV) and 476.0 ± 13.0 ps (250–750 keV) using CFD alone. [1][11]

- **FPGA-based digital CFD:** Achieved 28 ps intrinsic time resolution (measured with a pulse generator) using CAEN V1751 1 GS/s digitisers and a Xilinx Virtex-6 FPGA. [11] Total time dispersion of less than 500 ps with two LaBr₃(Ce) detectors and a ²²Na source. [11]

- **Digital CFD (BaF₂ scintillators, 1 GS/s ADC):** Average timing resolution of 456±8 ps, which is slightly higher than the analog average resolution of 419±7 ps. [1]

- **SAMPIC waveform digitizer with CFD algorithm:** Timing resolutions down to 4 ps with synthesized signals and 40 ps with silicon detector signals. [20][10]

- **PICOSEC gaseous detector with CFD:** Timing resolution of 50.5 ps for the complete dataset and 24.4 ps for events fully embedded in the detector area. [13]

#### 3.3 Limitations and Drawbacks

1. **Excessive Walk with Large Dynamic Range:** CFDs are designed to minimize walk compared to leading-edge discriminators but "can still exhibit excessive walk, especially with large dynamic ranges of input signals or improper user adjustments." [6] "Excessive walk is defined here as any walk that leads to an overall timing resolution that is much greater than the intrinsic timing resolution of the detection system." [6]

2. **Rise Time Dependence:** The CFD technique assumes identical rise times across all signals. "For work with channel plates or SBD's, we care only about minimizing amplitude walk. Time resolution is relatively insensitive to the actual fraction set on the constant fraction." [8] However, for signals with varying rise times (e.g., scintillation detectors with varying photoelectron statistics), the CFD does not fully eliminate walk.

3. **Complexity of Analog Circuitry:** "Typical analog CFD circuits utilize multiple high-bandwidth operational amplifiers. Such devices must be able to operate up to 100 MHz or more, to reproduce the steep leading edge (few ns) of the detector signal. Suitable amplifier ICs tend to be costly and consume significant amounts of power." [9]

4. **Power Consumption:** High-bandwidth analog CFDs are power-hungry. The SAMPIC ASIC, which includes CFD functionality, has total power consumption less than 200 mW for 16 channels (~10 mW per channel in low-current mode). [6] The FastIC ASIC has power consumption ~6 mW/channel at 1.2 V. [12]

5. **Delay Line Requirements:** Analog CFDs require precision delay lines (typically implemented as coaxial cables or lumped-element delay lines), which add to board space and cost. The Twin_Peaks_CFD1 design uses "16× 50 cm (1.3 mm thick) coaxial cables providing 2.5 ns delay, connected via U.F.L miniature coax connectors." [19] This makes the physical implementation bulky.

6. **Pulse Pair Resolution (Dead Time):** Different CFD models have varying pulse pair resolutions: Tennelec TC453 (10 ns), Ortec 934 (7-10 ns), Ortec 935 (5 ns), CF4000 (15-20 ns), and CF8000 (30 ns). [8] This limits the maximum count rate.

7. **Threshold Setting Trade-offs:** The threshold setting affects pulse width and pulse pair resolution. For noisy signals, "a 40% fraction may be needed instead of 20%." [8] Update mode gives best pulse pair resolution; blocking mode prevents ringing. [8]

8. **Noise Sensitivity:** The CFD is sensitive to noise at the zero-crossing point of the bipolar shaped signal, particularly for low-amplitude signals.

9. **Off-line Correction Sometimes Required:** The off-line correction method for CFD walk was developed because the method can "reduce the contribution to the overall timing resolution from the walk to a value that is equal to or less than the intrinsic timing resolution of the detectors." [6] The method relies on two conditions: "(1) a measure of the amplitude of the pulse from the scintillator is recorded on an event-by-event basis along with the timing information, and (2) there is a class of events in the data stream that has a wide dynamic range of signal amplitudes and has its timing information known a priori." [6]

10. **Digital CFD Limitations:** Digital CFD (dCFD) methods improve timing by "only up to 20% compared to the basic analog method. This improvement decreases when the consecutive samples are correlated." [14] For totally correlated samples (e.g., low-pass-filtered white noise oversampled, or correlated clock jitter in SCA devices), "there is no improvement compared to the analog method." [14] For partially correlated samples (e.g., white noise filtered by a low-pass filter with time constant τ), when T/τ < 1, "samples used for the interpolation are strongly correlated and the noise improvement factor will be of only 10% or less." [14]

### 4. WAVEFORM SAMPLING WITH INTERPOLATION/FITTING METHODS

#### 4.1 Operating Principle

Waveform sampling with interpolation/fitting methods digitize the entire detector signal or a portion of its leading edge, and then apply digital algorithms to extract the arrival time. These methods offer the most flexibility and highest potential accuracy, as they preserve the full waveform information for offline analysis.

The key methods include:

- **Digital Constant Fraction Discrimination (dCFD):** Algorithms extract time marks from digitized signals using interpolation (e.g., cubic polynomial interpolation) to find the constant fraction crossing point. The method achieves "time resolution about two orders of magnitude smaller than the 10 ns sampling period." [7]

- **Digital Leading Edge with Interpolation:** Linear interpolation between samples around the threshold crossing improves timing performance. For Moku:Pro sampling at 1.25 GSa/s (800 ps period), "linear interpolation improves timing performance by ~100x, but assumes the rising edge is linear between sample points around the threshold crossing." [21]

- **Cross-correlation Methods:** A software framework using "either a constant fraction discriminator or a fast cross-correlation algorithm" to extract timing information from SAMPIC output data. [20][10]

- **Machine Learning/Neural Network Methods:** A feedforward neural network with 4 hidden layers was evaluated for the LHCb ECAL Upgrade II (PicoCal), achieving ~18.3 ps without pile-up and ~66.2 ps with pile-up, showing significant improvement over digital CFD (~43.5 ps without pile-up, ~94.5 ps with pile-up). [9]

- **Multi Charge-over-Threshold (mCoT):** Using charge-over-threshold values from multiple thresholds, the mCoT method achieved 44.9 ps for the complete dataset and 23.2 ps for embedded events, outperforming CFD. [13]

- **Pulse-shape Fitting:** The χ² reference timing method, particularly when using the very beginning of the leading edge of the pulse, achieves the best timing resolution. [16]

- **Fourth-order Polynomial Fitting:** Applied to correct time-walk effects from leading-edge discriminator triggers, achieving timing performance improvement of about 10% (max 25.2%). [3][21]

- **Waveform Resampling (LMN Method):** A variant of trigonometric interpolation that implements optimized resampling in the frequency domain, achieving "mean squared error (MSE) very close to or identical to zero across all signal frequencies." [22]

#### 4.2 Typical Time Resolution Achieved

- **SAMPIC waveform digitizer:** Timing resolutions down to 4 ps with synthesized signals and 40 ps with silicon detector signals. [20][10] After TINL correction, time resolution reduced to 3.5 ps RMS. [6]

- **Digital CFD with cubic polynomial interpolation (100 MS/s, 12-bit):** Total time walk less than 120 ps for a dynamic range of 250:1. Single time-mark determination of ~100 ps FWHM with 300 μm NTD Silicon detector. [7]

- **WaveCatcher (3.2 GS/s, 12-bit):** Timing resolution consistent with commercial Ortec 9327CFD, TAC588, and 14-bit ADC114 electronics. σ_single_detector ~18.1 ps with MCP-PMTs. [16]

- **Neural Network (LHCb ECAL Upgrade II):** ~18.3 ps without pile-up, ~66.2 ps with pile-up. [9]

- **Digital CFD (ILL, 1 GS/s, Xilinx Virtex-6):** 28 ps intrinsic time resolution with pulse generator, <500 ps total time dispersion with LaBr₃(Ce) detectors. [11]

- **Digital Timing (BaF₂ scintillators, 1 GS/s):** 456±8 ps with constant-fraction discrimination. [1]

- **Digital Pulse Processing (Pixie-4, LSO):** 886 ps FWHM; 576 ps for LaBr₃. The DPP itself achieved 57 ps resolution using a pulser. [12]

- **Multi Charge-over-Threshold (PICOSEC):** 44.9 ps for complete dataset, 23.2 ps for embedded events. [13]

- **Long plastic scintillator (3 m, EJ-200) with SAMPIC:** Time resolution from a single PMT varies from 80 ps (near PMT) to 340 ps (far end); average from both PMTs ~140 ps. Weighted average approach provides 100 ps resolution over the entire 3 m bar length. [8]

#### 4.3 Limitations and Drawbacks

1. **High Data Throughput:** Waveform digitization generates massive amounts of data. As noted, "traditional ADCs" produce "high data rates" requiring significant data transfer bandwidth and storage. [6] The SAMPIC chip addresses this with a "Waveform Time to Digital Converter (WTDC)" concept that combines waveform sampling with TDC-like self-triggering and low data output. [6]

2. **Sampling Rate and ADC Resolution Trade-offs:** The time resolution is "primarily determined by the number of effective bits of the converter (10.8 ENOB in their system) rather than the sampling rate, provided the signal risetime contains a few sampling periods. Higher sampling rates cannot compensate for poorer bit resolution." [7]

3. **Interpolation Bias:** For linear interpolation, "faster edge rates cause interpolation bias (distribution biases toward multiples of sample period), degrading accuracy and jitter." [21] There are two competing requirements: "edges must be fast to minimize amplitude noise coupling into timing, but slow enough to preserve linear interpolation assumptions." [21] The "goldilocks" edge rate for Moku:Pro is an optimum rise time of 6 ns (~7.5 sample periods). [21]

4. **Power Consumption:** High-speed digitizers consume significant power. The SAMPIC ASIC consumes less than 200 mW total for 16 channels (~10 mW per channel) in low-current mode. [6] The WaveCatcher board has bandwidth of 500 MHz and 3.2 GS/s sampling. Larger systems require substantial power: 5.5 W for 32 channels and 7.5 W for 64 channels of SAMPIC. [6]

5. **Complexity of Digital Processing:** The offline processing of digitized waveforms requires significant computational resources. The FPGA-based digital CFD for the ILL system uses a Xilinx Virtex-6 FPGA and "real-time processing algorithm running in the processor is able to handle total event rates of more than 1 MHz." [11]

6. **Quantization and Noise:** The study of digital timing with BaF₂ scintillators concluded that "advantages of digital methods include reduced drift, data archiving, and better control over analysis parameters, while limitations include quantization in time and amplitude." [1]

7. **INL/DNL Correction Required:** Integral nonlinearity (INL) correction is critical for waveform digitizers. "Without it, resolution worsens from 17.2 ps to 27.3 ps for the WaveCatcher." [16] For the SAMPIC, "once the TINL correction is applied, the TDR is reduced to 3.5 ps rms." [6]

8. **Bandwidth Limitations:** The TARGET chip performed worse than the WaveCatcher "due to (a) lower bandwidth (~150 MHz vs 500 MHz) and (b) a worse S/N ratio (~50-60 vs ~450)." [16] The WaveCatcher board has 500 MHz bandwidth, 3.2 GS/s, 12-bit resolution. [16]

9. **Dead Time/Count Rate Limitations:** The SAMPIC chip has 64 analog switched-capacitor sampling cells per channel, limiting the number of waveforms that can be stored before readout. [6] The ILL system handles "total event rates of more than 1 MHz" but this requires significant processing power. [11]

10. **Cost and Complexity:** While "ASIC-based waveform recording electronics are well-suited to large-scale applications," the initial development cost of ASICs is high. "Although commercial CFD-based electronics are readily available and perform very well, they are impractical for large scale systems." [16] The time and cost of FPGA design is also significant: "median design time is 9 months (47% require 6-12 months, 27% over a year) and median cost is $360K (48% cost between $100K-$1M)." [13]

11. **Limited Improvement from Digital Methods:** The theoretical analysis of dCFD shows that "the use of the two uncorrelated noisy samples permits to improve (through interpolation) the time picking resolution by a factor sqrt(3/2) = 1.23 compared to the analog method. Note that it is significantly less than the sqrt(2) factor often used." [14] For correlated samples, the improvement is even less.

### 6. ANALOG VS. DIGITAL IMPLEMENTATIONS

#### 6.1 Analog Implementations

Analog implementations use continuous-time signal processing with dedicated electronic modules:

- **Advantages:** Lower latency, no quantization noise, proven technology, commercial availability (e.g., Ortec, Tennelec, Surface Concept CFDs). "Analog simulation uses continuous signal models to represent varying voltages and currents in real time. Rather than looking at on/off or binary states, analog methods treat signals as uninterrupted waveforms, providing a direct view of physical phenomena." [6]
- **Disadvantages:** Bulky (NIM modules), high power consumption, temperature drift, limited flexibility, component aging, difficult to scale to large channel counts. "Although commercial CFD-based electronics are readily available and perform very well, they are impractical for large scale systems." [16]
- **Recent innovations:** The maker-friendly CFD design and Twin_Peaks_CFD1 demonstrate that minimalist analog CFDs using RF transistors and LVDS receivers can achieve competitive performance (60 ps precision) with lower power and cost, using "a complete lack of op-amps — to save power, costs and board space." [9][19]

#### 6.2 Digital Implementations

Digital implementations use ADCs, FPGAs, or ASICs to digitize and process signals:

- **Advantages:** Flexibility, reconfigurability, drift-free operation, data archiving, advanced algorithms (ML, neural networks), scalability. "The DSP system offers significant advantages over the analog system in the areas of cost, accuracy, and efficiency by eliminating a need for extra electronic modules." [4][17] "In digital signal processing (DSP) technique, the detector preamplifier outputs are directly digitized without any analog signal shaping and then, according to specific application, processed to deduce desired results." [4][17]
- **Disadvantages:** Higher power consumption for high-speed digitization, quantization noise, limited sampling rate, data throughput bottlenecks, initial development cost. "The major difference between analog and digital signal processing is that with the digital method after signal conditioning, the preamplifier pulse is digitized immediately and all operations are carried out in digital filters. With the analog signal processing method, the filtering must be completed in relatively slower analog circuits." [4][17]
- **Key ASICs:** SAMPIC (16-channel, 1-10 GS/s, 0.18 μm CMOS, <200 mW total), [6] FastIC (8-channel, 25 ps time resolution, ~6 mW/channel), [12] SPIDER (for LHCb ECAL Upgrade II), [9] Timepix4 (sub-100 ps, 65 nm CMOS). [11]

#### 1.1 Time-Walk and Timing-Shift Correction for Dual-Ended Readout TOF-DOI PET
**Soure 2**: H. Wang, J. Xie, J. Qi, S. R. Cherry, and J. Du, "A Time-Walk and Timing-Sift Correction Method for Dual-Ended Readout TOF-DOI PET Detectors," *IEEE Transations on Radiation and Plasma Medical Sciences*, 2024.

This paper presents a combined time-walk and timing-shift correction method for dual-ended readout time-of-flight (TOF) PET detectors with depth-of-interaction (DOI) capability. Two dual-ended readout detectors were constructed using Hamamatsu S14161-3050-08 SiPM arrays coupled to 8×8 arrays of 3.1×3.1×20 mm³ LYSO crystals (3.2 mm pitch). The PETsys TOFPET2 readout system was used for data acquisition. Events were categorized into DOI layers based on the ratio of energies detected by the two SiPM arrays. The correction method uses the relationship between threshold crossing time differences and the natural logarithm of energy ratios (e.g., t₂-t₃ vs. ln(E₂/E₃)) to derive correction parameters (c for time-walk, b for timing-sift) for each DOI layer pair.
- CTR improved from 260.7 ± 1.0 ps to 229.4 ± 1.0 ps (improvement of ~31 ps) using a 400–650 keV energy window.
- Correcting time-walk alone improved CTR by 12.6 ps; DOI correction added ~20 ps further improvement.
- Optimal number of DOI layers was determined to be 4; beyond 4 layers, improvement plateaued (228.8 ps at 8 layers).
- Detector had a DOI resolution of 2.6 mm.
- Method also corrects timing offsets from readout electronics, improving localization accuracy along the LOR.
- Supported by NIH grants R01 EB028806 and R01 EB031961.

#### 2.1 Deep Neural Networks for Fast-Sampled Partice Timing Detectors (CMS-PPS Diamond Detectors)
**Soure 1 & 3**: M. Kocot, K. Misan, V. Avati, E. Bossini, L. Grzanka, and N. Minafra, "Using deep neural networks to improve the precision of fast-sampled particle timing detectors," *Computer Science*, 10 Decmber 2023. DOI: 10.7494/csci.2024.25.1.5784. arXiv:2312.05883.

This paper invesigates using deep neural networks to imprve the timing precision of the CMS-TOTEM Precision Proton Spectrometer (PPS) diamond timing detectors. The key problem addressed is the "time walk efect" — statistical fluctations in charge deposited by particles that cause errors in arival time measurements. The standard method, the Constant Fraction Disriminator (CFD) algorithm, is simple and efctive but does not utilize all voltage samples in a time series.

**Mehodoogy**: The researchers used data from the DESY-II synchrotron test beam facility (2020), where both PPS diamond timing detectrs and a high-precision MCP-PMT (Microchane Plate Photomultiplier Tube) detector were installed. The MCP served as the ground-truth reference (precision ~10 ps, compared to diamond sensors' 50-100 ps). The SAMPIC readout chip sampled signals every 156.25 pu, producing 64-sample wavforms within a 10 ns window. Afer preprocesing (version, fitering of nois/saturated events, riming to 48 samples, baseline substraction, and amplitude normlization). the final dataset conained aproximatly 500,000 waveform entries (reduced from 5.5 GB to 126 MB).

**Ntwork Architctures Tsted**: Three architectures were evaluated using hyperparmeter tuning with KerasTuner and Bayesan optmiation: (1) Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) — 2,737 parameters, (2) Convolutonal Neural Network (CNN) — 36,865 parameters, (3) UNet-based model — 456,965 parameters. The UNet architecture, which uses an encoder-decoder structure with skip connection, performed best.

**Key esults**:
- The UNet-based model achieved the best timing precision (60.71 ps in cross-valiation) compared to CNN (62.83 ps) and MLP (63.90 ps).
- Against the baseline CFD algorithm, improvements ranged from 8% to 23% acorss difrent detector readout channels.
- In the base experiment, precision improved by 17% (from 71.6 ps with CFD to 58.4 ps with UNet).
- Under LHC-like conditions (24-sample time series instead of 48), precision improved from 73.3 ps to 62.1 ps (15% improvement).
- The inference requires only ~10 millisecons of CPU time, making it suitale for online processing, such as in the high-level trigger reconstructon chain.
- Networks generally required training on specific channels to achieve optimal results.

#### 2.2 Timing Measurements with 3D Silicon Sensor on Timepix3
**Soure6 (from seon search)**: "Timing measurements with a 3D silicon sensor on Timepix3," arXiv:2105.11800.

Test beam measurements of timing performance compaing a 3D ilicon sensor and a thin planar sensor, both bump-bonded to Timepix3 ASICs, conducted at the CERN SPS H8 beame with 180 GeV/c mixed hadrons. The study used the LHCb VELO Timepix3 Telscope for track reconstruction and scintiators for reference timing.

Key indings:
- Perpendicuar incedence: The 3D sensor achieves an overall time resolution of 567±6 ps (with charge cut) comped to 683±8 ps for the thin planar sensor. The 3D sensor benfits from larger signals (~22 ke⁻ MPV vs ~3.3 ke⁻ for the thin planar) due to its 300 μm thickness versus 50 μm, resulting in less timewalk. However, the 3D sensor has higher pixel capacitance, leading to more analog front-end jitter.
- Graing incedence: The thin planar detector achieves better time resolution for small signals because its lower pixel capacitance reduces jiter. A non-depleted region near the backside of the 3D sensor was observed (z > ~250 μm), causing long charge colction times.
- Multi-hit resolution: Combining multiple hits from the same cluster improves time resolution signifiantly. The thin planar detector achieves ~100 ps with 50-60 hits, while the 3D detector achieves ~250 ps with ~40 hits.
- Timewalk correcions based on charge alone provided most of the improvement; spatial correcions added only ~1% improvement for perpendicuar incedence.

#### 2.6 Silicon Detector Technologies for Precision Track Timing (Review)
**Soure17 (from third search)**: G. Kramberger, "Silicon detector technologies for precision track timing," *PoS(Pixel2022)010*, 2022.

Paper presented at the 10th Internationl Workshop on Semiconductor Pixel Detectors (Pixel2022) in Decembr 2022. Discusses key technologies for tens-of-picosecond time resolution:

**LGADs**: Plaar sensors with a gain laer (p+) providing avalanche muplication (~10x gain). Achieve excelent time resolution (~30 ps) for larg pads (~1 mm). Main drawbacks: radiaion tolerance limited to ~few×10^15 cm^-2 due to acceptor removal in the gain layr (mitigated by carbon enrichmen), and poor file factor (large interpad gaps of ~50 μm). varints to improve file factor: Inverse-LGAD, AC-LGAD, DC-Resistive-LGAD, and Trench-Isolated LGAD (few μm interpad gaps).

**Monolithic sensors**: Eectronic and sensor on same wafer. Two designs: small-electode (low capacitance, low noise, but large weighting field contribution) and large-electode (similar to conventional planar). Novel PicoAD detector uses thin active layr (5 μm) with gain, aiming for ~10 ps resolution.

**3D sensors**: Eectrodes (columns or trenches) extend through the sensor thickness, decoupling drift distance from signal generaton. Column-3D (50×50 μm² cells) achieved ~20-30 ps resolution. Trench-3D (Time Spot project) reached ~20 ps with <10 ps weighting field contribution. Very radiation hard (up to 3×10^16 cm^-2). Drawbacks: larger capacitance, file factor issues, complex production.

**Time resolution contributions**: Noise jtter (σ_j ~ t_p/(S/N)), time walk from Landau fluctations (σ_lf), and weighting field efects (σ_wf). For 10 ps resolution, gain is necessary for planar detectors. 3D sensors minimize σ_lf due to short drift distances.

#### 2.7 4D-Tracking with Silcon Detectors: LGAD, AC-LGAD, DC-RSD
**Soure19 (from thir search)**: R. Arcidiacono, "4D-tracking with silicon detectors," *XXXIII Bonaudi-Chiava International School on Particle Deteors*, 2024.

This presenation covers a decaded of developmens in 4D-tracking with silion detectors, paricularly LGAD technology. Key points:
- LGAD uses an inernal moderate gain layr (thin p+ doping) providing large signals with short rise time and low noise. State-of-the-art LGADs achieve 25-40 ps time resolution with 1.3×1.3 mm² pixels.
- The time resolution equation: σ²t = σ²Jitter + σ²TimeWalk + σ²LandauNoise + σ²Distortion + σ²TDC.
- LGADs face accetor removal effect under irradiation, with pre-irradiated devices achieving ~30 ps timing; after irradiation to 1.5×10¹⁵ neq/cm², resolution degrades to ~50-60 ps.
- Resistive AC-Coupled LGADs (RSD/AC-LGAD): Overcomes inter-pad dead area problem using continuous gain layr with resistive n+ layr and AC-coupled readout pads, achieving 100% file factor. Spatial resolution of ~3% of pitch size demonstated (e.g., ~40 µm for 1300 µm pitch, ~15 µm for 450 µm pitch). Time jitter of ~20 ps achieved at gain ~30.
- DC-RSD evolution: Next generaton (DC-coupled Resistive Silicon Detectors) removes the oxide layr for AC-couping, implants readout electrodes directy on the resistive layr, and adds charge containment structures (isolting trenches). Advantages include: no signal disperion, no bipolar signals (~1 ns pulses), no baseline fluctations, improved SNR, and feasibility of O(cm²) active surface devices. First production completed at FBK in November 2024: DC-RSD1.

#### 4.1 Tme-Varant Front-End Read-Out Electronics for Hih-Data-Rate Detetors
**Soure10 (from first search)**: S. Sharifi et al., "Time-Variant Front-End Read-Out Electronics for High-Data-Rate Detectors," *Electronics*, 2021, Volume10, Issue13, 1528.

This paper addresses the trade-off between signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and data-rate in read-out electronics for high-energy physics detectors, particular for ATLAS Monitored Drit Tube (MDT) detectors. The authors propose time-variant (TV) solutions that use a long time constant (high fitering) during the event measurment (EM) phase for high SNR, and a shorter (or nul) time constant during the baseline recovery (BLR) phase to minimize tail and enable higher data-rates.

- TV-ToT sigificanty reduces BLR time compared to TI-ToT for the same SNR.
- TV-RE outpeforms both TI-ToT and TV-ToT, achieving the shorst BLR times and highest potential data-rates.
- For the ATLAS MDT detector case study (with a50 ns time constant): TI-ToT BLR = 380 ns, TV-ToT BLR = 110 ns, TV-RE BLR = 44 ns.
- With a ~50 ns reset phase, TV-RE enables data-rates up to 10 MHz, sufcient for small-diameter MDT detectors.
- TV architectures require minimal additional hardware (an extra logic unit for reset, and an extra discriminator for TV-RE) with small power consumtion growth.

### 5. CMS MIP Timing Detector (MTD) and Timing Performance

#### 5.1 CMS MTD Overview
**Soure6 (from third search)**: CMS - "New precision timing detector for the CMS HL-LHC upgrade," CERN, 2024.

The CMS experiment will deploy a new MIP Timing Detector (MTD) for the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) upgrade expected after 2027. The HL-LHC will deliver about 20 times more data than Run 2, with pile-up reaching 140-200 per buch crossing. The MTD will provide precision timing information with a resolution of about 35 ps. The MTD uses crystal scintilators with silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) in the central barre and Low Gain Silicon Detectors (LGADs) in the end-caps. Successful test demonstrated a time resolution of 25 ps with prototypes.

#### 5.2 CMS MTD Barrel Timing Layer (BTL)
**Soure7 (from third search)**: R. Tramontano on behal of the CMS Collaboration, "Precision Timing with the CMS MTD Barrel Timing Layer," CERN CDS.

The BTL covers pseudorapidity |η| < 1.5 and uses LYSO:Ce crystal bars (57 × 3.12 mm front face, ~3 mm thick) with double-sided Silicon Photomultiptier (SiPM) readout. A time resolution of ~30 ps would reduce effective PU to ~33 (comparable to current LHC levels), while 60 ps would yield ~70 effective PU. Test beam results from Setember 2018 at CERN's H4 faciliy, using 80 GeV pions, demonstated that amplitude walk (AW) correction improved time resolution from 46 ps to less than 30 ps, meeting the MTD target of σt = 30 ps.

**Soure9 (from third search)**: "CMS MTD BTL Timing Detector in Phase2 Upgrade," Presenation at 14th National Particle Physics Conference, Shanghai, Aug 15, 2024.

Key details:
- BTL measures time-of-arival for MIPs (>0.7 GeV) with ~30-60 ps precision, covering |η| < 1.5, using ~10k sensor modules (each with 16 LYSO crystal bars and two 16-channel SiPM arrays), read out by TOFHIR2 ASIC, mounted on CO2-cooled trays.
- 25 μm SiPM cell size showed best time resolution.
- Detector Module consists of sensor module, FE board (with TOFHIR2 readout chip achieving <60 ps), and copper shell.
- BTL Tray: Each tray covers 10 degrees and 2.5m at η; 72 trays total. First complete tray produced Jy 2024 at CERN.
- Sensor design approved Jun 2023; first complete detector module end of 2023; first Readout Unit March 2024.

#### 5.3 CMS MTD Endcap Timing Layer (ETL)
**Soure8 (from third search)**: "The Precision Endcap Timing Layer of the CMS MIP Timing Detector," IPRD25, September 2025.

The ETL covers |η| 1.6-3.0, with ~14 m² area and ~8.5 million channels. Uses n-in-p planar silicon Low-Gain Avalanche Diode (LGAD) technology, ~50 µm active thickness with internal gain of 10-30. Radiation fluence: up to 1.6×10¹⁵ neq/cm². 16×16 pixel matrix, 1.3 mm pitch, file factor ~90%. The ASIC (ETIROC/ETROC): ETROC2 first full-size, full-functionality prototype finalized May 2025, 16×16 array, 1.3 mm pitch, TSMC CMOS 65 nm technology, featuring Pre-Amplifier + Disriminator + TDC, Time of Arival (ToA), Time over Threshold (ToT), low power: 1W/chip (240 mW/cm²). Timing resolution results: Beam tests at DESY (4 GeV e⁺/e⁻) and SPS H6 (120 GeV p/π) show timing resolution of ~35 ps with ETROC2 + HPK LGADs.

## (1) Time Resolution Improvement: AI Methods vs. Traditional Methods

### DNN-based Time-Walk Correction for CMS-PPS Diamond Timing Detectors (CERN)
A study published in *Computer Science* (2024) by researchers at CERN investigated using deep neural networks to replace the Constant Fraction Discriminator (CFD) algorithm for time-walk correction in the Precision Proton Spectrometer (PPS) subsystem of the CMS detector at the LHC. The neural networks used all voltage samples in a waveform time series. Three architectures were evaluated: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and a UNet-based model. The UNet-based model achieved the best results, improving timing precision by 8% to 23% depending on the detector's readout channel. The base experiment showed a 17% improvement over CFD, from 71.6 ps to 58.4 ps. The networks were also tested under LHC-like conditions with 24-sample time series, achieving a 15% improvement (73.3 ps to 62.1 ps). The study used data from DESY-II synchrotron test beam facilities, employing MCP-PMT detectors as a reference (10 ps precision) alongside PPS diamond timing detectors (50-100 ps precision). The dataset consisted of ~500,000 waveform entries. [Source 7, Source 12]

### LSTM-based Timing Correction for MRPC TOF Detectors (EIC)
A proposal (July 2022) for the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) described a sealed MRPC (sMRPC) with 32 gas gaps of 104 µm thickness achieving 16 ps intrinsic resolution in cosmic-ray tests using standard gas. A new analysis based on the deep learning method using a Long-Short-Term-Memory (LSTM) network further improved the time resolution to ~16.8 ps, compared to 23 ps with the traditional Time-Over-Threshold (ToT) method. This represents an improvement of approximately 27% over the conventional ToT method. At high rates (15 kHz/cm²), the resolution degrades to ~20 ps. [Source 6]

### MLP Neural Network for PICOSEC Gaseous Detector Timing (CERN RD51)
A presentation by I. Manthos et al. (HEP 2021, Thessaloniki) investigated signal processing techniques for precise timing with the PICOSEC detector, targeting ~20-30 ps timing resolution for HL-LHC pileup mitigation. Methods tested on PICOSEC MIP data included:
- **Constant Fraction Discrimination (CFD):** Reference method achieved 50.5 ps (full dataset) and 24.4 ps (events fully embedded in detector area).
- **Leading Edge - multi Time-over-Threshold (mToT):** Used 7 thresholds (10-200 mV). Best thresholds: 10mV (73.5 ps), 100mV (29.2 ps). Combined: 48.8 ps overall.
- **Leading Edge - multi Charge-over-Threshold (mCoT):** Best thresholds: 10mV (54.8 ps), 100mV (26.7 ps). Combined: 44.9 ps overall; 23.2 ps for fully embedded events — **better than CFD**.
- **Neural Network (MLP):** Inputs from ToT at 10/50/100 mV thresholds. Achieved 46.0 ps overall; 25.2 ps for fully embedded events.

In sub-picosecond domain tests (70 p.e. dataset), both CFD (5.50 ps) and mCoT (5.52 ps) performed comparably. The key conclusion was that mCoT outperforms CFD when charge info is available from front-end electronics, and neural networks yield results comparable to analytical methods. [Source 2]

### CNN-based Time-Walk Correction for BGO TOF-PET Scintillators
A study published in *EJNMMI Physics* (2025) compared different timing estimation methods for BGO scintillators in TOF-PET, comparing leading-edge discrimination (LED), time-walk correction (TWC) using two thresholds, and a convolutional neural network (CNN) approach. For 2×2×3 mm³ crystals:
- LED: 157±3 ps CTR
- TWC: 129±2 ps (18% improvement)
- CNN: 115±2 ps (26% improvement)

For 2×2×20 mm³ crystals:
- LED: 280±8 ps
- TWC: 241±7 ps (14% improvement)
- CNN: 239±7 ps (15% improvement), showing similar performance between TWC and CNN for longer crystals.

The CNN demonstrated better tail suppression in coincidence time distributions, particularly evident in the full-width tenth-maximum (FWTM) metrics. The study concluded that for longer BGO crystals, a simpler two-threshold TWC approach captures most essential information, while the CNN offers marginal additional benefits. [Source 9]

### LED-based Self-Correction for PET Detectors
A study by Du et al. (2017) presented a self-calibrating time-walk correction method for PET detectors using leading edge discriminators (LEDs). Experimental validation used two SensL MicroFB SiPMs coupled to 2.5×2.5×20 mm polished LYSO crystals. Key results:
- Without correction: 389.0±12.0 ps (425–650 keV window) and 670.2±16.2 ps (250–750 keV)
- With LED-based self-correction: 367.3±0.5 ps (425–650 keV) and 413.7±0.9 ps (250–750 keV)
- With CFD: 442.8±12.8 ps (425–650 keV) and 476.0±13.0 ps (250–750 keV)
- With CFD-based reference detector correction: 367.3±0.4 ps (425–650 keV) and 413.4±0.9 ps (250–750 keV)

The LED-based self-correction method matched the performance of a dedicated CFD reference detector and outperformed standard CFD. The method was also successfully applied to large-area SiPM arrays, improving timing from 11.2±0.2 ns to 4.2±0.1 ns. [Source 1]

### Combined Time-Walk and Timing-Shift Correction for Dual-Ended Readout TOF-PET
A paper published in *IEEE Transactions on Radiation and Plasma Medical Sciences* (November 2024) by researchers at UC Davis presented a combined correction method for dual-ended readout TOF-PET detectors with DOI capability. Using two Hamamatsu S14161-3050-08 SiPM arrays coupled to 8×8 arrays of 3.1×3.1×20 mm³ LYSO crystals with a 400-650 keV energy window:
- CTR improved from 260.7 ± 1.0 ps to 229.4 ± 1.0 ps after correction (~31 ps improvement)
- Time-walk correction alone improved CTR by 12.6 ps
- DOI correction added another ~20 ps improvement
- The optimal number of DOI layers was 4 (228.8 ps at 8 layers)
- The detector had a DOI resolution of 2.6 mm [Source 3, Source 6]

### MAC/UMAC Autoencoder Architectures for Timing Reconstruction
A study published in *Particles* (MDPI, 2025) by Sofia University researchers presented convolutional neural networks with modified autoencoder (MAC) architectures for reconstructing pulse arrival times in scintillating crystal calorimeters. The MAC model showed a mean difference of 0.7 ns between true and predicted arrival time, while the UMAC (upsampling version) reduced this to −0.003 ns with a narrower distribution. The model is sensitive to sub-bin timing — it can distinguish arrival times with higher precision than the 1 ns time bin width. The UMAC significantly improves time resolution by adding two upsampling layers (factor of 2) in the decoder, achieving 4096-length labels (0.25 ns precision). [Source 14]

### ML-Aided Self-Calibration for FPGA-Based Time-to-Digital Converters (TDC)
A paper published in *Intelligent Systems with Applications* (May 2026) presented a novel FPGA-based TDC using machine learning-aided self-calibration. Three ML models (NN, DNN, CNN) were trained on over 300,000 raw TDC samples to correct residual non-linearities. On a Kintex UltraScale FPGA, the ML-aided TDC achieved timing precision below 15 ps (13.6 ps standard deviation), improving precision by more than 10.5× over conventional encoder-based FPGA TDC, and reaching performance comparable to state-of-the-art ASIC TDCs. ### hls4ml Implementation Strategies
hls4ml implements three strategies for constant matrix-vector multiplication (CMVM):
- **Latency:** Fully unrolled, weights embedded into multiplier circuits; suitable for small models with very low latency requirements
- **Resource:** Stores weights in BRAM with explicit parallelism control; better for larger models
- **Distributed Arithmetic (DA):** Decomposes CMVM into shift-and-add operations via adder graph; no DSP usage; lowest fabric utilization

Users control parallelism via Reuse Factor (RF) and Parallelization Factor (PF) per layer. Low reuse factor achieves the lowest latency and highest throughput but uses the most resources, while high reuse factor saves resources at the expense of longer latency and lower throughput. [Source 3, Source 5 (from second search)]
